0.title: Holy, Holy, Holy: The Book of Leviticus
0.overview:
The message. Leviticus answers the most serious question a sinner can ask: how can I live in the presence of a holy God and not be destroyed? Exodus ended with the glory of the LORD filling the tabernacle, so that even Moses “was not able to enter the tent of meeting” (Exodus 40:35). God had moved in, and no one could come near. Leviticus is his answer, given in sacrifice, priesthood, cleansing and a holy way of life: “You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy” (19:2). It is not a ladder up to God, but a door he opens for a people already rescued. Its message is that God is holy, and that God himself has made a way for sinners to come near.

Background: the writer. Leviticus is named after the Levites, the priestly tribe. More than thirty times it says that “the LORD spoke to Moses”, and it closes, “These are the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses for the people of Israel on Mount Sinai” (27:34). Jesus told a cleansed leper to offer “what Moses commanded” (Mark 1:44), and Paul introduces a verse of Leviticus with “Moses writes” (Romans 10:5, quoting 18:5). Many modern scholars assign the book to a “Priestly” source written down during or after the exile, in the sixth or fifth century BC. Others find much of it far older; its world is a wilderness camp with a tent at its centre, not a temple in a city. This commentary holds, though the question is debated, that its substance comes from Moses, as the book says.

When and where. The tabernacle was set up a year after the exodus (Exodus 40:17), and Numbers opens one month later (Numbers 1:1). Leviticus belongs in that month, with Israel camped at Sinai. Christians date the exodus either about 1446 BC (from 1 Kings 6:1) or about 1260 BC; this commentary, as in Exodus, leaves that open. Either way, these laws came to a nation of freed slaves, surrounded by peoples whose gods were thought to need feeding and whose worship could demand children (18:21; 20:2–5). Leviticus takes the familiar language of altar, priest and blood and fills it with new meaning: here God gives the blood himself, “to make atonement for your souls” (17:11).

The kind of writing. Leviticus is mostly law, held in a thin thread of story (chapters 8–10; 24:10–23). Read it as you would read the plans of a house you are going to live in: not every line will move you, but every line shows what the owner is like. Three words are the keys. Holy means set apart for God and marked by his character. Clean and unclean describe fitness to come near God’s dwelling, and they are not the same as innocent and guilty: a mother after childbirth was unclean without having done anything wrong (12:2–8). Atonement means the covering and cleansing of sin, so that a holy God and an unclean people can meet.

How the book makes its case. The book moves inward to God’s presence, then outward into life. First come the offerings (chapters 1–7): burnt, grain, peace, sin and guilt offerings, priced so that the poor could bring birds or flour. Then the priests (chapters 8–10): Aaron and his sons are ordained, the glory of the LORD appears, and the people “shouted and fell on their faces” (9:24); almost at once two of Aaron’s sons offer fire God had not commanded and die, for “Among those who are near me I will be sanctified” (10:3). Next, clean and unclean (chapters 11–15): food, childbirth, skin disease and bodily discharges, life in a world marked by death. At the centre stands the Day of Atonement (chapter 16), when once a year the high priest passed behind the curtain with blood, and a second goat carried the people’s sins away into the wilderness: “You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins” (16:30). Then holiness goes out into daily life (chapters 17–27, often called the Holiness Code): blood, sex and marriage, love of neighbour and care for the poor (17–20), holy priests and offerings (21–22), the feasts of the year (23), the Sabbath year and the Jubilee (25), blessings and curses (26), and gifts vowed to God (27). Near the end comes the promise everything has served: “I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people” (26:12).

Do these laws bind Christians? Christians are not under the law of Moses as a covenant, but the Reformed tradition reads it in three strands. The moral law, rooted in God’s character and repeated in the New Testament, remains the shape of love: “you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (19:18). The ceremonial law of sacrifices, priests, cleanness and feasts was “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:17), and Jesus “declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19). The civil law governed Israel as a nation and ended with it. Some Christians would apply Israel’s civil laws today; others see the whole law replaced by the law of Christ. This commentary’s view is the Reformed one: the moral law remains the rule of life, never a way to earn salvation.

Did the sacrifices really forgive? Leviticus promises that the sinner “shall be forgiven” (4:31). Hebrews says, “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). Both are true: the forgiveness was real for the Israelite who came trusting God’s promise, but the animals were never its ground. God “had passed over former sins” in his forbearance (Romans 3:25), until the sacrifice they all pointed to was made.

Where it leads: to Christ. Leviticus leads to Christ by pattern. Hebrews calls its worship “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (Hebrews 8:5), and every part of it is taken up in him. He is the offering wholly given to God and the peace offering that brings us to God’s table; John the Baptist pointed to him as “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). He is the high priest Aaron could only picture, “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26). On the true Day of Atonement “he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12), and like the second goat he carried his people’s sins away. Where the law could only examine a leper and send him outside the camp, Jesus touched one and said, “I will; be clean” (Mark 1:41). Mary brought the poor family’s offering of 12:8 after his birth (Luke 2:22–24), and he “suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12), taking the place of the unclean so that the unclean could come in.

For us. Leviticus corrects two opposite mistakes. We are tempted to think God is harmless, and the book shows a holiness that is a consuming fire. We are tempted to think we must make ourselves clean before we come, and the book shows God providing the blood, the priest and the way. In Christ both are answered: “we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19). So the call of 19:2 comes to us unchanged: “as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct” (1 Peter 1:15), in honest business, care for the poor and the stranger, purity of body and love for neighbours. Come expecting dust, and you may end, like Israel, on your face before the glory of God, and glad.

1.title: The Burnt Offering: Wholly the Lord's
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of you brings an offering to the LORD, you shall bring your offering of livestock from the herd or from the flock.<sup>3</sup>"If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without blemish. He shall bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting, that he may be accepted before the LORD.<sup>4</sup>He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.<sup>5</sup>Then he shall kill the bull before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests shall bring the blood and throw the blood against the sides of the altar that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>6</sup>Then he shall flay the burnt offering and cut it into pieces,<sup>7</sup>and the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire on the altar and arrange wood on the fire.<sup>8</sup>And Aaron's sons the priests shall arrange the pieces, the head, and the fat, on the wood that is on the fire on the altar;<sup>9</sup>but its entrails and its legs he shall wash with water. And the priest shall burn all of it on the altar, as a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>10</sup>"If his gift for a burnt offering is from the flock, from the sheep or goats, he shall bring a male without blemish,<sup>11</sup>and he shall kill it on the north side of the altar before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>12</sup>And he shall cut it into pieces, with its head and its fat, and the priest shall arrange them on the wood that is on the fire on the altar,<sup>13</sup>but the entrails and the legs he shall wash with water. And the priest shall offer all of it and burn it on the altar; it is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>14</sup>"If his offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, then he shall bring his offering of turtledoves or pigeons.<sup>15</sup>And the priest shall bring it to the altar and wring off its head and burn it on the altar. Its blood shall be drained out on the side of the altar.<sup>16</sup>He shall remove its crop with its contents and cast it beside the altar on the east side, in the place for ashes.<sup>17</sup>He shall tear it open by its wings, but shall not sever it completely. And the priest shall burn it on the altar, on the wood that is on the fire. It is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
1.overview:
Where we are. Exodus closed with the glory of the LORD filling the tabernacle, so that even Moses “was not able to enter the tent of meeting” (Exodus 40:35). Leviticus opens with God calling from inside that tent. Chapters 1–7 set out the offerings, and the burnt offering comes first.

The message. God opens the way to himself before he asks anything, and the way is a substitute wholly given. The worshipper lays his hand on an animal without blemish, it dies in his place and goes up to God entirely in smoke, and he is “accepted” and atoned for (v. 4). Whether he brings a bull, a sheep or a pair of birds, the result is the same: “a pleasing aroma to the LORD”.

Why it was said. A rescued people now had the holy God living in the middle of their camp (see the introduction). They needed to know that they could come near, how they could come near, and that the way did not depend on how much they owned.

How the chapter makes its case. God calls from the tent and opens the offering to “any one of you” (vv. 1–2). A bull from the herd is brought, the worshipper’s hand is laid on its head, he kills it, its blood is thrown against the altar, and the whole animal is burned (vv. 3–9). A sheep or goat is offered in exactly the same way (vv. 10–13). For the poor, turtledoves or pigeons, with the priest doing the killing (vv. 14–17). Each case ends on the same words of acceptance.

Where it leads. By pattern, which the New Testament itself draws. Paul describes the cross in the language of the burnt offering: Christ “gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2). He is the one “without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19), who held nothing back from the Father, “I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7), and who “appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26). His mother brought the poor family’s birds when he was presented in the temple (Luke 2:24).

For us. We come to God through Christ’s whole offering, accepted not on what we can afford but on what he gave. And because we are already accepted, we can give ourselves wholly back to God, “a living sacrifice” offered “by the mercies of God” (Romans 12:1), not to win his favour but because we have it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God opens a way for anyone to come near him, and the way is a whole life given in another’s place. After God’s call from the tent and his invitation to “any one of you” (vv. 1–2), three cases follow at three prices. A bull from the herd, the worshipper’s hand on its head, its blood thrown against the altar and the whole of it burned (vv. 3–9); a sheep or goat in the same way (vv. 10–13); and turtledoves or pigeons for the poor, with the priest doing the killing (vv. 14–17). Each case ends with the same words, “a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD”: one acceptance, whatever the price.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Leviticus Is For

God opens a way to come near to him, and prices it so that rich and poor alike can take it.
verseByVerse.examples: Three prices brought one and the same acceptance. No believer comes to God on a lesser footing than another, because all come through the same offering.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of you brings an offering to the LORD, you shall bring your offering of livestock from the herd or from the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has moved into the middle of his people, and his first word from the tent is an invitation: any ordinary person may bring an offering.

From the tent of meeting. Exodus ended with the glory filling the tabernacle so completely that Moses was not able to enter (Ex. 40:35). Leviticus opens with the next problem: God has moved in, and nobody can go near him. This book is not a legal appendix but the answer to the question Exodus left hanging: how do sinful people live next door to a holy God without being destroyed? Every sacrifice, washing and distinction between clean and unclean addresses that question.

When any one of you brings an offering. The first word about the offerings is a permission, not a demand. The Hebrew for any one of you is adam, a human being: not a priest or a leader, but any ordinary person. The door is opened as wide as the language allows before a single regulation follows.
verseByVerse.note: Leviticus takes its name from the Levites, the priestly tribe.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without blemish. He shall bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting, that he may be accepted before the LORD. He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him. Then he shall kill the bull before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests shall bring the blood and throw the blood against the sides of the altar that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting. Then he shall flay the burnt offering and cut it into pieces, and the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire on the altar and arrange wood on the fire. And Aaron's sons the priests shall arrange the pieces, the head, and the fat, on the wood that is on the fire on the altar; but its entrails and its legs he shall wash with water. And the priest shall burn all of it on the altar, as a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole animal goes up to God, and the worshipper who laid his hand on it is accepted and atoned for: a substitute dies, and he does not.

A burnt offering. Olah comes from the verb to go up: all of it goes up in smoke, except the skin (7:8), and it must be a male without blemish (v. 3), the best of the herd.

He shall lay his hand on the head. Verse 4 contains the whole logic of the system in one sentence. A man presses his hand on a living animal, and then the animal is killed and he is not. The verse says what this achieves: accepted for him, atonement for him. The acceptance is God’s provision, received, not earned.

Then he shall kill the bull. Not the priest: whoever brought the animal cut its throat and watched it die, while Aaron’s sons handled the blood and the fire. No worshipper was permitted to be sentimental about what sin costs.

What atonement means. The English word was built to say what it does: “at-one-ment”, two parties who were apart made one again. The Hebrew verb, kipper, has been taken to mean to cover or to wipe clean, and it is closely tied to kopher, a ransom: the price paid to set free a life that is forfeit, the word used for the half shekel each man paid as “a ransom for his life” (Exodus 30:12). So atonement is not God being talked round, nor a sinner trying harder: it is a life given so that a forfeited life may go free and be brought near. See also Atonement in the Theological Dictionary.

A pleasing aroma to the LORD. The last phrase of verse 9 is the one the New Testament picks up: Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Eph. 5:2). Paul describes the cross in the words of the burnt offering: the whole given, nothing held back, and accepted by the Father completely. Every one of these animals points to the lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet. 1:19), who came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45) and “has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26).

When an old sin accuses. We tend to manage guilt: we explain it, outweigh it with good deeds, or stop looking at it. Leviticus allows none of these: something has to die. So when an old sin comes back to accuse you, do not reach for an excuse or a better week. Lay your hand, as it were, on his head, and say: he died for that.

Everyone brings a burnt offering. It is easy to feel superior to a religion of altars and smoke, but the altars are still there. People give their evenings, their marriages and their health to a career, sleep to a screen, savings to an image. Whatever we treat as ultimate asks for the whole animal, and unlike the God of Leviticus it never tells us we have given enough or that we are accepted. The burnt offering turns that upside down: acceptance is promised first, and in Christ the one who receives the whole offering is first the one who makes it. Only someone that sure of being accepted can safely give everything back, which is why Paul calls for a living sacrifice offered “by the mercies of God” (Romans 12:1), not in order to win them.

Does God eat? If I were hungry, I would not tell you (Ps 50:12). Unlike the gods of Israel’s neighbours, he needs no feeding: “food offering” and “pleasing aroma” mean that the offering is accepted.

Where Christians differ. Some see the laid-on hand as passing the worshipper’s sin to the animal, as on the Day of Atonement (16:21); some as identifying him with it, so that its death stands for his; others as simply marking it as his own gift.

This commentary’s view. The hand identifies the worshipper with his animal, and the result the verse names, atonement for him, shows that its death is in his place: substitution, fulfilled when Christ bore the punishment our sins deserved.

Uncertain wording. “Food offering” (ishsheh) was once rendered “offering made by fire”, from esh, fire; many now link it with a word for a gift. Its origin is uncertain; its use is clear: an offering the LORD receives.
verseByVerse.note: Except for the skin (7:8), the whole animal was burned.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his gift for a burnt offering is from the flock, from the sheep or goats, he shall bring a male without blemish, and he shall kill it on the north side of the altar before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar. And he shall cut it into pieces, with its head and its fat, and the priest shall arrange them on the wood that is on the fire on the altar, but the entrails and the legs he shall wash with water. And the priest shall offer all of it and burn it on the altar; it is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A sheep or goat brings exactly the same acceptance as a bull: the poorer offering is not a lesser atonement.

Word for word. The sheep or goat is offered in identical terms, with the identical result, and the repetition is the point: the poorer man’s offering ends with the same phrase, word for word.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, then he shall bring his offering of turtledoves or pigeons. And the priest shall bring it to the altar and wring off its head and burn it on the altar. Its blood shall be drained out on the side of the altar. He shall remove its crop with its contents and cast it beside the altar on the east side, in the place for ashes. He shall tear it open by its wings, but shall not sever it completely. And the priest shall burn it on the altar, on the wood that is on the fire. It is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the poorest, who can bring only a bird, are received on the same terms, and the priest spares them the work of killing it.

Turtledoves or pigeons. These birds cost very little. Here the priest kills the bird rather than the worshipper, and he removes the crop and throws it beside the altar. The detail is almost tender: a man too poor to bring a lamb is not asked to do the killing or the messy work himself.

The same acceptance at every price. Three times, at three prices, the chapter ends on the identical sentence. God builds the poor into the system on the first page, and refuses to describe their offering in weaker terms than anyone else’s.

The offering of Jesus’ mother. When Mary and Joseph presented their firstborn, they brought a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons (Luke 2:24), the offering Leviticus allows a mother who cannot afford a lamb (12:8). The mother of the Lord could not afford a lamb. She had the Lamb of God in her arms.

Uncertain wording. The rare word translated its contents (v. 16) may instead mean the bird’s feathers (so the King James Version). Either way, what was unfit for the altar was removed first.
verseByVerse.note: Turtledoves and pigeons were the offering the poor could afford.

1.theology:
Substitutionary atonement. The laid-on hand and the slain animal teach that sin is dealt with not by human effort but by a substitute God provides, which is the heart of the cross.

Total consecration. The wholly consumed offering pictures the surrender Christ gave the Father, which the Spirit now works in us: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice" (Rom 12:1).

The pleasing aroma. What the burnt offering symbolised, Christ accomplished, and in him our worship rises acceptably.
1.examples:
Then: an Israelite pressed his hand on his own animal and watched it die and go up in flame: approaching God requires a substitute.

Now: we come through Christ's once-for-all offering, and give our whole selves to God not to be accepted but because we already are accepted in him.

keyVerse.quote: He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.
keyVerse.note: This verse holds the logic of the whole sacrificial system in one sentence: the worshipper identifies himself with an animal that dies, and God accepts him and covers his sin. Acceptance is God’s gift through a substitute, the pattern fulfilled when Christ gave himself for us.

1.reflection:
The worshipper pressed his hand on the animal and then killed it himself (vv. 4–5). Why might God have wanted the cost of sin to be seen so plainly, and how do we tend to hide it from ourselves?

A bull, a lamb or a pair of birds brought the same acceptance. What does that say to someone who feels they come to God with less than others?

Paul calls Christ’s death “a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2). What difference does it make to you that the Father fully accepted his Son’s offering?

Romans 12:1 asks for “a living sacrifice” offered “by the mercies of God”. What part of your life are you still holding back, and why does being already accepted make it safe to give it?

2.title: The Grain Offering: The Labor of Our Hands
2.text: <sup>1</sup>"When anyone brings a grain offering as an offering to the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour. He shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it<sup>2</sup>and bring it to Aaron's sons the priests. And he shall take from it a handful of the fine flour and oil, with all of its frankincense, and the priest shall burn this as its memorial portion on the altar, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>3</sup>But the rest of the grain offering shall be for Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the LORD's food offerings.<sup>4</sup>"When you bring a grain offering baked in the oven as an offering, it shall be unleavened loaves of fine flour mixed with oil or unleavened wafers smeared with oil.<sup>5</sup>And if your offering is a grain offering baked on a griddle, it shall be of fine flour unleavened, mixed with oil.<sup>6</sup>You shall break it in pieces and pour oil on it; it is a grain offering.<sup>7</sup>And if your offering is a grain offering cooked in a pan, it shall be made of fine flour with oil.<sup>8</sup>And you shall bring the grain offering that is made of these things to the LORD, and when it is presented to the priest, he shall bring it to the altar.<sup>9</sup>And the priest shall take from the grain offering its memorial portion and burn this on the altar, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>10</sup>But the rest of the grain offering shall be for Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the LORD's food offerings.<sup>11</sup>"No grain offering that you bring to the LORD shall be made with leaven, for you shall burn no leaven nor any honey as a food offering to the LORD.<sup>12</sup>As an offering of firstfruits you may bring them to the LORD, but they shall not be offered on the altar for a pleasing aroma.<sup>13</sup>You shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing from your grain offering; with all your offerings you shall offer salt.<sup>14</sup>"If you offer a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, you shall offer for the grain offering of your firstfruits fresh ears, roasted with fire, crushed new grain.<sup>15</sup>And you shall put oil on it and lay frankincense on it; it is a grain offering.<sup>16</sup>And the priest shall burn as its memorial portion some of the crushed grain and some of the oil with all of its frankincense; it is a food offering to the LORD.
2.overview:
Where we are. After the burnt offering, where a whole animal went up in smoke, comes an offering with no blood in it at all: the grain offering. It often went up alongside the burnt offering (Numbers 15:1–10), joining the gift of a life to the gift of its work.

The message. God receives the work of ordinary hands as worship. Flour that has been ploughed, sown, reaped, threshed and ground is brought to him; a handful is burned as a “memorial portion” and the rest feeds the priests. Nothing that sours may go on his altar, and nothing may lack “the salt of the covenant” (v. 13): what is offered must be pure, and it rests on his unfailing faithfulness.

Why it was said. Israel was on its way to a land of fields and harvests that God would give (see the introduction). The grain offering taught them that the harvest would be his gift and their labour his due, so that the whole of their working life would be lived before him.

How the chapter makes its case. Raw flour is brought with oil and frankincense, a handful is burned and the rest goes to the priests (vv. 1–3). The same offering may be baked in an oven, cooked on a griddle or in a pan, and every form is “most holy” (vv. 4–10). Leaven and honey are barred from the altar, but salt must go with every offering (vv. 11–13). Last come the firstfruits of the new grain, roasted and crushed (vv. 14–16).

Where it leads. Mostly by pattern, and the New Testament draws it at two points. Paul takes the chapter’s banned leaven as a picture of sin, because “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7), and he calls the risen Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). Many Christians have also seen in the fine flour, unleavened and passed through fire, a picture of Jesus’ sinless life offered to the Father. The text does not say so, but it fits the one who called himself “the bread of life” (John 6:35) and the grain of wheat that dies to bear much fruit (John 12:24).

For us. Because Christ’s offering has made us acceptable, our work and our giving can now be offered as worship: Paul calls the Philippians’ gift “a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18). Bring your ordinary days to God, keep out what corrupts, and rest in a covenant that does not spoil.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God receives the fruit of human work as worship, kept pure and seasoned with his covenant. The basic offering is fine flour with oil and frankincense: a handful, the memorial portion, is burned, and the rest belongs to Aaron and his sons (vv. 1–3). It may be brought baked in an oven, cooked on a griddle or in a pan, and every form is “most holy” (vv. 4–10). Two things are barred from the altar, leaven and honey, and one is required, salt, “the salt of the covenant with your God” (vv. 11–13). Last comes the grain offering of firstfruits, fresh ears roasted and crushed, with oil and frankincense as before (vv. 14–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
An Offering With No Blood in It

This is a gift of grain, kept free of leaven and seasoned with salt.
verseByVerse.examples: The offering fitted whatever kitchen the household had. God asks for what we have, not for what we lack.

verseByVerse.quote: "When anyone brings a grain offering as an offering to the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour. He shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it and bring it to Aaron's sons the priests. And he shall take from it a handful of the fine flour and oil, with all of its frankincense, and the priest shall burn this as its memorial portion on the altar, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. But the rest of the grain offering shall be for Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the LORD's food offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grain offering hands God the product of a person’s work: a handful is burned for him with all the frankincense, and the rest feeds the priests.

A grain offering. Minchah is used elsewhere for a gift brought to a superior, and what is brought is not a living animal but the product of work: grain sown, watched, harvested, threshed and ground by somebody’s hands, then mixed with oil. A man who brought this handed over a portion of his own labour, from a harvest God had given.

Its memorial portion. A handful, the memorial portion, is burned and stands for the whole, and the rest belongs to Aaron and his sons. All the frankincense went up with that handful (v. 2): a costly resin brought from Arabia (compare Jer. 6:20), it was never eaten, so the fragrance of the gift was the LORD’s alone. So the grain offering is also how the priesthood eats: Israel’s worship and Israel’s ministers are sustained by the same act. Paul argues from this that “those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14).

Work as worship. The New Testament carries the thought into every workplace: Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men (Col. 3:23). A day’s work done honestly and well, and a share of its wages given with thanks, is still a way of laying the fruit of one’s hands before the God who gave the strength to do it.

Uncertain wording. Memorial portion (azkarah) comes from the verb to remember, but its exact sense is uncertain: the portion that calls the worshipper to God’s remembrance, or a token standing for the whole offering, or both.
verseByVerse.note: The grain offering acknowledged God as the giver of the harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you bring a grain offering baked in the oven as an offering, it shall be unleavened loaves of fine flour mixed with oil or unleavened wafers smeared with oil. And if your offering is a grain offering baked on a griddle, it shall be of fine flour unleavened, mixed with oil. You shall break it in pieces and pour oil on it; it is a grain offering. And if your offering is a grain offering cooked in a pan, it shall be made of fine flour with oil. And you shall bring the grain offering that is made of these things to the LORD, and when it is presented to the priest, he shall bring it to the altar. And the priest shall take from the grain offering its memorial portion and burn this on the altar, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. But the rest of the grain offering shall be for Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the LORD's food offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baked, griddled or fried, the offering is equally “most holy”: God fixes what is offered and leaves the kitchen to the household.

Fitted to the household. Listing three ways of preparing it means the offering fits the household. A woman with an oven brings loaves; a family with only a griddle brings wafers. God specifies the flour and oil and leaves the kitchen arrangements to whoever is cooking, and every version is most holy.

verseByVerse.quote: "No grain offering that you bring to the LORD shall be made with leaven, for you shall burn no leaven nor any honey as a food offering to the LORD. As an offering of firstfruits you may bring them to the LORD, but they shall not be offered on the altar for a pleasing aroma. You shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing from your grain offering; with all your offerings you shall offer salt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing that ferments may be burned on God’s altar, and nothing may be offered without the salt that stands for his unbreakable covenant.

No leaven nor any honey. Both banned substances probably share one property: they ferment. Leaven (yeast) works through dough by souring it; honey ferments as it warms. Leaven is usually a picture of corruption in Scripture (1 Cor 5:8), though not always (Matt 13:33). Leavened loaves could still be brought as firstfruits (v. 12; 23:17), but never burned on the altar. Nothing that spreads by souring may go on the altar, which is the sense the New Testament gives it: a little leaven leavens the whole lump, so cleanse out the old leaven and keep the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5:6-8). Paul grounds that call in what has already happened: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor. 5:7).

The salt of the covenant. Salt does the opposite of leaven. It preserves, and in the ancient Near East a covenant sealed with a shared meal of salt was a bond that did not spoil. Every offering in Israel carried a pinch of the thing that stops decay, and God calls it the salt of the covenant: his own faithfulness, seasoning their gifts.

Salt in the disciples. Jesus handed the image to his disciples: You are the salt of the earth (Matt. 5:13), and Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another (Mark 9:50). Paul told the Colossians to let their speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt (Col. 4:6). What was sprinkled on every sacrifice is now said of the people who bring them.
verseByVerse.note: Numbers 18:19 and 2 Chronicles 13:5 also speak of a “covenant of salt”.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you offer a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, you shall offer for the grain offering of your firstfruits fresh ears, roasted with fire, crushed new grain. And you shall put oil on it and lay frankincense on it; it is a grain offering. And the priest shall burn as its memorial portion some of the crushed grain and some of the oil with all of its frankincense; it is a food offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first ripe grain, roasted and crushed, is given to God before the harvest is in, an act of trust that the rest will come from him.

A grain offering of firstfruits. Firstfruits are the first of the crop to ripen, brought before the rest of the harvest is in. To give them away is to act on the belief that the remainder is coming, and coming from God: the offering of a man not yet certain of his year who gives anyway.

Christ the firstfruits. Paul uses the word for the resurrection: Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor. 15:20). One sheaf brought in early guarantees the whole field behind it: because he rose, his people will.

2.theology:
Consecrated work. The fruit of human labour, offered to God, becomes worship. For the believer no honest work is merely secular.

The exclusion of corruption. Nothing that spreads by souring may go on the altar. Christ alone was wholly free of sin's leaven, the sinless bread offered to God.

The covenant of salt. God's covenant faithfulness does not decay. Christ kept that covenant perfectly, and his people are called to be salt.
2.examples:
Then: the farmer brought the ground fruit of his fields, salted and unleavened, to the God who gave the increase.

Now: we offer our work and wages to God as worship, not to earn his favour but because he has given us everything, and we look to Christ, the grain of wheat that died to bring forth much fruit.

keyVerse.quote: You shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing from your grain offering; with all your offerings you shall offer salt.
keyVerse.note: Every gift Israel brought was seasoned with the one thing that stops decay, and God calls it his covenant. Our offerings are acceptable not because they are fine enough but because they rest on his faithfulness, which does not spoil; and Jesus passes the image on to his people: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13).

2.reflection:
The grain offering was the product of months of ordinary work. Which parts of your working week do you find hardest to think of as offered to God, and why?

Leaven was barred from the altar, and Paul tells the church to “cleanse out the old leaven” (1 Corinthians 5:7). What small corruptions most easily spread through a life or a church?

Every offering carried “the salt of the covenant” (v. 13). How does God’s faithfulness, rather than the quality of our gifts, make our worship acceptable?

Giving firstfruits meant giving before you knew how the harvest would turn out. How does Christ, “the firstfruits” of the resurrection, give you confidence to give and to trust now?

3.title: The Peace Offering: Communion Restored
3.text: <sup>1</sup>"If his offering is a sacrifice of peace offering, if he offers an animal from the herd, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish before the LORD.<sup>2</sup>And he shall lay his hand on the head of his offering and kill it at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and Aaron's sons the priests shall throw the blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>3</sup>And from the sacrifice of the peace offering, as a food offering to the LORD, he shall offer the fat covering the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails,<sup>4</sup>and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins, and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys.<sup>5</sup>Then Aaron's sons shall burn it on the altar on top of the burnt offering, which is on the wood on the fire; it is a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>6</sup>"If his offering for a sacrifice of peace offering to the LORD is an animal from the flock, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish.<sup>7</sup>If he offers a lamb for his offering, then he shall offer it before the LORD,<sup>8</sup>lay his hand on the head of his offering, and kill it in front of the tent of meeting; and Aaron's sons shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>9</sup>Then from the sacrifice of the peace offering he shall offer as a food offering to the LORD its fat; he shall remove the whole fat tail, cut off close to the backbone, and the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails<sup>10</sup>and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys.<sup>11</sup>And the priest shall burn it on the altar as a food offering to the LORD.<sup>12</sup>"If his offering is a goat, then he shall offer it before the LORD<sup>13</sup>and lay his hand on its head and kill it in front of the tent of meeting, and the sons of Aaron shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>14</sup>Then he shall offer from it, as his offering for a food offering to the LORD, the fat covering the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails<sup>15</sup>and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys.<sup>16</sup>And the priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering with a pleasing aroma. All fat is the LORD's.<sup>17</sup>It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, that you eat neither fat nor blood."
3.overview:
Where we are. The burnt offering went wholly to God and the grain offering fed the priests. Now comes the peace offering, the only sacrifice in Leviticus whose meat the worshipper and his family eat themselves (7:15).

The message. The goal of sacrifice is not only that guilt be removed but that people sit down to eat in God’s presence. The animal is shared: the blood and the richest fat go to God, a portion to the priests (7:31–34), and the rest becomes a family feast. Yet even at the table God is honoured as host: the best is his, and “All fat is the LORD’s” (v. 16).

Why it was said. Israel had been rescued to live with God, not merely to be pardoned by him (see the introduction). The peace offering gave them a way to celebrate that life with him: in thanks for a mercy, in keeping a vow, or as a freewill gift (7:11–16).

How the chapter makes its case. From the herd, male or female: the worshipper lays his hand on it and kills it, the blood is thrown against the altar, and the fat around the inner organs is burned on top of the burnt offering (vv. 1–5). From the flock, a lamb, with its rich fat tail added to God’s portion (vv. 6–11). A goat in the same way, and then two lasting rules: all fat is the LORD’s, and Israel must eat neither fat nor blood (vv. 12–17).

Where it leads. By pattern and by covenant. Christ made “peace by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20), and “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). Paul sets Israelites who ate the sacrifices and were “participants in the altar” beside believers who share in Christ at the Lord’s Table (1 Corinthians 10:16–18). The sacrifice has been made once for all; the Table is no altar but a meal, where by faith we enjoy the peace he made.

For us. Peace with God is meant to be enjoyed, not merely believed. Come to the Lord’s Table glad, give God the first and best rather than the leftovers, and let thankfulness, not guilt, set the tone of your life with him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The peace offering is the meal of fellowship, and God’s portion comes first. From the herd, male or female, the worshipper lays his hand on the animal and kills it; the blood is thrown against the altar, and the fat around the entrails, the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver are burned on top of the burnt offering (vv. 1–5). From the flock, a lamb is offered in the same way, with the whole fat tail added to God’s portion (vv. 6–11). A goat follows the same pattern, and the chapter closes with two standing rules: “All fat is the LORD’s”, and Israel shall “eat neither fat nor blood” (vv. 12–17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Only Sacrifice the Worshipper Eats

This is a meal shared with God, and the best portion is his.
verseByVerse.examples: The best cut was put before the host. Thankful worship still gives God the first and best, not what is left over.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering is a sacrifice of peace offering, if he offers an animal from the herd, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish before the LORD. And he shall lay his hand on the head of his offering and kill it at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and Aaron's sons the priests shall throw the blood against the sides of the altar. And from the sacrifice of the peace offering, as a food offering to the LORD, he shall offer the fat covering the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails, and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins, and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys. Then Aaron's sons shall burn it on the altar on top of the burnt offering, which is on the wood on the fire; it is a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The peace offering is a meal shared with God: the blood and the best fat are his, and the worshipper’s family eat the rest in his presence.

A sacrifice of peace offering. The burnt offering was entirely consumed; the grain offering fed the priests. The shelamim is shared three ways: part to God on the altar, part to the priests, and part eaten by the worshipper and his family. It is the only sacrifice in Leviticus that the person who brought it gets to eat.

A meal with God. Nothing about it is solemn in the way the sin offering is solemn. It is dinner, in God’s presence. For most Israelite families meat was a rare luxury, so a peace offering meant a feast, and chapter 7 names the occasions that called for one: thanks for a mercy received, a vow fulfilled, or a freewill gift (7:11-16). It is not brought to fix anything. No guilt is named and no wrong put right. The peace offering is what you bring when things are well.

Yet it begins with blood. The feast starts exactly as the burnt offering did: a hand on the animal’s head and blood against the altar (v. 2). Fellowship with God is never simply assumed; it stands on a life given. So does the meal Christ gave his people: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood” (1 Corinthians 11:25).

Uncertain wording. Shelamim is related to shalom, peace and wholeness, but its exact sense is uncertain; translations say peace, fellowship or well-being offering. The long lobe of the liver (v. 4) is uncertain too: perhaps a lobe, perhaps the fatty covering of the liver.
verseByVerse.note: Some translations call it the “fellowship offering.”

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering for a sacrifice of peace offering to the LORD is an animal from the flock, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish. If he offers a lamb for his offering, then he shall offer it before the LORD, lay his hand on the head of his offering, and kill it in front of the tent of meeting; and Aaron's sons shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar. Then from the sacrifice of the peace offering he shall offer as a food offering to the LORD its fat; he shall remove the whole fat tail, cut off close to the backbone, and the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys. And the priest shall burn it on the altar as a food offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A sheep brings the same shared meal, and its choicest part, the fat tail, is named for God.

The whole fat tail. What goes to God is oddly precise, and in a fat-tailed desert sheep the tail is the choicest part, the store of energy, the piece anyone would want. It is specified for God by name.

A food offering to the LORD. Food offering is deliberately homely language (see on 1:9). Scripture is emphatic that God does not eat: if I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine (Ps. 50:12). The language describes a shared table rather than a transaction, and the best cut is put before the host.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering is a goat, then he shall offer it before the LORD and lay his hand on its head and kill it in front of the tent of meeting, and the sons of Aaron shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar. Then he shall offer from it, as his offering for a food offering to the LORD, the fat covering the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys. And the priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering with a pleasing aroma. All fat is the LORD's. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, that you eat neither fat nor blood."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A goat may be offered in the same way, and the chapter closes with two lasting rules: the fat belongs to God, and the blood may not be eaten.

All fat is the LORD’s. The fat is God’s because it is the best, and the rule guards against a natural drift: a man carving up his own peace offering, deciding the choice portion is wasted in smoke, and keeping it. When worship becomes something we manage instead of something we give, the best part is the first thing we keep back.

Why blood is not food. The blood is God’s for a different reason, given in full at 17:11: the life of the flesh is in the blood... it is the blood that makes atonement by the life. Blood is not food because blood is life, and life belongs to the one who gave it.

Peace with God. This offering puts together a shared meal in God’s presence, eaten in peace, with no guilt on the table, and so does the New Testament: Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 5:1). For he himself is our peace (Eph. 2:14).

Enjoyed at his table. Peace with God was always meant to be enjoyed at his table, not merely believed. Among the last pictures Scripture gives of it is a voice at the door: if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me (Rev. 3:20).

Where Christians differ. The ban on fat, the LORD’s portion at the altar, ended with the sacrifices. Does the ban on eating blood still bind? It was given to Noah before Israel (Gen 9:4), and the Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to keep it for the sake of fellowship with Jewish Christians (Acts 15:20, 29), so some Christians still abstain. Most hold that the rule has passed while its principle remains.

This commentary’s view. The New Testament declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19; 1 Tim 4:4), and the Acts 15 rules served fellowship at that time. The principle, reverence for the life God gives, remains, but eating meat that is not fully drained is not sin. The command concerns eating, not medicine; a blood transfusion gives life and does not break it.

3.theology:
Peace with God. Atonement leads to restored fellowship, the heart of shalom, fulfilled in Christ "who is our peace" (Eph 2:14).

The fellowship meal. The shared meal anticipates the Lord's Table, where the reconciled feast in God's presence.

God's claim on the best. God receives the choicest portion, not the leftovers.
3.examples:
Then: a reconciled family sat down to a joyful sacred meal in God's courts.

Now: at the Lord's Table we celebrate the peace Christ made by his blood, because the gospel's goal is not mere pardon but fellowship with our God.

keyVerse.quote: And the priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering with a pleasing aroma. All fat is the LORD’s.
keyVerse.note: At the one meal Israel shared with God, the best portion went to him first. Fellowship with God never makes him our equal: he is the host, honoured at his own table, and the peace we enjoy there was made by blood.

3.reflection:
The peace offering was brought when things were well, for thanks, a vow or a freewill gift. How often does your worship begin with thanks rather than with need?

Even this joyful meal began with a hand on the animal’s head and blood against the altar (vv. 2, 8, 13). Why does real fellowship with God always rest on atonement?

“All fat is the LORD’s” (v. 16). What would it look like to give God the best of your time, money or energy instead of what is left over?

How does the picture of a shared meal in God’s presence shape the way you come to the Lord’s Table?

4.title: The Sin Offering: Even Unintended Sin
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If anyone sins unintentionally in any of the LORD's commandments about things not to be done, and does any one of them,<sup>3</sup>if it is the anointed priest who sins, thus bringing guilt on the people, then he shall offer for the sin that he has committed a bull from the herd without blemish to the LORD for a sin offering.<sup>4</sup>He shall bring the bull to the entrance of the tent of meeting before the LORD and lay his hand on the head of the bull and kill the bull before the LORD.<sup>5</sup>And the anointed priest shall take some of the blood of the bull and bring it into the tent of meeting,<sup>6</sup>and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle part of the blood seven times before the LORD in front of the veil of the sanctuary.<sup>7</sup>And the priest shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense before the LORD that is in the tent of meeting, and all the rest of the blood of the bull he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>8</sup>And all the fat of the bull of the sin offering he shall remove from it, the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails<sup>9</sup>and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys<sup>10</sup>(just as these are taken from the ox of the sacrifice of the peace offerings); and the priest shall burn them on the altar of burnt offering.<sup>11</sup>But the skin of the bull and all its flesh, with its head, its legs, its entrails, and its dung—<sup>12</sup>all the rest of the bull—he shall carry outside the camp to a clean place, to the ash heap, and shall burn it up on a fire of wood. On the ash heap it shall be burned up.<sup>13</sup>"If the whole congregation of Israel sins unintentionally and the thing is hidden from the eyes of the assembly, and they do any one of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, and they realize their guilt,<sup>14</sup>when the sin which they have committed becomes known, the assembly shall offer a bull from the herd for a sin offering and bring it in front of the tent of meeting.<sup>15</sup>And the elders of the congregation shall lay their hands on the head of the bull before the LORD, and the bull shall be killed before the LORD.<sup>16</sup>Then the anointed priest shall bring some of the blood of the bull into the tent of meeting,<sup>17</sup>and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle it seven times before the LORD in front of the veil.<sup>18</sup>And he shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar that is in the tent of meeting before the LORD, and the rest of the blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>19</sup>And all its fat he shall take from it and burn on the altar.<sup>20</sup>Thus shall he do with the bull. As he did with the bull of the sin offering, so shall he do with this. And the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven.<sup>21</sup>And he shall carry the bull outside the camp and burn it up as he burned the first bull; it is the sin offering for the assembly.<sup>22</sup>"When a leader sins, doing unintentionally any one of all the things that by the commandments of the LORD his God ought not to be done, and realizes his guilt,<sup>23</sup>or the sin which he has committed is made known to him, he shall bring as his offering a goat, a male without blemish,<sup>24</sup>and shall lay his hand on the head of the goat and kill it in the place where they kill the burnt offering before the LORD; it is a sin offering.<sup>25</sup>Then the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out the rest of its blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering.<sup>26</sup>And all its fat he shall burn on the altar, like the fat of the sacrifice of peace offerings. So the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>27</sup>"If anyone of the common people sins unintentionally in doing any one of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, and realizes his guilt,<sup>28</sup>or the sin which he has committed is made known to him, he shall bring for his offering a goat, a female without blemish, for his sin which he has committed.<sup>29</sup>And he shall lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and kill the sin offering in the place of burnt offering.<sup>30</sup>And the priest shall take some of its blood with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out all the rest of its blood at the base of the altar.<sup>31</sup>And all its fat he shall remove, as the fat is removed from the peace offerings, and the priest shall burn it on the altar for a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>32</sup>"If he brings a lamb as his offering for a sin offering, he shall bring a female without blemish<sup>33</sup>and lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and kill it for a sin offering in the place where they kill the burnt offering.<sup>34</sup>Then the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out all the rest of its blood at the base of the altar.<sup>35</sup>And all its fat he shall remove as the fat of the lamb is removed from the sacrifice of peace offerings, and the priest shall burn it on the altar, on top of the LORD's food offerings. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed, and he shall be forgiven.
4.overview:
Where we are. The burnt, grain and peace offerings were largely freewill gifts. Now the tone changes. The sin offering is required, and it deals first with sins committed “unintentionally” (v. 2).

The message. Sin is measured by God’s holiness, not by our awareness: wrongs we never meant or noticed still defile and still need blood. The higher a person’s place, the further the defilement reaches and the costlier the offering. But the chapter’s refrain is grace: atonement is made, and “he shall be forgiven”.

Why it was said. The holy God now lived in Israel’s camp, and sin did not only stain the sinner; it defiled the sanctuary where God dwelt (see the introduction). Israel needed to know how even unnoticed sin could be cleansed, so that God could stay among them.

How the chapter makes its case. If the anointed priest sins, he brings a bull; its blood is carried into the tent, sprinkled before the veil and put on the incense altar, and the carcass is burned outside the camp (vv. 1–12). If the whole congregation sins, the same bull is brought, and the elders lay their hands on it for everyone (vv. 13–21). A leader brings a male goat (vv. 22–26), and an ordinary person a female goat or lamb (vv. 27–35), their blood put on the altar in the courtyard. Four times the chapter announces forgiveness (vv. 20, 26, 31, 35).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Hebrews says that “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4), and that Jesus, unlike the anointed priest, has no need to offer “first for his own sins” (Hebrews 7:27). As the bull was burned outside the camp, he “suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12): God “made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). On the cross he prayed for people who did not know what they were doing: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).

For us. We are guiltier than we know, and more forgiven than we dared hope. Christ’s blood covers the sins we cannot see, so we need neither trust our own flattering verdict on ourselves nor search anxiously and endlessly for hidden faults. We can afford to hear the truth about ourselves, and those who lead can own their failures openly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-12 — The Sin Offering: When the Anointed Priest Sins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Unintended sin still needs atonement, and the priest’s sin is the most serious of all. God introduces an offering for sins committed “unintentionally” (vv. 1–2). If the anointed priest sins, he brings guilt on the whole people, so he must bring a bull without blemish, lay his hand on it and kill it (vv. 3–4). Its blood is carried into the tent, sprinkled seven times before the veil and put on the horns of the incense altar, and the rest is poured out at the base of the altar of burnt offering (vv. 5–7). The fat is burned as with a peace offering (vv. 8–10), and everything else is carried outside the camp and burned on the ash heap (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Why Unintentional Sin Needs Atoning

The priest's sin is priced at the same rate as the whole nation's.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the priest's sin brought guilt on the people. Now: those who lead in the church carry a heavier responsibility, and need the same sacrifice as everyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If anyone sins unintentionally in any of the LORD's commandments about things not to be done, and does any one of them, if it is the anointed priest who sins, thus bringing guilt on the people, then he shall offer for the sin that he has committed a bull from the herd without blemish to the LORD for a sin offering. He shall bring the bull to the entrance of the tent of meeting before the LORD and lay his hand on the head of the bull and kill the bull before the LORD. And the anointed priest shall take some of the blood of the bull and bring it into the tent of meeting, and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle part of the blood seven times before the LORD in front of the veil of the sanctuary. And the priest shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense before the LORD that is in the tent of meeting, and all the rest of the blood of the bull he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And all the fat of the bull of the sin offering he shall remove from it, the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys (just as these are taken from the ox of the sacrifice of the peace offerings); and the priest shall burn them on the altar of burnt offering. But the skin of the bull and all its flesh, with its head, its legs, its entrails, and its dung— all the rest of the bull—he shall carry outside the camp to a clean place, to the ash heap, and shall burn it up on a fire of wood. On the ash heap it shall be burned up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin committed without meaning to is still sin, and the anointed priest’s sin falls on the whole people and needs the costliest offering.

If anyone sins unintentionally. The Hebrew shegagah means sin committed in error, without meaning to, and that raises the question a modern reader asks at once: why need atonement for something you did not know you were doing?

Why unknowing sin needs atonement. Guilt in Scripture is not measured by the offender’s awareness of it. A law broken unknowingly is still broken. Leviticus assumes what every honest person discovers: we are not reliable judges of our own record, and “I did not realise” explains what happened without making us innocent. David prayed out of the same conviction: Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults (Ps. 19:12).

If it is the anointed priest who sins. The first case is the high priest, with the most expensive animal and the most elaborate blood rite. His sin does not stay with him; it brings guilt on the people. And the same bull is required for the whole congregation, so a priest’s private failure costs as much as a national one. A leader’s sin weighs more, because it harms more people.

Into the tent of meeting. For the priest and the congregation the blood goes inside the tent, before the veil and on the incense altar (vv. 5–7); for a leader or an ordinary person, only to the altar in the courtyard (vv. 25, 30). It seems that sin defiles God’s dwelling, and the sins of the priest and the whole people reach further in, so the blood must go further in too.

Outside the camp. The rest of the bull is burned outside the camp, the detail Hebrews reaches for: the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Heb. 13:11-12).

The good person who never meant any harm. Most of us grade ourselves on our intentions and other people on their actions. I did not mean to hurt her; I did not know where the money came from; my heart was in the right place. That double standard lets nearly everyone believe they are basically good. Leviticus will not let intention be the whole story: a wrong done in ignorance still lands on someone and still needs dealing with. That sounds harsher, but it is far more hopeful. If my standing before God rested on my reading of my own heart, I would have to keep the reading flattering, and I could never be sure of it. Paul knew better: “I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me” (1 Corinthians 4:4). And the Judge has provided for the sins I cannot see: Christ’s blood covers faults I would never have thought to confess, so I can afford to find out the truth about myself.

What about deliberate sin? The one who sins with a high hand, in open defiance, had no sacrifice (Num 15:30–31). Yet David, guilty of adultery and murder, was forgiven when he confessed (2 Sam 12:13; Ps 51:16–17). The sacrifices covered sins of weakness; deliberate sin was cast on God’s mercy alone. In Christ every sin confessed is forgiven: the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7).

Uncertain wording. “Sin offering” translates chatta’t, the ordinary word for sin. Because its blood cleanses the sanctuary as well as the worshipper, many scholars prefer “purification offering”. Both are true to what it does.
verseByVerse.note: “Unintentionally” means by mistake (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13-21 — When the Whole Congregation Sins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A whole people can be guilty without knowing it. When the congregation’s hidden sin comes to light, the assembly brings the same costly offering as the anointed priest, a bull (vv. 13–14). The elders lay their hands on it on everyone’s behalf, and it is killed before the LORD (v. 15). Its blood is taken into the tent and sprinkled before the veil and put on the altar there, and its fat is burned (vv. 16–19). Then the chapter’s refrain sounds for the first time: “the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven” (v. 20). The bull is burned outside the camp like the first (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology:
Guilt Nobody Has Noticed

Once a community's hidden sin comes to light, one offering covers it.
verseByVerse.examples: A church, too, can share a blind spot no one has named. Because the sacrifice is already provided, it can afford to have that blind spot pointed out.

verseByVerse.quote: "If the whole congregation of Israel sins unintentionally and the thing is hidden from the eyes of the assembly, and they do any one of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, and they realize their guilt, when the sin which they have committed becomes known, the assembly shall offer a bull from the herd for a sin offering and bring it in front of the tent of meeting. And the elders of the congregation shall lay their hands on the head of the bull before the LORD, and the bull shall be killed before the LORD. Then the anointed priest shall bring some of the blood of the bull into the tent of meeting, and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle it seven times before the LORD in front of the veil. And he shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar that is in the tent of meeting before the LORD, and the rest of the blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And all its fat he shall take from it and burn on the altar. Thus shall he do with the bull. As he did with the bull of the sin offering, so shall he do with this. And the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven. And he shall carry the bull outside the camp and burn it up as he burned the first bull; it is the sin offering for the assembly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A whole nation can share a sin none of its members has noticed; once it comes to light, the elders lay their hands on one bull for all, and the people are forgiven.

If the whole congregation of Israel sins. A nation can be guilty of something none of its members has noticed, and that hidden shared sin is real enough to require the most expensive sacrifice in the system.

When the sin which they have committed becomes known. Dealing with it depends on discovery. Until the sin is recognised there is no offering, so the health of the arrangement depends on a community willing to have its blind spots pointed out, which is easier for a people who know a sacrifice is already provided.

The elders of the congregation shall lay their hands. The elders lay their hands on the bull for everybody. Representation runs right through this book: one animal, a few hands, a whole people covered (v. 20). John saw the pattern fulfilled when the high priest unknowingly prophesied “that Jesus would die for the nation” (John 11:51).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22-35 — When a Leader or a Common Person Sins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Leaders and ordinary people are forgiven in the same way, at a lower price. A leader who discovers his sin brings a male goat; its blood goes on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, its fat is burned, and “he shall be forgiven” (vv. 22–26). One of the common people brings a female goat (vv. 27–31) or a female lamb (vv. 32–35), with the same rite. The cost falls as the rank falls, but the promise does not change: each section ends with atonement made and forgiveness declared (vv. 26, 31, 35), stated as fact, not as hope.
verseByVerse.theology:
Forgiveness Stated as Fact

When atonement has been made, forgiveness is pronounced.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the offering shrank with the offender's rank, and every offender heard the same words of forgiveness. Now: Christ's blood does what the blood of goats only promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a leader sins, doing unintentionally any one of all the things that by the commandments of the LORD his God ought not to be done, and realizes his guilt, or the sin which he has committed is made known to him, he shall bring as his offering a goat, a male without blemish, and shall lay his hand on the head of the goat and kill it in the place where they kill the burnt offering before the LORD; it is a sin offering. Then the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out the rest of its blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering. And all its fat he shall burn on the altar, like the fat of the sacrifice of peace offerings. So the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin, and he shall be forgiven. "If anyone of the common people sins unintentionally in doing any one of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, and realizes his guilt, or the sin which he has committed is made known to him, he shall bring for his offering a goat, a female without blemish, for his sin which he has committed. And he shall lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and kill the sin offering in the place of burnt offering. And the priest shall take some of its blood with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out all the rest of its blood at the base of the altar. And all its fat he shall remove, as the fat is removed from the peace offerings, and the priest shall burn it on the altar for a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven. "If he brings a lamb as his offering for a sin offering, he shall bring a female without blemish and lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and kill it for a sin offering in the place where they kill the burnt offering. Then the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out all the rest of its blood at the base of the altar. And all its fat he shall remove as the fat of the lamb is removed from the sacrifice of peace offerings, and the priest shall burn it on the altar, on top of the LORD's food offerings. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed, and he shall be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A leader brings a male goat and an ordinary person a female goat or lamb, and each, once atonement is made, hears the same promise: he shall be forgiven.

The price falls with rank. The offering shrinks with the rank of the offender: the reverse of how most societies price wrongdoing, where the powerful make things go away more cheaply than the poor.

When a leader sins. One small difference in wording is pointed. For the priest and the congregation the text says if; for the leader it says when. Scripture does not entertain the possibility that a man in authority will get through his term without needing this.

He shall be forgiven. Every paragraph after the priest’s ends with the same formula, four times (vv. 20, 26, 31, 35): atonement made, and he shall be forgiven. Not “he may hope to be”, nor “he shall feel” forgiven. It is stated as accomplished fact, to a man who did not know he had done wrong until somebody told him. Hebrews observes that the sacrifices had to keep being repeated because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Heb. 10:4). The forgiveness announced here was real, resting on a payment not yet made: the death of Christ.

Forgiven at infinite cost. The refrain is now spoken over believers on the strength of Christ’s blood, and it covers what we cannot name. A Christian troubled by faults he cannot identify may rest here: “God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything” (1 John 3:20).

4.theology:
The gravity of unintentional sin. Guilt is measured by God's holiness, not by our awareness, and that leaves no room for self-righteousness.

Graded accountability. The higher the office, the costlier the offering (cf. James 3:1).

'They shall be forgiven.' This is the chapter's refrain of grace. Christ the sin offering secures the forgiveness the bulls and goats could only foreshadow (Heb 10:4).
4.examples:
Then: an Israelite, suddenly aware of a sin committed unawares, brought a goat, laid his hand on it, and heard the priest pronounce him forgiven.

Now: we are guiltier than we know, but in Christ more loved than we dared hope. This is no call to anxious, endless self-searching: the believer who cannot name every hidden fault may rest in the One who knows them all and has paid for them all (1 John 3:20).

keyVerse.quote: And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed, and he shall be forgiven.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s refrain, sounded four times, is spoken here over the most ordinary Israelite. Forgiveness is declared as fact once atonement is made, a promise that rested on a payment not yet made: the blood of Christ, which “cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

4.reflection:
Israel needed atonement even for sins committed unintentionally (v. 2). Why do we usually judge ourselves by our intentions, and what does this chapter say to that?

The anointed priest’s sin brought guilt on the whole people (v. 3). What does that mean for those who lead in churches and homes, and how should we pray for them?

A community’s sin could stay hidden until it became known (v. 14). How can a church become a place where blind spots can be named safely?

Four times the chapter says that the sinner “shall be forgiven”. How does knowing that Christ’s blood covers even the sins you cannot name free you from anxious self-examination?

5.title: The Guilt Offering: Forgiveness and Restoration
5.text: <sup>1</sup>"If anyone sins in that he hears a public adjuration to testify, and though he is a witness, whether he has seen or come to know the matter, yet does not speak, he shall bear his iniquity;<sup>2</sup>or if anyone touches an unclean thing, whether a carcass of an unclean wild animal or a carcass of unclean livestock or a carcass of unclean swarming things, and it is hidden from him and he has become unclean, and he realizes his guilt;<sup>3</sup>or if he touches human uncleanness, of whatever sort the uncleanness may be with which one becomes unclean, and it is hidden from him, when he comes to know it, and realizes his guilt;<sup>4</sup>or if anyone utters with his lips a rash oath to do evil or to do good, any sort of rash oath that people swear, and it is hidden from him, when he comes to know it, and he realizes his guilt in any of these;<sup>5</sup>when he realizes his guilt in any of these and confesses the sin he has committed,<sup>6</sup>he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed, a female from the flock, a lamb or a goat, for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin.<sup>7</sup>"But if he cannot afford a lamb, then he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering.<sup>8</sup>He shall bring them to the priest, who shall offer first the one for the sin offering. He shall wring its head from its neck but shall not sever it completely,<sup>9</sup>and he shall sprinkle some of the blood of the sin offering on the side of the altar, while the rest of the blood shall be drained out at the base of the altar; it is a sin offering.<sup>10</sup>Then he shall offer the second for a burnt offering according to the rule.
