And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin that he has committed, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>11</sup>"But if he cannot afford two turtledoves or two pigeons, then he shall bring as his offering for the sin that he has committed a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering. He shall put no oil on it and shall put no frankincense on it, for it is a sin offering.<sup>12</sup>And he shall bring it to the priest, and the priest shall take a handful of it as its memorial portion and burn this on the altar, on the LORD's food offerings; it is a sin offering.<sup>13</sup>Thus the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed in any one of these things, and he shall be forgiven. And the remainder shall be for the priest, as in the grain offering."<sup>14</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>15</sup>"If anyone commits a breach of faith and sins unintentionally in any of the holy things of the LORD, he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation, a ram without blemish out of the flock, valued in silver shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, for a guilt offering.<sup>16</sup>He shall also make restitution for what he has done amiss in the holy thing and shall add a fifth to it and give it to the priest. And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>17</sup>"If anyone sins, doing any of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, though he did not know it, then realizes his guilt, he shall bear his iniquity.<sup>18</sup>He shall bring to the priest a ram without blemish out of the flock, or its equivalent, for a guilt offering, and the priest shall make atonement for him for the mistake that he made unintentionally, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>19</sup>It is a guilt offering; he has indeed incurred guilt before the LORD."
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 set out the sin offering for unintentional sins. Chapter 5 finishes that teaching with some everyday cases and an offering scaled down for the poor, then introduces the last of the five offerings, the guilt offering, which runs on to 6:7.

The message. Sin is wider than we think: it includes the truth we keep back, the defilement we leave untended and the careless promise we forget, and when it comes to light it must be confessed by name. God has made the way back so cheap that no one is priced out of it, and yet so serious that what has been taken from him must be repaid in full and more. Grace does not excuse us from making things right; it is what makes us able to.

Why it was said. The holy God now lived in the middle of Israel’s camp (see the introduction). They needed to know that hidden and careless sins mattered, that the poorest Israelite was as welcome at the altar as the richest, and that worship could never be a way round repaying what had been taken.

How the chapter makes its case. Three cases of hidden or careless sin come first: the witness who stays silent, the uncleanness left untended and the rash oath (vv. 1–4). Each ends in confession and a female lamb or goat (vv. 5–6). If the sinner cannot afford a lamb, two birds will do (vv. 7–10); if not birds, a little flour (vv. 11–13); and each time “he shall be forgiven”. Then comes the guilt offering. Whoever has misused the LORD’s holy things brings a ram, repays the loss and adds a fifth (vv. 14–16), and even a wrong done without knowing it is real guilt that needs the ram (vv. 17–19).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Isaiah uses this chapter’s word for the guilt offering of the Servant of the LORD: “when his soul makes an offering for guilt” (Isaiah 53:10). Christ is both the ram and the repayment, giving back to God what our sin had stolen, and more. And the Son of God was born into a family that could afford only the poor man’s birds (Luke 2:24): “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

For us. Confess your sins by name, not only in general, and come however little you have to bring, because the price has been paid. Where your sin has cost someone, put it right, gladly and generously, because Christ has repaid far more for you than you could ever repay.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-13 — The Sin Offering Scaled to the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No sin is too hidden to need dealing with, and no sinner too poor to have it dealt with. Three cases open the section: the witness who keeps silent when the court calls for testimony, the person who has unknowingly become unclean and left it untended, and the one who swore rashly and forgot (vv. 1–4). When any of them realises his guilt, he must confess it and bring a female lamb or goat (vv. 5–6). Then God lowers the price: two turtledoves or pigeons for those who cannot afford a lamb (vv. 7–10), and for the poorest a tenth of an ephah of flour, burned on top of the blood offerings already on the altar (vv. 11–13). Each time the promise is the same: “he shall be forgiven.”
verseByVerse.theology:
A Sin Offering of Flour

The sinner confesses, and the offering is priced so that everyone can afford it.
verseByVerse.examples: The way back is open the moment a person admits the wrong, and no one is too poor to take it.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone sins in that he hears a public adjuration to testify, and though he is a witness, whether he has seen or come to know the matter, yet does not speak, he shall bear his iniquity; or if anyone touches an unclean thing, whether a carcass of an unclean wild animal or a carcass of unclean livestock or a carcass of unclean swarming things, and it is hidden from him and he has become unclean, and he realizes his guilt; or if he touches human uncleanness, of whatever sort the uncleanness may be with which one becomes unclean, and it is hidden from him, when he comes to know it, and realizes his guilt; or if anyone utters with his lips a rash oath to do evil or to do good, any sort of rash oath that people swear, and it is hidden from him, when he comes to know it, and he realizes his guilt in any of these; when he realizes his guilt in any of these and confesses the sin he has committed, he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed, a female from the flock, a lamb or a goat, for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keeping silent when you should speak, leaving an uncleanness untended and forgetting a rash oath are real sins, and once a person realises it he must confess and bring a sin offering.

Though he is a witness… yet does not speak. The first case is not an action at all. A public adjuration was a solemn curse pronounced on anyone who knew the facts of a case and would not come forward; Proverbs describes the thief’s partner who “hears the curse, but discloses nothing” (Proverbs 29:24). The man in this verse tells no lie. He simply keeps quiet while an injustice proceeds, and Leviticus files that under sin: silence when the truth is asked for is treated as an act, and he shall bear his iniquity.

If anyone touches an unclean thing… and it is hidden from him. Touching a carcass was not in itself a sin; whoever touched one was simply unclean until the evening and must wash (11:24–25). The fault seems to lie in what happened next: the person did not notice, the uncleanness went untended, and he might carry it near God’s holy things (see Uncertain wording below).

A rash oath to do evil or to do good. “Evil or good” is a Hebrew way of saying “anything at all”. A man swears in the heat of the moment to do something, and then forgets. Words spoken carelessly before God are still words spoken. Jesus pressed the point further: the answer to careless oaths is a life so truthful that oaths are not needed: “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37).

When he realizes his guilt… and confesses. All three cases end at the same door, and the remedy is waiting the moment a person admits his guilt. Here, for the first time in Leviticus, confession is required: the sin must be named (v. 5), not merely regretted. The offering was not a way of avoiding the admission but the way of making it. The order holds for us: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

The silent witness today. The silent witness has modern successors: the employee who knows the accounts are false, the church member who knows a child is being harmed, the friend who could clear an innocent name. When the truth is needed, keeping quiet is not neutral. Where someone is being abused or is in danger, tell the police or the proper authorities the same day, and the church’s leaders as well, never instead.

Uncertain wording. Two points are not certain. First, the text does not say exactly where the sin lay in vv. 2–3: in the contact, in the delay in cleansing, or in bringing uncleanness near holy things. Since the contact itself was not sin, most interpreters think the guilt lay in leaving it untended. Second, v. 6 calls the animal the sinner’s ’asham, the word for the guilt offering, yet says it is “for a sin offering”. The ESV’s “compensation” is probably right: the word here means the penalty he owes, not a different sacrifice, so vv. 1–13 belong with the sin offering of chapter 4.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if he cannot afford a lamb, then he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. He shall bring them to the priest, who shall offer first the one for the sin offering. He shall wring its head from its neck but shall not sever it completely, and he shall sprinkle some of the blood of the sin offering on the side of the altar, while the rest of the blood shall be drained out at the base of the altar; it is a sin offering. Then he shall offer the second for a burnt offering according to the rule. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin that he has committed, and he shall be forgiven. "But if he cannot afford two turtledoves or two pigeons, then he shall bring as his offering for the sin that he has committed a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering. He shall put no oil on it and shall put no frankincense on it, for it is a sin offering. And he shall bring it to the priest, and the priest shall take a handful of it as its memorial portion and burn this on the altar, on the LORD's food offerings; it is a sin offering. Thus the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed in any one of these things, and he shall be forgiven. And the remainder shall be for the priest, as in the grain offering."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God scales the sin offering down to what the poorest can bring, two birds or even a little flour, so that no one is ever priced out of forgiveness.

If he cannot afford a lamb. Literally, “if his hand cannot reach” a lamb. Then two turtledoves or pigeons, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering, and the priest offers “first the one for the sin offering” (v. 8). The order matters: the sin is dealt with first, and only then does the burnt offering give the forgiven person wholly back to God.

A tenth of an ephah of fine flour. For those who cannot manage even birds, a tenth of an ephah, about two litres of flour. Hebrews sums up the system, “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins”, and is careful to say that under the law “almost everything is purified with blood” (Hebrews 9:22), perhaps with exactly this case in mind. The text insists that it is still a sin offering, and closes with the same promise: “he shall be forgiven.”

He shall put no oil on it. Two details show that this is no exception to the rule of blood. There is no oil or frankincense, unlike the grain offering of chapter 2, because this is not a gift of gratitude but an offering for sin. And the priest burns a handful “on the LORD’s food offerings”, on top of the blood sacrifices already burning. The poor man’s flour goes into a fire that blood has already lit. His forgiveness is not bloodless; it rests on blood he did not bring.

Saved by a payment someone else made. That is the position of everyone who has ever been forgiven. Nobody’s atonement is self-funded, and the Israelite carrying a bag of flour to the altar is the plainest picture of it in Leviticus. When the Son of God came, he was born into a family in the poorer bracket, whose offering after his birth was a pair of birds (Luke 2:24; compare 12:8). “Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The one born at the bottom of the price scale paid the whole price himself.

What it does not mean. Not that a cheap offering meant a cheap view of sin. The poor man was asked for what was costly to him, and the rich man could not get away with flour; God weighs a gift by what it costs the giver (Mark 12:41–44). The gospel is offered on the same terms: “he who has no money, come, buy and eat!” (Isaiah 55:1).
verseByVerse.note: A tenth of an ephah was roughly two litres of flour.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Where sin has taken something that belongs to God, sorrow is not enough: the loss must be repaid. This is the guilt offering. Whoever commits “a breach of faith” by misusing the LORD’s holy things, even unintentionally, brings a ram without blemish, valued by the sanctuary’s standard, restores what he took and adds a fifth (vv. 14–16). Then the priest makes atonement, and he is forgiven. The last case reaches further: a man who broke a command “though he did not know it” has still “incurred guilt before the LORD” and must bring the same ram (vv. 17–19). Ignorance may explain a wrong, but it does not erase it; only atonement does.
verseByVerse.theology:
Repentance With an Arithmetic

The offender brings a ram, restores the loss and adds a fifth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: worship was no substitute for putting something right. Now: a forgiven Christian pays back what he took, gladly, because his own debt has been paid.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "If anyone commits a breach of faith and sins unintentionally in any of the holy things of the LORD, he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation, a ram without blemish out of the flock, valued in silver shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, for a guilt offering. He shall also make restitution for what he has done amiss in the holy thing and shall add a fifth to it and give it to the priest. And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering, and he shall be forgiven. "If anyone sins, doing any of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, though he did not know it, then realizes his guilt, he shall bear his iniquity. He shall bring to the priest a ram without blemish out of the flock, or its equivalent, for a guilt offering, and the priest shall make atonement for him for the mistake that he made unintentionally, and he shall be forgiven. It is a guilt offering; he has indeed incurred guilt before the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever wrongs the LORD by misusing what belongs to him, even unknowingly, must bring a ram, repay the loss in full and add a fifth; a wrong done without knowing it is still real guilt.

A breach of faith. The Hebrew ma’al is a word for unfaithfulness, used of a wife who “breaks faith” with her husband (Numbers 5:12) and of Israel’s treachery against God. Here it is specific: misusing the holy things of the LORD, perhaps by eating what belonged to the priests, holding back a tithe or using for oneself something dedicated to God. Taking what is God’s betrays a relationship; it does not merely break a rule.

A guilt offering. The ’asham deals not only with sin but with damage, a debt that is owed. Alongside the ram, “valued in silver shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary” (the shekel of standard weight used for payments to the sanctuary), the offender must restore what he took.

Add a fifth to it. Repentance here has an arithmetic. The wrong is repaid in full plus twenty per cent, so that the one wronged ends up better off, and the repayment goes with the sacrifice. Israel could not use worship as a substitute for putting something right. Zacchaeus shows the spirit of it: grace found him first, and then he repaid fourfold (Luke 19:8).

Though he did not know it. The closing case stretches the principle to its limit: a man who did something forbidden “though he did not know it” has “indeed incurred guilt before the LORD”. Ignorance and guilt do not cancel each other. That is why the sacrifices exist: not to make people feel as bad as their offence deserves, but to deal with the guilt that is really there.

The guilt offering who repaid. Isaiah uses this very word of the Servant of the LORD: “when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring” (Isaiah 53:10). Christ is the ram and the repayment together. He gave back to God the honour and obedience our sin had stolen, and more, for “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20). In a psalm the New Testament applies to Jesus again and again (John 2:17; Romans 15:3), the sufferer asks, “What I did not steal must I now restore?” (Psalm 69:4). At the cross the Innocent did exactly that.

Uncertain wording. “Valued in silver shekels” is compressed in Hebrew, literally “by your valuation, silver, shekels”. It may mean that the ram had to be worth at least two shekels (the plural), or that its value could be paid in silver instead, which “or its equivalent” (v. 18) may suggest. The case of vv. 17–19 is also unclear: it is hard to see how it differs from the unintentional sins of chapter 4. Jewish tradition read it as an offering for someone who suspects he may have trespassed on holy things but cannot be sure; others take it as the general rule. Either way the point stands: not knowing does not mean not guilty.
verseByVerse.note: The “shekel of the sanctuary” (v. 15) was the standard weight for payments to the sanctuary.

5.theology:
Confession. Sin must be named openly before God, the gateway to forgiveness (1 John 1:9).

Restitution. Grace does not bypass repair; it enables it, and true repentance pays back more than it took.

Christ our restorer. Isaiah says the Servant's soul "makes an offering for guilt" (Isa 53:10): he is himself the 'asham, paying far more than the added fifth and giving back what he never took away (Ps 69:4).
5.examples:
Then: an Israelite who had defrauded God or a neighbour confessed, repaid with a fifth added, and brought a ram.

Now: resting in Christ, the guilt offering who cancelled our debt, we make things right where we have wronged others, by the Spirit who makes a forgiven person generous. Where our repair falls short, his covers it.

keyVerse.quote: when he realizes his guilt in any of these and confesses the sin he has committed
keyVerse.note: For the first time Leviticus requires the sinner to confess: the sin must be named, not merely regretted. Everything else in the chapter, from the poor man’s flour to the restored fifth, comes through this door, and it is still the way back to God: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

5.reflection:
The witness of v. 1 sinned simply by saying nothing. Where are Christians most tempted to keep quiet when the truth is needed, and what makes speaking up costly?

Confession in v. 5 means naming the sin, not just feeling bad about it. Why is it easier to regret in general than to confess in particular, and how does God’s promise to forgive make it possible?

God lowered the price until even the poorest could bring a little flour (vv. 11–13), yet that flour burned on top of the blood offerings. What does this teach about who may come to God, and on what basis?

The guilt offering required repayment plus a fifth (v. 16). Is there anything you have taken, in money, time or someone’s good name, that you need to put right, and how does Christ’s payment for you change the way you go about it?

6.title: Laws for the Priests: The Fire That Never Goes Out
6.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"If anyone sins and commits a breach of faith against the LORD by deceiving his neighbor in a matter of deposit or security, or through robbery, or if he has oppressed his neighbor<sup>3</sup>or has found something lost and lied about it, swearing falsely—in any of all the things that people do and sin thereby—<sup>4</sup>if he has sinned and has realized his guilt and will restore what he took by robbery or what he got by oppression or the deposit that was committed to him or the lost thing that he found<sup>5</sup>or anything about which he has sworn falsely, he shall restore it in full and shall add a fifth to it, and give it to him to whom it belongs on the day he realizes his guilt.<sup>6</sup>And he shall bring to the priest as his compensation to the LORD a ram without blemish out of the flock, or its equivalent, for a guilt offering.<sup>7</sup>And the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD, and he shall be forgiven for any of the things that one may do and thereby become guilty."<sup>8</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>9</sup>"Command Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the burnt offering. The burnt offering shall be on the hearth on the altar all night until the morning, and the fire of the altar shall be kept burning on it.<sup>10</sup>And the priest shall put on his linen garment and put his linen undergarment on his body, and he shall take up the ashes to which the fire has reduced the burnt offering on the altar and put them beside the altar.<sup>11</sup>Then he shall take off his garments and put on other garments and carry the ashes outside the camp to a clean place.<sup>12</sup>The fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it; it shall not go out. The priest shall burn wood on it every morning, and he shall arrange the burnt offering on it and shall burn on it the fat of the peace offerings.<sup>13</sup>Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out.<sup>14</sup>"And this is the law of the grain offering. The sons of Aaron shall offer it before the LORD in front of the altar.<sup>15</sup>And one shall take from it a handful of the fine flour of the grain offering and its oil and all the frankincense that is on the grain offering and burn this as its memorial portion on the altar, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>16</sup>And the rest of it Aaron and his sons shall eat. It shall be eaten unleavened in a holy place. In the court of the tent of meeting they shall eat it.<sup>17</sup>It shall not be baked with leaven. I have given it as their portion of my food offerings. It is a thing most holy, like the sin offering and the guilt offering.<sup>18</sup>Every male among the children of Aaron may eat of it, as decreed forever throughout your generations, from the LORD's food offerings. Whatever touches them shall become holy."<sup>19</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>20</sup>"This is the offering that Aaron and his sons shall offer to the LORD on the day when he is anointed: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a regular grain offering, half of it in the morning and half in the evening.<sup>21</sup>It shall be made with oil on a griddle. You shall bring it well mixed, in baked pieces like a grain offering, and offer it for a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>22</sup>The priest from among Aaron's sons, who is anointed to succeed him, shall offer it to the LORD as decreed forever. The whole of it shall be burned.<sup>23</sup>Every grain offering of a priest shall be wholly burned. It shall not be eaten."<sup>24</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>25</sup>"Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the sin offering. In the place where the burnt offering is killed shall the sin offering be killed before the LORD; it is most holy.<sup>26</sup>The priest who offers it for sin shall eat it. In a holy place it shall be eaten, in the court of the tent of meeting.<sup>27</sup>Whatever touches its flesh shall be holy, and when any of its blood is splashed on a garment, you shall wash that on which it was splashed in a holy place.<sup>28</sup>And the earthenware vessel in which it is boiled shall be broken. But if it is boiled in a bronze vessel, that shall be scoured and rinsed in water.<sup>29</sup>Every male among the priests may eat of it; it is most holy.<sup>30</sup>But no sin offering shall be eaten from which any blood is brought into the tent of meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place; it shall be burned up with fire.
6.overview:
Where we are. The guilt offering of chapter 5 runs on into vv. 1–7, now for wrongs done to a neighbour. Then, from v. 8, the book turns from the worshippers to the priests, giving them the “law” of each offering: how it is to be handled at the altar (6:8–7:38).

The message. Wronging your neighbour is a breach of faith against the LORD, and there is no making peace with God while the person you cheated is still out of pocket. And the God who is a consuming fire orders his worship down to the ashes: the altar fire must never go out, the priests must remain worshippers themselves, and the holiness of the sin offering is never to be handled lightly. Nothing about approaching him is trivial.

Why it was said. Israel lived without banks, police or written contracts, so daily life depended on trust: goods left with a neighbour, a pledge, an oath before God. And the priests, about to begin their work (chapters 8–9), needed to know exactly how to handle what was most holy (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Wrongs against a neighbour are put right by repaying in full plus a fifth on the day the guilt is realised, and then by a ram (vv. 1–7). The law of the burnt offering: the fire must never go out, and the priest changes his clothes to carry the ashes away (vv. 8–13). The law of the grain offering: the priests eat it in a holy place, while the high priest offers his own every day, wholly burned (vv. 14–23). The law of the sin offering: it is most holy, and when its blood has been taken into the Holy Place it is burned, not eaten (vv. 24–30).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by contrast. The fire never went out because Israel never stopped sinning and the sacrifices were never finished; Christ “offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins” and sat down (Hebrews 10:12), and “he always lives to make intercession” for those who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). The high priest brought an offering for himself every day; Jesus needed none. And Hebrews takes the sin offering that no one could eat, burned outside the camp, as a picture of the Lord who “suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12).

For us. Faith in Christ shows in how you handle other people’s things: what you borrowed, found or were trusted with. Put wrongs right on the day you see them. And let the fire that never went out remind you that in Christ the way to God is never closed, at any hour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Restitution for Sins Against a Neighbor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cheating a neighbour is a sin against God, and it must be put right before the sinner comes to the altar. The list is drawn from ordinary life: lying about something left in your care or pledged to you, robbery, extortion, and keeping lost property and swearing falsely about it (vv. 1–3). Each is called “a breach of faith against the LORD”. The guilty person must restore what he took in full, add a fifth, and pay it to the owner “on the day he realizes his guilt” (vv. 4–5). Only then does he bring a ram for a guilt offering; the priest makes atonement, and “he shall be forgiven” (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology:
Wrongs Against People Are Breaches of Faith Against God

The neighbour is to be repaid on the very day the guilt is realised.
verseByVerse.examples: The neighbour was paid before God was approached. A Christian who has wronged someone puts it right as part of coming back to God, not as an optional extra afterwards.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "If anyone sins and commits a breach of faith against the LORD by deceiving his neighbor in a matter of deposit or security, or through robbery, or if he has oppressed his neighbor or has found something lost and lied about it, swearing falsely—in any of all the things that people do and sin thereby— if he has sinned and has realized his guilt and will restore what he took by robbery or what he got by oppression or the deposit that was committed to him or the lost thing that he found or anything about which he has sworn falsely, he shall restore it in full and shall add a fifth to it, and give it to him to whom it belongs on the day he realizes his guilt. And he shall bring to the priest as his compensation to the LORD a ram without blemish out of the flock, or its equivalent, for a guilt offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD, and he shall be forgiven for any of the things that one may do and thereby become guilty."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cheating or deceiving a neighbour is a sin against God himself, and the one who has done it must repay in full, plus a fifth, on the very day he admits it, before he brings his guilt offering.

A breach of faith against the LORD. Every offence in the list is committed against a person, and the verse calls all of them a breach of faith against the LORD. Cheating a neighbour over a deposit is not merely a matter between two people; it is a sin against God, done to a man.

A deposit or security… or has found something lost. The list reads like the ordinary dealings of a village without banks or police: goods left with a neighbour for safekeeping, a pledge, open robbery, extortion of the weak, and lost property kept and lied about. Most of these depended on trust and could never have been proved in court, and each could be sealed by swearing falsely, calling God to witness a lie. Leviticus reaches past what a court could detect to what the conscience knows.

On the day he realizes his guilt. The remedy has two halves in a fixed order. First, restore in full, add a fifth and pay it to the owner on the day he realizes his guilt: not when it is convenient. Then the guilt offering.

First the neighbour, then God. The wronged man is paid before God is approached. There was no arrangement in Israel for making peace with heaven while the defrauded person was still out of pocket, which is why Zacchaeus, the moment grace reached him, started calculating (Luke 19:8), and why Jesus told people to leave their gift at the altar and first be reconciled to a brother (Matthew 5:23–24). In both cases grace comes first; the repaying is its fruit.

The debt only Christ could pay. The ram of the guilt offering pictured what we owe God and cannot pay. Christ paid it, “canceling the record of debt that stood against us… nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14). People forgiven a debt like that do not haggle over the small debts they owe others; the servant in Jesus’ parable who did so showed that he had never understood his own release (Matthew 18:32–33).

What if I cannot repay? The law foresaw part of this: if the wronged person had died and left no next of kin, the restitution went to the LORD for the priest (Numbers 5:8), and many Christians in that position give the sum to the church or the poor. Restitution is the fruit of forgiveness, not its price, so where full repayment is impossible, confess, do what you can and trust God with the rest. Where contacting the person would harm them or you, as with someone who has been abusive, seek counsel from a pastor or biblical counsellor before acting. And God’s forgiveness does not cancel the law of the land: putting a crime right may mean facing its lawful consequences.

Uncertain wording. “Security” translates a phrase found only here, literally “a placing of the hand”. It may mean a pledge, a loan, or money put into a joint venture; the general sense, something entrusted to another on the strength of a handshake, is clear.
verseByVerse.note: Leviticus 6:1–7 is 5:20–26 in the Hebrew numbering (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — The Fire That Never Goes Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The altar fire must never go out. The law of the burnt offering, now given to the priests, says three times that the fire is to be kept burning (vv. 9, 12, 13). The offering lies on the hearth of the altar all night until morning (v. 9). Each morning the priest, in his linen garments, lifts the ashes to the side of the altar, then changes into other clothes to carry them outside the camp to a clean place (vv. 10–11). Then he lays fresh wood, arranges the burnt offering and burns the fat of the peace offerings (v. 12). Night and day, on feast days and ordinary days, the altar never went cold.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Fire Nobody Was Allowed to Let Die

The altar never goes cold, and the ashes are carried out in working clothes.
verseByVerse.examples: Somebody shovelled out yesterday's fire every morning. Unseen, repeated work in a church is service to God, and he sees it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the burnt offering. The burnt offering shall be on the hearth on the altar all night until the morning, and the fire of the altar shall be kept burning on it. And the priest shall put on his linen garment and put his linen undergarment on his body, and he shall take up the ashes to which the fire has reduced the burnt offering on the altar and put them beside the altar. Then he shall take off his garments and put on other garments and carry the ashes outside the camp to a clean place. The fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it; it shall not go out. The priest shall burn wood on it every morning, and he shall arrange the burnt offering on it and shall burn on it the fat of the peace offerings. Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fire on the altar of burnt offering must be kept burning day and night and never allowed to go out, and even its ashes are to be removed with care.

It shall not go out. One instruction is repeated three times in five verses (vv. 9, 12, 13). In chapter 9 fire will come from before the LORD onto this altar (9:24), and from then on Israel’s task is to keep it alight: through every festival and every ordinary Tuesday, the altar never goes cold.

On the hearth on the altar all night. The evening lamb, one of the two offered “day by day regularly” (Exodus 29:38–39), burned slowly through the night, so that there was always an offering on the altar. Israel slept under the smoke of a sacrifice.

He shall take up the ashes. The mechanics are given with odd care. The priest removes the ashes in his linen garments, then changes into other clothes to carry them outside the camp. The holy garments are for the altar; the ash run is done in working clothes. Yet even the ashes go to “a clean place”, not a rubbish heap: what has been given to God is treated with respect to the end.

Unseen work. Somebody had to shovel out yesterday’s fire before today’s offering, every morning, unseen by the nation. Most of what keeps worship going has always looked like that: the person who unlocks the building, sets out the chairs and washes the cups. God wrote that job into his law.

The fire that need burn no longer. The fire never went out because Israel never stopped sinning and the offerings were never finished. Christ “offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins” and then “sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12). What the fire said day and night, that the way to God was open, his finished offering says for ever, and “he always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near through him (Hebrews 7:25). The altar is cold now; the access is not.

A fair application. Christians have long taken the fire that never went out as a picture of prayer that does not stop (1 Thessalonians 5:17) and of zeal kept burning: “Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit” (Romans 12:11). That is an application, not the text’s own meaning, but a fair one. Fires are rarely lost in a moment; they go out when nobody brings wood in the morning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-23 — The Priests and the Grain Offering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who serve at the altar remain worshippers who must bring offerings of their own. The people’s grain offering is shared: a handful is burned as a memorial, and the rest is eaten by the priests, unleavened, in the court of the tent, as their most holy portion (vv. 14–18). But from the day of his anointing the high priest brings his own grain offering, a tenth of an ephah of flour, half in the morning and half in the evening, cooked with oil on a griddle (vv. 19–22). It is wholly burned, for no priest may eat his own grain offering (v. 23). The man who lives on the gifts of others gives one that feeds nobody.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priest Is Also a Worshipper

The men fed by the offerings bring one that feeds nobody.
verseByVerse.examples: No office, however holy, exempts a man from needing grace, and those who lead God's people bring their own need to him first.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the law of the grain offering. The sons of Aaron shall offer it before the LORD in front of the altar. And one shall take from it a handful of the fine flour of the grain offering and its oil and all the frankincense that is on the grain offering and burn this as its memorial portion on the altar, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And the rest of it Aaron and his sons shall eat. It shall be eaten unleavened in a holy place. In the court of the tent of meeting they shall eat it. It shall not be baked with leaven. I have given it as their portion of my food offerings. It is a thing most holy, like the sin offering and the guilt offering. Every male among the children of Aaron may eat of it, as decreed forever throughout your generations, from the LORD's food offerings. Whatever touches them shall become holy." The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "This is the offering that Aaron and his sons shall offer to the LORD on the day when he is anointed: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a regular grain offering, half of it in the morning and half in the evening. It shall be made with oil on a griddle. You shall bring it well mixed, in baked pieces like a grain offering, and offer it for a pleasing aroma to the LORD. The priest from among Aaron's sons, who is anointed to succeed him, shall offer it to the LORD as decreed forever. The whole of it shall be burned. Every grain offering of a priest shall be wholly burned. It shall not be eaten."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests eat the people’s grain offering as a most holy portion in the sanctuary court, but the high priest’s own daily grain offering is burned entire, for no priest may feed on his own offering.

A thing most holy. The priests’ share of the grain offering counts as their most sacred food. It is to be eaten unleavened, in the court of the tent: even their meal is an act of worship in God’s presence. God calls the offerings “my food offerings” and gives part of them to the priests (v. 17). They live at his table.

A regular grain offering. Then a striking provision. From the day of his anointing the high priest brings his own flour, morning and evening, and unlike the people’s grain offering it is wholly burned. The men who live off the offerings of others bring one that feeds nobody, every day of their lives. Nothing about the priesthood exempts a priest from being a worshipper, and those who lead God’s people today still need to come to him as needy worshippers, not only as professionals.

A better High Priest. Hebrews draws the contrast: Israel’s high priests offered daily, first for their own sins, but Jesus has no need to, since he offered up himself once for all (Hebrews 7:27). Nothing he does at the Father’s right hand is for himself; all of it is for us.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are uncertain. “Whatever touches them shall become holy” (v. 18, and again in v. 27) can also be translated “whoever touches them must be holy”, that is, only those consecrated may handle them. Haggai 2:12 shows that holy meat carried in a garment did not make other food holy, which some take to favour the second reading; the washing and breaking of vessels in vv. 27–28 favours the first. Either way, holy things were not to be handled casually. And “on the day when he is anointed” (v. 20) sits awkwardly with an offering made every morning and evening. It probably means “from the day of his anointing” onwards, as Jewish tradition took it; some think it was an offering for the day of ordination itself, made by each new high priest.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sin offering is most holy and must be handled with care. It is killed where the burnt offering is killed, and the priest who offers it eats it in the court of the tent (vv. 24–26). Its holiness reaches whatever it touches: a garment splashed with its blood must be washed in a holy place, an earthenware pot it was boiled in must be broken, and a bronze one scoured and rinsed (vv. 27–28). Every male priest may eat of it (v. 29). But when the blood of a sin offering has been carried into the Holy Place to make atonement, none of it may be eaten; it is burned (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology:
Holiness Running the Other Way

Whatever touches the sin offering is made holy.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: contact with this offering spread holiness. Now: Christ, touched by sinners, made them clean instead of being made unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the sin offering. In the place where the burnt offering is killed shall the sin offering be killed before the LORD; it is most holy. The priest who offers it for sin shall eat it. In a holy place it shall be eaten, in the court of the tent of meeting. Whatever touches its flesh shall be holy, and when any of its blood is splashed on a garment, you shall wash that on which it was splashed in a holy place. And the earthenware vessel in which it is boiled shall be broken. But if it is boiled in a bronze vessel, that shall be scoured and rinsed in water. Every male among the priests may eat of it; it is most holy. But no sin offering shall be eaten from which any blood is brought into the tent of meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place; it shall be burned up with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sin offering is most holy: the priest eats it in the holy place, whatever it touches is marked by its holiness, and if its blood has been taken into the Holy Place it must be burned, not eaten.

The priest who offers it for sin shall eat it. Why should the priest eat the sin offering? Leviticus later gives the reason: it was given to the priests “that you may bear the iniquity of the congregation, to make atonement for them before the LORD” (10:17). Eating it was part of the priest’s work of dealing with sin, not merely his wages.

Whatever touches its flesh shall be holy. The law of the sin offering dwells on how its holiness spreads: a splashed garment washed in a holy place, an earthenware pot broken, a bronze one scoured. In most of Leviticus contact spreads uncleanness: touch a corpse and you are unclean. The sin offering runs the other way. What touches it is marked by its holiness, and the porous pot cannot simply be reused, because something has soaked into it that cannot be scrubbed out (on the wording, see the note on vv. 14–23).

No sin offering shall be eaten. The one exception: any sin offering whose blood is brought into the tent is burned, not eaten. The offerings that go furthest in are the ones nobody shares, for the priest could not eat an offering made for his own sin or the whole people’s (4:3–21). Chapter 16 will show the greatest of them.

The offering we are given to eat. Hebrews builds directly on this law. “We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat”, it says, because the bodies of the animals whose blood was brought into the holy places were burned outside the camp: “So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:10–12). The altar is the cross, not a church table. The sin offering that no Israelite priest could ever eat, Christ gives his people to feed on by faith.

Holiness that heals. In Jesus the direction of v. 27 becomes the pattern of a whole ministry. When the woman with the flow of blood “touched his garment”, her uncleanness did not pass to him; his power went out to her, and “immediately the flow of blood dried up” (Mark 5:27–29).

6.theology:
The perpetual fire. The unceasing flame showed that atonement was always available and that a sinful people always needed it, a need answered once for all in Christ.

Daily devotion. The wood the priest laid on the fire each morning (v. 12) pictures tending the heart's fire, which God kindles and the Spirit keeps alight. "Do not quench the Spirit" (1 Thess 5:19). Older Reformed writers spoke of a daily putting to death of sin and a daily renewing of grace.

Provision for ministers. Those who serve at the altar share in what is offered there.
6.examples:
Then: before dawn the priest removed the night's ashes and laid on fresh wood, guarding the flame God himself had kindled.

Now: we tend devotion daily by the Word, prayer and the Spirit, resting in the finished sacrifice that ended the need for endless offerings, even as our hearts burn within us (Luke 24:32).

keyVerse.quote: Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out.
keyVerse.note: Repeated three times in five verses, this command kept Israel’s altar alight day and night: there was always an offering before God, and the way to him was never closed. The fire burned on because the offerings were never finished. Christ’s single sacrifice is finished, and through his blood the way into God’s presence stays open for good (Hebrews 10:12, 19–20).

6.reflection:
Verses 1–7 call cheating a neighbour “a breach of faith against the LORD”. How does seeing wrongs against people as wrongs against God change how seriously we take them?

Restitution had to be paid “on the day he realizes his guilt”, before the offering. Why do we put off making things right, and what would doing it promptly look like for you?

The altar fire was never allowed to go out, and someone carried out the ashes every morning (vv. 9–13). What unseen daily work keeps your faith and your church going, and how do you regard it?

The high priest brought an offering for himself every day, but Jesus needed none (Hebrews 7:27). What difference does it make to come to God through a priest like that?

7.title: The Portion of the Priests: Order in Holy Things
7.text: <sup>1</sup>"This is the law of the guilt offering. It is most holy.<sup>2</sup>In the place where they kill the burnt offering they shall kill the guilt offering, and its blood shall be thrown against the sides of the altar.<sup>3</sup>And all its fat shall be offered, the fat tail, the fat that covers the entrails,<sup>4</sup>the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins, and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys.<sup>5</sup>The priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering to the LORD; it is a guilt offering.<sup>6</sup>Every male among the priests may eat of it. It shall be eaten in a holy place. It is most holy.<sup>7</sup>The guilt offering is just like the sin offering; there is one law for them. The priest who makes atonement with it shall have it.<sup>8</sup>And the priest who offers any man's burnt offering shall have for himself the skin of the burnt offering that he has offered.<sup>9</sup>And every grain offering baked in the oven and all that is prepared on a pan or a griddle shall belong to the priest who offers it.<sup>10</sup>And every grain offering, mixed with oil or dry, shall be shared equally among all the sons of Aaron.<sup>11</sup>"And this is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings that one may offer to the LORD.<sup>12</sup>If he offers it for a thanksgiving, then he shall offer with the thanksgiving sacrifice unleavened loaves mixed with oil, unleavened wafers smeared with oil, and loaves of fine flour well mixed with oil.<sup>13</sup>With the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving he shall bring his offering with loaves of leavened bread.<sup>14</sup>And from it he shall offer one loaf from each offering, as a gift to the LORD. He shall not leave any of it until the morning.<sup>16</sup>But if the sacrifice of his offering is a vow offering or a freewill offering, it shall be eaten on the day that he offers his sacrifice, and on the next day what remains of it shall be eaten.<sup>17</sup>But what remains of the flesh of the sacrifice on the third day shall be burned up with fire.<sup>18</sup>If any of the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offering is eaten on the third day, he who offers it shall not be accepted, neither shall it be credited to him. It is tainted, and he who eats of it shall bear his iniquity.<sup>19</sup>"Flesh that touches any unclean thing shall not be eaten. It shall be burned up with fire. All who are clean may eat flesh,<sup>20</sup>but the person who eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of the LORD's peace offerings while an uncleanness is on him, that person shall be cut off from his people.<sup>21</sup>And if anyone touches an unclean thing, whether human uncleanness or an unclean beast or any unclean detestable creature, and then eats some flesh from the sacrifice of the LORD's peace offerings, that person shall be cut off from his people."<sup>22</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>23</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, You shall eat no fat, of ox or sheep or goat.<sup>24</sup>The fat of an animal that dies of itself and the fat of one that is torn by beasts may be put to any other use, but on no account shall you eat it.<sup>25</sup>For every person who eats of the fat of an animal of which a food offering may be made to the LORD shall be cut off from his people.<sup>26</sup>Moreover, you shall eat no blood whatever, whether of fowl or of animal, in any of your dwelling places.<sup>27</sup>Whoever eats any blood, that person shall be cut off from his people."<sup>28</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>29</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, Whoever offers the sacrifice of his peace offerings to the LORD shall bring his offering to the LORD from the sacrifice of his peace offerings.<sup>30</sup>His own hands shall bring the LORD's food offerings. He shall bring the fat with the breast, that the breast may be waved as a wave offering before the LORD.<sup>31</sup>The priest shall burn the fat on the altar, but the breast shall be for Aaron and his sons.<sup>32</sup>And the right thigh you shall give to the priest as a contribution from the sacrifice of your peace offerings.<sup>33</sup>Whoever among the sons of Aaron offers the blood of the peace offerings and the fat shall have the right thigh for a portion.<sup>34</sup>For the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed I have taken from the people of Israel, out of the sacrifices of their peace offerings, and have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons, as a perpetual due from the people of Israel.<sup>35</sup>This is the portion of Aaron and of his sons from the LORD's food offerings, from the day they were presented to serve as priests of the LORD.<sup>36</sup>The LORD commanded this to be given them by the people of Israel, from the day that he anointed them. It is a perpetual due throughout their generations."<sup>37</sup>This is the law of the burnt offering, of the grain offering, of the sin offering, of the guilt offering, of the ordination offering, and of the peace offering,<sup>38</sup>which the LORD commanded Moses on Mount Sinai, on the day that he commanded the people of Israel to bring their offerings to the LORD, in the wilderness of Sinai.
7.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 7 completes the priests’ handbook begun at 6:8. It gives the law of the guilt offering, then the book’s fullest instructions for the peace offering, the meal Israel shared in God’s presence, and it closes with a summary of all the offerings commanded at Sinai (vv. 37–38).

The message. God gives every part of his worship its proper place: what is his alone, what belongs to the priests, and what the worshipper may eat with joy. At the centre stands the peace offering, a feast of fellowship with God that must be eaten fresh, shared generously and approached clean. Around it run two lines no one may cross: the fat and the blood belong to God.

Why it was said. The priests would have no land of their own, so they needed to know what they could live on. Worshippers needed to know how to keep a feast in the presence of the holy God without treating it as an ordinary meal (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The guilt offering is most holy and is handled like the sin offering; its meat goes to the priest who makes atonement, as do the hide of a burnt offering and the cooked grain offerings (vv. 1–10). The peace offering comes in three kinds, thanksgiving, vow and freewill; the thanksgiving must be eaten the same day, and no one unclean may eat (vv. 11–21). No fat and no blood may be eaten at all (vv. 22–27). The worshipper brings God’s portion with his own hands; the breast is waved and given to the priests, and the right thigh to the priest who offers the blood (vv. 28–36). A summary closes the whole law of the offerings (vv. 37–38).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by contrast. Christ “is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14), “making peace by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20), so through him we “continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God” (Hebrews 13:15). The blood that no Israelite might drink, Jesus told his hearers to drink (John 6:53), because his life is given to be ours. And where Aaron’s sons stood daily offering the same sacrifices, Christ offered one and “sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12).

For us. Thanksgiving to God is not meant to stay private: like the peace offering, it is to be spoken aloud and shared at a table with others. Come to the Lord’s Table cleansed by confession, not kept away by fear. And gladly support those who serve the gospel, as Israel fed its priests.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-10 — The Guilt Offering and the Priests' Portions
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The guilt offering is most holy, and the priests who serve the altar are fed from it. It is killed where the burnt offering is killed, its blood thrown against the sides of the altar and its fat burned (vv. 1–5). Its meat is eaten by the priests in a holy place, because it follows the same law as the sin offering: the priest who makes atonement with it receives it (vv. 6–7). Then the priests’ other portions are settled: the hide of a burnt offering goes to the priest who offered it, grain offerings cooked in oven, pan or griddle to the priest who presents them, and the rest are shared equally among Aaron’s sons (vv. 8–10).
verseByVerse.theology:
Income Specified in Law

The priests' living is written into the offerings themselves.
verseByVerse.examples: A tribe with no land lived by written provision, and churches still owe a fair living to those who give their lives to teaching them.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the law of the guilt offering. It is most holy. In the place where they kill the burnt offering they shall kill the guilt offering, and its blood shall be thrown against the sides of the altar. And all its fat shall be offered, the fat tail, the fat that covers the entrails, the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins, and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys. The priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering to the LORD; it is a guilt offering. Every male among the priests may eat of it. It shall be eaten in a holy place. It is most holy. The guilt offering is just like the sin offering; there is one law for them. The priest who makes atonement with it shall have it. And the priest who offers any man's burnt offering shall have for himself the skin of the burnt offering that he has offered. And every grain offering baked in the oven and all that is prepared on a pan or a griddle shall belong to the priest who offers it. And every grain offering, mixed with oil or dry, shall be shared equally among all the sons of Aaron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The guilt offering is most holy and is handled like the sin offering, and its meat, like the hide of a burnt offering and the grain offerings, is given to the priests who serve at the altar.

This is the law of the guilt offering. Chapter 5 told the worshipper what to bring; now the priest learns what to do with it. Its blood is thrown against the sides of the altar, and its fat is burned, including the fat tail, the broad tail of the region’s sheep, which was prized as the richest part (compare 3:9).

The guilt offering is just like the sin offering. One law covers both: the priest who makes atonement with it eats it (v. 7), in a holy place. As with the sin offering, that eating belonged to the priest’s work of dealing with guilt (10:17), not merely to his wages.

The priests’ income. A short paragraph settles who gets what: the hide to the officiating priest, the cooked grain offerings to the one who presents them, the dry ones shared among Aaron’s sons. It reads like accountancy, and it does something important. Levi received no farmland, and the priests’ whole income was fixed by law rather than left to whoever turned up. Paul appeals to the arrangement when he argues that gospel workers should be supported: “Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple… In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:13–14).

What it does not mean. Not that Christian ministers are priests who offer sacrifices. Paul uses the arrangement only as a pattern for supporting those who preach; in Christ every believer belongs to “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), and ministers are elders, not a priestly caste.

The offering for guilt. The ram of the guilt offering died for one man’s debt. Isaiah saw a Servant whose soul would make “an offering for guilt” and who would “make many to be accounted righteous” (Isaiah 53:10–11). What the priest handled on one man’s behalf, Christ accomplished for a multitude (see the note on 5:14–19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11-21 — The Peace Offering: Thanksgiving and Vows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The peace offering is a feast with God, to be eaten fresh, shared and kept clean. Brought for thanksgiving, it comes with unleavened loaves and wafers and with leavened bread, one of each going to the priest (vv. 11–14), and all its meat must be eaten that same day (v. 15). A vow or freewill offering may be eaten over two days, but whatever is left on the third day must be burned; meat eaten then is “tainted”, and the offering is not accepted (vv. 16–18). Meat that touches anything unclean is burned, and anyone who eats while unclean is cut off from his people (vv. 19–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
Gratitude That Cannot Be Stored

The thanksgiving offering is eaten the same day, and nothing may be kept to the third.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: gratitude had to be spent at once, in company. Now: thanks for what God has done is still meant to be told and shared with others.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings that one may offer to the LORD. If he offers it for a thanksgiving, then he shall offer with the thanksgiving sacrifice unleavened loaves mixed with oil, unleavened wafers smeared with oil, and loaves of fine flour well mixed with oil. With the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving he shall bring his offering with loaves of leavened bread. And from it he shall offer one loaf from each offering, as a gift to the LORD. It shall belong to the priest who throws the blood of the peace offerings. And the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving shall be eaten on the day of his offering. He shall not leave any of it until the morning. But if the sacrifice of his offering is a vow offering or a freewill offering, it shall be eaten on the day that he offers his sacrifice, and on the next day what remains of it shall be eaten. But what remains of the flesh of the sacrifice on the third day shall be burned up with fire. If any of the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offering is eaten on the third day, he who offers it shall not be accepted, neither shall it be credited to him. It is tainted, and he who eats of it shall bear his iniquity. "Flesh that touches any unclean thing shall not be eaten. It shall be burned up with fire. All who are clean may eat flesh, but the person who eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of the LORD's peace offerings while an uncleanness is on him, that person shall be cut off from his people. And if anyone touches an unclean thing, whether human uncleanness or an unclean beast or any unclean detestable creature, and then eats some flesh from the sacrifice of the LORD's peace offerings, that person shall be cut off from his people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The peace offering is a feast with God, brought in thanksgiving, to keep a vow or freely; its meat must be eaten fresh and shared, and no one unclean may eat it.

Thanksgiving, vow and freewill. The distinctions matter. A thanksgiving offering is brought for something God has done; a vow offering keeps a promise made to God, often in trouble; a freewill offering is brought for no stated reason at all, simply out of love.

Loaves of leavened bread. Leaven was banned from anything burned on the altar (2:11), but these leavened loaves were eaten at the meal, not burned. One loaf of each kind went to the priest (v. 14). The thanksgiving feast was a real meal, with ordinary bread on the table.

He shall not leave any of it until the morning. Consider what the one-day rule does to a family. A whole animal must be eaten before morning, far more than most households can manage. So the thanksgiving offering in effect forced a party: neighbours are called in, and they will want to know what is being celebrated. Gratitude for what God had done could not be kept private or stored. It had to be spent at once, in company, on people. The psalmist knew it: “I will offer to you the sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD. I will pay my vows to the LORD in the presence of all his people” (Psalm 116:17–18).

The sacrifice of praise. The peace offering pictured fellowship with God, and Christ has made that peace “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20). So the thanksgiving offering has not ended; it has changed form: “Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name” (Hebrews 13:15).

Closed to the unclean. The meal is closed to anyone who is unclean (vv. 20–21). Paul brings the same concern to the Lord’s Table: “Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:27). That warning, like this one, sends us to the cleansing God provides, not away from his table.

What does “cut off from his people” mean? Interpreters differ: execution by the community, exclusion from the covenant people, or God’s own judgment, an early death or a family line that dies out. The likeliest reading is that God himself would cut the person off; where the law means execution, it says so plainly.

Uncertain wording. “Tainted” (v. 18) translates a rare word used for meat that has become foul or unfit (compare 19:7; Isaiah 65:4). Whether it means meat that has literally begun to spoil or meat that has become ritually unacceptable is not certain; either way, a sacrifice eaten late is not accepted. It is also unclear whether “neither shall it be credited to him” means the offering is cancelled after the event, or simply that it never did him any good.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two things God keeps for himself: the fat and the blood. Israel must eat no fat of ox, sheep or goat; the fat of an animal that died naturally or was killed by wild beasts may be put to other uses, but never eaten (vv. 22–24). Whoever eats the fat of an animal fit for the altar is cut off from his people (v. 25). And no blood at all may be eaten, of bird or beast, in any of their homes (vv. 26–27). The fat was the choicest part, and the blood carried the life (17:11). Both belong to the Giver, and these rules held not only at the altar but at every Israelite meal.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Heaviest Penalty in the Dietary Law

Eating fat or blood cuts a person off from his people.
verseByVerse.examples: The reason for the ban waits until 17:11, but its seriousness was plain to everyone at once: life belongs to God.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, You shall eat no fat, of ox or sheep or goat. The fat of an animal that dies of itself and the fat of one that is torn by beasts may be put to any other use, but on no account shall you eat it. For every person who eats of the fat of an animal of which a food offering may be made to the LORD shall be cut off from his people. Moreover, you shall eat no blood whatever, whether of fowl or of animal, in any of your dwelling places. Whoever eats any blood, that person shall be cut off from his people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must never eat the fat of sacrificial animals or any blood at all, because the best part and the life belong to God.

You shall eat no fat. “All fat is the LORD’s” (3:16). The fat around the organs, the richest part of the animal, was reserved for the altar, and the ban covers ox, sheep and goat, the animals that could be offered. Even the fat of an animal that died of itself or was torn by beasts, which could never go on the altar, might be put to other uses but never eaten. God’s claim on the best did not lapse when no sacrifice was involved.

The heaviest penalty. The reason for the blood is held back until 17:11, “the life of the flesh is in the blood”, but the severity is clear already: of all the food rules in this book, fat and blood carry the heaviest penalty. When the first Christian council released Gentile converts from circumcision and the food laws, this is one of the four things they kept: “that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood” (Acts 15:29).

The blood we are told to drink. To ears trained by this law, nothing Jesus said could have sounded more shocking: “unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you” (John 6:53). Many of his disciples “turned back and no longer walked with him” (John 6:66). Blood was withheld because the life was in it and belonged to God. Jesus offers his own life, given in death, to be ours. He did not mean a literal eating: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:63). We receive him by faith.

Must Christians still avoid eating blood? The ban is older than Israel (Genesis 9:4), and the Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to keep it so that they could share a table with Jewish Christians (Acts 15:20, 29). Yet the New Testament declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19; 1 Timothy 4:4). So most Christians hold that reverence for the life God gives remains, while meat not fully drained is not sin. And a blood transfusion is not eating at all: it gives life rather than taking it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The worshipper brings God’s portion with his own hands, and the priests receive theirs as God’s gift. The one who offers a peace offering brings the fat and the breast himself; the fat is burned, the breast is waved before the LORD and given to Aaron and his sons, and the right thigh goes to the priest who offers the blood (vv. 28–33). These are the priests’ perpetual due, granted by God from the day of their anointing (vv. 34–36). A summary closes the whole law: burnt, grain, sin, guilt, ordination and peace offerings, all commanded on Mount Sinai (vv. 37–38). The ordination itself comes next.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Remarkable Provision, and a Provisional One

Seven chapters describe a single system for approaching God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the priests stood daily, offering again. Now: Christ has offered one sacrifice and sat down.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, Whoever offers the sacrifice of his peace offerings to the LORD shall bring his offering to the LORD from the sacrifice of his peace offerings. His own hands shall bring the LORD's food offerings. He shall bring the fat with the breast, that the breast may be waved as a wave offering before the LORD. The priest shall burn the fat on the altar, but the breast shall be for Aaron and his sons. And the right thigh you shall give to the priest as a contribution from the sacrifice of your peace offerings. Whoever among the sons of Aaron offers the blood of the peace offerings and the fat shall have the right thigh for a portion. For the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed I have taken from the people of Israel, out of the sacrifices of their peace offerings, and have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons, as a perpetual due from the people of Israel. This is the portion of Aaron and of his sons from the LORD's food offerings, from the day they were presented to serve as priests of the LORD. The LORD commanded this to be given them by the people of Israel, from the day that he anointed them. It is a perpetual due throughout their generations." This is the law of the burnt offering, of the grain offering, of the sin offering, of the guilt offering, of the ordination offering, and of the peace offering, which the LORD commanded Moses on Mount Sinai, on the day that he commanded the people of Israel to bring their offerings to the LORD, in the wilderness of Sinai.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The worshipper brings God’s portion with his own hands, the breast and right thigh go to the priests as their lasting share, and a summary closes the whole law of the offerings given at Sinai.

His own hands shall bring. The worshipper does not hand his offering over for others to deal with; he carries the LORD’s portions himself. The breast is waved before the LORD and then given to the priests, and the right thigh goes to the priest who offers the blood. The priests’ portion comes to them from God’s hand: “I have taken from the people of Israel… and have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons” (v. 34).

What it does not mean. Not that the priests could help themselves. In Eli’s day his sons demanded their meat before the fat was even burned, and took it by force if refused, so that “the men treated the offering of the LORD with contempt” (1 Samuel 2:17). Those who serve God’s people receive what is given; they do not seize it.

The system as a whole. Stand back before the narrative resumes. Israel now has a way to approach God for devotion, for gratitude, for guilt known and unknown, for damage that needed repaying, and for ordinary fellowship, scaled from a bull to a bag of flour so that nobody was priced out. It is a remarkable provision, and, apart from the break of the exile, it ran for well over a thousand years, until the temple fell in AD 70.

Provisional, not primitive. The New Testament’s verdict is not that the system was primitive but that it was provisional: “every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:11–12). The detail that carries the argument is the sitting. No chair stood among the tabernacle’s furniture, because the work was never finished. He sat down.

Uncertain wording. The exact gesture of the “wave offering” is not known. The older view is that the priest moved the portion to and fro before the altar; many now think it was lifted up before the LORD, an “elevation offering”. Either way it presented to God what he then gave to the priests. The “contribution” of the thigh (older versions, “heave offering”) means a portion set apart. And the part itself is uncertain: “thigh” is likely, though older translations have “shoulder”.

7.theology:
The order of worship. God's careful regulation of holy things reflects that he is "not a God of confusion but of peace" (1 Cor 14:33).

The sanctity of blood. The life is in the blood, and the blood belongs to God: the foundation of atonement, fulfilled in the precious blood of Christ.

The sacrifice of thanksgiving. The todah (thanksgiving) offering becomes, in Christ, the continual sacrifice of praise (Heb 13:15).
7.examples:
Then: the reconciled Israelite shared a thanksgiving feast the same day, and the priests received their portion.

Now: we offer the sacrifice of praise through Christ, support those who serve God's people, and marvel that the blood once forbidden as food is now, in Christ, the cup of salvation, received in bread and wine at his table.

keyVerse.quote: And the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving shall be eaten on the day of his offering. He shall not leave any of it until the morning.
keyVerse.note: This small rule turned gratitude into a feast: an animal eaten in a day had to be shared, and the neighbours would hear why. Thanksgiving to God was meant to be spent at once, in company. Through Christ, who made peace by his blood, we still “offer up a sacrifice of praise to God” (Hebrews 13:15).

7.reflection:
The thanksgiving offering had to be eaten on the day it was offered, so it became a feast with others (v. 15). How could your thankfulness to God become more spoken and more shared?

No one unclean could eat the peace offering (vv. 19–21). How should Paul’s warning about the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:27–28) lead us to Christ’s cleansing rather than keep us away from the table?

The fat and the blood belonged to God alone (vv. 22–27). What might it mean for you to give God the best, and to treat every life as his?

Israel’s priests stood daily and their work was never done, but Christ “sat down” (Hebrews 10:12). Where do you still live as if your standing with God depended on repeated effort?

8.title: The Ordination of Aaron: Consecrated by Blood and Oil
8.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Take Aaron and his sons with him, and the garments and the anointing oil and the bull of the sin offering and the two rams and the basket of unleavened bread.<sup>3</sup>And assemble all the congregation at the entrance of the tent of meeting."<sup>4</sup>And Moses did as the LORD commanded him, and the congregation was assembled at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>5</sup>And Moses said to the congregation, "This is the thing that the LORD has commanded to be done."<sup>6</sup>And Moses brought Aaron and his sons and washed them with water.<sup>7</sup>And he put the coat on him and tied the sash around his waist and clothed him with the robe and put the ephod on him and tied the skillfully woven band of the ephod around him, binding it to him with the band.<sup>8</sup>And he placed the breastpiece on him, and in the breastpiece he put the Urim and the Thummim.<sup>9</sup>And he set the turban on his head, and on the turban, in front, he set the golden plate, the holy crown, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>10</sup>Then Moses took the anointing oil and anointed the tabernacle and all that was in it, and consecrated them.<sup>11</sup>And he sprinkled some of it on the altar seven times, and anointed the altar and all its utensils and the basin and its stand, to consecrate them.<sup>12</sup>And he poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron's head and anointed him to consecrate him.<sup>13</sup>And Moses brought Aaron's sons and clothed them with coats and tied sashes around their waists and bound caps on them, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>14</sup>Then he brought the bull of the sin offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the bull of the sin offering.<sup>15</sup>And he killed it, and Moses took the blood, and with his finger put it on the horns of the altar around it and purified the altar and poured out the blood at the base of the altar and consecrated it to make atonement for it.<sup>16</sup>And he took all the fat that was on the entrails and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with their fat, and Moses burned them on the altar.<sup>17</sup>But the bull and its skin and its flesh and its dung he burned up with fire outside the camp, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>18</sup>Then he presented the ram of the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram.<sup>19</sup>And he killed it, and Moses threw the blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>20</sup>He cut the ram into pieces, and Moses burned the head and the pieces and the fat.<sup>21</sup>He washed the entrails and the legs with water, and Moses burned the whole ram on the altar. It was a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering for the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>22</sup>Then he presented the other ram, the ram of ordination, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram.<sup>23</sup>And he killed it, and Moses took some of its blood and put it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot.<sup>24</sup>Then he presented Aaron's sons, and Moses put some of the blood on the lobes of their right ears and on the thumbs of their right hands and on the big toes of their right feet. And Moses threw the blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>25</sup>Then he took the fat and the fat tail and all the fat that was on the entrails and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with their fat and the right thigh,<sup>26</sup>and out of the basket of unleavened bread that was before the LORD he took one unleavened loaf and one loaf of bread with oil and one wafer and placed them on the pieces of fat and on the right thigh.<sup>27</sup>And he put all these in the hands of Aaron and in the hands of his sons and waved them as a wave offering before the LORD.<sup>28</sup>Then Moses took them from their hands and burned them on the altar with the burnt offering. This was an ordination offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>29</sup>And Moses took the breast and waved it for a wave offering before the LORD. It was Moses' portion of the ram of ordination, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>30</sup>Then Moses took some of the anointing oil and of the blood that was on the altar and sprinkled it on Aaron and his garments, and also on his sons and his sons' garments.
