So he consecrated Aaron and his garments, and his sons and his sons' garments with him.<sup>31</sup>And Moses said to Aaron and his sons, "Boil the flesh at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and there eat it and the bread that is in the basket of ordination offerings, as I commanded, saying, 'Aaron and his sons shall eat it.'<sup>32</sup>And what remains of the flesh and the bread you shall burn up with fire.<sup>33</sup>And you shall not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days, until the days of your ordination are completed, for it will take seven days to ordain you.<sup>34</sup>As has been done today, the LORD has commanded to be done to make atonement for you.<sup>35</sup>At the entrance of the tent of meeting you shall remain day and night for seven days, performing what the LORD has charged, so that you do not die, for so I have been commanded."<sup>36</sup>And Aaron and his sons did all the things that the LORD commanded by Moses.
8.overview:
Where we are. The instructions on the offerings now give way to story. Chapters 8–10 tell of the ordination of Aaron and his sons, their first day of service and the disaster that follows. Chapter 8 carries out, step by step, the plan God gave in Exodus 29, with Moses acting as priest to install the priests.

The message. No one can make himself a priest. God chooses, washes, clothes, anoints and consecrates with blood the men who will stand between him and his people, and he does it in public, exactly as he commanded. Every step is done to Aaron by another, and the sinner chosen to serve must first be atoned for himself.

Why it was said. Israel had lately watched Aaron make the golden calf (Exodus 32). They needed to see that his priesthood rested not on his merit or his own claim but on God’s call and on sacrifice, done openly before the whole congregation (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The congregation gathers at the tent (vv. 1–5). Aaron and his sons are washed, Aaron is dressed in the high priest’s garments (vv. 6–9), the tabernacle and then Aaron are anointed, and his sons are clothed (vv. 10–13). A bull is offered as a sin offering and a ram as a burnt offering, the priests laying their hands on both (vv. 14–21). Then the ram of ordination: its blood on right ear, thumb and toe, the portions placed in the priests’ hands and waved, and oil and blood sprinkled on the men and their garments (vv. 22–30). For seven days they stay at the door of the tent, and they do all that the LORD commanded (vv. 31–36).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by contrast. Christ too “did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by him” (Hebrews 5:5), and “God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38). But Aaron needed a sin offering before he could serve, while Jesus is “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26). The law appointed weak men, but God’s oath “appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever” (Hebrews 7:28). He consecrated himself for us (John 17:19), and by his blood he has made his people “a kingdom, priests to his God and Father” (Revelation 1:6).

For us. Every Christian has been “washed” and “sanctified” in the name of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 6:11), clothed in a righteousness not his own. So the ears, hands and feet the blood has claimed belong to God: offer them to him. And let those who lead the church be called and recognised, never self-appointed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s priests are prepared in public, and everything is done to them. The LORD tells Moses to bring Aaron, his sons, the garments, the oil and the offerings, and to gather the whole congregation at the entrance of the tent (vv. 1–5). Moses washes Aaron and his sons with water, then dresses Aaron piece by piece: coat, sash, robe, ephod, breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim, turban and golden plate (vv. 6–9). He anoints the tabernacle and everything in it, sprinkles the altar seven times and pours oil on Aaron’s head; then he clothes Aaron’s sons (vv. 10–13). Washed, clothed and anointed, Aaron brings nothing but himself.
verseByVerse.theology:
Anointed

Aaron is washed, robed and anointed by another, in front of everyone.
verseByVerse.examples: The priesthood was installed in public, before the people it would serve. Leaders in the church, too, are called and recognised openly, not self-appointed.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Take Aaron and his sons with him, and the garments and the anointing oil and the bull of the sin offering and the two rams and the basket of unleavened bread. And assemble all the congregation at the entrance of the tent of meeting." And Moses did as the LORD commanded him, and the congregation was assembled at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And Moses said to the congregation, "This is the thing that the LORD has commanded to be done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Moses to ordain Aaron and his sons before the whole congregation, because Israel’s priests are appointed by God’s command, not by themselves.

Take Aaron and his sons. Seven chapters of instruction end and the story resumes. The design given in Exodus 29 is now carried out, and Moses, who was not himself a priest by office, does the priest’s work: the mediator of the covenant installs the mediators of worship. A psalm can even count him among them: “Moses and Aaron were among his priests” (Psalm 99:6).

Assemble all the congregation. The first thing the text insists on is the audience. The whole nation is called to watch men become priests. Israel needs to see who has been appointed, by whose authority and at what cost, because a priesthood that installs itself is answerable to nobody. The New Testament says the same of the same office: “no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was” (Hebrews 5:4).

This is the thing that the LORD has commanded. Moses grounds the whole ceremony in God’s word before anything is done. Nothing in it is his own invention, and the rest of the chapter keeps reminding us that each step was done “as the LORD commanded Moses”.

Called, not self-appointed. The principle reaches the church. Those who lead God’s people should be called and recognised, tested and publicly set apart (1 Timothy 3:10; Acts 6:3–6), not self-appointed and unaccountable.

Where Christians differ. Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold that the church still has a priesthood, ordained by a sacrament to offer the sacrifice of the Mass, and they have read Aaron’s ordination as one of its patterns. Most Protestants hold that Aaron’s priesthood is fulfilled in Christ, the one High Priest, and that all believers now share a priesthood of praise and service (1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:6).

This commentary’s view. Every believer is a priest; ministers are elders, not priests, and ordination is the church’s recognition and commissioning, not a sacrament. Christ’s sacrifice is complete and is never repeated.
verseByVerse.note: Moses follows the instructions of Exodus 29 point by point.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses brought Aaron and his sons and washed them with water. And he put the coat on him and tied the sash around his waist and clothed him with the robe and put the ephod on him and tied the skillfully woven band of the ephod around him, binding it to him with the band. And he placed the breastpiece on him, and in the breastpiece he put the Urim and the Thummim. And he set the turban on his head, and on the turban, in front, he set the golden plate, the holy crown, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses washes Aaron and his sons and dresses Aaron in the high priest’s garments, so that he comes before God cleansed and clothed in what God has provided.

Washed them with water. Washing comes before a single garment goes on. Whatever else ordination is, it begins with a man being cleaned by somebody else.

He put the coat on him. Then Aaron is dressed, piece by piece, in clothes he did not make or choose: coat, sash, robe, ephod, breastpiece, turban. He is clothed in what God provided. The prophets later used the picture of a sinner given clean clothes: when Joshua the high priest stood in filthy garments, the LORD said, “I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments” (Zechariah 3:4).

The breastpiece. Exodus explains that Aaron “shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place” (Exodus 28:29). The high priest carried the tribes before God on his heart. Our High Priest carries his people the same way, for “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

The golden plate, the holy crown. Exodus tells us what was engraved on the golden plate: ‘Holy to the LORD’ (Exodus 28:36). Aaron wore those words on his forehead, where everyone could read them and he could not. It was there so that the people’s gifts would be “accepted before the LORD” (Exodus 28:38). A man was declared holy by an inscription he could never see for himself, and the holiness he wore covered the imperfect gifts of others. Our offerings too are “acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 2:5), not through their own quality.

Uncertain wording. The Urim and Thummim were most likely sacred lots kept in the breastpiece, by which the high priest asked God for a yes or a no (Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 14:41). What they looked like and how they worked are not known, and even the meaning of the names is uncertain (perhaps “lights and perfections”). They disappear after the early monarchy; God now guides his people through his completed word.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses took the anointing oil and anointed the tabernacle and all that was in it, and consecrated them. And he sprinkled some of it on the altar seven times, and anointed the altar and all its utensils and the basin and its stand, to consecrate them. And he poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron's head and anointed him to consecrate him. And Moses brought Aaron's sons and clothed them with coats and tied sashes around their waists and bound caps on them, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses anoints the tabernacle and its furnishings, pours oil on Aaron’s head to consecrate him, and then clothes Aaron’s sons.

Anointed the tabernacle. The oil touches objects first: the tabernacle, the altar seven times, the basin. Only then is it poured on Aaron. The dwelling and its servants are consecrated together, set apart for God’s use.

Poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron’s head. The furnishings are anointed; Aaron’s head has the oil poured on it. A psalm pictures the scene: “It is like the precious oil on the head, running down on the beard, on the beard of Aaron, running down on the collar of his robes!” (Psalm 133:2).

Anointed him to consecrate him. The Hebrew for “anointed one” is mashiach, messiah. Priests, kings and prophets were anointed, and each anointing pointed ahead to the one man who would hold all three offices at once. Jesus was anointed not with oil but with the Spirit: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Luke 4:18; compare Acts 10:38). Many Christians have seen Psalm 133 come true in him: the Spirit poured on the Head runs down to his whole body, so that John can tell ordinary believers, “you have been anointed by the Holy One” (1 John 2:20).

Clothed them with coats. Then Aaron’s sons are clothed. The office is not his alone and does not end with him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-21 — The Sin Offering and Burnt Offering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the new priests serve anyone else, sacrifices must be made for them. Aaron and his sons lay their hands on a bull for a sin offering; Moses puts its blood on the horns of the altar to purify it, pours out the rest at its base and burns the fat, and the rest of the bull is burned outside the camp (vv. 14–17). Then they lay their hands on a ram for a burnt offering, and Moses burns the whole of it on the altar, “a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma” to the LORD (vv. 18–21). Guilt is dealt with first, and then the priests are given wholly to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priest Needed What He Was Appointed to Administer

The sin offering comes first, then the burnt offering.
verseByVerse.examples: Guilt was dealt with before devotion was expressed. Christians still come to God in that order: forgiven first, then offering themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought the bull of the sin offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the bull of the sin offering. And he killed it, and Moses took the blood, and with his finger put it on the horns of the altar around it and purified the altar and poured out the blood at the base of the altar and consecrated it to make atonement for it. And he took all the fat that was on the entrails and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with their fat, and Moses burned them on the altar. But the bull and its skin and its flesh and its dung he burned up with fire outside the camp, as the LORD commanded Moses. Then he presented the ram of the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram. And he killed it, and Moses threw the blood against the sides of the altar. He cut the ram into pieces, and Moses burned the head and the pieces and the fat. He washed the entrails and the legs with water, and Moses burned the whole ram on the altar. It was a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering for the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Aaron and his sons can serve anyone, a bull dies as their sin offering and a ram as their burnt offering: the priests must first be atoned for, and then given wholly to God.

Laid their hands on the head of the bull. The men about to become the nation’s mediators must first stand where any guilty Israelite stands, hands pressed on an animal dying in their place. Then comes the ram, wholly burned. Guilt is dealt with before devotion is expressed.

Purified the altar… to make atonement for it. Even the altar needs cleansing before it can be used, because it stands in the middle of a sinful people. Everything that comes near God, people and things alike, must be made fit by blood.

Burned up with fire outside the camp. As in 4:11–12, the body of the sin offering is carried out of the camp and burned. Hebrews sees Christ in that detail: “So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12).

A priest who needed atonement. Nothing about ordination made Aaron less of a sinner. He needed the remedy he was appointed to administer, and the fact that he needed it first is what Hebrews seizes on in describing a better priest: “He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself” (Hebrews 7:27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ordination ram marks the priests, body and clothes, as belonging to God. After they lay their hands on it, Moses puts its blood on the right ear, right thumb and right big toe of Aaron and of each of his sons, and throws the rest against the altar (vv. 22–24). He places the fat, the right thigh and three kinds of bread in their hands, waves them before the LORD and burns them on the altar, and the breast is his own portion (vv. 25–29). Last, he sprinkles anointing oil and blood from the altar on Aaron and his sons and on their garments (v. 30). Hands filled and bodies marked, the priests are consecrated.
verseByVerse.theology:
Ear, Thumb, Toe

Blood is put on the faculties a priest uses, and on his new clothes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the new vestments were splashed with blood on their first day. Now: what we hear, do and walk toward belongs to the one who bought us.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he presented the other ram, the ram of ordination, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram. And he killed it, and Moses took some of its blood and put it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot. Then he presented Aaron's sons, and Moses put some of the blood on the lobes of their right ears and on the thumbs of their right hands and on the big toes of their right feet. And Moses threw the blood against the sides of the altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blood of the ordination ram is put on the priests’ right ear, thumb and big toe: their hearing, their doing and their going now belong to God.

The lobe of Aaron’s right ear. This is the strangest gesture in the ceremony, and the three points are not random. The ear hears God’s word. The thumb does the work; no hand grips anything without it. The big toe is what a man stands and walks on. Hearing, working, going: the blood is applied to the faculties a priest will actually use.

The same marks for the outcast. Leviticus uses this rite once more, and in a surprising place. When a man healed of a skin disease was restored to the camp, the priest put blood “on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot” (14:14). The outcast brought back from outside the camp receives the same marks as the high priest. Grace does not merely readmit the unclean; it consecrates them.

The ear that was opened. Christ is the priest whose whole body was given to God. The Servant says, “The Lord GOD has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious” (Isaiah 50:5): his ear perfectly heard the Father, his hands only did good, and his feet never strayed from the road to the cross. What the blood on Aaron claimed, Jesus gave.

A claim on the body. Consecration is not an inward mood but a claim on the parts of a person that do things. Paul asks the same “by the mercies of God”: “present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1). Not your sentiments but your body, the thing that turns up places and handles things, offered because it has already been bought.
verseByVerse.note: The right side was the side of strength and honour in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he took the fat and the fat tail and all the fat that was on the entrails and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with their fat and the right thigh, and out of the basket of unleavened bread that was before the LORD he took one unleavened loaf and one loaf of bread with oil and one wafer and placed them on the pieces of fat and on the right thigh. And he put all these in the hands of Aaron and in the hands of his sons and waved them as a wave offering before the LORD. Then Moses took them from their hands and burned them on the altar with the burnt offering. This was an ordination offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. And Moses took the breast and waved it for a wave offering before the LORD. It was Moses' portion of the ram of ordination, as the LORD commanded Moses. Then Moses took some of the anointing oil and of the blood that was on the altar and sprinkled it on Aaron and his garments, and also on his sons and his sons' garments. So he consecrated Aaron and his garments, and his sons and his sons' garments with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses fills the priests’ hands with the offering, waves it before the LORD and burns it, then sprinkles oil and blood on the priests and their garments: they are ordained and consecrated.

In the hands of Aaron. Moses places the fat, the thigh and the bread in their hands, waves them before the LORD and then takes them back and burns them (vv. 27–28). The Hebrew idiom for ordaining a priest is to “fill his hand”, and here it is acted out: a man was made a priest by having his hands filled with something he then gave away.

It was Moses’ portion. The breast, which normally belonged to the priests (7:31), goes to Moses, because on this day he is the one serving as priest.

Sprinkled it on Aaron and his garments. Then oil and blood together, on the men and on their clothes. Those vestments were the finest work in Israel, gold thread and blue and scarlet, and on the day they were first worn they were splashed with sacrificial blood. The garments that made a priest look holy were marked for good with the evidence of what holiness had cost. John saw the same paradox in heaven: the redeemed “have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7:14).

Uncertain wording. Where the idiom “fill the hand” came from is not certain. It may come from the portions placed in the priest’s hands, as here, or from paying a priest his due (Micah “ordained”, literally “filled the hand of”, one of his sons in Judges 17:5). The ordination offering itself is called by a word meaning “fillings”. The Greek Old Testament translated it with words for “completion”, which may lie behind Hebrews’ description of Christ as a Son “made perfect forever” (Hebrews 7:28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31-36 — Seven Days at the Door
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ordination takes a week, spent at God’s door. Aaron and his sons are to boil the meat at the entrance of the tent and eat it with the bread of ordination, burning whatever is left (vv. 31–32). For seven days they must not leave the entrance of the tent, day or night, because the LORD has commanded it to make atonement for them, “so that you do not die” (vv. 33–35). The chapter ends with a simple sentence that the next two chapters will test: Aaron and his sons did all that the LORD commanded by Moses (v. 36).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sentence Laid Down Before It Detonates

A week at the threshold ends in full obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: The ordination took a week of waiting at the threshold. Some of God's best preparation of his servants looks like staying put.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to Aaron and his sons, "Boil the flesh at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and there eat it and the bread that is in the basket of ordination offerings, as I commanded, saying, 'Aaron and his sons shall eat it.' And what remains of the flesh and the bread you shall burn up with fire. And you shall not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days, until the days of your ordination are completed, for it will take seven days to ordain you. As has been done today, the LORD has commanded to be done to make atonement for you. At the entrance of the tent of meeting you shall remain day and night for seven days, performing what the LORD has charged, so that you do not die, for so I have been commanded." And Aaron and his sons did all the things that the LORD commanded by Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For seven days Aaron and his sons eat the ordination meal and stay at the entrance of the tent, and they do all that the LORD commanded.

Boil the flesh… and there eat it. The ordination ram, like a peace offering, ends in a meal, eaten at the door of God’s house. The new priests eat in his presence before they serve in it, and whatever is left is burned, as with the most holy offerings.

You shall not go outside. The last instruction is about staying put. The ceremony is not a morning’s event but a week, “for it will take seven days to ordain you”, and for that week Aaron and his sons live at the threshold of the tent, day and night, the offerings repeated each day (Exodus 29:35–36). Their ministry begins not with activity but with waiting at God’s door.

So that you do not die. The warning is not decoration. These men were living next to the holy God, and holiness handled carelessly kills, as chapter 10 will show.

All the things that the LORD commanded. The chapter ends with a sentence Leviticus uses like a refrain: they did all the things that the LORD commanded by Moses. Chapters 8 and 9 turn on that clause, and chapter 10 opens with two men who offered what the LORD “had not commanded them” (10:1). The narrator sets up the contrast before the disaster comes.

The priest who always obeyed. Aaron’s obedience lasted a week before his own sons failed. Only one priest has ever done all that the LORD commanded, every day of his life: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). Our standing with God rests on his obedience, not on the faithfulness of our own week.

8.theology:
Priesthood conferred from outside. Aaron is washed, robed, anointed and atoned for by another; in the same way we are made priests by grace.

Whole-life consecration. Blood on ear, hand and foot claims the entire person for God, as Christ claims every faculty of those he saves.

The anointing of the Spirit. The oil poured on Aaron foreshadows the Spirit who anointed Christ at his baptism and now anoints his people (1 John 2:20; Acts 10:38).
8.examples:
Then: for seven days Moses washed, robed, anointed and marked with blood Aaron and his sons, setting apart Israel's priesthood with fearful reverence.

Now: Christ is our consecrated High Priest, and by his blood and Spirit he makes us "a royal priesthood" (1 Pet 2:9), our whole lives set apart for God.

keyVerse.quote: And he poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron’s head and anointed him to consecrate him.
keyVerse.note: Aaron did not take the office; it was poured on him. The word “anoint” gives us “Messiah”, and every anointed priest, king and prophet in Israel pointed ahead to Jesus, whom “God anointed… with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38), the High Priest who needs no cleansing and makes his people priests to God.

8.reflection:
Aaron did nothing to make himself a priest: he was washed, clothed and anointed by another (vv. 6–12). How does this picture what God has done for every believer in Christ (1 Corinthians 6:11; 1 Peter 2:9)?

Before serving anyone else, Aaron laid his hands on a sin offering for himself (v. 14). Why does it matter that leaders know themselves to be forgiven sinners, and why is it good news that Jesus needed no such offering?

Blood was put on ear, hand and foot (vv. 23–24). What would it look like this week to present your hearing, your work and your going to God (Romans 12:1)?

The chapter ends, “Aaron and his sons did all the things that the LORD commanded” (v. 36), yet chapter 10 tells of failure. How does Christ’s perfect obedience comfort you when your own obedience falls short?

9.title: The Glory Appears: Fire from Heaven
9.text: <sup>1</sup>On the eighth day Moses called Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel,<sup>2</sup>and he said to Aaron, "Take for yourself a bull calf for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering, both without blemish, and offer them before the LORD.<sup>3</sup>And say to the people of Israel, 'Take a male goat for a sin offering, and a calf and a lamb, both a year old without blemish, for a burnt offering,<sup>4</sup>and an ox and a ram for peace offerings, to sacrifice before the LORD, and a grain offering mixed with oil, for today the LORD will appear to you.'"<sup>5</sup>And they brought what Moses commanded in front of the tent of meeting, and all the congregation drew near and stood before the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And Moses said, "This is the thing that the LORD commanded you to do, that the glory of the LORD may appear to you."<sup>7</sup>Then Moses said to Aaron, "Draw near to the altar and offer your sin offering and your burnt offering and make atonement for yourself and for the people, and bring the offering of the people and make atonement for them, as the LORD has commanded."<sup>8</sup>So Aaron drew near to the altar and killed the calf of the sin offering, which was for himself.<sup>9</sup>And the sons of Aaron presented the blood to him, and he dipped his finger in the blood and put it on the horns of the altar and poured out the blood at the base of the altar.<sup>10</sup>But the fat and the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver from the sin offering he burned on the altar, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>11</sup>The flesh and the skin he burned up with fire outside the camp.<sup>12</sup>Then he killed the burnt offering, and Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he threw it against the sides of the altar.<sup>13</sup>And they handed the burnt offering to him, piece by piece, and the head, and he burned them on the altar.<sup>14</sup>And he washed the entrails and the legs and burned them with the burnt offering on the altar.<sup>15</sup>Then he presented the people's offering and took the goat of the sin offering that was for the people and killed it and offered it as a sin offering, like the first one.<sup>16</sup>And he presented the burnt offering and offered it according to the rule.<sup>17</sup>And he presented the grain offering, took a handful of it, and burned it on the altar, besides the burnt offering of the morning.<sup>18</sup>Then he killed the ox and the ram, the sacrifice of peace offerings for the people. And Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he threw it against the sides of the altar.<sup>19</sup>But the fat pieces of the ox and of the ram, the fat tail and that which covers the entrails and the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver—<sup>20</sup>they put the fat pieces on the breasts, and he burned the fat pieces on the altar,<sup>21</sup>but the breasts and the right thigh Aaron waved for a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses commanded.<sup>22</sup>Then Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them, and he came down from offering the sin offering and the burnt offering and the peace offerings.<sup>23</sup>And Moses and Aaron went into the tent of meeting, and when they came out they blessed the people, and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people.<sup>24</sup>And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the pieces of fat on the altar, and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces.
9.overview:
Where we are. For seven days Aaron and his sons have stayed at the door of the tent of meeting while they were ordained (8:33–35). Now comes the eighth day, the first day the priesthood actually works. Everything since God gave Moses the plans of the tabernacle (Exodus 25) has been heading for this morning.

The message. God will show his glory to sinners, but only when atonement has been made in the way he commanded. The offerings come first, for the priest and then for the people; then the glory of the LORD appears, and fire from God’s presence consumes the sacrifice. That fire is God’s own answer: he has accepted the offering, so the people can see his glory and live.

Why it was said. This was a nation that had trembled at Sinai from a distance, and had only lately bowed down to a golden calf that Aaron himself had made (Exodus 32). Could such a people, with such a priest, have the holy God in their camp? (See the introduction.) The chapter answers: yes, through the sacrifices God himself has given.

How the chapter makes its case. Moses gives the order of the day and the promise that “today the LORD will appear to you” (vv. 1–7). Aaron offers a sin offering and a burnt offering for himself, step by careful step (vv. 8–14). Then come the people’s offerings in their order: sin, burnt, grain and peace (vv. 15–21). Last, Aaron blesses the people, the glory appears, and the fire falls, and the people shout and fall on their faces (vv. 22–24).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Aaron had to offer first for his own sins; Jesus had no sins of his own and offered himself “once for all” (Hebrews 7:27). Aaron went into the tent and came out to bless; Christ was carried into heaven with his hands raised in blessing (Luke 24:50–51), and will appear a second time to save (Hebrews 9:28). God showed that he accepted Christ’s sacrifice not by fire on an altar but by raising him from the dead: he was “raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25). And the glory that Israel saw in fire we now see “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

For us. No one can stand before the glory of God except through a sacrifice God has accepted, and in Christ we have one. So Christian worship holds together what Israel did that day: a shout of joy and a face to the ground. We come gladly, because we are accepted, and reverently, because “our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The day begins with God’s order of service and God’s promise. Moses calls the priests and the elders and lists the offerings: a bull calf and a ram for Aaron, and a goat, a calf, a lamb, an ox, a ram and a grain offering for the people (vv. 1–4). The whole congregation draws near and stands before the LORD, and Moses gives the reason for it all: “that the glory of the LORD may appear to you” (v. 6). But atonement must come first, and it must begin with the priest himself: “make atonement for yourself and for the people” (v. 7). The glory is promised; the way to it is sacrifice.
verseByVerse.theology: Even the man who will stand between God and the people must first be covered himself. Every human mediator in Israel was a sinner in need of the sacrifice he offered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: everything since Exodus 25 led to this one day. Now: we come to God through a priest who never had to offer anything for himself, and so his whole work is for us.

verseByVerse.quote: On the eighth day Moses called Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel, and he said to Aaron, "Take for yourself a bull calf for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering, both without blemish, and offer them before the LORD. And say to the people of Israel, 'Take a male goat for a sin offering, and a calf and a lamb, both a year old without blemish, for a burnt offering, and an ox and a ram for peace offerings, to sacrifice before the LORD, and a grain offering mixed with oil, for today the LORD will appear to you.'" And they brought what Moses commanded in front of the tent of meeting, and all the congregation drew near and stood before the LORD. And Moses said, "This is the thing that the LORD commanded you to do, that the glory of the LORD may appear to you." Then Moses said to Aaron, "Draw near to the altar and offer your sin offering and your burnt offering and make atonement for yourself and for the people, and bring the offering of the people and make atonement for them, as the LORD has commanded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the first day of their service, God tells the priests to make atonement, first for Aaron and then for the people, and promises that when it is done his glory will appear.

On the eighth day. The seven days of ordination are over (8:33–35), and this is the first day the priesthood actually works. Like the eighth day on which a boy was circumcised (12:3), it marks a new beginning: Israel’s worship starts here.

A bull calf for a sin offering. The word for calf is the word used for the golden calf that Aaron made at Sinai (Exodus 32:4). Some interpreters, Jewish and Christian, have seen a fitting reminder in it: the man who made the calf now brings a calf to atone for his own sin. The text does not draw the line itself, but it does not let us forget that Israel’s high priest was a forgiven sinner.

Today the LORD will appear to you. Moses gives the reason for the whole day: for today the LORD will appear to you, that the glory of the LORD may appear to you (vv. 4, 6). Everything since Exodus 25 has been arranged so that a nation of former slaves can survive the presence of God in their camp. The elders and all the congregation drew near and stood before the LORD (v. 5): the whole people is there to see him come.

For yourself first. Before anything else comes an order the New Testament never stops pointing at: make atonement for yourself and for the people. Aaron cannot carry anyone else’s guilt until his own has been dealt with. Hebrews builds on this sequence to show why we needed a different priest, one “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners”, who has no need “to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people” (Hebrews 7:26–27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before Aaron can serve anyone else, his own sin must be dealt with. He kills the calf of the sin offering “which was for himself” (v. 8), puts its blood on the horns of the altar and pours out the rest, burns the fat on the altar, and burns the flesh and skin outside the camp (vv. 9–11). Then he offers his burnt offering, his sons handing him the blood and the pieces (vv. 12–14). Every step is done “as the LORD commanded Moses”. The section shows the priest of Israel kneeling, as it were, at the same altar as everyone else.
verseByVerse.theology: In Leviticus the careful procedure is itself the message: God is approached in the way he has given, not in a way we invent.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the whole day rested on Aaron doing exactly what he was told. Now: our peace with God rests on what Christ did exactly as the Father willed, not on how well we perform our worship.

verseByVerse.quote: So Aaron drew near to the altar and killed the calf of the sin offering, which was for himself. And the sons of Aaron presented the blood to him, and he dipped his finger in the blood and put it on the horns of the altar and poured out the blood at the base of the altar. But the fat and the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver from the sin offering he burned on the altar, as the LORD commanded Moses. The flesh and the skin he burned up with fire outside the camp. Then he killed the burnt offering, and Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he threw it against the sides of the altar. And they handed the burnt offering to him, piece by piece, and the head, and he burned them on the altar. And he washed the entrails and the legs and burned them with the burnt offering on the altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aaron offers the sin offering and the burnt offering for himself exactly as God commanded: the priest must be cleansed before he can serve.

So Aaron drew near to the altar. The narrator slows down to record each step: the calf which was for himself, blood on the horns of the altar and poured out at its base, the fat burned, the burnt offering handed to him piece by piece. A man in new clothes is carefully doing what he was told, in order, while a nation watches, and the weight of the day rests on his getting it right. Twice the text says it was done as the LORD commanded Moses (v. 10; compare v. 7).

Outside the camp. The flesh and the skin he burned up with fire outside the camp (v. 11). A priest could not eat the sin offering made for his own sin, so it was carried away from the holy place and burned (4:11–12). Hebrews sees Christ in this detail: the bodies of such sin offerings were burned outside the camp, “So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12).

The priest we needed. Aaron had to stand at the altar for himself before he could stand there for anyone else. Jesus never did. He has no need, “like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself” (Hebrews 7:27). Our confidence before God rests on a priest who had nothing of his own to atone for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15-24 — The People's Offerings, and the Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the people’s offerings are made, and God answers. Aaron offers the sin offering, burnt offering, grain offering and peace offerings for the people, in that order: guilt removed, the whole life given, daily bread offered, and then a shared meal in God’s presence (vv. 15–21). Then he lifts his hands and blesses the people; he and Moses go into the tent and come out to bless them again; the glory of the LORD appears to all, and fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes what is on the altar (vv. 22–24). The people see it, shout for joy and fall on their faces. The promise of verse 6 is kept.
verseByVerse.theology: The fire is God's answer. It shows that he has accepted the sacrifice offered in his appointed way, and so has accepted the people for whom it was offered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the people knew they were accepted because they saw the fire fall. Now: we know we are accepted because God raised Jesus from the dead, his public sign that the sacrifice was received.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he presented the people's offering and took the goat of the sin offering that was for the people and killed it and offered it as a sin offering, like the first one. And he presented the burnt offering and offered it according to the rule. And he presented the grain offering, took a handful of it, and burned it on the altar, besides the burnt offering of the morning. Then he killed the ox and the ram, the sacrifice of peace offerings for the people. And Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he threw it against the sides of the altar. But the fat pieces of the ox and of the ram, the fat tail and that which covers the entrails and the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver— they put the fat pieces on the breasts, and he burned the fat pieces on the altar, but the breasts and the right thigh Aaron waved for a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses commanded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people’s offerings follow in the order of the gospel: sin removed, the whole life given to God, daily bread offered to him, and last a meal of peace in his presence.

The order of the offerings. First the sin offering, like the first one (v. 15), then the burnt offering, then the grain offering, and last the peace offering, the one Israel eats. The order runs from guilt removed to a family sitting down to dinner in God’s presence, and that is the shape of the whole book compressed into one morning. It is also the order of the gospel: “since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1).

Besides the burnt offering of the morning. The daily burnt offering, made every morning and evening (Exodus 29:38–42), had already been offered (v. 17). The great day did not push aside the ordinary worship of every day; it was added to it.

As Moses commanded. One detail is easy to miss: the breasts and the right thigh Aaron waved for a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses commanded (v. 21). Even on the greatest day of his life, Aaron is guided not by his own instinct but by what he was told. The next chapter shows what happens when priests do otherwise.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them, and he came down from offering the sin offering and the burnt offering and the peace offerings. And Moses and Aaron went into the tent of meeting, and when they came out they blessed the people, and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the pieces of fat on the altar, and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the offerings complete, Aaron blesses the people, the glory of the LORD appears, and God’s own fire consumes the sacrifice: heaven accepts it, and the people fall down in joyful awe.

Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people. Aaron lifts his hands and blesses the people, and comes down from the altar. He and Moses go into the tent, come out, and bless the people again. The words are not given; many think of the blessing God later gave the priests to speak, The LORD bless you and keep you (Numbers 6:24).

Fire came out from before the LORD. This is what the whole day, and the whole book so far, has been building toward: not the fire as spectacle, but the fire as answer. God had specified an offering; the offering was made exactly as specified; and God came out and took it. Many interpreters have taken this to be the fire the priests were to keep burning on the altar and never let go out (6:13). Fire falls again at other great beginnings, on Elijah’s altar on Carmel (1 Kings 18:38) and at the dedication of Solomon’s temple (2 Chronicles 7:1).

They shouted and fell on their faces. The verb for shouted is usually a cry of joy. Joy and awe arrive together: the shout and the faces in the dust are the response of people who have just watched heaven accept something on their behalf.

Our High Priest’s blessing. Many Christians have seen here a picture of our own High Priest. Jesus lifted up his hands and blessed his disciples as he was carried up into heaven (Luke 24:50–51), and Hebrews says that, having entered the true holy place, he “will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him” (Hebrews 9:28). And God’s answer to his sacrifice was not fire on an altar but an empty tomb: he “was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25).

The same fire, the opposite outcome. In the very next chapter the same sentence returns: And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them (10:2). The words are the same and the outcome is the opposite, and the difference is not in the fire but in what it fell on: an offering God had commanded, or one he had not.

Fire that did not consume. Centuries later, in a house in Jerusalem, divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them (Acts 2:3). Fire came down and settled on people, and they were not consumed. God had not become less holy. By then the offering had been made, once, outside a city wall, and accepted; so when the fire came to rest on human beings, it came to dwell in them, not to judge them.

Joy and awe in our worship. Christian worship should carry both halves of verse 24. Without the shout it turns grim and fearful; without the faces on the ground it turns casual. Hebrews holds them together: “let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:28–29), and we do it as those who are “receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken”.

9.theology:
The goal of worship is glory. All the offerings aim at the appearing of God's glory (9:6, 23). That glory is now seen "in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6).

Acceptance through a substitute. The fire from heaven seals God's acceptance of the sacrifice. The judgment that the altar pictured fell, at the last, on Christ, and because it fell on him it need never fall on those who trust him.
9.examples:
Then: Israel saw the fire fall, and shouted and fell on their faces.

Now: Because the fire of judgment fell on Christ, we behold God's glory not in terror but in worship. The right response to grace is still both: glad praise and humble awe before the God who accepts us in his Son.

keyVerse.quote: And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the pieces of fat on the altar, and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces.
keyVerse.note: The whole day, and every offering of chapters 1–8, leads to this moment: God himself answers the sacrifice he commanded and accepts it in fire. The people’s shout and their faces in the dust show the right response to an accepted sacrifice, joy and awe together, which Christians share before the cross and the empty tomb.

9.reflection:
Aaron had to offer a sacrifice for his own sin before he could serve anyone else (vv. 7–8). What comfort is there in knowing that Jesus needed no sacrifice for himself?

The glory of the LORD appeared only after the offerings were made (vv. 6, 23). Why can sinners see God’s glory and live only through a sacrifice he has accepted?

The people shouted for joy and fell on their faces (v. 24). Which of these comes less naturally to you in worship, and what would help you hold them together?

God accepted Christ’s sacrifice by raising him from the dead (Romans 4:25). How might that truth change the way you come to God when you feel unworthy?

10.title: Nadab and Abihu: Unauthorized Fire
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer and put fire in it and laid incense on it and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them.<sup>2</sup>And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, and they died before the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Then Moses said to Aaron, "This is what the LORD has said: 'Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.'" And Aaron held his peace.<sup>4</sup>And Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron, and said to them, "Come near; carry your brothers away from the front of the sanctuary and out of the camp."<sup>5</sup>So they came near and carried them in their coats out of the camp, as Moses had said.<sup>6</sup>And Moses said to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar his sons, "Do not let the hair of your heads hang loose, and do not tear your clothes, lest you die, and wrath come upon all the congregation; but let your brothers, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning that the LORD has kindled.<sup>7</sup>And do not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting, lest you die, for the anointing oil of the LORD is upon you." And they did according to the word of Moses.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD spoke to Aaron, saying,<sup>9</sup>"Drink no wine or strong drink, you or your sons with you, when you go into the tent of meeting, lest you die. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations.<sup>10</sup>You are to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean,<sup>11</sup>and you are to teach the people of Israel all the statutes that the LORD has spoken to them by Moses."<sup>12</sup>Moses spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his surviving sons: "Take the grain offering that is left of the LORD's food offerings, and eat it unleavened beside the altar, for it is most holy.<sup>13</sup>You shall eat it in a holy place, because it is your due and your sons' due, from the LORD's food offerings, for so I am commanded.<sup>14</sup>But the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed you shall eat in a clean place, you and your sons and your daughters with you, for they are given as your due and your sons' due from the sacrifices of the peace offerings of the people of Israel.<sup>15</sup>The thigh that is contributed and the breast that is waved they shall bring with the food offerings of the fat pieces to wave for a wave offering before the LORD, and it shall be yours and your sons' with you as a due forever, as the LORD has commanded."<sup>16</sup>Now Moses diligently inquired about the goat of the sin offering, and behold, it was burned up! And he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, the surviving sons of Aaron, saying,<sup>17</sup>"Why have you not eaten the sin offering in the place of the sanctuary, since it is a thing most holy and has been given to you that you may bear the iniquity of the congregation, to make atonement for them before the LORD?<sup>18</sup>Behold, its blood was not brought into the inner part of the sanctuary. You certainly ought to have eaten it in the sanctuary, as I commanded."<sup>19</sup>And Aaron said to Moses, "Behold, today they have offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and yet such things as these have happened to me! If I had eaten the sin offering today, would the LORD have approved?"<sup>20</sup>And when Moses heard that, he approved.
10.overview:
Where we are. It is still the day of chapter 9 (10:19). The glory of the LORD has appeared, fire has consumed the offering, and the people have shouted for joy. Before the day is out, two of Aaron’s sons offer “unauthorized fire” (v. 1), and the same fire that accepted the sacrifice consumes them.

The message. The God who has come near is holy, and he will be approached in the way he has commanded, not in the way we choose: “Among those who are near me I will be sanctified” (v. 3). The nearer people stand to him, the more seriously his holiness must be honoured. Yet the same chapter ends with that holy God making room for a grieving father who could not bring himself to eat.

Why it was said. Israel’s worship had just begun, and its priests were setting the pattern for every generation after them. Their neighbours approached their gods however they pleased (see the introduction); on the first day God showed that he is not one more god to be handled on our terms.

How the chapter makes its case. Nadab and Abihu offer fire God had not commanded and die; Aaron is silent, and the priests may not mourn in public (vv. 1–7). God speaks to Aaron: no wine on duty, for the priests must tell holy from common and clean from unclean, and teach the people (vv. 8–11). Moses tells the surviving priests to eat their holy portions (vv. 12–15). Moses is angry that the sin offering was burned, not eaten, but accepts Aaron’s answer (vv. 16–20).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. On its first day the priesthood failed; Aaron’s house could not secure our access to God. We need a priest who never offered God anything he had not commanded, who could say, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). Christ is that priest, and on the cross the fire of judgment fell on him in our place, so that we come to God by “the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:20). In him we also see what verses 16–20 glimpse: a holy God who has a High Priest able “to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15).

For us. We come to God by the way he has opened in Christ, not by routes of our own devising, and we worship as he has said, with reverence. But we need not fear that he is a machine: the God who is a consuming fire also hears the honest words of a broken heart, and in Christ he receives us with both holiness and mercy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will be honoured as holy by those who come nearest to him. Nadab and Abihu offer fire he had not commanded, and fire from before the LORD consumes them (vv. 1–2). Moses gives God’s explanation, “Among those who are near me I will be sanctified”, and Aaron is silent (v. 3). Their cousins carry the bodies out of the camp (vv. 4–5). Aaron and his remaining sons may not show the signs of mourning or leave the tent, because the anointing oil is on them, while the whole nation weeps for them (vv. 6–7). The cost is shown in full, and so is the holiness of God.
verseByVerse.theology: The same fire that accepted the offering in chapter 9 now judges presumption. God's holiness is the reason for both: it is life to those who come his way and danger to those who do not.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Aaron had to let God be right on the worst day of his life. Now: a believer may grieve openly and still trust, for our High Priest has wept beside a grave himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer and put fire in it and laid incense on it and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, and they died before the LORD. Then Moses said to Aaron, "This is what the LORD has said: 'Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.'" And Aaron held his peace. And Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron, and said to them, "Come near; carry your brothers away from the front of the sanctuary and out of the camp." So they came near and carried them in their coats out of the camp, as Moses had said. And Moses said to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar his sons, "Do not let the hair of your heads hang loose, and do not tear your clothes, lest you die, and wrath come upon all the congregation; but let your brothers, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning that the LORD has kindled. And do not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting, lest you die, for the anointing oil of the LORD is upon you." And they did according to the word of Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two of Aaron’s sons offer fire God had not commanded, and fire from the LORD kills them: those who come nearest to God must treat him as holy.

Unauthorized fire … which he had not commanded them. Nadab and Abihu were Aaron’s eldest sons, who had gone up the mountain and seen the God of Israel (Exodus 24:9–11). Each takes a censer, puts fire and incense in it, and offers it before the LORD. The text does not say they meant harm; it says only that God had not commanded it. On the day God had shown exactly how he would be approached, they approached him their own way.

They died before the LORD. The happiest day becomes the most terrible, and the same fire that had blessed now kills (compare 9:24). Moses explains it in God’s own words: Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified. No one stood nearer to God than these priests, and the nearer a person stands, the more seriously God’s holiness must be honoured. He will not be treated as common or worshipped however we please. Yes, God has flung open a way to himself; but he is still “a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29), and we come with reverence and awe, not casual familiarity.

Carry your brothers away. Mishael and Elzaphan, Aaron’s cousins (Exodus 6:22), carry the bodies out in their coats, the priestly tunics the young men had been dressed in only days before (8:13). The fire took their lives but did not burn their clothes: this was no ordinary blaze but the judgment of God.

Why Aaron may not weep. Loose hair and torn clothes were Israel’s customary signs of grief, and Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar may not show them, nor leave the tent, lest you die. Not because grief was wrong: the whole nation is told to bewail the burning that the LORD has kindled. The nation may weep; the father may not. Two reasons stand together. The anointing oil of the LORD is upon you: they have only just been ordained, and to walk out now would be to desert the post God had just given them. And for the priests to take up the public signs of mourning would be a public protest, a way of saying before all Israel that God’s verdict was wrong. They must stand in the hour of their own bereavement and let God be right.

And Aaron held his peace. Read verse 3 again in that light. It is faith bowing before God, saying in silence something like what Job said in words: “the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21). But it is the silence of a father with two dead sons and a command not to weep, not of a man who felt little, as verse 19 shows.

The High Priest who wept. Israel had a high priest who was not permitted to weep at a tomb. We have a High Priest who wept at one: standing at the grave of his friend, knowing he was about to raise him, Jesus wept (John 11:35). And he did more than weep. He offered nothing to God that God had not commanded, and on the cross he bore the fire of God’s judgment himself, so that the fire which fell on Nadab and Abihu need never fall on those who trust him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that believers today must hide their grief. Aaron’s silence belonged to his office on that day; the rest of Israel wept, and so did Jesus. Christians grieve, though not “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

Does their death mean Nadab and Abihu were lost for ever? Scripture does not say. It records a judgment in this life on a public sin at a decisive moment, much like the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira at the start of the church (Acts 5:1–11), and leaves their eternal state with God. Such sudden judgments are rare in Scripture and come mostly at new beginnings, as warnings written down for all who come after (1 Corinthians 10:11). The warning is real; so is the way of approach God has opened in Christ.

Where Christians differ. Does this chapter establish the regulative principle of worship? The Reformed tradition holds that God may be worshipped only in the ways he commands in Scripture (Deuteronomy 12:32; Matthew 15:9; Westminster Confession 21.1). Others hold the normative principle: whatever Scripture does not forbid is allowed. Faithful Christians differ here, and both sides agree on the chapter’s main lesson: worship is shaped by what pleases God, not by what pleases us.

This commentary’s view. The death of Nadab and Abihu shows that God cares how he is worshipped, and the regulative principle, applied with wisdom, is the safer course: the elements of worship are reading and preaching the word, prayer, singing and the sacraments, while circumstances such as time and place are left to wisdom.

Uncertain wording. Unauthorized fire is literally “strange” or “foreign” fire (so the ESV note and older versions). What made it strange is not said. Most likely they took coals from somewhere other than the altar (compare 16:12), or offered incense at a time and in a way God had not prescribed; the warning against drink in verse 9 suggests to some that they had also been drinking. In verse 6 the phrase rendered do not let the hair of your heads hang loose may instead refer to uncovering the head (so the King James Version); either way it is a sign of mourning.
verseByVerse.note: “Unauthorized fire” can be rendered “strange fire” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-11 — Distinguish the Holy from the Common
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God speaks to Aaron himself, and the subject is a clear head for holy work. Priests on duty must not drink wine or strong drink, on pain of death (vv. 8–9). The reason opens up their whole calling: “to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean” (v. 10), and to teach Israel all that the LORD has spoken through Moses (v. 11). Coming straight after the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, it shows that careless worship begins with a mind that can no longer tell holy things from common ones. These distinctions also open the next five chapters.
verseByVerse.theology: The priest's essential work was to tell the holy from the common and to teach God's people to see the difference.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: what the priest discerned, he taught. Now: pastors and parents still do this work, and need clear heads and a steady diet of Scripture to do it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Aaron, saying, "Drink no wine or strong drink, you or your sons with you, when you go into the tent of meeting, lest you die. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations. You are to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean, and you are to teach the people of Israel all the statutes that the LORD has spoken to them by Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Aaron that priests must not drink when they serve, because their work is to tell holy from common and clean from unclean, and to teach God’s word.

And the LORD spoke to Aaron. Everywhere else in Leviticus God speaks to Moses, or to Moses and Aaron together. Here, on the day of his loss, he speaks to Aaron alone, and gives the grieving priest his calling.

Drink no wine or strong drink. The command comes straight after the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, and the timing suggests a connection: careless, perhaps intoxicated, worship. It applies when you go into the tent of meeting, that is, while on duty, and it is a statute forever.

To distinguish between the holy and the common. The reason opens up the whole calling of the priest, and the heartbeat of Leviticus. Everything is either holy (set apart for God) or common (ordinary); and common things are either clean or unclean. The priests must keep these distinctions clear-headed, and they must teach the people of Israel: “the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth” (Malachi 2:7). Chapters 11–15 spell out the distinctions in detail. When a people can no longer tell these things apart, holiness itself is lost (Ezekiel 22:26).

A royal priesthood with clear heads. In Christ every believer is part of “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), and the same Peter writes, “Be sober-minded; be watchful” (1 Peter 5:8). Learning to call holy what God calls holy is still the work of God’s word in his people, training us “to distinguish good from evil” (Hebrews 5:14). Whatever dulls that judgment, drink, screens or busyness, is a danger to worship.

Must Christians abstain from wine before worship or ministry? This command was for priests on duty. Scripture does not require total abstinence (Psalm 104:15; John 2:1–11), but it forbids drunkenness and bids us be filled with the Spirit instead (Ephesians 5:18), and elders must not be a drunkard (1 Timothy 3:3). The principle remains: a clear head for holy things. If drink has a hold on you, do not carry it alone: speak to your pastor or a biblical counsellor, and see a doctor as well.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-20 — Grief and Grace at the Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s provision goes on after the disaster, and his law is administered with mercy. Moses tells Aaron and his surviving sons to eat the grain offering beside the altar and the priests’ portions of the peace offerings with their families, because these are their due from the LORD (vv. 12–15). Then Moses finds that the people’s sin offering has been burned instead of eaten, and he is angry (vv. 16–18). Aaron, speaking for the first time in the chapter, says that after what has happened to him that day God would not have been pleased if he had eaten it, and Moses accepts his answer (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology: The law was never a machine. The holy God who judged presumption also weighs the heart of a grieving man.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a grieving father's reason was accepted. Now: in seasons of loss, when ordinary duties are beyond us, we may tell God so honestly and expect to be understood.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his surviving sons: "Take the grain offering that is left of the LORD's food offerings, and eat it unleavened beside the altar, for it is most holy. You shall eat it in a holy place, because it is your due and your sons' due, from the LORD's food offerings, for so I am commanded. But the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed you shall eat in a clean place, you and your sons and your daughters with you, for they are given as your due and your sons' due from the sacrifices of the peace offerings of the people of Israel. The thigh that is contributed and the breast that is waved they shall bring with the food offerings of the fat pieces to wave for a wave offering before the LORD, and it shall be yours and your sons' with you as a due forever, as the LORD has commanded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even on the day of their loss, the surviving priests are to eat their holy portions as God provided: his arrangement of grace is not cancelled by the sin that happened within it.

Eat it unleavened beside the altar. With two bodies just carried out of the camp, Moses turns to Aaron and his surviving sons and tells them to eat their dinner. The grain offering is most holy and is eaten beside the altar (6:16); the breast and thigh of the peace offerings may be eaten in a clean place at home.

Why the meal goes on. It sounds almost brutal until you see what it is doing. The offerings are still holy, the priests are still priests, and the arrangement God made has not been suspended because a disaster happened inside it. Aaron is being told that his sons’ sin has not disqualified the office or contaminated the food. Life at the altar goes on, and he is to sit down and eat as the law provides: it is your due.

Your sons and your daughters with you. There is a particular mercy in the detail your sons and your daughters with you (v. 14). The family that has just lost two of its men is named, together, as the people who will eat this. Grief does not put a household outside the provision of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses diligently inquired about the goat of the sin offering, and behold, it was burned up! And he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, the surviving sons of Aaron, saying, "Why have you not eaten the sin offering in the place of the sanctuary, since it is a thing most holy and has been given to you that you may bear the iniquity of the congregation, to make atonement for them before the LORD? Behold, its blood was not brought into the inner part of the sanctuary. You certainly ought to have eaten it in the sanctuary, as I commanded." And Aaron said to Moses, "Behold, today they have offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and yet such things as these have happened to me! If I had eaten the sin offering today, would the LORD have approved?" And when Moses heard that, he approved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests burn the sin offering instead of eating it, and Moses is angry; but Aaron explains that on such a day God would not have been pleased if he had eaten it, and Moses accepts his answer.

It was burned up! Moses diligently inquired about the goat of the people’s sin offering and found it burned. Since its blood had not been taken inside the sanctuary, the priests should have eaten it in the holy place (6:26, 30). Eating it was part of the atonement: it had been given to them that you may bear the iniquity of the congregation (v. 17). After the morning’s deaths, Moses fears another breach of God’s command, and he is angry with Eleazar and Ithamar.

Such things as these have happened to me. Aaron answers for his sons, and it is the only thing he says in the whole chapter. In verse 3 he held his peace; here a father who was forbidden to tear his clothes or let his hair down says the one sentence he is allowed, and his grief finally surfaces. His argument is not a technicality. To eat the sin offering was to act for the people before God, confident of God’s acceptance; on the day God had killed his sons for presumption, he could not do that with a whole heart, and to go through the motions would have been the very sin the day had just punished.

And when Moses heard that, he approved. This shows something about God which the rest of the chapter might have hidden. In the same chapter fire came out and killed two men for doing what was not commanded, and it ends with a man not doing what was commanded, giving his reason, and being told he was right. The difference is the heart: Nadab and Abihu presumed, Aaron trembled. The law was never a machine. It was always administered by a God who knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14), and who does not break a bruised reed (Isaiah 42:3).

The priest who bears iniquity. The priests ate the sin offering to bear the iniquity of the congregation. Their bearing was a sign; Christ’s was the reality: “he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12). And he is a High Priest who knows grief from the inside: “we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15).

Both things stand. Both truths stand in the same twenty verses, and neither cancels the other. God is a consuming fire, and he makes room for a father who cannot eat. So we may bring him our honest grief and our trembling scruples, never our presumption.

Uncertain wording. Aaron’s answer in verse 19 is compressed, and his exact reasoning is not spelled out. Some think he means that a mourner was unfit to eat holy food (compare Deuteronomy 26:14, “I have not eaten of the tithe while I was mourning”). Others think he means that the day’s sin and death had defiled the sanctuary, so that the offering should be treated like one whose blood was taken inside and burned (4:11–12, 21). Others think he simply could not eat it with the confidence it required. All agree on the result: Moses, and through him God, accepted his answer.

10.theology:
The holiness of God. God must be approached on his terms, not ours, and the greater the privilege, the greater the responsibility: those brought nearest must honour him most.

The only way. There is one acceptable approach to the Father, and it is Christ (John 14:6), who bore the judgment we deserved.
10.examples:
Then: Aaron's sons were consumed, and their father bowed in silence before the holiness of God.

Now: we are warned against casual, self-styled worship, and we are also shown a God who hears the honest grief of his servants.

keyVerse.quote: Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.
keyVerse.note: God’s own words explain the death of Nadab and Abihu and the whole chapter: nearness to God does not make his holiness less serious but more. Everyone who comes near him, priest or people, must treat him as holy, and Christians do so by coming through the one way he has opened in Christ.

10.reflection:
Nadab and Abihu offered fire “which he had not commanded them” (v. 1). In what ways are Christians today tempted to worship God on their own terms rather than his?

Aaron was told not to mourn in public, yet Jesus wept at a grave (John 11:35). How does Jesus’ grief help you bring your own grief to God?

The priests were to “distinguish between the holy and the common” (v. 10). What dulls your ability to tell holy things from common ones, and what sharpens it?

The chapter that begins with fire ends with God accepting a grieving father’s honest answer (vv. 19–20). How do God’s holiness and his compassion meet in Christ, and how does that shape the way you come to him?

11.title: Clean and Unclean: A People Set Apart
11.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying to them,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, These are the living things that you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth.<sup>3</sup>Whatever parts the hoof and is cloven-footed and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat.<sup>4</sup>Nevertheless, among those that chew the cud or part the hoof, you shall not eat these: The camel, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you.<sup>5</sup>And the rock badger, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you.<sup>6</sup>And the hare, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you.<sup>7</sup>And the pig, because it parts the hoof and is cloven-footed but does not chew the cud, is unclean to you.<sup>8</sup>You shall not eat any of their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses; they are unclean to you.<sup>9</sup>"These you may eat, of all that are in the waters. Everything in the waters that has fins and scales, whether in the seas or in the rivers, you may eat.<sup>10</sup>But anything in the seas or the rivers that does not have fins and scales, of the swarming creatures in the waters and of the living creatures that are in the waters, is detestable to you.<sup>11</sup>You shall regard them as detestable; you shall not eat any of their flesh, and you shall detest their carcasses.<sup>12</sup>Everything in the waters that does not have fins and scales is detestable to you.<sup>13</sup>"And these you shall detest among the birds; they shall not be eaten; they are detestable: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture,<sup>14</sup>the kite, the falcon of any kind,<sup>15</sup>every raven of any kind,<sup>16</sup>the ostrich, the nighthawk, the sea gull, the hawk of any kind,<sup>17</sup>the little owl, the cormorant, the short-eared owl,<sup>18</sup>the barn owl, the tawny owl, the carrion vulture,<sup>19</sup>the stork, the heron of any kind, the hoopoe, and the bat.<sup>20</sup>"All winged insects that go on all fours are detestable to you.<sup>21</sup>Yet among the winged insects that go on all fours you may eat those that have jointed legs above their feet, with which to hop on the ground.<sup>22</sup>Of them you may eat: the locust of any kind, the bald locust of any kind, the cricket of any kind, and the grasshopper of any kind.<sup>23</sup>But all other winged insects that have four feet are detestable to you.<sup>24</sup>"And by these you shall become unclean. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening,<sup>25</sup>and whoever carries any part of their carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening.<sup>26</sup>Every animal that parts the hoof but is not cloven-footed or does not chew the cud is unclean to you. Everyone who touches them shall be unclean.<sup>27</sup>And all that walk on their paws, among the animals that go on all fours, are unclean to you. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening,<sup>28</sup>and he who carries their carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening; they are unclean to you.<sup>29</sup>"And these are unclean to you among the swarming things that swarm on the ground: the mole rat, the mouse, the great lizard of any kind,<sup>30</sup>the gecko, the monitor lizard, the lizard, the sand lizard, and the chameleon.<sup>31</sup>These are unclean to you among all that swarm. Whoever touches them when they are dead shall be unclean until the evening.<sup>32</sup>And anything on which any of them falls when they are dead shall be unclean, whether it is an article of wood or a garment or a skin or a sack, any article that is used for any purpose. It must be put into water, and it shall be unclean until the evening; then it shall be clean.<sup>33</sup>And if any of them falls into any earthenware vessel, all that is in it shall be unclean, and you shall break it.<sup>34</sup>Any food in it that could be eaten, on which water comes, shall be unclean. And all drink that could be drunk from every such vessel shall be unclean.<sup>35</sup>And everything on which any part of their carcass falls shall be unclean. Whether oven or stove, it shall be broken in pieces. They are unclean and shall remain unclean for you.<sup>36</sup>Nevertheless, a spring or a cistern holding water shall be clean, but whoever touches a carcass in them shall be unclean.<sup>37</sup>And if any part of their carcass falls upon any seed grain that is to be sown, it is clean,<sup>38</sup>but if water is put on the seed and any part of their carcass falls on it, it is unclean to you.<sup>39</sup>"And if any animal which you may eat dies, whoever touches its carcass shall be unclean until the evening,<sup>40</sup>and whoever eats of its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening. And whoever carries the carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening.<sup>41</sup>"Every swarming thing that swarms on the ground is detestable; it shall not be eaten.<sup>42</sup>Whatever goes on its belly, and whatever goes on all fours, or whatever has many feet, any swarming thing that swarms on the ground, you shall not eat, for they are detestable.<sup>43</sup>You shall not make yourselves detestable with any swarming thing that swarms, and you shall not defile yourselves with them, and become unclean through them.<sup>44</sup>For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy. You shall not defile yourselves with any swarming thing that crawls on the ground.<sup>45</sup>For I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God.
