You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy."<sup>46</sup>This is the law about beast and bird and every living creature that moves through the waters and every creature that swarms on the ground,<sup>47</sup>to make a distinction between the unclean and the clean and between the living creature that may be eaten and the living creature that may not be eaten.
11.overview:
Where we are. The priests have just been told that their work is “to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean” (10:10). Chapters 11–15 now teach that distinction, beginning with what Israel may eat and what makes a person unclean by touch.

The message. God’s people must be different at every meal, because their God is holy and he has redeemed them: “You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy” (v. 45). The lines the chapter draws, between clean and unclean animals and between the living and the dead, taught Israel day by day that they belonged to the living God and that death has no place at his table.

Why it was said. Israel was a rescued nation living among other peoples, and God meant them to be visibly his (see the introduction). Later Leviticus ties the food laws directly to that calling: “I the LORD am holy and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine” (20:26). Every meal was to remind them whose they were.

How the chapter makes its case. Land animals must both part the hoof and chew the cud (vv. 1–8); water creatures must have fins and scales (vv. 9–12); birds are forbidden by a list, and winged insects except the locust family (vv. 13–23). The law then moves from eating to touching: carcasses make a person unclean until evening (vv. 24–28), dead swarming things defile pots, food and ovens (vv. 29–38), even a clean animal that dies defiles, and swarming things are not to be eaten (vv. 39–43). The chapter closes with its reason: God’s holiness and his redemption (vv. 44–47).

Where it leads. By pattern and by covenant. The food laws were “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:17). Jesus “declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19), and in Peter’s vision God opened his table to the Gentiles (Acts 10). More than that, Jesus touched what the law kept at a distance, a leper, a dead girl’s hand, a funeral bier, and instead of becoming unclean he made them clean and alive. The command to be holy remains, now resting on the blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:15–19).

For us. Christians are free to eat what God has made clean, and to welcome to their table those he has made clean. But the reason behind the old menu still stands: those whom Christ has bought are to be holy in all their conduct, not to earn God’s favour, but because they belong to the living God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God marks out what his people may eat, and the marks are simple enough for anyone to use. Land animals must both part the hoof and chew the cud, and the camel, rock badger, hare and pig are named because they pass one test and fail the other (vv. 1–8). Water creatures must have fins and scales (vv. 9–12). Birds are handled by a list, mostly birds of prey and scavengers (vv. 13–19). Winged insects are forbidden, except the locust family, which hop on jointed legs (vv. 20–23). No priest was needed at the market or the riverbank: at every meal an ordinary Israelite could tell what God had called clean.
verseByVerse.theology: The tests are simple enough for any Israelite to use at a market stall. God's holiness was not kept among the experts; it was to be practised by ordinary people in ordinary choices.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: every shopping trip trained Israel to tell one thing from another, the very skill God asked of the priests in 10:10. Now: Christians are trained in the same habit of discernment, though the choices now concern conduct rather than menus.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying to them, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, These are the living things that you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof and is cloven-footed and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat. Nevertheless, among those that chew the cud or part the hoof, you shall not eat these: The camel, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you. And the rock badger, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you. And the hare, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you. And the pig, because it parts the hoof and is cloven-footed but does not chew the cud, is unclean to you. You shall not eat any of their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses; they are unclean to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel may eat land animals that both part the hoof and chew the cud, and no others: a simple test that set God’s people apart at every meal.

A double test. The dietary laws arrive without a word of explanation for the individual rules, and the test for land animals is doubled: an animal must both part the hoof and chew the cud. Cattle, sheep and goats pass both tests (compare Deuteronomy 14:4–5).

Four disqualified animals. Four animals are named and disqualified precisely because they pass one test and fail the other: the camel, the rock badger and the hare chew but do not part the hoof; the pig parts the hoof but does not chew. You shall not touch their carcasses (v. 8) already points to the chapter’s second theme: contact with death.

The hare. Sceptics point out that the hare is not a ruminant like the cow. True, but the law is describing what an ordinary observer sees, a creature that keeps chewing, and the hare does in fact eat its own droppings to digest its food a second time. Scripture classifies animals by appearance and use, not by the categories of modern zoology, and is not in error for doing so.

The test, not the reason. What the text itself gives, over and over, is not the reason for each rule but the test. Israel was to obey because the LORD had spoken, and the final reason comes at the end: be holy, for I am holy (v. 44). For what happened to these laws in the New Testament, see the note on verses 44–47.

Where Christians differ. Why these animals? Some see hygiene: pork and shellfish can carry disease. Some see a rejection of pagan worship, in which certain animals were sacrificed. Some, following the anthropologist Mary Douglas, see a symbolism of order: clean animals are the normal members of their kind, and those that cross categories are unclean. Others see a line between life and death: many forbidden creatures live on flesh or carrion. Most also note that the laws marked Israel off from the nations (20:24–26).

This commentary’s view. The clearest thread is the one the chapter itself keeps touching: many forbidden creatures feed on flesh or carrion, and every rule about touching concerns carcasses, so the laws kept death away from the table of the living God. Alongside that, they made Israel visibly different at every meal, as 20:24–26 says. Hygiene may be a side benefit, but the text never gives it as the reason.

Uncertain wording. The rock badger is probably the rock hyrax, a small animal of the rocky hills that seems to chew constantly (the King James Version has “coney”). Like the hare, it is described as it appears, not by modern classification.
verseByVerse.note: Deuteronomy 14:3-21 repeats these food laws with small differences.

verseByVerse.quote: "These you may eat, of all that are in the waters. Everything in the waters that has fins and scales, whether in the seas or in the rivers, you may eat. But anything in the seas or the rivers that does not have fins and scales, of the swarming creatures in the waters and of the living creatures that are in the waters, is detestable to you. You shall regard them as detestable; you shall not eat any of their flesh, and you shall detest their carcasses. Everything in the waters that does not have fins and scales is detestable to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Water creatures may be eaten only if they have both fins and scales; all others are detestable to Israel.

Detestable to you. Detestable comes four times in three verses. The rule sweeps out shellfish, eels and every bottom-feeder at a stroke. An Israelite standing at a market stall did not need a priest. He needed only to look for fins and scales. Detestable to you describes how Israel was to regard them, not what God thinks of the creatures he made and called good (Genesis 1:21).

Why do Christians eat shellfish (11:10) yet still hold to the sexual laws of chapter 18? Because the New Testament itself draws the line. The food laws marked Israel off from the nations, and Jesus and the apostles lift them explicitly (see vv. 44–47). The sexual laws rest on creation (Genesis 2:24), were binding on the Canaanites too (18:24–25), and are repeated by the apostles (Romans 1:26–27; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11). That is following the apostles, not picking and choosing. Israel’s civil penalties ended with Israel’s state, and the gospel offers washing to every sinner: such were some of you.

verseByVerse.quote: "And these you shall detest among the birds; they shall not be eaten; they are detestable: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture, the kite, the falcon of any kind, every raven of any kind, the ostrich, the nighthawk, the sea gull, the hawk of any kind, the little owl, the cormorant, the short-eared owl, the barn owl, the tawny owl, the carrion vulture, the stork, the heron of any kind, the hoopoe, and the bat. "All winged insects that go on all fours are detestable to you. Yet among the winged insects that go on all fours you may eat those that have jointed legs above their feet, with which to hop on the ground. Of them you may eat: the locust of any kind, the bald locust of any kind, the cricket of any kind, and the grasshopper of any kind. But all other winged insects that have four feet are detestable to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Birds of prey and scavengers are forbidden, as are winged insects, except the locust family that hops on jointed legs.

These you shall detest among the birds. Birds are handled not by criteria but by a list: eagle, vultures, kite, falcon, raven, ostrich, nighthawk, sea gull, hawk, owls, cormorant, stork, heron, hoopoe and bat. The bat is here because the Hebrew word means winged creatures, not birds in the modern scientific sense. Many of them are birds of prey or scavengers, creatures that live on flesh, and often on flesh that is already dead. That fits the thread this commentary follows through the chapter: whatever feeds on death is kept away from the table of a people who worship the living God.

Winged insects that go on all fours. Insects have six legs, and the law knows it: on all fours is an everyday way of saying creatures that walk or creep along the ground, as opposed to those that hop. The locust family is the surprising exception, because it has jointed legs above their feet, with which to hop on the ground (v. 21).

Locusts and wild honey. Centuries later a man would live in the wilderness on locusts and wild honey (Mark 1:6), and Mark’s first readers would have recognised that John the Baptist was eating clean food, in the desert, off the land.

Uncertain wording. The identity of many of these birds is uncertain, as the ESV note says. The Hebrew names are rare, and translations differ widely: what one version calls an owl another calls a swan or a pelican. The same is true of the four kinds of locust in verse 22. What is clear is the general pattern: most of the forbidden birds are hunters or scavengers.
verseByVerse.note: The identity of many of these birds is uncertain (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24-47 — Uncleanness, Death, and 'Be Holy, for I Am Holy'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The law moves from the table to the touch, and from the altar into the kitchen, and ends with its reason. Touching or carrying the carcass of an unclean animal makes a person unclean until evening (vv. 24–28). Eight swarming creatures defile whatever they fall on when dead: clothes and sacks are washed, earthenware pots and ovens broken, though springs and dry seed stay clean (vv. 29–38). Even a clean animal that dies of itself defiles, and swarming things are not to be eaten (vv. 39–43). The reason is God himself: “be holy, for I am holy”, the God who brought Israel out of Egypt (vv. 44–47).
verseByVerse.theology: Uncleanness here is not sin. It comes from contact with death, and it is removed by washing and waiting, which taught Israel that death does not belong in God's presence.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a dead mouse in the flour was a matter for God's law. Now: no corner of an ordinary day is too small for a Christian to live it before God.

verseByVerse.quote: "And by these you shall become unclean. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening, and whoever carries any part of their carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening. Every animal that parts the hoof but is not cloven-footed or does not chew the cud is unclean to you. Everyone who touches them shall be unclean. And all that walk on their paws, among the animals that go on all fours, are unclean to you. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening, and he who carries their carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening; they are unclean to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Touching or carrying the carcass of an unclean animal makes a person unclean until evening: the issue is not guilt but contact with death.

Whoever touches their carcass. From eating to touching, and the pattern that governs the rest of the book appears: uncleanness is contracted from carcasses. This is not a moral judgment. A man who picked up a dead animal had done nothing wrong, and the remedy is to wash his clothes and wait until the evening, when a new day began (see How days were counted). All that walk on their paws (v. 27), such as dogs, cats and bears, are unclean too.

The one who touched the dead. The law kept death at a distance from God’s people. Jesus walked straight towards it. He took a dead girl by the hand (Mark 5:41) and touched the bier of a widow’s only son (Luke 7:14), and instead of uncleanness passing to him, life passed from him: both of them rose. In him the living God came near enough to touch death, and to defeat it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And these are unclean to you among the swarming things that swarm on the ground: the mole rat, the mouse, the great lizard of any kind, the gecko, the monitor lizard, the lizard, the sand lizard, and the chameleon. These are unclean to you among all that swarm. Whoever touches them when they are dead shall be unclean until the evening. And anything on which any of them falls when they are dead shall be unclean, whether it is an article of wood or a garment or a skin or a sack, any article that is used for any purpose. It must be put into water, and it shall be unclean until the evening; then it shall be clean. And if any of them falls into any earthenware vessel, all that is in it shall be unclean, and you shall break it. Any food in it that could be eaten, on which water comes, shall be unclean. And all drink that could be drunk from every such vessel shall be unclean. And everything on which any part of their carcass falls shall be unclean. Whether oven or stove, it shall be broken in pieces. They are unclean and shall remain unclean for you. Nevertheless, a spring or a cistern holding water shall be clean, but whoever touches a carcass in them shall be unclean. And if any part of their carcass falls upon any seed grain that is to be sown, it is clean, but if water is put on the seed and any part of their carcass falls on it, it is unclean to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Small swarming creatures make whatever they fall on unclean when they die, reaching God’s holiness into every kitchen, pot and store of food.

Anything on which any of them falls. Eight small creatures that swarm on the ground, rodents and lizards, defile whatever their dead bodies touch. Wood, cloth, skin and sacks are put into water and are clean again at evening (v. 32).

Any earthenware vessel. An earthenware pot is broken rather than washed, probably because unglazed clay is porous: whatever soaked into it cannot be scrubbed out. Ovens and stoves of clay are broken too (v. 35). The rule is not superstition; it follows from what the pot is made of.

A spring or a cistern. There are sensible limits. A spring or a cistern stays clean (v. 36), so that a household’s water supply is not lost, though whoever lifts out the carcass is unclean. Dry seed for sowing stays clean, but wet seed does not (vv. 37–38), since moisture was thought to carry uncleanness.

Into the kitchen. The holiness of God does not stay in the tabernacle. It reaches into the kitchen, the pantry and the water supply, and it comes up in the middle of an ordinary morning when something has died in the flour. For Christians the rules have gone (see vv. 44–47), but the lesson has not: there is no corner of life that does not belong to God (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Uncertain wording. The eight creatures of verses 29–30 are hard to identify. The ESV offers mole rat, mouse and six kinds of lizard, but the King James Version has weasel, tortoise, ferret, snail and mole among them. The general sense is clear: small creatures that scurry along the ground.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if any animal which you may eat dies, whoever touches its carcass shall be unclean until the evening, and whoever eats of its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening. And whoever carries the carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening. "Every swarming thing that swarms on the ground is detestable; it shall not be eaten. Whatever goes on its belly, and whatever goes on all fours, or whatever has many feet, any swarming thing that swarms on the ground, you shall not eat, for they are detestable. You shall not make yourselves detestable with any swarming thing that swarms, and you shall not defile yourselves with them, and become unclean through them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even a clean animal that dies of itself makes a person unclean, and creatures that swarm on the ground are not to be eaten at all.

If any animal which you may eat dies. Even the clean ox found dead in the field is not ordinary food: touching, carrying or eating its carcass makes a person unclean until evening. What dies of itself defiles, however clean the animal was in life.

Whatever goes on its belly. Swarming things, whether they slither, walk on all fours or have many feet, are detestable: You shall not make yourselves detestable with them (v. 43). The phrase goes on its belly echoes the curse on the serpent in Eden, on your belly you shall go (Genesis 3:14), and many readers have heard in it a reminder of where death came from. The reason for the ban follows in the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy. You shall not defile yourselves with any swarming thing that crawls on the ground. For I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy." This is the law about beast and bird and every living creature that moves through the waters and every creature that swarms on the ground, to make a distinction between the unclean and the clean and between the living creature that may be eaten and the living creature that may not be eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The food laws rest on God himself: because the LORD who brought Israel out of Egypt is holy, his people must be holy too.

I am the LORD your God. The food laws were never finally about the food. They were about a people who had to be recognisably different in the most ordinary and unavoidable area of life, because the God who took them out of Egypt was different. An Israelite could not eat a meal without remembering whose he was. And the order matters: I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt comes before You shall therefore be holy. Holiness is the grateful response of a redeemed people, not the price of their redemption.

All foods clean. Two things happened to this chapter in the New Testament. The first is that Jesus set the food rules aside. Arguing that defilement comes out of a person rather than going into him, he pointed out that whatever enters the stomach is expelled, and Mark adds: Thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). Then Peter, on a rooftop in Joppa, was shown a sheet of unclean animals three times and told to eat, and the voice said What God has made clean, do not call common (Acts 10:15); while he was still turning it over, Gentiles knocked at the door. Once the food laws were lifted, Jew and Gentile could eat together, and the mission to the nations could go forward.

Be holy, for I am holy. The second is that the verse this chapter ends on was not set aside at all. Peter, the same man from the rooftop, quotes it directly: as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:15–16).

The menu and the reason. The menu changed; the reason for the menu did not. What was once practised over a cooking pot is now required in all your conduct, which is far harder than checking a hoof. But Peter grounds it in a ransom already paid with the blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19) and in the Spirit’s sanctifying work (1 Peter 1:2). In practice that means the same daily habit of telling one thing from another, now applied to speech, money, entertainment and friendships: not to earn God’s favour, but because those he has bought take on the family likeness.

We still have food laws. A chapter like this can look like proof that the Bible belongs to a superstitious age. Yet our own age is full of purity codes. We speak of “clean eating” and detoxes, feel guilty over sugar and virtuous over kale, and police the purity of opinions online like zealous Levites. Mary Douglas, in Purity and Danger (1966), argued that every society, our own included, draws lines between clean and unclean, because every society needs to say what belongs where. The real question is what the lines are for. Ours mostly sort the righteous from the rest and offer no way back across. Israel’s lines taught a whole people, at every meal, that God is holy and that death does not belong at his table, and they came with washings and offerings that brought the unclean home. Then Jesus moved the line to where it had always pointed: “There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him” (Mark 7:15). No diet reaches that far. Only “the blood of Christ” can “purify our conscience” (Hebrews 9:14), and he does what no purity code has ever done: he makes the unclean clean.

Where Christians differ. Seventh-day Adventists and some Messianic Jews still keep the food laws, holding that they remain God’s will or a fitting part of Jewish identity. Most Christians hold that they were fulfilled in Christ and no longer bind anyone (Mark 7:19; Acts 10; Colossians 2:16–17).

This commentary’s view. All foods are clean. Jewish believers are free to keep these customs as devotion, but never as the way of salvation or as a test of fellowship, and no Christian may impose them on another (Romans 14:14; Colossians 2:16).

11.theology:
Separation unto God. The food laws trained Israel, at every meal, to be a people visibly set apart, and to distinguish between holy and common.

Holiness grounded in grace. The call to be holy rests on who God is and on what he has done in rescuing his people. In Christ the boundary no longer runs between Jew and Gentile, but between those who are in him and those who are not, and the call to holiness endures (1 Pet 1:16).
11.examples:
Then: every meal reminded an Israelite whose he was.

Now: we are no longer bound by Israel's food laws, but the call to be holy and distinct reaches every part of life, and the Spirit who calls us also enables us (1 Pet 1:15).

keyVerse.quote: For I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.
keyVerse.note: The verse gives the reason behind every rule in the chapter: God’s own holiness, and the redemption by which he made Israel his. Its order is the order of the gospel, rescue first and holiness in response, and Peter applies its command to every Christian (1 Peter 1:15–16).

11.reflection:
Israel could not eat a single meal without remembering that they belonged to God. What everyday habits help you remember whose you are?

The chapter puts redemption before holiness: “I am the LORD who brought you up … You shall therefore be holy” (v. 45). Why does that order matter for the way we pursue holiness?

Jesus touched the dead and made them alive instead of becoming unclean (Mark 5:41; Luke 7:14). What does that show you about him, and about what he can do with what is unclean in you?

Peter learned not to call common what God has made clean (Acts 10:15). Are there people you find it hard to welcome to your table, and what would it mean to welcome them as Christ has welcomed you?

12.title: Purification After Childbirth: The Offering of the Poor
12.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If a woman conceives and bears a male child, then she shall be unclean seven days. As at the time of her menstruation, she shall be unclean.<sup>3</sup>And on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.<sup>4</sup>Then she shall continue for thirty-three days in the blood of her purifying. She shall not touch anything holy, nor come into the sanctuary, until the days of her purifying are completed.<sup>5</sup>But if she bears a female child, then she shall be unclean two weeks, as in her menstruation. And she shall continue in the blood of her purifying for sixty-six days.<sup>6</sup>"And when the days of her purifying are completed, whether for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring to the priest at the entrance of the tent of meeting a lamb a year old for a burnt offering, and a pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering,<sup>7</sup>and he shall offer it before the LORD and make atonement for her. Then she shall be clean from the flow of her blood. This is the law for her who bears a child, either male or female.<sup>8</sup>And if she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean."
12.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 dealt with uncleanness from what Israel ate and touched. Now the clean and unclean laws (chapters 11–15) turn to the human body, and they begin at the beginning of life: a mother after childbirth.

The message. Even the joy of a new birth takes place in a world marked by death, and a mother who has lost blood in giving life needs to be cleansed before she comes near the holy God. Her uncleanness is not sin, and God himself provides the way back to his presence, at a price even the poorest family can pay.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that the holy God who lived among them cared about the most intimate moments of family life, and that his holiness reached even there. “Unclean” in Leviticus means unfit to approach the sanctuary for a time, not guilty (see the introduction): childbirth was a blessing God had commanded, not a fault.

How the chapter makes its case. After the birth of a son the mother is unclean for seven days, as in her monthly period; the boy is circumcised on the eighth day; and she waits a further thirty-three days before touching anything holy or entering the sanctuary. After a daughter the times are doubled (vv. 1–5). When her days are complete she brings a lamb for a burnt offering and a bird for a sin offering, and the priest makes atonement for her; if she cannot afford a lamb, two birds will do (vv. 6–8).

Where it leads. By fulfilment in a single, tender scene. When Jesus was forty days old, Mary and Joseph brought him to the temple and offered “a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons” (Luke 2:24), the poor mother’s offering of verse 8. The Son of God was “born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Galatians 4:4–5), and he came into a family that could not afford a lamb: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The chapter also shows the need he came to meet: every child is born into a world of death and needs redemption.

For us. Every child is a gift, and every child needs the Saviour. Mothers are not unclean before God in Christ, and the poor are not second-class: the Lord himself was born among them. We can thank God for each new life, and bring each one to the One who was offered for at forty days old.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God provides for a mother to be restored to his presence after giving birth, at a price within reach of the poorest. After a son she is unclean for seven days, as in her period, the boy is circumcised on the eighth day, and she waits thirty-three more days in “the blood of her purifying”, touching nothing holy (vv. 1–4). After a daughter the times are doubled, fourteen and sixty-six days (v. 5). When the days are complete she brings a year-old lamb for a burnt offering and a pigeon or turtledove for a sin offering, the same for a son or a daughter, and the priest makes atonement for her (vv. 6–7). If she cannot afford a lamb, two birds are enough (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Unclean does not mean sinful. The law marks a moment when new life came with the loss of blood, and then provides a way back, open to rich and poor alike.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: no mother was kept from God because she was poor. Now: no one is too poor, too lowly or too worn out to be welcomed by him.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If a woman conceives and bears a male child, then she shall be unclean seven days. As at the time of her menstruation, she shall be unclean. And on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised. Then she shall continue for thirty-three days in the blood of her purifying. She shall not touch anything holy, nor come into the sanctuary, until the days of her purifying are completed. But if she bears a female child, then she shall be unclean two weeks, as in her menstruation. And she shall continue in the blood of her purifying for sixty-six days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After giving birth a mother is ritually unclean for a set time, not because birth is sinful but because the loss of blood marks her with mortality; until her purification is complete she may not come near the sanctuary.

She shall be unclean. Two misunderstandings need clearing away. The first: unclean in Leviticus does not mean sinful. It is a ritual status, not a moral verdict, and here it attaches to something God himself commanded: “Be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:28). Nobody thought childbirth was wrong. Uncleanness meant only that, for a time, she could not touch anything holy, nor come into the sanctuary (v. 4).

The blood of her purifying. What she had done was lose a great deal of blood, and blood, in this book, is life (17:11). Every law about discharge, disease and death works on the same principle: where life visibly drains away, a person is for a time kept back from the living God. The rule is a statement about mortality, not morality. Since Eden birth has come with pain (Genesis 3:16), and every child is born into a world where death reigns.

On the eighth day. In the middle of the mother’s law comes the son’s: on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised, the sign of God’s covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:12). Her first seven days of uncleanness end as he receives the covenant sign. Jesus too was circumcised on the eighth day and named (Luke 2:21).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a woman’s body, or motherhood, is shameful to God. The law brings a mother back, publicly and with God’s own provision, into the worship of his people. Nor does it make Christian mothers unclean today (see the note on verses 6–8).

Son and daughter. The second difficulty is the doubling, forty days for a son and eighty for a daughter, and honesty requires saying that the text gives no reason for it. Various suggestions have been made, but none is certain. What can be said is what the chapter does not say: nothing about the daughter being worth less, and nothing about her being more defiling. The offering at the end is identical for both, whether for a son or for a daughter (v. 6). Whatever the doubling means, it does not affect the price of restoration.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the days of her purifying are completed, whether for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring to the priest at the entrance of the tent of meeting a lamb a year old for a burnt offering, and a pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering, and he shall offer it before the LORD and make atonement for her. Then she shall be clean from the flow of her blood. This is the law for her who bears a child, either male or female. And if she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When her days are complete the mother brings a burnt offering and a sin offering, and the priest makes atonement so that she is clean; a poor mother may bring two birds instead of a lamb.

A lamb … and a pigeon or a turtledove. The lamb is a burnt offering, the whole life given to God; the bird is a sin offering, which cleanses her from the flow of her blood. Then she shall be clean, free to come again to the sanctuary with God’s people.

If she cannot afford a lamb. This clause is why the chapter matters more than its length suggests. When Mary and Joseph brought the child to the temple, Luke records exactly what they offered: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons (Luke 2:24). They brought the poor woman’s offering, the allowance of this verse, written for a household that could not manage a lamb. The Lord was born into a family poor enough to need it.

Born under the law. There is more in it than poverty. The whole scene is a family bringing a sin offering on behalf of a household that included the sinless Son of God, submitting to a purification law that had nothing in him to purify: born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). He lived under that law from forty days old, before he could hold his head up. The family could not afford a lamb, yet the Lamb of God was lying in the arms of the woman who came to offer the birds.

If childbirth is not sin, why a sin offering? The offering’s name can also be translated “purification offering”: it cleansed from the uncleanness of the flow of blood, not from moral guilt (compare 14:19). Mary offered it after Jesus’ birth (Luke 2:22–24), not because his birth was sinful, but in obedience to the law.

Do these laws bind Christian mothers? No. The purity laws were regulations for the body until the time of reformation (Hebrews 9:10), and Christ has fulfilled them. A Christian mother is as welcome at the Lord’s table the week after giving birth as on any other day. What remains is the heart of the chapter: thanksgiving to God for a child, and the knowledge that every child needs the Saviour this law once received at forty days old.
verseByVerse.note: Turtledoves and pigeons were the cheapest animals the law accepted; the same allowance for the poor appears in 5:7 and 14:21-22.

12.theology:
Born into a mortal world. Even the gift of birth, marked by blood and pain, shows that every life comes into a world of death and needs God's cleansing.

Atonement within reach of the poor. The provision for those who could not afford a lamb shows that no one is shut out from God by want.

The poverty of Christ. The Lamb of God entered the world in real poverty, and was presented under the law he came to fulfil.
12.examples:
Then: a new mother brought a lamb, or two birds if she could not, and was pronounced clean.

Now: a Christian mother gives thanks for her child without any rite of cleansing, and she may also bring her grief to the same God if a pregnancy or birth has ended in loss. The King of glory met us in poverty and weakness; no one is too lowly for his grace.

keyVerse.quote: And if she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean.
keyVerse.note: God made the way back to his presence affordable for the poorest mother, and gave her the same atonement and the same cleanness. This is the offering Mary brought for Jesus (Luke 2:24): the Son of God was born into a family that could not afford a lamb, and he himself became the Lamb.

12.reflection:
Leviticus calls a mother “unclean” after childbirth, yet she had done nothing wrong (vv. 2–5). How does the difference between unclean and guilty help you read this chapter, and the whole book?

The offering was the same for a son or a daughter, and the poor could bring birds instead of a lamb (vv. 6–8). What does that tell you about the way God receives people?

Mary and Joseph brought the poor family’s offering for Jesus (Luke 2:24). What does it mean to you that the Lord was born into poverty and “under the law” (Galatians 4:4)?

How could your church or home group thank God for new births and support new parents, including those who are struggling?

13.title: Skin Disease: The Priest Who Examines
13.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying,<sup>2</sup>"When a person has on the skin of his body a swelling or an eruption or a spot, and it turns into a case of leprous disease on the skin of his body, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons the priests,<sup>3</sup>and the priest shall examine the diseased area on the skin of his body. And if the hair in the diseased area has turned white and the disease appears to be deeper than the skin of his body, it is a case of leprous disease. When the priest has examined him, he shall pronounce him unclean.<sup>4</sup>But if the spot is white in the skin of his body and appears no deeper than the skin, and the hair in it has not turned white, the priest shall shut up the diseased person for seven days.<sup>5</sup>And the priest shall examine him on the seventh day, and if in his eyes the disease is checked and the disease has not spread in the skin, then the priest shall shut him up for another seven days.<sup>6</sup>And the priest shall examine him again on the seventh day, and if the diseased area has faded and the disease has not spread in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him clean; it is only an eruption. And he shall wash his clothes and be clean.<sup>7</sup>But if the eruption spreads in the skin, after he has shown himself to the priest for his cleansing, he shall appear again before the priest.<sup>8</sup>And the priest shall look, and if the eruption has spread in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a leprous disease.<sup>9</sup>"When a man is afflicted with a leprous disease, he shall be brought to the priest,<sup>10</sup>and the priest shall look. And if there is a white swelling in the skin that has turned the hair white, and there is raw flesh in the swelling,<sup>11</sup>it is a chronic leprous disease in the skin of his body, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean. He shall not shut him up, for he is unclean.<sup>12</sup>And if the leprous disease breaks out in the skin, so that the leprous disease covers all the skin of the diseased person from head to foot, so far as the priest can see,<sup>13</sup>then the priest shall look, and if the leprous disease has covered all his body, he shall pronounce him clean of the disease; it has all turned white, and he is clean.<sup>14</sup>But when raw flesh appears on him, he shall be unclean.<sup>15</sup>And the priest shall examine the raw flesh and pronounce him unclean. Raw flesh is unclean, for it is a leprous disease.<sup>16</sup>But if the raw flesh recovers and turns white again, then he shall come to the priest,<sup>17</sup>and the priest shall examine him, and if the disease has turned white, then the priest shall pronounce the diseased person clean; he is clean.<sup>18</sup>"If there is in the skin of one's body a boil and it heals,<sup>19</sup>and in the place of the boil there comes a white swelling or a reddish-white spot, then it shall be shown to the priest.<sup>20</sup>And the priest shall look, and if it appears deeper than the skin and its hair has turned white, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is a case of leprous disease that has broken out in the boil.<sup>21</sup>But if the priest examines it and there is no white hair in it and it is not deeper than the skin, but has faded, then the priest shall shut him up seven days.<sup>22</sup>And if it spreads in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a disease.<sup>23</sup>But if the spot remains in one place and does not spread, it is the scar of the boil, and the priest shall pronounce him clean.<sup>24</sup>"Or, when the body has a burn on its skin and the raw flesh of the burn becomes a spot, reddish-white or white,<sup>25</sup>the priest shall examine it, and if the hair in the spot has turned white and it appears deeper than the skin, then it is a leprous disease. It has broken out in the burn, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a case of leprous disease.<sup>26</sup>But if the priest examines it and there is no white hair in the spot and it is no deeper than the skin, but has faded, the priest shall shut him up seven days,<sup>27</sup>and the priest shall examine him the seventh day. If it is spreading in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a case of leprous disease.<sup>28</sup>But if the spot remains in one place and does not spread in the skin, but has faded, it is a swelling from the burn, and the priest shall pronounce him clean, for it is the scar of the burn.<sup>29</sup>"When a man or woman has a disease on the head or the beard,<sup>30</sup>the priest shall examine the disease. And if it appears deeper than the skin, and the hair in it is yellow and thin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is an itch, a leprous disease of the head or the beard.<sup>31</sup>And if the priest examines the itching disease and it appears no deeper than the skin and there is no black hair in it, then the priest shall shut up the person with the itching disease for seven days,<sup>32</sup>and on the seventh day the priest shall examine the disease. If the itch has not spread, and there is in it no yellow hair, and the itch appears to be no deeper than the skin,<sup>33</sup>then he shall shave himself, but the itch he shall not shave; and the priest shall shut up the person with the itching disease for another seven days.<sup>34</sup>And on the seventh day the priest shall examine the itch, and if the itch has not spread in the skin and it appears to be no deeper than the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him clean. And he shall wash his clothes and be clean.<sup>35</sup>But if the itch spreads in the skin after his cleansing,<sup>36</sup>then the priest shall examine him, and if the itch has spread in the skin, the priest need not seek for the yellow hair; he is unclean.<sup>37</sup>But if in his eyes the itch is unchanged and black hair has grown in it, the itch is healed and he is clean, and the priest shall pronounce him clean.<sup>38</sup>"When a man or a woman has spots on the skin of the body, white spots,<sup>39</sup>the priest shall look, and if the spots on the skin of the body are of a dull white, it is leukoderma that has broken out in the skin; he is clean.<sup>40</sup>"If a man's hair falls out from his head, he is bald; he is clean.<sup>41</sup>And if a man's hair falls out from his forehead, he has baldness of the forehead; he is clean.<sup>42</sup>But if there is on the bald head or the bald forehead a reddish-white diseased area, it is a leprous disease breaking out on his bald head or his bald forehead.<sup>43</sup>Then the priest shall examine him, and if the diseased swelling is reddish-white on his bald head or on his bald forehead, like the appearance of leprous disease in the skin of the body,<sup>44</sup>he is a leprous man, he is unclean. The priest must pronounce him unclean; his disease is on his head.<sup>45</sup>"The leprous person who has the disease shall wear torn clothes and let the hair of his head hang loose, and he shall cover his upper lip and cry out, 'Unclean, unclean.'<sup>46</sup>He shall remain unclean as long as he has the disease. He is unclean. He shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp.<sup>47</sup>"When there is a case of leprous disease in a garment, whether a woolen or a linen garment,<sup>48</sup>in warp or woof of linen or wool, or in a skin or in anything made of skin,<sup>49</sup>if the disease is greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the skin or in the warp or the woof or in any article made of skin, it is a case of leprous disease, and it shall be shown to the priest.<sup>50</sup>And the priest shall examine the disease and shut up that which has the disease for seven days.<sup>51</sup>Then he shall examine the disease on the seventh day. If the disease has spread in the garment, in the warp or the woof, or in the skin, whatever be the use of the skin, the disease is a persistent leprous disease; it is unclean.<sup>52</sup>And he shall burn the garment, or the warp or the woof, the wool or the linen, or any article made of skin that is diseased, for it is a persistent leprous disease. It shall be burned in the fire.<sup>53</sup>"And if the priest examines, and if the disease has not spread in the garment, in the warp or the woof or in any article made of skin,<sup>54</sup>then the priest shall command that they wash the thing in which is the disease, and he shall shut it up for another seven days.<sup>55</sup>And the priest shall examine the diseased thing after it has been washed. And if the appearance of the diseased area has not changed, though the disease has not spread, it is unclean. You shall burn it in the fire, whether the rot is on the back or on the front.<sup>56</sup>"But if the priest examines, and if the diseased area has faded after it has been washed, he shall tear it out of the garment or the skin or the warp or the woof.<sup>57</sup>Then if it appears again in the garment, in the warp or the woof, or in any article made of skin, it is spreading. You shall burn with fire whatever has the disease.<sup>58</sup>But the garment, or the warp or the woof, or any article made of skin from which the disease departs when you have washed it, shall then be washed a second time, and be clean."<sup>59</sup>This is the law for a case of leprous disease in a garment of wool or linen, either in the warp or the woof, or in any article made of skin, to determine whether it is clean or unclean.
13.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 11–15 teach Israel the difference between clean and unclean, so that the holy God can live in their camp (see the introduction). After food and childbirth, chapter 13 turns to the longest single case: a skin condition the ESV calls “leprous disease”, and the same kind of blight in cloth and leather.

The message. Whatever bears the marks of death cannot dwell in the presence of the living God, and God wants that line drawn truly, never carelessly. The priest does not cure; he looks, waits and gives an honest verdict, as careful to declare the healthy clean as to declare the sick unclean. And the stakes are high, because an unclean verdict meant a life alone outside the camp.

Why it was said. Israel lived in a camp around God’s tent. Skin disease was common and frightening, and it made a living person look like one of the dead (Numbers 12:12). Careful rules protected the camp without letting fear drive people out on rumour.

How the chapter makes its case. Swellings, eruptions and spots are examined, with seven-day waits before any verdict (vv. 1–8). A chronic case is unclean at once, yet a man turned white from head to foot is clean (vv. 9–17). Boils and burns may prove to be only scars (vv. 18–28). Sores of the scalp and beard are sorted from harmless white spots and plain baldness (vv. 29–44). Then two verses show the cost of an unclean verdict: torn clothes, the cry “Unclean, unclean”, and a dwelling outside the camp (vv. 45–46). Finally the same patient examination is applied to garments and leather (vv. 47–59).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes and by pattern. The law could diagnose but never heal, and it could only send the unclean away. Jesus did what it could not: when a leper knelt before him, “he stretched out his hand and touched him” (Mark 1:41), and instead of the clean becoming unclean, the unclean became clean. Then he went outside the camp himself, for “Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). Christians have long seen the disease as a picture of sin, which spreads, disfigures and isolates: a fair picture, if held carefully, since the law never treats the sufferer as guilty.

For us. Christ tells us the truth about our uncleanness and then takes it away himself, so we need neither hide it nor despair of it. His people should judge as slowly and fairly as this priest, never treat illness as a sign of special sin, and go out to the lonely as he did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-46 — Leprous Disease and the Priest's Examination
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priest’s task is to tell the truth about a frightening disease, patiently and fairly, because a verdict of unclean meant exclusion from God’s camp. Case after case is brought to him: swellings, eruptions and spots (vv. 1–8), a chronic disease (vv. 9–17), boils and burns (vv. 18–28), and sores of the head and beard (vv. 29–44). In each he looks for the same signs, whether the hair has turned white and whether the mark lies deeper than the skin, and where he is unsure he waits seven days and looks again. Scars, harmless spots and baldness are declared clean. Only then come the two verses that show what was at stake: the unclean person mourned, cried a warning and lived alone outside the camp (vv. 45–46).
verseByVerse.theology: The priest's work is careful judgment. He waits, looks again, and refuses to condemn too soon, and the law protects the healthy from a wrong verdict as much as it protects the camp from disease.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the priest was told to look twice before he spoke. Now: Christians, quick to judge one another, can learn the same patience before deciding what is wrong with someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, "When a person has on the skin of his body a swelling or an eruption or a spot, and it turns into a case of leprous disease on the skin of his body, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons the priests, and the priest shall examine the diseased area on the skin of his body. And if the hair in the diseased area has turned white and the disease appears to be deeper than the skin of his body, it is a case of leprous disease. When the priest has examined him, he shall pronounce him unclean. But if the spot is white in the skin of his body and appears no deeper than the skin, and the hair in it has not turned white, the priest shall shut up the diseased person for seven days. And the priest shall examine him on the seventh day, and if in his eyes the disease is checked and the disease has not spread in the skin, then the priest shall shut him up for another seven days. And the priest shall examine him again on the seventh day, and if the diseased area has faded and the disease has not spread in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him clean; it is only an eruption. And he shall wash his clothes and be clean. But if the eruption spreads in the skin, after he has shown himself to the priest for his cleansing, he shall appear again before the priest. And the priest shall look, and if the eruption has spread in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a leprous disease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a suspicious mark appears on someone’s skin, the priest must examine it carefully and give God’s verdict, clean or unclean, without rushing to condemn.

A case of leprous disease. The Hebrew is tsara’at. It is not modern leprosy (Hansen’s disease), and the traditional English rendering has caused much confusion. It covers surface conditions on skin, cloth and even house walls, some of which plainly heal on their own (see the box below).

He shall be brought to Aaron the priest. Not to a physician. No treatment is prescribed anywhere in the chapter: the priest is there not to cure but to say which of two words applies, clean or unclean, and so whether this person may come near the place where God lives.

Unhurried judgment. If the signs are doubtful (the hair not white, the mark no deeper than the skin), the priest shuts the person away for seven days, looks again, and if need be waits seven more: two weeks before anyone is declared anything. A mark that faded was “only an eruption” (v. 6), and washing his clothes was enough.

Was the sufferer being punished for sin? Not as a rule. A few people in Scripture were struck with this disease as a judgment (Miriam, Gehazi, King Uzziah), but the law here makes no accusation and requires no confession. Unclean is not the same as sinful. The disease made a person unfit to enter the camp where God dwelt because, as Aaron said of Miriam, its sufferer looked “as one dead, whose flesh is half eaten away” (Numbers 12:12), and death has no place in the presence of the living God. Quarantine also protected the community, but the chief lesson is theological.

The priest who heals. Aaron’s sons could pronounce but never heal; Jesus declared a leper clean and made him so with one word (Matthew 8:2–3). These rules no longer bind Christians as law, but their lesson stands. Illness is no sign of greater sin (John 9:2–3), and a church should judge as slowly as this priest.

Uncertain wording. The exact meaning of tsara’at is unknown. It covers skin, fabric and walls, and its signs (white hair, a patch deeper than the skin, spreading) match no single modern disease. The Greek translation used lepra, a general word for scaly skin, which gave us “leprosy”. Likely it means a family of spreading, flaking or discoloured conditions that looked like decay. The “itch” (v. 30) and “leukoderma” (v. 39) are also best guesses.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprous disease” is the ESV's rendering; older versions have simply “leprosy”.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man is afflicted with a leprous disease, he shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall look. And if there is a white swelling in the skin that has turned the hair white, and there is raw flesh in the swelling, it is a chronic leprous disease in the skin of his body, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean. He shall not shut him up, for he is unclean. And if the leprous disease breaks out in the skin, so that the leprous disease covers all the skin of the diseased person from head to foot, so far as the priest can see, then the priest shall look, and if the leprous disease has covered all his body, he shall pronounce him clean of the disease; it has all turned white, and he is clean. But when raw flesh appears on him, he shall be unclean. And the priest shall examine the raw flesh and pronounce him unclean. Raw flesh is unclean, for it is a leprous disease. But if the raw flesh recovers and turns white again, then he shall come to the priest, and the priest shall examine him, and if the disease has turned white, then the priest shall pronounce the diseased person clean; he is clean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A long-established case with raw flesh is unclean, but, against all instinct, a man turned white from head to foot is clean. The priest judges by God’s signs, not by how bad it looks.

A chronic leprous disease. Where a white swelling shows raw flesh, the disease is settled and there is no waiting: “He shall not shut him up, for he is unclean” (v. 11).

It has all turned white, and he is clean. When the condition covers the whole body and has turned white, the man is clean; raw flesh makes him unclean again, and when it heals over white he is clean once more. Whatever the medical reason (perhaps white skin was healed skin, and raw flesh active disease), the priest plainly applies God’s standard, not his own reaction.

For us. Appearances mislead: some who look worst may be nearest to healing. Only God sees truly (1 Samuel 16:7).

verseByVerse.quote: "If there is in the skin of one's body a boil and it heals, and in the place of the boil there comes a white swelling or a reddish-white spot, then it shall be shown to the priest. And the priest shall look, and if it appears deeper than the skin and its hair has turned white, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is a case of leprous disease that has broken out in the boil. But if the priest examines it and there is no white hair in it and it is not deeper than the skin, but has faded, then the priest shall shut him up seven days. And if it spreads in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a disease. But if the spot remains in one place and does not spread, it is the scar of the boil, and the priest shall pronounce him clean. "Or, when the body has a burn on its skin and the raw flesh of the burn becomes a spot, reddish-white or white, the priest shall examine it, and if the hair in the spot has turned white and it appears deeper than the skin, then it is a leprous disease. It has broken out in the burn, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a case of leprous disease. But if the priest examines it and there is no white hair in the spot and it is no deeper than the skin, but has faded, the priest shall shut him up seven days, and the priest shall examine him the seventh day. If it is spreading in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a case of leprous disease. But if the spot remains in one place and does not spread in the skin, but has faded, it is a swelling from the burn, and the priest shall pronounce him clean, for it is the scar of the burn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A boil or burn that has healed with a scar is clean; only a mark that goes deeper and spreads is declared unclean.

It is the scar of the boil. For boil and burn alike, white hair and a mark deeper than the skin mean disease; otherwise the priest waits seven days. If the spot stays in one place, the finding is “it is the scar of the boil” (v. 23) or “it is the scar of the burn” (v. 28), and the man is pronounced clean.

Protecting the healthy. The chapter is as concerned not to condemn the healthy as to identify the sick: a scar marks a wound that has healed, and must not be mistaken for one that is spreading.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man or woman has a disease on the head or the beard, the priest shall examine the disease. And if it appears deeper than the skin, and the hair in it is yellow and thin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is an itch, a leprous disease of the head or the beard. And if the priest examines the itching disease and it appears no deeper than the skin and there is no black hair in it, then the priest shall shut up the person with the itching disease for seven days, and on the seventh day the priest shall examine the disease. If the itch has not spread, and there is in it no yellow hair, and the itch appears to be no deeper than the skin, then he shall shave himself, but the itch he shall not shave; and the priest shall shut up the person with the itching disease for another seven days. And on the seventh day the priest shall examine the itch, and if the itch has not spread in the skin and it appears to be no deeper than the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him clean. And he shall wash his clothes and be clean. But if the itch spreads in the skin after his cleansing, then the priest shall examine him, and if the itch has spread in the skin, the priest need not seek for the yellow hair; he is unclean. But if in his eyes the itch is unchanged and black hair has grown in it, the itch is healed and he is clean, and the priest shall pronounce him clean. "When a man or a woman has spots on the skin of the body, white spots, the priest shall look, and if the spots on the skin of the body are of a dull white, it is leukoderma that has broken out in the skin; he is clean. "If a man's hair falls out from his head, he is bald; he is clean. And if a man's hair falls out from his forehead, he has baldness of the forehead; he is clean. But if there is on the bald head or the bald forehead a reddish-white diseased area, it is a leprous disease breaking out on his bald head or his bald forehead. Then the priest shall examine him, and if the diseased swelling is reddish-white on his bald head or on his bald forehead, like the appearance of leprous disease in the skin of the body, he is a leprous man, he is unclean. The priest must pronounce him unclean; his disease is on his head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sores of the scalp and beard need the same careful sorting, and harmless white spots and ordinary baldness are declared clean.

Fine distinctions. For the scalp the signs change: yellow, thin hair shows disease, and black hair growing back shows healing (vv. 30, 37). The person shaves around the patch but not the patch itself, so the priest can watch its edges (v. 33).

Trained to tell the difference. As with the food laws, someone must be trained to tell one thing from another, and the whole community depends on his getting it right. A wrong verdict either way does damage: a diseased man left in the camp, or a healthy man put out of it.

He is bald; he is clean. A mercy easily missed: dull white spots are only leukoderma, and “he is clean” (v. 39); “If a man’s hair falls out from his head, he is bald; he is clean” (v. 40). In a chapter this alert to skin, someone had to say so. Only a reddish-white sore on the bald patch counts as disease (vv. 42–44).

verseByVerse.quote: "The leprous person who has the disease shall wear torn clothes and let the hair of his head hang loose, and he shall cover his upper lip and cry out, 'Unclean, unclean.' He shall remain unclean as long as he has the disease. He is unclean. He shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The person declared unclean must live as a mourner, warn others away and dwell alone outside the camp, cut off from God’s house and from human touch.

Wear torn clothes. Two verses carry the human weight of the whole chapter. Torn clothes and loosened hair are the signs of mourning, the very signs Aaron was forbidden three chapters earlier (10:6). A man with this condition dresses for a funeral, and the funeral is his own. He must cover his upper lip and cry his own defilement aloud, “Unclean, unclean”, so that nobody comes near by accident. Then comes the starkest sentence in Leviticus: “He shall live alone.”

Outside the camp. He is not merely ill. Outside the camp means away from the tabernacle, from the worship of God and from every human touch, for as long as the disease lasts. In a book about drawing near, here is a man who may not.

The touch that made clean. This is why the Gospels keep bringing lepers to Jesus, and why what he does with them is never merely a healing: “And a leper came to him, imploring him, and kneeling said to him, ‘If you will, you can make me clean.’ Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him” (Mark 1:40–41). He did not have to touch him; he healed an official’s son without going near him (John 4:46–53). He touched this man because very likely nobody had touched him since the priest pronounced him unclean. And the direction of that touch is the gospel in a single gesture. Under this chapter, contact with the unclean made the clean unclean; here the clean one made the unclean clean. He could, because in time he would go outside the camp himself, for “Jesus also suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12), and bear the outcast’s sentence in his place.

The loneliness we chose. “He shall live alone” was the worst sentence this chapter could pass. Modern Western life has turned it, for many, into a lifestyle we call freedom. In 2023 the United States Surgeon General, Vivek Murthy, issued a public advisory calling loneliness and isolation an epidemic, with effects on health he compared to smoking. No priest had to put us outside the camp; we walked out, thinking belonging would cost too much. Yet “It is not good that the man should be alone” (Genesis 2:18). Jesus was put outside the camp and was truly alone, forsaken even by his Father (Mark 15:34), so that no one who belongs to him ever would be. And he saves people not into a private spirituality but into a family, a new camp with himself at its centre, where those who once cried “Unclean” are welcomed to the table.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The uncleanness that marks the body can get into the things people wear and use, and it must be dealt with there too. Wool, linen and leather showing greenish or reddish patches are shown to the priest and shut away for seven days (vv. 47–50). If the patch has spread, the article is burned (vv. 51–52). If not, it is washed and watched another week, and burned if the patch is unchanged (vv. 53–55). If it has faded, the patch is torn out, and an article from which the blight has gone is washed a second time and declared clean (vv. 56–58). A closing summary ends the law (v. 59). Nothing is destroyed in haste, and nothing tainted is kept.
verseByVerse.theology: Decay was not treated as a purely personal matter. It could get into the things people owned, and it had to be dealt with there too.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a garment was washed and watched, and burned only as a last resort. Now: it is worth asking whether something we own, or a habit attached to it, keeps drawing us away from God, and dealing with it patiently but firmly.

verseByVerse.quote: "When there is a case of leprous disease in a garment, whether a woolen or a linen garment, in warp or woof of linen or wool, or in a skin or in anything made of skin, if the disease is greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the skin or in the warp or the woof or in any article made of skin, it is a case of leprous disease, and it shall be shown to the priest. And the priest shall examine the disease and shut up that which has the disease for seven days. Then he shall examine the disease on the seventh day. If the disease has spread in the garment, in the warp or the woof, or in the skin, whatever be the use of the skin, the disease is a persistent leprous disease; it is unclean. And he shall burn the garment, or the warp or the woof, the wool or the linen, or any article made of skin that is diseased, for it is a persistent leprous disease. It shall be burned in the fire. "And if the priest examines, and if the disease has not spread in the garment, in the warp or the woof or in any article made of skin, then the priest shall command that they wash the thing in which is the disease, and he shall shut it up for another seven days. And the priest shall examine the diseased thing after it has been washed. And if the appearance of the diseased area has not changed, though the disease has not spread, it is unclean. You shall burn it in the fire, whether the rot is on the back or on the front. "But if the priest examines, and if the diseased area has faded after it has been washed, he shall tear it out of the garment or the skin or the warp or the woof. Then if it appears again in the garment, in the warp or the woof, or in any article made of skin, it is spreading. You shall burn with fire whatever has the disease. But the garment, or the warp or the woof, or any article made of skin from which the disease departs when you have washed it, shall then be washed a second time, and be clean." This is the law for a case of leprous disease in a garment of wool or linen, either in the warp or the woof, or in any article made of skin, to determine whether it is clean or unclean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same patient inspection applies to cloth and leather: an article with a spreading blight must be burned, but one that washes clean may be kept.

Leprous disease in a garment. Probably mould or mildew (v. 49). Nothing is destroyed in haste: the article is shut away, washed and examined again, and burned only if the patch spreads or will not change (vv. 51–55).

Not a purely personal matter. Corruption could get into the things people owned and wore, and it had to be looked for there too. The next chapter takes it one step further and finds it in the walls of a house (14:33–53).

For us. Jude borrows the picture: show mercy to sinners, “hating even the garment stained by the flesh” (Jude 23). Whatever we own that keeps drawing us from God deserves this chapter’s treatment, patient but firm.

Uncertain wording. “Warp or woof” normally means the lengthwise and crosswise threads of weaving, but in finished cloth these could hardly be affected separately. Perhaps yarn prepared for weaving is meant, or two kinds of material; the exact sense is unclear, though the point is plain: any article of wool, linen or leather.

13.theology:
Sin's nature pictured. Skin disease, working beneath the surface and breaking out visibly, is a picture of sin: it defiles, spreads, disfigures and cuts off from God. The sufferer himself is not accused.

The priest who heals. The priest could diagnose and declare but not cure; only the Great High Priest both pronounces and heals.

Outside the camp. The exile of the leper is reversed by Christ, who took the outcast's place to bring the outcast home.
13.examples:
Then: the diseased lived alone outside the camp, cut off from worship and community.

Now: we bring our defilement honestly to the Great Priest, who does not banish us but touches us and makes us clean. And those whose illness has cut them off from church and friends can know that he is not ashamed to come near.

keyVerse.quote: He shall remain unclean as long as he has the disease. He is unclean. He shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp.
keyVerse.note: Every careful examination in the chapter leads towards or away from this sentence, and it shows what uncleanness finally means: exclusion from God’s presence and from his people. It is the sentence Jesus reversed when he touched a leper, and the place he went himself when he suffered outside the gate so that the excluded could be brought home.

13.reflection:
The priest waited, looked again and refused to condemn too soon, and he was as careful to declare the healthy clean as to declare the sick unclean. What would it look like for us to judge one another with the same patience and fairness?

Leviticus never treats the person with skin disease as guilty, yet many people still assume that suffering means special sin. Why is that assumption so persistent, and how should we speak to someone who is ill?

“He shall live alone” (v. 46) was the hardest sentence in the chapter. Who around you lives “outside the camp” today, by circumstance or by choice, and how could your church go out to them as Jesus did?

Jesus touched the leper and made him clean instead of becoming unclean himself. What does that tell you about how he receives you, and what might you need to bring to him that you have kept hidden?

14.title: The Cleansing of the Leper: Two Birds and Living Water
14.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"This shall be the law of the leprous person for the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest,<sup>3</sup>and the priest shall go out of the camp, and the priest shall look. Then, if the case of leprous disease is healed in the leprous person,<sup>4</sup>the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two live clean birds and cedarwood and scarlet yarn and hyssop.<sup>5</sup>And the priest shall command them to kill one of the birds in an earthenware vessel over fresh water.<sup>6</sup>He shall take the live bird with the cedarwood and the scarlet yarn and the hyssop, and dip them and the live bird in the blood of the bird that was killed over the fresh water.<sup>7</sup>And he shall sprinkle it seven times on him who is to be cleansed of the leprous disease. Then he shall pronounce him clean and shall let the living bird go into the open field.<sup>8</sup>And he who is to be cleansed shall wash his clothes and shave off all his hair and bathe himself in water, and he shall be clean. And after that he may come into the camp, but live outside his tent seven days.<sup>9</sup>And on the seventh day he shall shave off all his hair from his head, his beard, and his eyebrows. He shall shave off all his hair, and then he shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and he shall be clean.<sup>10</sup>"And on the eighth day he shall take two male lambs without blemish, and one ewe lamb a year old without blemish, and a grain offering of three tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil, and one log of oil.<sup>11</sup>And the priest who cleanses him shall set the man who is to be cleansed and these things before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>12</sup>And the priest shall take one of the male lambs and offer it for a guilt offering, along with the log of oil, and wave them for a wave offering before the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And he shall kill the lamb in the place where they kill the sin offering and the burnt offering, in the place of the sanctuary. For the guilt offering, like the sin offering, belongs to the priest; it is most holy.<sup>14</sup>The priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering, and the priest shall put it on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot.<sup>15</sup>Then the priest shall take some of the log of oil and pour it into the palm of his own left hand<sup>16</sup>and dip his right finger in the oil that is in his left hand and sprinkle some oil with his finger seven times before the LORD.<sup>17</sup>And some of the oil that remains in his hand the priest shall put on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot, on top of the blood of the guilt offering.<sup>18</sup>And the rest of the oil that is in the priest's hand he shall put on the head of him who is to be cleansed. Then the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD.<sup>19</sup>The priest shall offer the sin offering, to make atonement for him who is to be cleansed from his uncleanness. And afterward he shall kill the burnt offering.<sup>20</sup>And the priest shall offer the burnt offering and the grain offering on the altar. Thus the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be clean.<sup>21</sup>"But if he is poor and cannot afford so much, then he shall take one male lamb for a guilt offering to be waved, to make atonement for him, and a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering, and a log of oil;<sup>22</sup>also two turtledoves or two pigeons, whichever he can afford. The one shall be a sin offering and the other a burnt offering.<sup>23</sup>And on the eighth day he shall bring them for his cleansing to the priest, to the entrance of the tent of meeting, before the LORD.<sup>24</sup>And the priest shall take the lamb of the guilt offering and the log of oil, and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before the LORD.<sup>25</sup>And he shall kill the lamb of the guilt offering. And the priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering and put it on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot.<sup>26</sup>And the priest shall pour some of the oil into the palm of his own left hand,<sup>27</sup>and shall sprinkle with his right finger some of the oil that is in his left hand seven times before the LORD.<sup>28</sup>And the priest shall put some of the oil that is in his hand on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot, in the place where the blood of the guilt offering was put.<sup>29</sup>And the rest of the oil that is in the priest's hand he shall put on the head of him who is to be cleansed, to make atonement for him before the LORD.<sup>30</sup>And he shall offer, of the turtledoves or pigeons, whichever he can afford,<sup>31</sup>one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering, along with a grain offering. And the priest shall make atonement before the LORD for him who is being cleansed.<sup>32</sup>This is the law for him in whom is a case of leprous disease, who cannot afford the offerings for his cleansing."<sup>33</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying,<sup>34</sup>"When you come into the land of Canaan, which I give you for a possession, and I put a case of leprous disease in a house in the land of your possession,<sup>35</sup>then he who owns the house shall come and tell the priest, 'There seems to me to be some case of disease in my house.'<sup>36</sup>Then the priest shall command that they empty the house before the priest goes to examine the disease, lest all that is in the house be declared unclean. And afterward the priest shall go in to see the house.<sup>37</sup>And he shall examine the disease. And if the disease is in the walls of the house with greenish or reddish spots, and if it appears to be deeper than the surface,<sup>38</sup>then the priest shall go out of the house to the door of the house and shut up the house seven days.<sup>39</sup>And the priest shall come again on the seventh day, and look. If the disease has spread in the walls of the house,<sup>40</sup>then the priest shall command that they take out the stones in which is the disease and throw them into an unclean place outside the city.<sup>41</sup>And he shall have the inside of the house scraped all around, and the plaster that they scrape off they shall pour out in an unclean place outside the city.<sup>42</sup>Then they shall take other stones and put them in the place of those stones, and he shall take other plaster and plaster the house.<sup>43</sup>"If the disease breaks out again in the house, after he has taken out the stones and scraped the house and plastered it,<sup>44</sup>then the priest shall go and look.
