And if the disease has spread in the house, it is a persistent leprous disease in the house; it is unclean.<sup>45</sup>And he shall break down the house, its stones and timber and all the plaster of the house, and he shall carry them out of the city to an unclean place.<sup>46</sup>Moreover, whoever enters the house while it is shut up shall be unclean until the evening,<sup>47</sup>and whoever sleeps in the house shall wash his clothes, and whoever eats in the house shall wash his clothes.<sup>48</sup>"But if the priest comes and looks, and if the disease has not spread in the house after the house was plastered, then the priest shall pronounce the house clean, for the disease is healed.<sup>49</sup>And for the cleansing of the house he shall take two small birds, with cedarwood and scarlet yarn and hyssop,<sup>50</sup>and shall kill one of the birds in an earthenware vessel over fresh water<sup>51</sup>and shall take the cedarwood and the hyssop and the scarlet yarn, along with the live bird, and dip them in the blood of the bird that was killed and in the fresh water and sprinkle the house seven times.<sup>52</sup>Thus he shall cleanse the house with the blood of the bird and with the fresh water and with the live bird and with the cedarwood and hyssop and scarlet yarn.<sup>53</sup>And he shall let the live bird go out of the city into the open country. So he shall make atonement for the house, and it shall be clean."<sup>54</sup>This is the law for any case of leprous disease: for an itch,<sup>55</sup>for leprous disease in a garment or in a house,<sup>56</sup>and for a swelling or an eruption or a spot,<sup>57</sup>to show when it is unclean and when it is clean. This is the law for leprous disease.
14.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 13 taught the priest to diagnose skin disease and sent the unclean outside the camp. Chapter 14 provides for the day the disease has gone: the ceremony that brings the healed man home, and then a law for disease in the walls of houses.

The message. God does not only shut the unclean out; he makes a way back in, complete and open to rich and poor alike. The man who lived as one dead is cleansed by the blood of a substitute, washed, and anointed like a priest, and so restored to his family and to the worship of God.

Why it was said. A diagnosis with no road back would have left a healed man an outcast for life. Israel needed to know that recovery was not the end: the man had to be declared clean and brought before God again. And a people about to receive houses in Canaan needed to know that their homes were under God’s eye too (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The priest goes out to the healed man; one bird dies, and the other is dipped in its blood and set free (vv. 1–7). The man washes, shaves and waits a week (vv. 8–9). On the eighth day come four offerings, with blood and oil on his ear, thumb and toe (vv. 10–20), and the same rite at lower cost for the poor (vv. 21–32). Then houses in the land: inspection, repair or demolition (vv. 33–47), and cleansing with two birds, before a summary closes chapters 13 and 14 (vv. 48–57).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern. The law had a ceremony for a cure it could not give, and when Jesus healed lepers he sent them to the priests to offer “what Moses commanded” (Mark 1:44), living evidence that the healer had come. The New Testament does not interpret the two birds, so the picture should be held lightly, but its shape is plain, and it returns with the two goats of chapter 16: one dies, and the other goes free marked by its blood. In Christ the outcast is not merely let back in but made part of “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9).

For us. Grace does not leave us at the edge of the camp. Christ brings the unclean all the way home, the poor as fully as the rich, and his people should welcome back those long absent, through illness or failure, as patiently and completely as this chapter does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-32 — The Cleansing of the Leper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God restores the healed outcast completely, step by step, and the poor man as fully as the rich. The priest goes out of the camp to the man and, if the disease has healed, performs the rite of the two birds: one is killed over fresh water, and the other, dipped in its blood, is released (vv. 1–7). The man washes, shaves and waits a week inside the camp but outside his tent (vv. 8–9). On the eighth day come the guilt, sin, burnt and grain offerings, with blood and oil placed on his right ear, thumb and big toe, as at the ordination of the priests (vv. 10–20). If he is poor, birds replace two of the lambs, but every part of the ceremony done to him remains (vv. 21–32).
verseByVerse.theology: Restoration is God's work from start to finish. The priest goes out to the man, the rites bring him in, and nothing depends on whether he can afford the full price.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the man who had lived alone was walked back into the camp step by step. Now: a church welcoming back someone long absent, through illness or failure, can do the same: patiently and completely.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "This shall be the law of the leprous person for the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall go out of the camp, and the priest shall look. Then, if the case of leprous disease is healed in the leprous person, the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two live clean birds and cedarwood and scarlet yarn and hyssop. And the priest shall command them to kill one of the birds in an earthenware vessel over fresh water. He shall take the live bird with the cedarwood and the scarlet yarn and the hyssop, and dip them and the live bird in the blood of the bird that was killed over the fresh water. And he shall sprinkle it seven times on him who is to be cleansed of the leprous disease. Then he shall pronounce him clean and shall let the living bird go into the open field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the disease has healed, the priest goes out to the man and declares him clean through a rite in which one bird dies and the other goes free marked by its blood.

The priest shall go out of the camp. The man cannot come in until he is pronounced clean, so the priest walks out to where he is. The healing has already happened (v. 3): the law does not heal, but it recognises a healing God has given.

Two live clean birds. One bird is killed in a clay pot over “fresh water”, literally “living water”. The other, with cedarwood, scarlet yarn and hyssop, is dipped in its blood; the man is sprinkled seven times, the number of completeness, and the living bird is released over open country. Everyone standing there watched a bird fly off wearing the blood of its substitute.

Two birds, two goats. Chapter 16 will do this again with two goats: one dies; the other goes free, marked by that death, and carries the uncleanness out of sight. The New Testament does not interpret the birds, so the picture should be held lightly; some have also heard in the blood over living water an echo of the blood and water from Christ’s side (John 19:34).

Hyssop. A small bushy plant used as a brush. With hyssop Israel painted the blood on their doorposts at Passover (Exodus 12:22), and on hyssop the sour wine was lifted to the mouth of Christ on the cross (John 19:29). John seems to want his readers to notice.

Show yourself to the priest. This is the ceremony Jesus had in view when he healed lepers and told them, “go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, for a proof to them” (Mark 1:44; Luke 17:14). The law had a rite for a cure it could not give. When Jesus sent cleansed men to the priests, he was handing them evidence that the One who heals had come.
verseByVerse.note: “Fresh water” is literally “living water” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And he who is to be cleansed shall wash his clothes and shave off all his hair and bathe himself in water, and he shall be clean. And after that he may come into the camp, but live outside his tent seven days. And on the seventh day he shall shave off all his hair from his head, his beard, and his eyebrows. He shall shave off all his hair, and then he shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and he shall be clean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cleansed man washes, shaves off all his hair and waits seven more days, coming home step by step.

Shave off all his hair. Twice, even his eyebrows: a clean break with the old condition. He may come into the camp, but must still “live outside his tent seven days” (v. 8).

Slow, but not a punishment. Restoration was complete, and slow, but every stage brought him one step nearer home. Hebrews uses the same language for the believer’s approach to God: “our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22).

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the eighth day he shall take two male lambs without blemish, and one ewe lamb a year old without blemish, and a grain offering of three tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil, and one log of oil. And the priest who cleanses him shall set the man who is to be cleansed and these things before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And the priest shall take one of the male lambs and offer it for a guilt offering, along with the log of oil, and wave them for a wave offering before the LORD. And he shall kill the lamb in the place where they kill the sin offering and the burnt offering, in the place of the sanctuary. For the guilt offering, like the sin offering, belongs to the priest; it is most holy. The priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering, and the priest shall put it on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot. Then the priest shall take some of the log of oil and pour it into the palm of his own left hand and dip his right finger in the oil that is in his left hand and sprinkle some oil with his finger seven times before the LORD. And some of the oil that remains in his hand the priest shall put on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot, on top of the blood of the guilt offering. And the rest of the oil that is in the priest's hand he shall put on the head of him who is to be cleansed. Then the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD. The priest shall offer the sin offering, to make atonement for him who is to be cleansed from his uncleanness. And afterward he shall kill the burnt offering. And the priest shall offer the burnt offering and the grain offering on the altar. Thus the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be clean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the eighth day the cleansed man brings offerings, and blood and oil are put on his ear, thumb and toe as at the ordination of priests: he is not merely readmitted but brought near to God.

Ear, thumb and toe. After the guilt offering, the first of four, its blood and then oil go on his right ear, thumb and big toe. This echoes the ordination of Aaron and his sons, where blood was put on the same three places and they were anointed with oil (8:23–24, 30). And it is now done to a man who a few weeks ago lived alone outside the camp crying “Unclean”. Many have seen in it the whole person claimed for God: the ear to hear him, the hand to serve him, the foot to walk in his ways.

Why does a healed man need offerings? His disease had shut him out of God’s presence, and the offerings restored him. Some cases were judgments (Numbers 12:10; 2 Chronicles 26:19), but Leviticus does not say every case was punishment for sin.

Made a priest. In Christ the outcast is welcomed in the same way: not to the back row, but into a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), washed and anointed by his Spirit (1 John 2:20).
verseByVerse.note: A log was about a third of a litre (the ESV note gives 1/3 quart).

verseByVerse.quote: "But if he is poor and cannot afford so much, then he shall take one male lamb for a guilt offering to be waved, to make atonement for him, and a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering, and a log of oil; also two turtledoves or two pigeons, whichever he can afford. The one shall be a sin offering and the other a burnt offering. And on the eighth day he shall bring them for his cleansing to the priest, to the entrance of the tent of meeting, before the LORD. And the priest shall take the lamb of the guilt offering and the log of oil, and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before the LORD. And he shall kill the lamb of the guilt offering. And the priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering and put it on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot. And the priest shall pour some of the oil into the palm of his own left hand, and shall sprinkle with his right finger some of the oil that is in his left hand seven times before the LORD. And the priest shall put some of the oil that is in his hand on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot, in the place where the blood of the guilt offering was put. And the rest of the oil that is in the priest's hand he shall put on the head of him who is to be cleansed, to make atonement for him before the LORD. And he shall offer, of the turtledoves or pigeons, whichever he can afford, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering, along with a grain offering. And the priest shall make atonement before the LORD for him who is being cleansed. This is the law for him in whom is a case of leprous disease, who cannot afford the offerings for his cleansing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the man is poor, God lowers the cost of the animals but not one part of what is done for him: he is restored as fully as the rich.

If he is poor and cannot afford so much. Birds replace two of the lambs and the flour is reduced (vv. 21–22). But read what is not reduced. The blood still goes on the ear, the thumb and the big toe; the oil still goes on top of it; the seven sprinklings still happen. Every symbolic element survives intact; only the cost comes down (compare 5:7–10).

No half-restoration. God will not have a poor man half restored. Mary brought the poor family’s birds for her own purification (Luke 2:24; Leviticus 12:8), and the Son of God grew up among people who needed this paragraph. In the gospel there is no cheaper grace for the poor and no better grace for the rich: all come with nothing, and all receive the whole of Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s care reaches the houses his people will live in, and he provides for trouble before they meet it. In Canaan, a householder who sees signs of disease in his walls tells the priest, who has the house emptied first so that its contents are not declared unclean (vv. 33–36). Infected stones are removed and the walls scraped and replastered (vv. 37–42). If the disease returns, the house is pulled down, and anyone who entered it while it was shut up must wash (vv. 43–47). If it does not, the house is cleansed with the same rite of two birds used for a healed person, so that even a building is made clean by a death (vv. 48–53). A summary closes the laws of chapters 13 and 14 (vv. 54–57).
verseByVerse.theology: God's care reaches homes as well as bodies, and he provides for trouble before his people meet it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a family whose walls were spotted with mould had a law to turn to. Now: no part of a household's life, its repairs and worries included, lies outside God's concern.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, "When you come into the land of Canaan, which I give you for a possession, and I put a case of leprous disease in a house in the land of your possession, then he who owns the house shall come and tell the priest, 'There seems to me to be some case of disease in my house.' Then the priest shall command that they empty the house before the priest goes to examine the disease, lest all that is in the house be declared unclean. And afterward the priest shall go in to see the house. And he shall examine the disease. And if the disease is in the walls of the house with greenish or reddish spots, and if it appears to be deeper than the surface, then the priest shall go out of the house to the door of the house and shut up the house seven days. And the priest shall come again on the seventh day, and look. If the disease has spread in the walls of the house, then the priest shall command that they take out the stones in which is the disease and throw them into an unclean place outside the city. And he shall have the inside of the house scraped all around, and the plaster that they scrape off they shall pour out in an unclean place outside the city. Then they shall take other stones and put them in the place of those stones, and he shall take other plaster and plaster the house. "If the disease breaks out again in the house, after he has taken out the stones and scraped the house and plastered it, then the priest shall go and look. And if the disease has spread in the house, it is a persistent leprous disease in the house; it is unclean. And he shall break down the house, its stones and timber and all the plaster of the house, and he shall carry them out of the city to an unclean place. Moreover, whoever enters the house while it is shut up shall be unclean until the evening, and whoever sleeps in the house shall wash his clothes, and whoever eats in the house shall wash his clothes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the land is theirs, a house showing signs of disease is to be examined, repaired and, if need be, pulled down, with care for the family’s belongings.

When you come into the land of Canaan. A law for houses in a land Israel had not yet entered. Strikingly, God says “I put a case of leprous disease in a house” (v. 34): even the mould is not outside his rule.

Lest all that is in the house be declared unclean. The house is emptied before the priest goes in (v. 36), so nobody loses their furniture to a diagnosis not yet made.

Repair before demolition. Infected stones are replaced and the walls replastered (vv. 40–42); only if the disease returns is the house pulled down (vv. 43–45). As with garments: patient, but final when it must be.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if the priest comes and looks, and if the disease has not spread in the house after the house was plastered, then the priest shall pronounce the house clean, for the disease is healed. And for the cleansing of the house he shall take two small birds, with cedarwood and scarlet yarn and hyssop, and shall kill one of the birds in an earthenware vessel over fresh water and shall take the cedarwood and the hyssop and the scarlet yarn, along with the live bird, and dip them in the blood of the bird that was killed and in the fresh water and sprinkle the house seven times. Thus he shall cleanse the house with the blood of the bird and with the fresh water and with the live bird and with the cedarwood and hyssop and scarlet yarn. And he shall let the live bird go out of the city into the open country. So he shall make atonement for the house, and it shall be clean." This is the law for any case of leprous disease: for an itch, for leprous disease in a garment or in a house, and for a swelling or an eruption or a spot, to show when it is unclean and when it is clean. This is the law for leprous disease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A house that stays clean after repair is pronounced clean and cleansed with the rite of two birds, and the long law of skin disease comes to an end.

Two small birds. The ritual of vv. 4–7 is used again: “So he shall make atonement for the house” (v. 53). Even a building is cleansed by a death and a release.

Before they arrive. These are houses they did not build in a land given as a gift, and God tells them in advance that corruption will be found there too, and provides the remedy before they arrive.

This is the law for leprous disease. The closing summary gathers chapters 13 and 14, “to show when it is unclean and when it is clean” (v. 57). The aim was never simply to expel, but to see truly and to restore. No part of a household’s life, its walls and repairs and worries included, lies outside God’s concern.

14.theology:
The rite Jesus pointed to. Jesus sent the lepers he cleansed to the priest with the offering of this chapter (Mark 1:44), proof that the Healer the law could only wait for had come.

From outcast to priest. The cleansed leper is consecrated like a priest; grace does not merely let the forgiven back in; it raises them to holy service.
14.examples:
Then: a healed leper was sprinkled, washed, and brought home.

Now: every sinner cleansed by Christ is brought home in the same way, not merely let back in but made a priest to God, however little he had to bring.

keyVerse.quote: And he shall sprinkle it seven times on him who is to be cleansed of the leprous disease. Then he shall pronounce him clean and shall let the living bird go into the open field.
keyVerse.note: This is the moment the outcast hears the word he has waited for: clean. It comes only after a death, and the living bird flies off marked with the blood of the one that died, a picture the Day of Atonement will repeat with two goats. It points to the cleansing Christ gives, freely, by his own blood.

14.reflection:
The priest went out of the camp to the healed man, because the man could not come in (v. 3). How does this picture what God has done for us in Christ, and what might it mean for us to go out to people rather than wait for them to come to us?

The cleansed man was given the same blood and oil on ear, thumb and toe as the priests (vv. 14–17). How does it change the way you see yourself to know that God does not merely tolerate forgiven sinners but brings them near?

The poor man brought cheaper offerings, but nothing was left out of what was done for him (vv. 21–32). Where might our churches, perhaps without meaning to, offer the poor a smaller welcome than the rich?

Restoration took eight days, with washing and waiting at each stage. How can a church welcome back someone long absent, through illness, failure or discipline, patiently and completely?

15.title: Bodily Discharges: The Pervasiveness of Defilement
15.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any man has a discharge from his body, his discharge is unclean.<sup>3</sup>And this is the law of his uncleanness for a discharge: whether his body runs with his discharge, or his body is blocked up by his discharge, it is his uncleanness.<sup>4</sup>Every bed on which the one with the discharge lies shall be unclean, and everything on which he sits shall be unclean.<sup>5</sup>And anyone who touches his bed shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>6</sup>And whoever sits on anything on which the one with the discharge has sat shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>7</sup>And whoever touches the body of the one with the discharge shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>8</sup>And if the one with the discharge spits on someone who is clean, then he shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>9</sup>And any saddle on which the one with the discharge rides shall be unclean.<sup>10</sup>And whoever touches anything that was under him shall be unclean until the evening. And whoever carries such things shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>11</sup>Anyone whom the one with the discharge touches without having rinsed his hands in water shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>12</sup>And an earthenware vessel that the one with the discharge touches shall be broken, and every vessel of wood shall be rinsed in water.<sup>13</sup>"And when the one with a discharge is cleansed of his discharge, then he shall count for himself seven days for his cleansing, and wash his clothes. And he shall bathe his body in fresh water and shall be clean.<sup>14</sup>And on the eighth day he shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons and come before the LORD to the entrance of the tent of meeting and give them to the priest.<sup>15</sup>And the priest shall use them, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD for his discharge.<sup>16</sup>"If a man has an emission of semen, he shall bathe his whole body in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>17</sup>And every garment and every skin on which the semen comes shall be washed with water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>18</sup>If a man lies with a woman and has an emission of semen, both of them shall bathe themselves in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>19</sup>"When a woman has a discharge, and the discharge in her body is blood, she shall be in her menstrual impurity for seven days, and whoever touches her shall be unclean until the evening.<sup>20</sup>And everything on which she lies during her menstrual impurity shall be unclean. Everything also on which she sits shall be unclean.<sup>21</sup>And whoever touches her bed shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>22</sup>And whoever touches anything on which she sits shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>23</sup>Whether it is the bed or anything on which she sits, when he touches it he shall be unclean until the evening.<sup>24</sup>And if any man lies with her and her menstrual impurity comes upon him, he shall be unclean seven days, and every bed on which he lies shall be unclean.<sup>25</sup>"If a woman has a discharge of blood for many days, not at the time of her menstrual impurity, or if she has a discharge beyond the time of her impurity, all the days of the discharge she shall continue in uncleanness. As in the days of her impurity, she shall be unclean.<sup>26</sup>Every bed on which she lies, all the days of her discharge, shall be to her as the bed of her impurity. And everything on which she sits shall be unclean, as in the uncleanness of her menstrual impurity.<sup>27</sup>And whoever touches these things shall be unclean, and shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>28</sup>But if she is cleansed of her discharge, she shall count for herself seven days, and after that she shall be clean.<sup>29</sup>And on the eighth day she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons and bring them to the priest, to the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>30</sup>And the priest shall use one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. And the priest shall make atonement for her before the LORD for her unclean discharge.<sup>31</sup>"Thus you shall keep the people of Israel separate from their uncleanness, lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst."<sup>32</sup>This is the law for him who has a discharge and for him who has an emission of semen, becoming unclean thereby;<sup>33</sup>also for her who is unwell with her menstrual impurity, that is, for anyone, male or female, who has a discharge, and for the man who lies with a woman who is unclean.
15.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 15 closes the section on clean and unclean (chapters 11–15), just before the Day of Atonement. After food, childbirth and skin disease, it turns to the most private facts of bodily life: discharges from the sexual organs of men and women.

The message. Uncleanness is not something only wrongdoers catch. It reaches every ordinary body, through illness and through the normal workings of life, marriage included. None of it is sin and no one is blamed, but none of it may be carried carelessly into the presence of the holy God who lives among his people (v. 31).

Why it was said. God had pitched his tent in a camp full of mortal bodies (see the introduction). Israel needed to know how to live so near to him, and the law taught them to treat the body’s weaknesses openly, in a law read aloud to everyone, rather than with secrecy or shame.

How the chapter makes its case. A man with a chronic discharge passes his uncleanness to beds, seats and people (vv. 1–12), and when healed he is cleansed with seven days, a bath and two birds (vv. 13–15). Ordinary emissions and marital relations need only washing and waiting until evening (vv. 16–18). A woman’s monthly period lasts seven days (vv. 19–24), and her chronic bleeding is treated exactly like the man’s chronic discharge, with the same offering (vv. 25–30). Then comes the reason for it all: God’s tabernacle is “in their midst” (vv. 31–33).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes. The chapter shows that no one gets through life in a body without being made unfit for God’s presence, and the next chapter supplies the remedy. In the Gospels a woman unclean under verses 25–30 for twelve years touched Jesus, and instead of defiling him she was healed: “immediately the flow of blood dried up” (Mark 5:29). Jesus does not catch our uncleanness; he heals it. And he did not let her slip away, but called her “Daughter”.

For us. Christians need not be embarrassed about the body God made, or about its weaknesses and illnesses; we may bring all of it to him without shame. The ceremonial rules are fulfilled in Christ, but their lesson remains: we need a cleansing we cannot give ourselves, and in him we have it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every kind of discharge from the sexual organs, in men and in women, normal and abnormal, makes a person ceremonially unclean, and God provides a way to be clean again. A man with a chronic discharge passes uncleanness to his bed, his seat and anyone he touches; when he is healed, he waits seven days, washes and brings two birds (vv. 1–15). An emission of semen, within marriage as well, needs only washing and waiting until evening (vv. 16–18). A woman’s monthly period lasts seven days (vv. 19–24), and chronic bleeding is treated exactly like the man’s chronic discharge, with the same offering (vv. 25–30). The reason for all of it is that God’s tabernacle stands in their midst (vv. 31–33).
verseByVerse.theology: None of these conditions is a sin. They are the ordinary and painful facts of living in a mortal body, and the law treats men and women alike, with the same remedies.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: no part of bodily life was untouched by uncleanness. Now: Christians need not be embarrassed about the body God made, and may bring its weaknesses and illnesses to him without shame.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any man has a discharge from his body, his discharge is unclean. And this is the law of his uncleanness for a discharge: whether his body runs with his discharge, or his body is blocked up by his discharge, it is his uncleanness. Every bed on which the one with the discharge lies shall be unclean, and everything on which he sits shall be unclean. And anyone who touches his bed shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. And whoever sits on anything on which the one with the discharge has sat shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. And whoever touches the body of the one with the discharge shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. And if the one with the discharge spits on someone who is clean, then he shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. And any saddle on which the one with the discharge rides shall be unclean. And whoever touches anything that was under him shall be unclean until the evening. And whoever carries such things shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. Anyone whom the one with the discharge touches without having rinsed his hands in water shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. And an earthenware vessel that the one with the discharge touches shall be broken, and every vessel of wood shall be rinsed in water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man with a chronic discharge is unclean, and his uncleanness spreads to his bed, his seat and anyone he touches; it is an illness, not a sin.

When any man has a discharge from his body. “Body” is literally “flesh”, here a polite word for the genitals, and the discharge is a disease, whether it flows or is “blocked up” (v. 3). No part of human life lies outside God’s holiness or his care.

His discharge is unclean. These are not sins. The man did not choose his illness, yet it shuts him out of worship, and its effect spreads: to every bed and seat, to a saddle, to anyone he spits on or touches with unwashed hands, and to clay pots, which must be broken (vv. 4–12). In the old order uncleanness passed by touch in a way holiness did not (Haggai 2:12–13).

A body in a fallen world. The effect was a constant, quiet reminder that to live in a body in a fallen world is to be touched by decay without having done anything wrong. Uncleanness is not what happens when you misbehave; it is the condition you live in, and it needs a cleansing we cannot provide.

Uncertain wording. The condition is not identified. Older writers often took it to be gonorrhoea, but the words fit several chronic diseases; what is clear is a lasting, abnormal flow, distinct from the ordinary emission of v. 16.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the one with a discharge is cleansed of his discharge, then he shall count for himself seven days for his cleansing, and wash his clothes. And he shall bathe his body in fresh water and shall be clean. And on the eighth day he shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons and come before the LORD to the entrance of the tent of meeting and give them to the priest. And the priest shall use them, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD for his discharge. "If a man has an emission of semen, he shall bathe his whole body in water and be unclean until the evening. And every garment and every skin on which the semen comes shall be washed with water and be unclean until the evening. If a man lies with a woman and has an emission of semen, both of them shall bathe themselves in water and be unclean until the evening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A healed man is restored with washing, waiting and a simple offering, and ordinary emissions, including the union of husband and wife, need only washing and waiting until evening.

When the one with a discharge is cleansed. Seven days, a bath in “fresh water” (literally “living water”), and on the eighth day two turtledoves or pigeons, an offering within anyone’s reach (vv. 13–15). Atonement is made “for his discharge” (v. 15), not because he had sinned, but because his condition had kept him from God’s presence.

An emission of semen. The ordinary cases, an emission of semen and the marriage act, need nothing more than washing and waiting until evening, with no offering at all (vv. 16–18). This chapter has been misread for centuries as a verdict on the body and on marriage, and it is not. What God commanded in Genesis 1:28 cannot be sinful in Leviticus 15. The rule probably concerns the loss of fluid that carries life, not wrongdoing, and its remedy is the mildest in the book.

What it does mean. Sex and worship were kept apart (compare Exodus 19:15): Israel’s God was not worshipped through sex, and marriage was honoured in its own place (Hebrews 13:4).

verseByVerse.quote: "When a woman has a discharge, and the discharge in her body is blood, she shall be in her menstrual impurity for seven days, and whoever touches her shall be unclean until the evening. And everything on which she lies during her menstrual impurity shall be unclean. Everything also on which she sits shall be unclean. And whoever touches her bed shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. And whoever touches anything on which she sits shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. Whether it is the bed or anything on which she sits, when he touches it he shall be unclean until the evening. And if any man lies with her and her menstrual impurity comes upon him, he shall be unclean seven days, and every bed on which he lies shall be unclean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman’s monthly period makes her ceremonially unclean for seven days, and her bed and seat pass that status on; it is a normal part of life, handled openly, not a shame.

When a woman has a discharge. Two things are easy to miss. The first is how much of an Israelite woman’s life this covered: a week in many months, for decades. The second is that the law made the condition public and ordinary rather than hidden and shameful. It is legislated for in the same breath as the male cases, with the same kind of remedies, in a book read aloud to everyone.

No offering. Like a man’s emission, a woman’s ordinary period needs no sacrifice; after seven days it is over. A man who lies with her during it shares her uncleanness for seven days (v. 24), and a later law forbids it outright (18:19; 20:18).

Do these laws apply to women in church today? No. Ritual uncleanness belonged to the tabernacle system, fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 9:9–10). Jesus did not shrink when a woman with a flow of blood touched him; he healed her and called her “Daughter” (Mark 5:34). “What God has made clean, do not call common” (Acts 10:15).

verseByVerse.quote: "If a woman has a discharge of blood for many days, not at the time of her menstrual impurity, or if she has a discharge beyond the time of her impurity, all the days of the discharge she shall continue in uncleanness. As in the days of her impurity, she shall be unclean. Every bed on which she lies, all the days of her discharge, shall be to her as the bed of her impurity. And everything on which she sits shall be unclean, as in the uncleanness of her menstrual impurity. And whoever touches these things shall be unclean, and shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. But if she is cleansed of her discharge, she shall count for herself seven days, and after that she shall be clean. And on the eighth day she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons and bring them to the priest, to the entrance of the tent of meeting. And the priest shall use one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. And the priest shall make atonement for her before the LORD for her unclean discharge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman with long-lasting bleeding stays unclean for as long as it lasts, and is cleansed with the same offering as a man; this was the condition of the woman who touched Jesus.

A discharge of blood for many days. In practice every bed she lay on and everything she sat on was unclean, and anyone who touched them had to wash and wait until evening. She could not embrace her husband or her children without passing her status on, and she was shut out of the tabernacle for as long as it lasted. If the bleeding did not stop, neither did the exclusion. When it stopped, she counted seven days and brought two birds, exactly as the man did (vv. 28–30): the law treats men and women alike.

The woman in Mark 5. “There was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse” (Mark 5:25–26). Twelve years under these verses: nobody could touch her without consequence, she was shut out of worship, and every physician’s bill made it worse. She came up behind Jesus in a crowd she was defiling with every step, touched his cloak, and hoped nobody would notice.

Holiness flows the other way. By this chapter, her uncleanness should have passed to him. Instead “immediately the flow of blood dried up” (Mark 5:29). Healing passed from him to her, as it had with the leper, and as it does every time holiness meets uncleanness in the Gospels.

Not allowed to slip away. Then he did the thing she dreaded. He stopped the crowd and asked who had touched him, and she came “in fear and trembling” and told him the whole truth in public (Mark 5:33), twelve years of it. He could have let her slip away healed; he would not let her leave as a woman who had stolen something. He let everyone hear that she was clean, and then he called her “Daughter” (Mark 5:34), the only individual the Gospels record him addressing by that word. The uncleanness of this chapter reaches everywhere, but the grace of Christ reaches further.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus you shall keep the people of Israel separate from their uncleanness, lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst." This is the law for him who has a discharge and for him who has an emission of semen, becoming unclean thereby; also for her who is unwell with her menstrual impurity, that is, for anyone, male or female, who has a discharge, and for the man who lies with a woman who is unclean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reason for all these rules is that the holy God lives among his people, and his dwelling must not be defiled.

Defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst. The danger is not the uncleanness itself but uncleanness brought into God’s presence. God has chosen, in grace, to pitch his tent in the middle of a camp full of mortal, leaking, dying people, and living so near to him calls for care.

The whole block together. Take chapters 11–15 together (food, childbirth, skin disease, discharges) and the message is unmistakable: no area of ordinary human life is untouched by corruption, and none of it can be argued away as somebody’s fault. Many have seen here a picture of total depravity: not that we are as bad as we could be, but that no part of us is untouched by the fall.

Why the next chapter. This is the problem the next chapter exists to solve. After five chapters showing that uncleanness reaches everywhere and never stops, Leviticus provides one day in the year when all of it, known and unknown, is dealt with at once (16:16).

15.theology:
Uncleanness is not guilt. The chapter blames no one. It describes the condition of mortal bodies in a fallen world, and so teaches humility without shame.

Guarding God's presence. The purity laws exist to protect the dwelling of God among his people (15:31), the very thing Israel could not live without.

The reversal in Christ. Under the law uncleanness spread by touch. In Christ it is holiness that spreads, and cleansing flows from him to us.
15.examples:
Then: ordinary bodily life made every Israelite unclean again and again.

Now: like the woman in the crowd, we come to Jesus as we are, and he does not shrink from us. He makes us clean, and calls us his own.

keyVerse.quote: Thus you shall keep the people of Israel separate from their uncleanness, lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst.
keyVerse.note: This verse gives the reason for the whole chapter, and for chapters 11–15. The rules exist because God has chosen to live in the middle of a mortal, unclean people, and his nearness is both their greatest gift and their greatest danger. The next chapter, and finally the cross, answer the problem this verse states.

15.reflection:
This chapter insists that ordinary bodily life, including marriage, made a person unclean without being sinful. Why is it important to keep “unclean” and “sinful” distinct, and where have Christians sometimes confused them?

The law handled the most private matters openly, in words read aloud to everyone. What might it look like for a church to speak about the body, illness and sexuality without either embarrassment or crudeness?

The woman of Mark 5 had lived for twelve years under verses 25–30. Read her story (Mark 5:25–34). What does Jesus’ insistence on finding her, and calling her “Daughter”, show about how he treats people who feel unclean or ashamed?

Verse 31 says the rules existed because God lived in their midst. How does God’s nearness to us in Christ make holiness both more serious and more joyful?

16.title: The Day of Atonement: The Heart of the Gospel
16.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses after the death of the two sons of Aaron, when they drew near before the LORD and died,<sup>2</sup>and the LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron your brother not to come at any time into the Holy Place inside the veil, before the mercy seat that is on the ark, so that he may not die. For I will appear in the cloud over the mercy seat.<sup>3</sup>But in this way Aaron shall come into the Holy Place: with a bull from the herd for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering.<sup>4</sup>He shall put on the holy linen coat and shall have the linen undergarment on his body, and he shall tie the linen sash around his waist, and wear the linen turban; these are the holy garments. He shall bathe his body in water and then put them on.<sup>5</sup>And he shall take from the congregation of the people of Israel two male goats for a sin offering, and one ram for a burnt offering.<sup>6</sup>"Aaron shall offer the bull as a sin offering for himself and shall make atonement for himself and for his house.<sup>7</sup>Then he shall take the two goats and set them before the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>8</sup>And Aaron shall cast lots over the two goats, one lot for the LORD and the other lot for Azazel.<sup>9</sup>And Aaron shall present the goat on which the lot fell for the LORD and use it as a sin offering,<sup>10</sup>but the goat on which the lot fell for Azazel shall be presented alive before the LORD to make atonement over it, that it may be sent away into the wilderness to Azazel.<sup>11</sup>"Aaron shall present the bull as a sin offering for himself, and shall make atonement for himself and for his house. He shall kill the bull as a sin offering for himself.<sup>12</sup>And he shall take a censer full of coals of fire from the altar before the LORD, and two handfuls of sweet incense beaten small, and he shall bring it inside the veil<sup>13</sup>and put the incense on the fire before the LORD, that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat that is over the testimony, so that he does not die.<sup>14</sup>And he shall take some of the blood of the bull and sprinkle it with his finger on the front of the mercy seat on the east side, and in front of the mercy seat he shall sprinkle some of the blood with his finger seven times.<sup>15</sup>"Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering that is for the people and bring its blood inside the veil and do with its blood as he did with the blood of the bull, sprinkling it over the mercy seat and in front of the mercy seat.<sup>16</sup>Thus he shall make atonement for the Holy Place, because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel and because of their transgressions, all their sins. And so he shall do for the tent of meeting, which dwells with them in the midst of their uncleannesses.<sup>17</sup>No one may be in the tent of meeting from the time he enters to make atonement in the Holy Place until he comes out and has made atonement for himself and for his house and for all the assembly of Israel.<sup>18</sup>Then he shall go out to the altar that is before the LORD and make atonement for it, and shall take some of the blood of the bull and some of the blood of the goat, and put it on the horns of the altar all around.<sup>19</sup>And he shall sprinkle some of the blood on it with his finger seven times, and cleanse it and consecrate it from the uncleannesses of the people of Israel.<sup>20</sup>"And when he has made an end of atoning for the Holy Place and the tent of meeting and the altar, he shall present the live goat.<sup>21</sup>And Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel, and all their transgressions, all their sins. And he shall put them on the head of the goat and send it away into the wilderness by the hand of a man who is in readiness.<sup>22</sup>The goat shall bear all their iniquities on itself to a remote area, and he shall let the goat go free in the wilderness.<sup>23</sup>"Then Aaron shall come into the tent of meeting and shall take off the linen garments that he put on when he went into the Holy Place and shall leave them there.<sup>24</sup>And he shall bathe his body in water in a holy place and put on his garments and come out and offer his burnt offering and the burnt offering of the people and make atonement for himself and for the people.<sup>25</sup>And the fat of the sin offering he shall burn on the altar.<sup>26</sup>And he who lets the goat go to Azazel shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and afterward he may come into the camp.<sup>27</sup>And the bull for the sin offering and the goat for the sin offering, whose blood was brought in to make atonement in the Holy Place, shall be carried outside the camp. Their skin and their flesh and their dung shall be burned up with fire.<sup>28</sup>And he who burns them shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and afterward he may come into the camp.<sup>29</sup>"And it shall be a statute to you forever that in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you shall afflict yourselves and shall do no work, either the native or the stranger who sojourns among you.<sup>30</sup>For on this day shall atonement be made for you to cleanse you. You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins.<sup>31</sup>It is a Sabbath of solemn rest to you, and you shall afflict yourselves; it is a statute forever.<sup>32</sup>And the priest who is anointed and consecrated as priest in his father's place shall make atonement, wearing the holy linen garments.<sup>33</sup>He shall make atonement for the holy sanctuary, and he shall make atonement for the tent of meeting and for the altar, and he shall make atonement for the priests and for all the people of the assembly.<sup>34</sup>And this shall be a statute forever for you, that atonement may be made for the people of Israel once in the year because of all their sins." And Aaron did as the LORD commanded Moses.
16.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 16 stands at the centre of Leviticus. Chapter 10 showed what happens when priests come near carelessly, and chapters 11–15 showed uncleanness reaching every part of life. Now God provides one day in the year when all of it is dealt with.

The message. A holy God can go on living among an unclean and sinful people only because he himself provides the way: a priest, a sacrifice and a substitute. On this day sin was both paid for, by blood brought before God’s throne, and removed, carried away into the wilderness, and the people heard the promise, “You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins” (v. 30).

Why it was said. Day after day Israel’s sins and uncleannesses polluted the sanctuary where God lived “in the midst of their uncleannesses” (v. 16). Without a yearly cleansing, God’s presence among them could not continue (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Aaron may enter only in plain linen, with a bull for himself and two goats for the people (vv. 1–10). Behind the veil, under a cloud of incense, he sprinkles the blood of the bull and then of the goat, cleansing the Holy Place, the tent and the altar (vv. 11–19). He lays both hands on the live goat, confesses all Israel’s sins over it and sends it into the wilderness; then he puts on his own garments and offers burnt offerings, while the remains of the sin offerings are burned outside the camp (vv. 20–28). The day is fixed for ever: the people humble themselves and rest, and are made clean (vv. 29–34).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern, and Hebrews 9–10 is the New Testament’s commentary on the day. Christ is the priest who needed no offering for himself and the sacrifice whose blood was brought before God: “he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12). He is also the sin-bearer, for “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6), and like the remains of the sin offerings he “suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12). At his death the veil was torn in two (Matthew 27:51), and what was done once a year has been done once for all.

For us. Our sin has been paid for and carried away, never to be brought against us again. So we come to God not once a year through a priest, but any day through Christ (Hebrews 10:19–22): humbled about our sin, and resting from every attempt to cleanse ourselves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-10 — Before the Veil: How Aaron May Enter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nobody, not even the high priest, may come into God’s presence when and how he pleases; God himself sets out the way. The day opens with a reminder of the death of Aaron’s two sons, who came near in a way God had not commanded (vv. 1–2). Aaron may enter the Most Holy Place only on God’s terms: bathed, dressed in plain linen, with a bull for his own sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering (vv. 3–5). From the people he takes two goats and casts lots over them: one for the LORD, to be a sin offering, and one for Azazel, to be sent away alive into the wilderness (vv. 6–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Access to God is God's gift. Nobody, not even the high priest, may decide for himself when and how to approach. The way in exists only because God opens it and describes it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: even the high priest had to atone for himself before he could act for anyone else. Now: our High Priest is "holy, innocent, unstained" and needs no sacrifice for himself (Heb. 7:26-27), so we can trust him entirely with ours.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses after the death of the two sons of Aaron, when they drew near before the LORD and died, and the LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron your brother not to come at any time into the Holy Place inside the veil, before the mercy seat that is on the ark, so that he may not die. For I will appear in the cloud over the mercy seat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After two of his sons died for approaching God carelessly, Aaron is told he may not enter the Most Holy Place whenever he likes, because God himself appears there.

After the death of the two sons of Aaron. The chapter is dated by a death. Nadab and Abihu had offered “unauthorized fire before the LORD” and were consumed (10:1–2). Now their father, Aaron, is told why the veil exists. It is not decoration but a barrier, a “keep out” woven in blue, purple and scarlet (Exodus 26:31), guarding the mercy seat, the golden lid of the ark, where God says, “I will appear in the cloud over the mercy seat.”

The veil torn. The Holy One cannot be approached on a whim, in a way of our own choosing. The wonder of the gospel is not that God lowered the barrier but that he himself passed through it, and then, at the cross, tore it from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51; Hebrews 10:19–20). The God who warned Aaron “so that he may not die” would one day die himself so that we might live.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew name of the day, Yom Kippur (23:27), comes from the same root as kapporet, the word for the mercy seat (see vv. 11-14).

verseByVerse.quote: But in this way Aaron shall come into the Holy Place: with a bull from the herd for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering. He shall put on the holy linen coat and shall have the linen undergarment on his body, and he shall tie the linen sash around his waist, and wear the linen turban; these are the holy garments. He shall bathe his body in water and then put them on. And he shall take from the congregation of the people of Israel two male goats for a sin offering, and one ram for a burnt offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God shows the way in: Aaron must come with sacrifices, bathed, and dressed not in his glorious robes but in plain linen.

But in this way. Four words of pure grace. God does not only bar the door; he shows the way through it: a bull for Aaron’s own sin, a ram for a burnt offering, and two goats supplied by the people, for it is their sin being dealt with (v. 5).

The holy linen coat. On other days the high priest blazed with gold and precious stones (Exodus 28); today he bathes and puts on plain white linen, dressed like the humblest servant. The greater the day, the lower he stoops. Many have seen here a picture of our Lord, who “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), laying aside his glory to do the work of atonement.

verseByVerse.quote: "Aaron shall offer the bull as a sin offering for himself and shall make atonement for himself and for his house. Then he shall take the two goats and set them before the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And Aaron shall cast lots over the two goats, one lot for the LORD and the other lot for Azazel. And Aaron shall present the goat on which the lot fell for the LORD and use it as a sin offering, but the goat on which the lot fell for Azazel shall be presented alive before the LORD to make atonement over it, that it may be sent away into the wilderness to Azazel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aaron must first make atonement for his own sin; then lots divide two goats, one to die as a sin offering and the other to be sent alive into the wilderness to Azazel.

A sin offering for himself. Before Aaron can carry anyone else’s sin, he must deal with his own. The mediator kneels as a sinner first, a quiet confession that no son of Aaron is clean enough to save. This is the flaw in the old priesthood that makes us long for a better one: a priest who has “no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins” (Hebrews 7:27).

Aaron shall cast lots. The choice is left to God (Proverbs 16:33). Together they make one sin offering for the people (v. 5): one goat shows sin paid for, the other sin removed.

Not an offering to Satan. Whatever Azazel means, the goat was not an offering to Satan or to anyone else: it was sent, not sacrificed. Its work was to carry Israel’s sins out of the camp and out of sight, beyond return.

Uncertain wording. The meaning of Azazel is uncertain; the word occurs only in this chapter. Later Jewish tradition made it a wilderness demon. Others take it as a place, perhaps a rugged cliff, or as “the goat that departs”. This commentary takes the likeliest reading to be the wilderness itself, the barren realm cut off from God’s camp, to which the sins were sent away.
verseByVerse.note: The English word “scapegoat” comes from Tyndale's 1530 translation, which read Azazel as “the goat that escapes”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11-19 — Within the Veil: Blood on the Mercy Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behind the veil, the blood of a substitute is brought before the throne of God, and the whole sanctuary is cleansed. Aaron kills the bull for himself, carries burning incense inside the veil so that its cloud covers the mercy seat and he does not die, and sprinkles the bull’s blood on and before the mercy seat (vv. 11–14). Then he does the same with the blood of the people’s goat, making atonement for the Holy Place and the tent, polluted by Israel’s uncleannesses and sins, while no one else may be in the tent (vv. 15–17). Finally he cleanses the altar outside with the blood of both animals (vv. 18–19). This is the heart of the day, and of the whole book.
verseByVerse.theology: Here the chapter teaches propitiation: God's just anger at sin is turned away, not because it is ignored, but because a life is given in the sinner's place and God himself accepts it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: one man, once a year, sprinkled blood on a golden lid that no one else ever saw. Now: what was hidden behind the veil has been set out in public at the cross, and every believer may come to God through Christ, any day of the year.

verseByVerse.quote: "Aaron shall present the bull as a sin offering for himself, and shall make atonement for himself and for his house. He shall kill the bull as a sin offering for himself. And he shall take a censer full of coals of fire from the altar before the LORD, and two handfuls of sweet incense beaten small, and he shall bring it inside the veil and put the incense on the fire before the LORD, that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat that is over the testimony, so that he does not die. And he shall take some of the blood of the bull and sprinkle it with his finger on the front of the mercy seat on the east side, and in front of the mercy seat he shall sprinkle some of the blood with his finger seven times.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shielded by a cloud of incense, Aaron carries the blood of his own sin offering behind the veil and sprinkles it on and before the mercy seat, where the broken law lies beneath and God’s presence above.

The cloud of the incense. A cloud shrouds the mercy seat, for no man, not even Aaron, can gaze on the unveiled glory and live. The incense is a mercy: it hides him, “so that he does not die” (v. 13).

Seven times. Then he sprinkles the blood of his own bull on the front of the mercy seat and seven times before it, seven being the number of completeness: atonement fully made. The ark below holds the tablets of the law Israel has broken; the blood falls above them, between the broken law and the God who gave it. That golden lid is the most important object in the world that day, because it is where wrath and mercy meet. Here is the gospel in shadow: the law accuses from beneath, the blood answers from above, and God looks down not on our sin but on the sprinkled blood.

Why blood? How can killing an animal answer moral guilt? To Israel blood meant life: “the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls” (17:11). Sin is rebellion against the God of life, and it ends in death. The animal’s death said, in a form no one could miss, that sin costs a life, and that God in mercy accepted a life given in the sinner’s place. Yet an animal does not understand, consent or share our nature, and Hebrews says plainly that “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). The sacrifices were God’s appointed sign and promise, pointing to a willing human substitute who would give his own life.

The mercy seat. The Hebrew word for the lid is kapporet, the place of covering or atonement. When Jewish scholars put the Old Testament into Greek they rendered it hilasterion, and that is the word Paul reaches for to describe what God did at the cross: “whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith” (Romans 3:25). Many interpreters think Paul is calling Christ the mercy seat itself, since Hebrews uses the same word for the golden lid (Hebrews 9:5); others take it more generally as the means by which wrath is turned away. Either way, what the mercy seat showed in picture, Christ is in fact: the place where the blood answers the broken law.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering that is for the people and bring its blood inside the veil and do with its blood as he did with the blood of the bull, sprinkling it over the mercy seat and in front of the mercy seat. Thus he shall make atonement for the Holy Place, because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel and because of their transgressions, all their sins. And so he shall do for the tent of meeting, which dwells with them in the midst of their uncleannesses. No one may be in the tent of meeting from the time he enters to make atonement in the Holy Place until he comes out and has made atonement for himself and for his house and for all the assembly of Israel. Then he shall go out to the altar that is before the LORD and make atonement for it, and shall take some of the blood of the bull and some of the blood of the goat, and put it on the horns of the altar all around. And he shall sprinkle some of the blood on it with his finger seven times, and cleanse it and consecrate it from the uncleannesses of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blood of the people’s goat is brought behind the veil too, cleansing the sanctuary itself from the pollution of Israel’s sins and uncleannesses so that God can go on living among them.

Inside the veil. The blood is carried where no Israelite could go and sprinkled where only God could see, “because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel and because of their transgressions, all their sins” (v. 16). Not only the people are cleansed but the place: the Holy Place, the tent and the altar (vv. 16–19).

In the midst of their uncleannesses. “Unclean” in Leviticus does not simply mean dirty, nor is it always sin. It marks whatever belongs to the realm of death and decay (a corpse, a disease, a bodily discharge) and so cannot come near the God of life without cleansing. Israel’s sins and uncleannesses polluted even the tent where God consented to dwell, and once a year it had to be cleansed so that he could go on living among them. Hebrews says the heavenly things themselves needed “better sacrifices than these” (Hebrews 9:23).

No one may be in the tent. While Aaron works, he is alone (v. 17): atonement is lonely work. On the true Day of Atonement the Mediator too was utterly alone: all the disciples left him and fled (Mark 14:50), and on the cross he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34), so that we might never be forsaken.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-28 — Outside the Camp: Sin Carried Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sin that has been paid for must also be removed, and the second goat carries it away. Aaron lays both hands on the live goat, confesses over it all Israel’s iniquities, transgressions and sins, and sends it into the wilderness with a man appointed for the task (vv. 20–22). Then he takes off the linen garments, bathes, puts on his own garments and offers the burnt offerings for himself and the people (vv. 23–25). Those who handled the uncleanness, the man who led the goat away and the man who burned the remains of the sin offerings outside the camp, must wash before they return (vv. 26–28). Two movements make one atonement: sin paid for, and sin carried away.
verseByVerse.theology: The second goat shows expiation, the removal of sin. Forgiveness does not only cancel a debt; it takes the guilt away from the sinner so that it no longer stands between him and God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel stood and watched their sin walk away into the wilderness. Now: when an old sin comes back to accuse you, you may answer that it has already been carried away, and God does not send for it again.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he has made an end of atoning for the Holy Place and the tent of meeting and the altar, he shall present the live goat. And Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel, and all their transgressions, all their sins. And he shall put them on the head of the goat and send it away into the wilderness by the hand of a man who is in readiness. The goat shall bear all their iniquities on itself to a remote area, and he shall let the goat go free in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aaron lays Israel’s sins on the live goat, pressing both hands on its head and confessing them all, and the goat carries them away into the wilderness, never to return.

Aaron shall lay both his hands. Not a light touch but a leaning weight. Over the goat he names every kind of sin: “iniquities” (the crookedness of the heart), “transgressions” (deliberate rebellions) and “sins” (the failures and misses). Three words to leave nothing out: a whole nation’s guilt for a whole year, named over one head.

To a remote area. A man standing ready leads the goat away, and it bears all their iniquities “to a remote area” (v. 22), literally a land cut off. Israel did not merely hear that their sin was forgiven; they watched it walk away: “as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12).

Laid on him. So with your sin. Your Saviour took it on his own head, for “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6), and “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). It is not filed away. It is gone.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then Aaron shall come into the tent of meeting and shall take off the linen garments that he put on when he went into the Holy Place and shall leave them there. And he shall bathe his body in water in a holy place and put on his garments and come out and offer his burnt offering and the burnt offering of the people and make atonement for himself and for the people. And the fat of the sin offering he shall burn on the altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the sin carried away, Aaron lays aside the linen, washes, puts on his own garments again and offers burnt offerings: once atonement is made, worship can rise.

Take off the linen garments. The mood changes. Aaron washes, leaves the plain linen in the tent and puts his glorious garments back on: the servant’s work done, the splendour restored. Many have seen in it a picture of our Lord, who after his humiliation was “crowned with glory and honor” (Hebrews 2:9).

His burnt offering and the burnt offering of the people. Whole animals given up to God. The order never changes: first atonement, then adoration. We do not worship our way into acceptance; we are accepted, and so we worship.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who lets the goat go to Azazel shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and afterward he may come into the camp. And the bull for the sin offering and the goat for the sin offering, whose blood was brought in to make atonement in the Holy Place, shall be carried outside the camp. Their skin and their flesh and their dung shall be burned up with fire. And he who burns them shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and afterward he may come into the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The remains of the sin offerings are burned outside the camp, and the men who handled them and the goat must wash before returning, for sin’s uncleanness clings to everything near it.

Outside the camp. The bodies of the animals whose blood went into the Holy Place are burned up outside the camp (v. 27). The writer of Hebrews sees his Lord in that lonely fire beyond the gate: “So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood. Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured” (Hebrews 13:12–13).

The place of shame. Golgotha was outside the city wall. The sin-bearer was cast out as unclean, treated as sin itself (2 Corinthians 5:21), so that the unclean might be brought in. The place of shame became the place of cleansing, and the call to us is to go out to him there, willing to share his reproach.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29-34 — A Statute Forever: The Sabbath of Atonement
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God fixes the day in Israel’s calendar for ever, and the people’s part is to humble themselves and rest while atonement is made for them. On the tenth day of the seventh month, native and stranger alike are to afflict themselves and do no work, for on this day they are cleansed from all their sins (vv. 29–31). The anointed priest of each generation will repeat the rite, making atonement for the sanctuary, the tent, the altar, the priests and all the people, once in the year (vv. 32–34). The chapter ends with obedience: Aaron did as the LORD commanded. Yet the yearly return of the day showed that the final atonement was still to come.
verseByVerse.theology: The people's part is to humble themselves and to rest. Their cleansing is something done for them, not something they achieve.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the day came round again every autumn. Now: there is no annual reckoning to wait for; a believer who sins comes back to God the same day, through the same finished sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall be a statute to you forever that in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you shall afflict yourselves and shall do no work, either the native or the stranger who sojourns among you. For on this day shall atonement be made for you to cleanse you. You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins. It is a Sabbath of solemn rest to you, and you shall afflict yourselves; it is a statute forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every year on this day all Israel, native and stranger alike, must humble themselves and rest from work, for God makes atonement to cleanse them from all their sins.

You shall afflict yourselves and shall do no work. A strange pairing. Israel must feel the weight of sin (this was the one fast day in the law, a day to humble the soul), and yet must lift not a finger towards its own cleansing. Both are the gospel: we come empty-handed, mourning our sin, and we rest, because the work is the priest’s, not ours.

You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins. Not some, but all; not partly, but clean. It is “a Sabbath of solemn rest” (v. 31), the deepest rest of the year, because the deepest rest a soul can know is to be clean before God, having contributed nothing but need. That rest has a name: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). The stranger living among Israel shared the day (v. 29), an early hint that this cleansing would not be for one nation alone.

How Jewish readers take it. Yom Kippur remains the holiest day of the Jewish year. Rabbinic tradition teaches that repentance, prayer and deeds of kindness now bring atonement, and the Mishnah (Yoma 8:9) adds that the day does not atone for wrongs against a neighbour until the wrongdoer has made peace with him. Both readings agree that sin is real, that cleansing is God’s gift, and that it is received with humbled hearts. This commentary reads the day as a shadow fulfilled when Christ entered the holy places once for all by his own blood (Hebrews 9:11–12).
verseByVerse.note: “Afflict yourselves” may mean “fast” (ESV note). The seventh month is September–October.

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest who is anointed and consecrated as priest in his father's place shall make atonement, wearing the holy linen garments. He shall make atonement for the holy sanctuary, and he shall make atonement for the tent of meeting and for the altar, and he shall make atonement for the priests and for all the people of the assembly. And this shall be a statute forever for you, that atonement may be made for the people of Israel once in the year because of all their sins." And Aaron did as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each generation’s high priest is to repeat the rite once a year, for the sanctuary and all the people; its very repetition shows that the final atonement was still to come.

Once in the year. The atonement reaches everything (sanctuary, tent, altar, priests and “all the people of the assembly”). Yet one phrase exposes the system’s limit: “once in the year” (v. 34). Each high priest died and another served “in his father’s place” (v. 32; compare Hebrews 7:23–25), and the yearly return of the day was God’s own admission that the real atonement was still to come (Hebrews 10:1–4). The chapter ends with “once in the year”; the gospel answers with “once for all” (Hebrews 9:26).

Do Christians keep the Day of Atonement? No, because what the Day of Atonement pictured has been done: “Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin” (Hebrews 10:18). Jewish people still keep it as Yom Kippur, with prayer and fasting but without sacrifice, since the temple fell in AD 70. For the Christian the curtain is torn, and every day is a day of open access to God.

16.theology:
Propitiation. The blood on the mercy seat turns away God's just anger and satisfies his justice. Christ is the propitiation for our sins (Rom 3:25; 1 John 2:2), not someone else winning over an unwilling God, but God himself providing the sacrifice he requires.

Expiation. The living goat carries confessed sin away. Both goats are needed to show one atonement: Christ's death pays for sin and removes it.

A finished work. Aaron entered yearly with another's blood and went out again; Christ entered with his own and sat down (Heb 10:12). The veil torn at his death (Matt 27:51) leaves the way open for ever.
16.examples:
Then: once a year Israel waited outside while the high priest went in with blood, wondering whether he would come out alive.

Now: Christ is both the goat that died and the goat sent away, and he has come out of the sanctuary alive, never to die again. So we no longer wait outside. We draw near with confidence (Heb 10:19-22), resting on his own word from the cross: "It is finished" (John 19:30).

keyVerse.quote: For on this day shall atonement be made for you to cleanse you. You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins.
keyVerse.note: This is the promise the whole day exists to deliver, and the heart of Leviticus: not some sins but all, not partly clean but clean, and all of it done for the people rather than by them. Hebrews shows that the promise is finally kept by Christ, who “has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26).

16.reflection:
The chapter opens with the death of Aaron’s sons and the warning “so that he may not die” (vv. 1–2). Why do we need to feel the danger of approaching God before we can appreciate the way he has opened? How does the torn veil change the way we pray?

One goat was killed and its blood brought before God; the other carried the people’s sins away into the wilderness. What does each goat teach about what Christ has done for us, and which do you most need to remember when guilt returns?

On this day the people were to humble themselves and do no work (v. 29). How do both parts, mourning sin and resting from self-improvement, belong to real repentance?

The yearly repetition showed that the old system could never finish its work (v. 34). How should knowing that Christ’s sacrifice was “once for all” shape the way you deal with your sin today?

17.title: The Sanctity of Blood: Life Given for Life
17.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to Aaron and his sons and to all the people of Israel and say to them, This is the thing that the LORD has commanded.<sup>3</sup>If any one of the house of Israel kills an ox or a lamb or a goat in the camp, or kills it outside the camp,<sup>4</sup>and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting to offer it as a gift to the LORD in front of the tabernacle of the LORD, bloodguilt shall be imputed to that man.
