He has shed blood, and that man shall be cut off from among his people.<sup>5</sup>This is to the end that the people of Israel may bring their sacrifices that they sacrifice in the open field, that they may bring them to the LORD, to the priest at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and sacrifice them as sacrifices of peace offerings to the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And the priest shall throw the blood on the altar of the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting and burn the fat for a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>So they shall no more sacrifice their sacrifices to goat demons, after whom they whore. This shall be a statute forever for them throughout their generations.<sup>8</sup>"And you shall say to them, Any one of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn among them, who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice<sup>9</sup>and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting to offer it to the LORD, that man shall be cut off from his people.<sup>10</sup>"If any one of the house of Israel or of the strangers who sojourn among them eats any blood, I will set my face against that person who eats blood and will cut him off from among his people.<sup>11</sup>For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life.<sup>12</sup>Therefore I have said to the people of Israel, No person among you shall eat blood, neither shall any stranger who sojourns among you eat blood.<sup>13</sup>"Any one also of the people of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn among them, who takes in hunting any beast or bird that may be eaten shall pour out its blood and cover it with earth.<sup>14</sup>For the life of every creature is its blood: its blood is its life. Therefore I have said to the people of Israel, You shall not eat the blood of any creature, for the life of every creature is its blood. Whoever eats it shall be cut off.<sup>15</sup>And every person who eats what dies of itself or what is torn by beasts, whether he is a native or a sojourner, shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening; then he shall be clean.<sup>16</sup>But if he does not wash them or bathe his flesh, he shall bear his iniquity."
17.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 16, the Day of Atonement, was the summit of the book. Now the second half of Leviticus begins, often called the Holiness Code (chapters 17–27), which carries holiness out of the sanctuary into the camp, the field and the home. It opens with blood.

The message. Life belongs to God, and so does the blood that carries it. God has given blood on his altar for one purpose, to make atonement, so it may not be offered anywhere else or to anyone else, and it may not be eaten as ordinary food.

Why it was said. Israel came out of Egypt with old habits, and some were still killing animals in the open field as offerings to “goat demons” (v. 7). The peoples around them thought gods needed feeding and that blood carried power (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Every ox, lamb or goat killed in or near the camp must be brought to the entrance of the tent of meeting as a peace offering, so that its blood goes on the LORD’s altar and not to goat demons (vv. 1–7). The same holds for every burnt offering and sacrifice, by Israelite or sojourner (vv. 8–9). No one may eat blood, because the life is in the blood and God has given it on the altar to atone (vv. 10–12). Even a hunter must pour out the blood and cover it (vv. 13–14), and eating an undrained carcass makes a person unclean (vv. 15–16).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and fulfilment. Verse 11 states the principle beneath every sacrifice in the book: a life given for a life, and God himself giving it. Hebrews shows where it ends: Christ entered the holy places “by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12). The one altar at the one door gives way to the “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). And the blood Israel was forbidden to drink is the blood Christ offers in the cup: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood” (1 Corinthians 11:25).

For us. There is no bloodless gospel: we are forgiven because a life was given in our place, and God gave it. We come to him by the way he has provided, not by private arrangements of our own, and we cannot share “the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Corinthians 10:21). At the Lord’s Supper we receive with thanks the life poured out for us.
17.theology:
Substitutionary atonement. The giving of a life in place of the forfeit life is the heart of the sacrificial system and of the cross.

Atonement as God's gift. God does not need to be talked round into mercy. He provides the sacrifice himself, from a heart already set on saving (John 3:16).

The blood that speaks mercy. Abel's blood cried out for justice; Christ's blood "speaks a better word than the blood of Abel" (Heb 12:24).
17.examples:
Then: every time an Israelite drained an animal's blood, he was reminded that life belongs to God.

Now: each time we take the cup at the Lord's Supper we receive, with awe and thankfulness, what that blood pointed to.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All sacrifice belongs at one place, before the LORD, so that no life is quietly offered to anyone else. Any ox, lamb or goat killed in the camp or outside it must be brought to the entrance of the tent of meeting; to kill it elsewhere brings bloodguilt (vv. 1–4). The reason follows: Israelites had been sacrificing in the open field to goat demons, and now the blood must go on the LORD’s altar and the fat be burned as a pleasing aroma to him (vv. 5–7). The rule reaches every burnt offering and sacrifice, by Israelite or sojourner alike (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: False worship thrives in private. By bringing every sacrifice to one door, God removed the hiding places where Israel's old idolatries could survive.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel worshipped at one altar, in full view. Now: a faith kept entirely private, out of the sight of other believers, is the faith most likely to drift; we need the fellowship of the church.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and his sons and to all the people of Israel and say to them, This is the thing that the LORD has commanded. If any one of the house of Israel kills an ox or a lamb or a goat in the camp, or kills it outside the camp, and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting to offer it as a gift to the LORD in front of the tabernacle of the LORD, bloodguilt shall be imputed to that man. He has shed blood, and that man shall be cut off from among his people. This is to the end that the people of Israel may bring their sacrifices that they sacrifice in the open field, that they may bring them to the LORD, to the priest at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and sacrifice them as sacrifices of peace offerings to the LORD. And the priest shall throw the blood on the altar of the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting and burn the fat for a pleasing aroma to the LORD. So they shall no more sacrifice their sacrifices to goat demons, after whom they whore. This shall be a statute forever for them throughout their generations. "And you shall say to them, Any one of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn among them, who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting to offer it to the LORD, that man shall be cut off from his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every animal killed in the camp was to be brought to the LORD’s altar, so that no Israelite could quietly offer its life to anyone else. The law is aimed not at butchery but at secret sacrifice.

Bloodguilt shall be imputed to that man. Bloodguilt sounds severe for killing an animal at home until verse 7 gives the reason: goat demons. Israel may well have picked up the habit in Egypt, and killing an animal out in the open field was how it was kept alive: a quiet offering, away from the tent, to something else.

To the entrance of the tent of meeting. The remedy is one place for every sacrifice: one altar, one door, in full view. Worship that no one else can see drifts, and God removes the privacy in which it drifts.

One door still. The single door of the tent becomes a single person, the “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). God has opened one way to himself at great cost, and every other altar leads elsewhere (1 Corinthians 10:20).

Does this contradict Deuteronomy 12? No. In the wilderness everyone lived near the tent; once Israel spread across the land, Deuteronomy allowed animals to be killed for food in the towns, while keeping the heart of this chapter: “Only be sure that you do not eat the blood” (Deuteronomy 12:23).

Uncertain wording. Goat demons translates a word that usually means male goats; the ESV renders it “goat idols” in 2 Chronicles 11:15, and older versions have “devils” or “satyrs”. Whether these were spirits imagined in goat form or goat-shaped images is unclear; either way, false gods were receiving what belonged to the LORD. Cut off from among his people (vv. 4, 9) may mean expulsion, early death at God’s hand, or the ending of a family line; many think it describes God’s own judgment rather than a sentence carried out by the community.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-16 — The Life Is in the Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blood may never be eaten, because the life is in the blood and God has given it on the altar to make atonement. Whoever eats blood, Israelite or sojourner, faces God’s own face set against him (vv. 10–12). Verse 11, the heart of the chapter, gives the reason behind every blood rule in the book: atonement is made by a life given, and God himself provides it. Even an animal caught far from the altar must have its blood poured out and covered with earth, given back to the God who gave its life (vv. 13–14). Eating an animal that died of itself, its blood never drained, leaves a person unclean until he washes (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Blood belongs to God because life belongs to God, and he has set it apart for one purpose: atonement.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a meal could be a lesson in reverence. Now: Christians are free to eat, but not free to treat lightly the death of Christ by which they were bought.

verseByVerse.quote: "If any one of the house of Israel or of the strangers who sojourn among them eats any blood, I will set my face against that person who eats blood and will cut him off from among his people. For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life. Therefore I have said to the people of Israel, No person among you shall eat blood, neither shall any stranger who sojourns among you eat blood. "Any one also of the people of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn among them, who takes in hunting any beast or bird that may be eaten shall pour out its blood and cover it with earth. For the life of every creature is its blood: its blood is its life. Therefore I have said to the people of Israel, You shall not eat the blood of any creature, for the life of every creature is its blood. Whoever eats it shall be cut off. And every person who eats what dies of itself or what is torn by beasts, whether he is a native or a sojourner, shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening; then he shall be clean. But if he does not wash them or bathe his flesh, he shall bear his iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blood may never be eaten, because the life is in the blood and God has given it on the altar as the price of atonement. The whole sacrificial system rests on verse 11.

The life of the flesh is in the blood. Three things are packed into the verse. First, blood is life: where life resides, so that spilling blood is spending a life. Second, the altar is a gift: I have given it for you. The sacrifices were not Israel’s device for placating God; God handed them to Israel so that they might live with him and not die. Third, atonement happens by the life: not by the ritual, nor by the sincerity of the worshipper, but by a life given in place of a life forfeited.

No person among you shall eat blood. To eat it would be to treat as ordinary food the one thing God had reserved as the price of atonement. Even game killed in the hunt, far from any altar, had its blood poured out and covered with earth (v. 13): the life was given back to God, by Israelite and sojourner alike. An animal that died of itself or was torn by beasts had never been drained, so eating it left a person unclean until he washed (vv. 15–16).

The price paid. Hebrews builds directly on this verse: “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins” (Hebrews 9:22). Peter names the final price: “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:18–19). As at the altar, God himself provided it.

Christ’s blood given to drink. There is one more turn, and Israel would have found it staggering. The book that forbids eating blood on pain of being cut off points forward to the Christ who says, “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:54). His hearers were appalled, and by Leviticus 17 they had reason to be. He meant receiving him and his death by faith. Blood was withheld because it was the means of atonement; in him it is offered, because he is the atonement, and the life in his blood is given to us rather than kept from us.

Does the ban on eating blood still bind? It was given to Noah before Israel (Genesis 9:4), and the Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to keep it for the sake of fellowship with Jewish Christians (Acts 15:20, 29). But the New Testament declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19; 1 Timothy 4:4), and most Christians conclude that reverence for the life God gives remains, while eating meat not fully drained is not sin. The command concerns eating, not medicine: a blood transfusion gives life and does not break it.

Uncertain wording. The last phrase of verse 11, by the life, can also be read “for the soul” (so the King James Version); the Hebrew allows either. Both say that a life given is what atones.

keyVerse.quote: For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life.
keyVerse.note: This is the Bible’s plainest statement of why sacrifice atones: a life is given in place of a life, and God himself provides it. It explains every altar in Leviticus and every blood rule in this chapter, and it prepares for the cross, where the life given was the Son’s own (Hebrews 9:12–14).

17.reflection:
Verses 3–7 close the door on private sacrifices in the open field. Where might worship that no one else sees drift in our own lives, and how does the fellowship of the church help to keep it true?

Verse 11 says God has “given” the blood on the altar to make atonement. How does it change the way you think about the cross to see atonement as God’s gift rather than something we offer to win him over?

Israel was forbidden to eat blood, yet Jesus says, “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:54). What does that contrast teach us about what Christ gives us, and about the Lord’s Supper?

Christians are free to eat what Israel could not. In what ordinary ways can we still show reverence for life, and for the death of Christ by which we were bought?

18.title: Sexual Ethics: A People Called to Be Different
18.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, I am the LORD your God.<sup>3</sup>You shall not do as they do in the land of Egypt, where you lived, and you shall not do as they do in the land of Canaan, to which I am bringing you. You shall not walk in their statutes.<sup>4</sup>You shall follow my rules and keep my statutes and walk in them. I am the LORD your God.<sup>5</sup>You shall therefore keep my statutes and my rules; if a person does them, he shall live by them: I am the LORD.<sup>6</sup>"None of you shall approach any one of his close relatives to uncover nakedness. I am the LORD.<sup>7</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father, which is the nakedness of your mother; she is your mother, you shall not uncover her nakedness.<sup>8</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife; it is your father's nakedness.<sup>9</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, your father's daughter or your mother's daughter, whether brought up in the family or in another home.<sup>10</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your son's daughter or of your daughter's daughter, for their nakedness is your own nakedness.<sup>11</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife's daughter, brought up in your father's family, since she is your sister.<sup>12</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's sister; she is your father's relative.<sup>13</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother's sister, for she is your mother's relative.<sup>14</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's brother, that is, you shall not approach his wife; she is your aunt.<sup>15</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your daughter-in-law; she is your son's wife, you shall not uncover her nakedness.<sup>16</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife; it is your brother's nakedness.<sup>17</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and of her daughter, and you shall not take her son's daughter or her daughter's daughter to uncover her nakedness; they are relatives; it is depravity.<sup>18</sup>And you shall not take a woman as a rival wife to her sister, uncovering her nakedness while her sister is still alive.<sup>19</sup>"You shall not approach a woman to uncover her nakedness while she is in her menstrual uncleanness.<sup>20</sup>And you shall not lie sexually with your neighbor's wife and so make yourself unclean with her.<sup>21</sup>You shall not give any of your children to offer them to Molech, and so profane the name of your God: I am the LORD.<sup>22</sup>You shall not lie with a male as with a woman; it is an abomination.<sup>23</sup>And you shall not lie with any animal and so make yourself unclean with it, neither shall any woman give herself to an animal to lie with it: it is perversion.<sup>24</sup>"Do not make yourselves unclean by any of these things, for by all these the nations I am driving out before you have become unclean,<sup>25</sup>and the land became unclean, so that I punished its iniquity, and the land vomited out its inhabitants.<sup>26</sup>But you shall keep my statutes and my rules and do none of these abominations, either the native or the stranger who sojourns among you<sup>27</sup>(for the people of the land, who were before you, did all of these abominations, so that the land became unclean),<sup>28</sup>lest the land vomit you out when you make it unclean, as it vomited out the nation that was before you.<sup>29</sup>For everyone who does any of these abominations, the persons who do them shall be cut off from among their people.<sup>30</sup>So keep my charge never to practice any of these abominable customs that were practiced before you, and never to make yourselves unclean by them: I am the LORD your God."
18.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 17 guarded blood, the life God gives. Chapter 18 guards the springs of life itself: sex, marriage and the family. It opens and closes with “I am the LORD your God” (vv. 2, 30).

The message. Israel belongs to the LORD, so its sexual life is to be shaped by him, not by the culture it has left or the one it is entering. God made sex for the covenant of marriage and set firm boundaries around the household, so that home would be a place of safety, not of danger. Crossing those boundaries defiles people and land alike, and his statutes are the way of life (v. 5).

Why it was said. Israel had lived for centuries in Egypt and was about to enter Canaan, and both had customs that God calls abominations (vv. 3, 24–27). In large, crowded households the women and the young were the most exposed.

How the chapter makes its case. God first says who he is, forbids Israel to copy Egypt or Canaan, and promises life to those who keep his ways (vv. 1–5). He forbids sexual relations with close relatives (vv. 6–18), then adds five further commands, from adultery to Molech (vv. 19–23). Then he warns that the land had vomited out the nations for these things, and will vomit out Israel too if it does the same (vv. 24–30).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes and by covenant. Verse 5 promises life to the one who keeps these statutes, and Paul quotes it to show that no sinner has earned that life (Galatians 3:12); Israel did not keep them, and the land did vomit it out in exile. One man kept them, and “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). The faithful marriage these laws protect pictures his love for the church (Ephesians 5:25). And the one who sets the boundaries washes those who have crossed them: “But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

For us. Our culture also draws sexual lines and finds its own obvious; the question is whose lines we live by. God’s are a fence around a gift, and they protect the vulnerable. Those who have failed find cleansing in Christ, and those who have been wronged find in him a refuge and a God who names the wrong as wrong.
18.theology:
Holiness grounded in God. Sexual ethics flow from God's character and the identity of a redeemed people, not from arbitrary rule.

A people called to be different. Neither Egypt behind nor Canaan ahead is to shape God's people (18:3); the church too is called not to be conformed to this world (Rom 12:2).

The dignity of the body. God's boundaries protect persons and help them flourish; in Christ the body becomes a temple of the Spirit.
18.examples:
Then: Israel was called to be visibly different from Egypt and Canaan.

Now: the church faces the same fierce pressure to conform. We hold God's design as wisdom and gift, not a cage, and we offer the cleansing of Christ to all who have failed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-30 — Holiness in the Family and the Marriage Bed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people are to live by his statutes, not by the sexual customs of the nations, because he is the LORD their God. He sets out the principle and the promise of life (vv. 1–5), then guards the household: no sexual relations with close relatives by blood or marriage, so that home is safe for the women and the young (vv. 6–18). Five further commands follow, forbidding relations during a woman’s period, adultery, child sacrifice to Molech, sex between men and sex with animals (vv. 19–23). The chapter ends with a warning that cuts both ways: the land vomited out the nations for these things, and it will vomit out Israel too if it copies them (vv. 24–30).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people are shaped neither by the culture they came from nor by the one they are entering, but by the God who redeemed them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: these laws made the home safe for the women and the young. Now: churches and families are called to be places where the vulnerable are protected, and where those who have fallen find both truth and a way back.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, I am the LORD your God. You shall not do as they do in the land of Egypt, where you lived, and you shall not do as they do in the land of Canaan, to which I am bringing you. You shall not walk in their statutes. You shall follow my rules and keep my statutes and walk in them. I am the LORD your God. You shall therefore keep my statutes and my rules; if a person does them, he shall live by them: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is to live by the LORD’s ways, not by the customs of Egypt or Canaan, because he is their God, and his statutes lead to life. The chapter is first about belonging to him, and only then about rules.

You shall not do as they do. Two cultures are named, Egypt behind and Canaan ahead, and Israel is to resemble neither. The people receiving these laws had spent four centuries in Egypt watching one of those cultures.

He shall live by them. Verse 5 promises life to the person who keeps these statutes. Paul quotes it twice (Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12) to show that the law offers life for perfect obedience, and that no sinner has ever earned it. One man did: Christ kept these statutes in our place, and by his obedience the many are made righteous (Romans 5:19). Whoever has failed here comes back by confession, to a mercy already secured.

Isn’t this just the morality of its time? Verse 3 answers that: these laws cut against both cultures Israel knew. And our views are the views of our time too; a morality that simply follows the age will always feel enlightened and will always date. Scripture offers something steadier: the purposes of the Maker, who made sex for covenant faithfulness and delight (see the note on Song of Songs 8:6–7), and who opposes both contempt for the body and the consumption of it. (The argument from consent is weighed in the note on 1 Corinthians 6:19–20.) The chapter does not ask what our time thinks, but whose we are (v. 2). And the one who sets the boundary washes all who have crossed it, in any century (1 Corinthians 6:11).

verseByVerse.quote: "None of you shall approach any one of his close relatives to uncover nakedness. I am the LORD. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father, which is the nakedness of your mother; she is your mother, you shall not uncover her nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife; it is your father's nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, your father's daughter or your mother's daughter, whether brought up in the family or in another home. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your son's daughter or of your daughter's daughter, for their nakedness is your own nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife's daughter, brought up in your father's family, since she is your sister. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's sister; she is your father's relative. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother's sister, for she is your mother's relative. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's brother, that is, you shall not approach his wife; she is your aunt. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your daughter-in-law; she is your son's wife, you shall not uncover her nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife; it is your brother's nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and of her daughter, and you shall not take her son's daughter or her daughter's daughter to uncover her nakedness; they are relatives; it is depravity. And you shall not take a woman as a rival wife to her sister, uncovering her nakedness while her sister is still alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sexual relations with close relatives, by blood or by marriage, are forbidden, so that the home is a place of safety rather than danger. Verse 6 gives the principle; the list spells it out.

None of you shall approach any one of his close relatives. Picture the crowded, many-generation household, where the most vulnerable were the women and the young. These laws make the home a place where a woman is safe from the men she lives among.

Your own nakedness. The reasons given are about belonging: a granddaughter’s nakedness “is your own nakedness” (v. 10). Marriage makes one flesh (Genesis 2:24), so to violate one member of the family is to violate the bond itself. Paul was appalled to find the sin of verse 8 in Corinth (1 Corinthians 5:1).

A rival wife to her sister. Verse 18 forbids marrying two sisters at once. Jacob had done it before the law was given, and Genesis shows the misery that followed: “she envied her sister” (Genesis 30:1). The law shuts the door on that rivalry.

The brother’s widow. Deuteronomy 25:5–10 commands a man to marry his dead brother’s childless widow. That was a specific exception, to raise up an heir; verse 16 forbids taking a brother’s wife while he lives, as Herod did (Mark 6:17–18).

The household of God. The church is a family too, where women are treated “as mothers … as sisters, in all purity” (1 Timothy 5:2).

A word to the abused. If you were abused within your own family, this chapter is on your side. God named these acts as wrongs, and the shame of them belongs to the one who did them, not to you. Seek safety and help at once, and tell someone who can protect you; abuse must be reported, and it is never to be hidden or tolerated in the name of family or faith.

Uncertain wording. In verse 18, a woman … to her sister is read by a few as an idiom for one woman and another, forbidding a second wife at all. Most take it literally, as the ESV does.
verseByVerse.note: “Uncover nakedness” means sexual relations.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not approach a woman to uncover her nakedness while she is in her menstrual uncleanness. And you shall not lie sexually with your neighbor's wife and so make yourself unclean with her. You shall not give any of your children to offer them to Molech, and so profane the name of your God: I am the LORD. You shall not lie with a male as with a woman; it is an abomination. And you shall not lie with any animal and so make yourself unclean with it, neither shall any woman give herself to an animal to lie with it: it is perversion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five further commands forbid relations during a woman’s period, adultery, giving children to Molech, sex between men and sex with animals; one of them is not sexual at all, and all of them guard life and the covenant of marriage.

Her menstrual uncleanness … your neighbor’s wife. Verse 19 forbids relations during a wife’s period, closely tied to the purity laws of chapter 15 (15:24). Verse 20 forbids adultery, and calls it defilement.

To offer them to Molech. Verse 21 is the command that is not sexual. Canaanite religion included the burning of children, and the ban stands here because it belongs to the same subject: what a society does with its offspring, and whether the vulnerable exist for the convenience of the powerful.

You shall not lie with a male as with a woman. Verse 22 forbids male homosexual practice. It is not a mistranslation, no amount of context removes it, and the New Testament reaffirms it (Romans 1:26–27; 1 Corinthians 6:9–10).

It is an abomination. “Abomination” means what God detests; the word is also used of idolatry and dishonest scales (Deuteronomy 7:25; Proverbs 11:1). It names the act, not a person beyond redemption.

Addressed to everyone. Verse 22 stands in a list that also forbids adultery and incest: a chapter addressed to everyone’s sexuality, not to one group’s. And the New Testament paragraph naming this sin names beside it the greedy, the drunkards and the swindlers, and then says: “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 6:11). That describes not who is beyond reach but whom the church has always been made of. This chapter is no licence for anyone to feel clean by comparison.

Does the verse condemn people who experience same-sex attraction? The verse addresses an act. Every one of us carries desires bent by the fall that need Christ’s mercy and the Spirit’s renewal (Romans 7:18–25). Many believers who never chose these attractions walk in costly faithfulness, and deserve the church’s friendship, not suspicion.

Molech and abortion. Abortion is not the same act, but it shares the same evil wherever an unborn child’s life is ended for another’s sake; God forms the child in the womb (Psalm 139:13–16). For anyone who carries that grief, the washing of 1 Corinthians 6:11 is offered in full.

Why condemn same-sex intercourse from Leviticus 18:22 but eat shellfish (11:10)? The food laws were ceremonial: they marked Israel off from the nations, and the New Testament lifts them explicitly (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). The sexual laws of this chapter are moral: they rest on creation (Genesis 2:24), the nations were judged for breaking them (vv. 24–25), and the New Testament repeats them (Romans 1:26–27; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11). Christians are not picking and choosing; they are following the apostles. The death penalty of 20:13 belonged to Israel’s civil law and ended with it, and the gospel offers washing to every sinner.

Where Christians differ: does verse 19 still bind? Most treat it, with chapter 15, as a purity law fulfilled in Christ; some think it still binds, or at least still teaches tender respect for a wife’s body. This commentary’s view: it is a purity law and does not bind Christian couples, but the care for a wife it expressed is never out of date.

Uncertain wording. Who or what Molech was is not certain. Most take it as a god’s name (20:5 speaks of “whoring after Molech”); some think it named a kind of offering. To offer them is literally to make them pass over, and whether the children were always burned is debated, though 2 Kings 23:10 speaks of burning them.
verseByVerse.note: The name Molech may be a deliberate mockery, joining the Hebrew melek, “king”, to the vowels of the word for “shame”.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not make yourselves unclean by any of these things, for by all these the nations I am driving out before you have become unclean, and the land became unclean, so that I punished its iniquity, and the land vomited out its inhabitants. But you shall keep my statutes and my rules and do none of these abominations, either the native or the stranger who sojourns among you (for the people of the land, who were before you, did all of these abominations, so that the land became unclean), lest the land vomit you out when you make it unclean, as it vomited out the nation that was before you. For everyone who does any of these abominations, the persons who do them shall be cut off from among their people. So keep my charge never to practice any of these abominable customs that were practiced before you, and never to make yourselves unclean by them: I am the LORD your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations of Canaan were being driven out for these very sins, and Israel would be expelled in the same way if it copied them, for God judges his own people by the same standard. The land itself is pictured as sickened.

The land vomited out its inhabitants. The image should stop anyone using this chapter as a weapon against outsiders. Canaan is cleared not because God prefers Israelites, but because of what was done there, and he had waited centuries, until “the iniquity of the Amorites” was complete (Genesis 15:16).

Lest the land vomit you out. And God turns the same warning on Israel, native and sojourner alike (v. 26). The land is not Israel’s by right of blood; it will treat Israel as it treated those before them.

Exile and a promise. Centuries later it did, and Ezekiel named these very defilements as Jerusalem’s guilt (Ezekiel 22:10–11). Yet the same prophet promised cleansing, a new heart and God’s own Spirit: “I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27). That is what Christ gives his people now.

What it does not mean. Not that every disaster is judgment for some particular sin. Jesus refused that reading of a fallen tower, and turned it into a call to all: “unless you repent, you will all likewise perish” (Luke 13:5).

keyVerse.quote: You shall not do as they do in the land of Egypt, where you lived, and you shall not do as they do in the land of Canaan, to which I am bringing you. You shall not walk in their statutes.
keyVerse.note: This is the chapter’s call in a sentence: God’s people are shaped neither by the culture they came from nor by the one around them, but by the God who redeemed them. The laws that follow went against both cultures at once, and the church hears the same call: “Do not be conformed to this world” (Romans 12:2).

18.reflection:
The chapter begins and ends with “I am the LORD your God” (vv. 2, 30). How does knowing whose we are change the way we think about sex and the body?

Verse 3 tells Israel not to copy Egypt or Canaan. Which assumptions about sex and relationships in our own culture do Christians find hardest to resist, and why?

These laws made the household safe for the women and the young (vv. 6–18). What would it look like for your church and your home to be places where the vulnerable are protected, and where abuse is never hidden?

Paul writes, “And such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11). How can we hold God’s boundaries firmly and still welcome those who have crossed them?

19.title: The Holiness Code: Love Your Neighbor
19.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to all the congregation of the people of Israel and say to them, You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.<sup>3</sup>Every one of you shall revere his mother and his father, and you shall keep my Sabbaths: I am the LORD your God.<sup>4</sup>Do not turn to idols or make for yourselves any gods of cast metal: I am the LORD your God.<sup>5</sup>"When you offer a sacrifice of peace offerings to the LORD, you shall offer it so that you may be accepted.<sup>6</sup>It shall be eaten the same day you offer it or on the day after, and anything left over until the third day shall be burned up with fire.<sup>7</sup>If it is eaten at all on the third day, it is tainted; it will not be accepted,<sup>8</sup>and everyone who eats it shall bear his iniquity, because he has profaned what is holy to the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from his people.<sup>9</sup>"When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field right up to its edge, neither shall you gather the gleanings after your harvest.<sup>10</sup>And you shall not strip your vineyard bare, neither shall you gather the fallen grapes of your vineyard. You shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner: I am the LORD your God.<sup>11</sup>"You shall not steal; you shall not deal falsely; you shall not lie to one another.<sup>12</sup>You shall not swear by my name falsely, and so profane the name of your God: I am the LORD.<sup>13</sup>"You shall not oppress your neighbor or rob him. The wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night until the morning.<sup>14</sup>You shall not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God: I am the LORD.<sup>15</sup>"You shall do no injustice in court. You shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great, but in righteousness shall you judge your neighbor.<sup>16</sup>You shall not go around as a slanderer among your people, and you shall not stand up against the life of your neighbor: I am the LORD.<sup>17</sup>"You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but you shall reason frankly with your neighbor, lest you incur sin because of him.<sup>18</sup>You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge against the sons of your own people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD.<sup>19</sup>"You shall keep my statutes. You shall not let your cattle breed with a different kind. You shall not sow your field with two kinds of seed, nor shall you wear a garment of cloth made of two kinds of material.<sup>20</sup>"If a man lies sexually with a woman who is a slave, assigned to another man and not yet ransomed or given her freedom, a distinction shall be made. They shall not be put to death, because she was not free;<sup>21</sup>but he shall bring his compensation to the LORD, to the entrance of the tent of meeting, a ram for a guilt offering.<sup>22</sup>And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering before the LORD for his sin that he has committed, and he shall be forgiven for the sin that he has committed.<sup>23</sup>"When you come into the land and plant any kind of tree for food, then you shall regard its fruit as forbidden. Three years it shall be forbidden to you; it must not be eaten.<sup>24</sup>And in the fourth year all its fruit shall be holy, an offering of praise to the LORD.<sup>25</sup>But in the fifth year you may eat of its fruit, to increase its yield for you: I am the LORD your God.<sup>26</sup>"You shall not eat any flesh with the blood in it. You shall not interpret omens or tell fortunes.<sup>27</sup>You shall not round off the hair on your temples or mar the edges of your beard.<sup>28</sup>You shall not make any cuts on your body for the dead or tattoo yourselves: I am the LORD.<sup>29</sup>"Do not profane your daughter by making her a prostitute, lest the land fall into prostitution and the land become full of depravity.<sup>30</sup>You shall keep my Sabbaths and reverence my sanctuary: I am the LORD.<sup>31</sup>"Do not turn to mediums or necromancers; do not seek them out, and so make yourselves unclean by them: I am the LORD your God.<sup>32</sup>"You shall stand up before the gray head and honor the face of an old man, and you shall fear your God: I am the LORD.<sup>33</sup>"When a stranger sojourns with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong.<sup>34</sup>You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.<sup>35</sup>"You shall do no wrong in judgment, in measures of length or weight or quantity.<sup>36</sup>You shall have just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.<sup>37</sup>And you shall observe all my statutes and all my rules, and do them: I am the LORD."
19.overview:
Where we are. After blood (chapter 17) and the family (chapter 18), chapter 19 shows what holiness looks like across the whole of ordinary life. It opens with the book’s defining command, “You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy” (v. 2),.

The message. To be holy is to be like God, and God’s likeness shows not in withdrawal from the world but in the field, the workplace, the courtroom, the market and the heart: in how we treat the people around us. At the centre stands “you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (v. 18). Fifteen times the chapter says “I am the LORD”, tying every command to his character: worship and the way we treat people cannot be separated.

Why it was said. Israel was a redeemed people (v. 36) about to become a nation of farms, courts and markets, where it would be easy to keep holiness at the sanctuary and do business as usual. Many of these commands guard people who could not protect themselves, and Israel had been one of them: “you were strangers in the land of Egypt” (v. 34).

How the chapter makes its case. The call is applied at home and in worship (vv. 1–8), in the field (vv. 9–10), in work, court and conversation (vv. 11–16), and in the heart, where hatred gives way to frank speech and love (vv. 17–18). Laws on mixed kinds, a slave woman, fruit trees, pagan rites, daughters and the dead follow (vv. 19–31). The chapter ends with honour for the old, love for the stranger and honest weights (vv. 32–37).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God revealed in him and by the need it exposes. Jesus named verse 18 the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39) and showed in the Samaritan who our neighbour is (Luke 10:29–37). He alone ever kept this chapter. He kept it for us, “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19), and he loved even his enemies (Romans 5:8). The Spirit he gives now grows that love in his people, for “love is the fulfilling of the law” (Romans 13:10).

For us. Holiness still wears work clothes: the timesheet, the wages, the words about an absent colleague, the seat offered to the old, the welcome to the foreigner. We do it not to become God’s people but because we already are, and “we love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).
19.theology:
Practical holiness. God's holiness is reflected not in withdrawal from the world but in justice, generosity, honesty and love in everyday life.

Love fulfils the law. The command to love one's neighbour sits at the heart of these laws, and the New Testament calls it the fulfilment of them all.

The law kept for us. The One who gave this law also kept it perfectly. Jesus, the true neighbour, loved not himself but us, became poor that we might be rich, and pours his own love into our hearts by the Spirit so that we may love as we have been loved.
19.examples:
Then: an Israelite farmer reflected God’s holiness in everyday mercy: field edges left, wages paid, honest scales.

Now: holiness still wears work clothes. We honour God in how we treat employees, the vulnerable, the elderly and the stranger, loving our neighbour as ourselves because Christ first loved us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-37 — 'You Shall Be Holy, for I Am Holy'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Be holy as God is holy, and you will look like him in every corner of ordinary life. The call is applied first to parents, Sabbaths, idols and the peace offering (vv. 1–8). Then it reaches the field, where the edges are left for the poor; the workplace, where wages are paid by nightfall; the court and the conversation, where there is no partiality and no slander; and the heart, where hatred gives way to frank speech and love of neighbour (vv. 9–18). Laws on mixed kinds, a slave woman, young fruit trees, pagan rites, daughters and mediums follow (vv. 19–31), and the chapter ends with honour for the old, love for the stranger and honest weights (vv. 32–37), sealed again and again with “I am the LORD”.
verseByVerse.theology: Being holy means becoming like God, and this chapter shows that God's likeness is seen first in how we treat parents, the poor, workers, the disabled, neighbours and strangers.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: an Israelite farmer showed God's holiness by the corners he left unharvested. Now: a Christian shows it in the margins of an ordinary week: time, money and attention left over for someone in need.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to all the congregation of the people of Israel and say to them, You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy. Every one of you shall revere his mother and his father, and you shall keep my Sabbaths: I am the LORD your God. Do not turn to idols or make for yourselves any gods of cast metal: I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the LORD is holy, his whole people must be holy, and that holiness begins at home: honouring mother and father, keeping his Sabbaths and refusing idols.

You shall be holy. The sentence the whole book has been circling is addressed not to the priests but to “all the congregation”. Holiness is not for the clergy alone. And it begins unexpectedly: look after your parents; take a day off. In this chapter imitating God consists almost entirely of how you treat the people around you.

What it means to be holy. We hear “holy” and picture stained glass or someone too pious to enjoy a joke. At its root it means set apart, in a class of one. God is holy because there is no one like him, “majestic in holiness” (Exodus 15:11). A holy people belong to him so completely that they begin to resemble him. Left to ourselves we drift towards whatever keeps us safe and admired, so holiness is first something God gives: “we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10). It is not the price of getting in but the family likeness of those already brought in. This week it may mean being the same person at home as at church. See also Holiness in the Theological Dictionary.

His mother and his father. The mother is named first, reversing the usual order of the fifth commandment; a small touch, and probably not an accident.

Where Christians differ: what of the Sabbath for Christians? Many godly believers, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (the classic Presbyterian and Reformed Baptist statements of faith), hold Sunday as a binding Christian Sabbath. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), and the Lord’s Day is a gift Christians gladly set apart for worship and rest; faithful Christians differ, and no one may bind another’s conscience (Romans 14:5).

verseByVerse.quote: "When you offer a sacrifice of peace offerings to the LORD, you shall offer it so that you may be accepted. It shall be eaten the same day you offer it or on the day after, and anything left over until the third day shall be burned up with fire. If it is eaten at all on the third day, it is tainted; it will not be accepted, and everyone who eats it shall bear his iniquity, because he has profaned what is holy to the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the peace offering, eaten with family and friends, had to be finished within two days, so that what was holy to the LORD was never treated as leftovers. The rule repeats chapter 7.

Worship and conduct together. It sits among commands about daily conduct because the two are not separate subjects. In Leviticus the way you handle the holy things and the way you handle people are one topic.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field right up to its edge, neither shall you gather the gleanings after your harvest. And you shall not strip your vineyard bare, neither shall you gather the fallen grapes of your vineyard. You shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner: I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Farmers were to leave the edges of their fields and the fallen grapes for the poor and the sojourner, so that the needy could feed themselves with dignity.

Right up to its edge. God does not command a handout; he commands a margin. The corners are left standing, the dropped grapes are left lying, and the poor come and do the gathering. A man who receives a parcel is a recipient; a man who reaps a corner is a harvester, who keeps his dignity and never has to ask.

Ruth in Boaz’s field. This is the law under which Ruth, a Moabite widow, went into the field of Boaz, fed her mother-in-law, and met the relative who would marry her and buy back the family’s land. The whole book of Ruth happens inside these two verses, and it ends with a son whose grandson was David (Ruth 4:17). Through a gleaner from a foreign land, the line ran on to Christ (Matthew 1:5).
verseByVerse.note: The same provision is repeated in 23:22 and Deuteronomy 24:19-22.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not steal; you shall not deal falsely; you shall not lie to one another. You shall not swear by my name falsely, and so profane the name of your God: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not steal, deceive or lie, and never call on God’s name to cover a lie: honesty with one another is honour to the LORD.

You shall not swear by my name falsely. The last command links the other three to God himself. A false oath does not merely wrong the man deceived; it drags God’s name into the deception as a guarantor, making him a witness to the fraud.

Simply yes or no. That is why Jesus’ teaching on oaths cuts where it does: “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). An elaborate oath implies that your ordinary word could not be trusted.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not oppress your neighbor or rob him. The wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night until the morning. You shall not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not exploit those who cannot protect themselves: pay the day labourer before nightfall, and never take advantage of the deaf or the blind, because God sees what they cannot.

Wages overnight. Take the clause concretely. A day labourer is paid at the end of the day because he has no reserves. Hold his wages until morning and his family does not eat tonight. The law reaches into the gap between an employer’s convenience and a worker’s supper, and sides with the supper. James is still angry about it centuries later: the withheld wages “are crying out against you” (James 5:4).

The deaf and the blind. Both crimes are undetectable. A deaf man does not know he has been cursed; a blind man who trips never learns the obstacle was placed there on purpose. No victim can testify, which is exactly why “but you shall fear your God” is attached: this is law for the moments when nobody is watching. Paul applies the stumbling block to anything that trips a weaker brother (Romans 14:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall do no injustice in court. You shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great, but in righteousness shall you judge your neighbor. You shall not go around as a slanderer among your people, and you shall not stand up against the life of your neighbor: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judge fairly, favouring neither poor nor powerful, and do not destroy a neighbour with your tongue.

You shall not be partial to the poor. In court the even-handedness cuts both ways. Favouring the powerful is the obvious corruption; favouring the poor because they are poor is named as the same crime. A sentimental verdict is still a false one. The Messiah would judge this way, “with righteousness he shall judge the poor” (Isaiah 11:4).

As a slanderer among your people. Slander and standing “against the life of your neighbor” belong together. Talk is placed alongside bloodshed, because a reputation destroyed in conversation and a man destroyed in court are closer than we like to think.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but you shall reason frankly with your neighbor, lest you incur sin because of him. You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge against the sons of your own people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not nurse hatred or revenge; speak honestly to the one who has wronged you, and love your neighbour as yourself.

Reason frankly. The alternative to hatred is not silence but speech: going to the man and telling him plainly what he has done (compare Matthew 18:15). Swallowing a grievance is not presented as the meek option; hatred kept hidden in the heart is a way of becoming guilty yourself.

Love your neighbor as yourself. The New Testament quotes this more than any other sentence in the book. Jesus named it the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39). Paul says “the whole law is fulfilled in one word” (Galatians 5:14), and James calls it “the royal law” (James 2:8). Notice what comes just before it: loving your neighbour, in the verse that defines it, includes telling him the truth to his face.

The neighbour who loved his enemies. Jesus took the command further than anyone had: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). And he did it, praying for the men driving in the nails, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). We were the enemies he loved (Romans 5:8), and that love is the power to obey this verse.

Does “as yourself” command self-love? It assumes the care that all people already have for themselves (Ephesians 5:29) and turns it outward. It is not a command to build self-esteem first. And Jesus answers “who is my neighbor?” with the Samaritan: anyone in need whom I can help (Luke 10:29–37).

Uncertain wording. Lest you incur sin because of him can be read two ways: if you hide your grievance, the hatred becomes your sin; or if you say nothing, you share the guilt of the wrong you failed to name. Either way, silence is not the safe course.
verseByVerse.note: “Neighbor” here first means a fellow Israelite; verse 34 widens the same love to the foreigner.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall keep my statutes. You shall not let your cattle breed with a different kind. You shall not sow your field with two kinds of seed, nor shall you wear a garment of cloth made of two kinds of material. "If a man lies sexually with a woman who is a slave, assigned to another man and not yet ransomed or given her freedom, a distinction shall be made. They shall not be put to death, because she was not free; but he shall bring his compensation to the LORD, to the entrance of the tent of meeting, a ram for a guilt offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering before the LORD for his sin that he has committed, and he shall be forgiven for the sin that he has committed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel was to keep distinct kinds distinct in breeding, sowing and clothing, and a man who slept with a slave woman promised to another must bring a guilt offering, for he had sinned against God.

Two kinds of seed. The rules on mixing kinds give no reason, and the honest thing is to say so rather than invent one. Most likely they belong with the food laws: a nation trained, in a hundred daily particulars, to keep distinct things distinct.

A woman who is a slave. Then a case of very different weight. She is not free, so the law of adultery does not apply as to a free woman, but the text refuses to let the matter drop. There is an inquiry, and the man brings a guilt offering; he is not excused because the woman was a slave. Neither is put to death, which also spares the woman, who as a slave may have had little power to refuse. In many ancient codes an offence involving a slave woman was a matter of damages owed to her owner. Here it is an offence against God that requires atonement.

Do Christians cherry-pick by ignoring the mixed-fabric law? These laws were signs of Israel’s separateness, fulfilled in Christ, who has “broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14). The moral laws of this chapter, love your neighbour, honest weights, no slander, are repeated in the New Testament; the symbolic laws are not.

Uncertain wording. A distinction shall be made translates a word found only here. It may mean an inquiry, a payment of damages, or a punishment short of death. The point is clear: the matter must be dealt with, but not as adultery with a free woman.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you come into the land and plant any kind of tree for food, then you shall regard its fruit as forbidden. Three years it shall be forbidden to you; it must not be eaten. And in the fourth year all its fruit shall be holy, an offering of praise to the LORD. But in the fifth year you may eat of its fruit, to increase its yield for you: I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fruit of a newly planted tree was left for three years, given to God in the fourth, and eaten only from the fifth: the first and best belongs to him.

Three years it shall be forbidden to you. The Hebrew says the fruit is to be treated as “uncircumcised”, not yet fit for God or for use. Four years of tending something you may not touch trains patience and teaches that the tree is God’s before it is yours. The reason given at the end is practical (to increase its yield for you): God attaches a blessing to an act of restraint, as Proverbs does: “Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce” (Proverbs 3:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not eat any flesh with the blood in it. You shall not interpret omens or tell fortunes. You shall not round off the hair on your temples or mar the edges of your beard. You shall not make any cuts on your body for the dead or tattoo yourselves: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must not copy the pagan practices of divination and of mourning rites for the dead, because the LORD, not omens or the dead, governs life and death.

For the dead. This cluster is aimed at the religion of the surrounding nations, and for the dead explains it. These were funeral practices. Israel’s neighbours cut themselves in mourning to appease or attract the gods of the dead. These acts said something untrue about death and about who governs it.

Grief with hope. Christ has gone through death and come back. Christians still mourn, but “not … as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

Are tattoos sin today? The command forbade marking the body in mourning rites for the dead, a pagan practice (Deuteronomy 14:1). It is not repeated in the New Testament. Christians should think carefully about what they put on bodies that belong to the Lord (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), but a tattoo is a matter of wisdom and conscience, not a breach of this law.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated tattoo yourselves occurs only here, and its exact practice is unknown: it may mean marks cut or inked into the skin. What was meant by rounding off the hair and marring the beard is also unclear, probably a mourning or cultic custom. The setting, rites “for the dead”, is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not profane your daughter by making her a prostitute, lest the land fall into prostitution and the land become full of depravity. You shall keep my Sabbaths and reverence my sanctuary: I am the LORD. "Do not turn to mediums or necromancers; do not seek them out, and so make yourselves unclean by them: I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not sell your daughter into prostitution, keep God’s Sabbaths and honour his sanctuary, and do not consult the dead: a holy people protects its vulnerable and seeks the living God.

Do not profane your daughter. The ban covers both the cult prostitution of Canaan and the trafficking of a child by her own father for money, and beside it stand the Sabbaths. A society that sells its daughters and a society that keeps its Sabbaths are set side by side, and the second is offered as the alternative to the first. What a nation does with its rest and what it does with its vulnerable are connected.

Mediums or necromancers. They consult the dead. Israel is not to go looking for answers from that quarter, for the same reason as the mourning marks: it treats the dead, rather than the living God, as the place to go. Isaiah asks, “should not a people inquire of their God? Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living?” (Isaiah 8:19). At the empty tomb the question was turned round: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” (Luke 24:5).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall stand up before the gray head and honor the face of an old man, and you shall fear your God: I am the LORD. "When a stranger sojourns with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong. You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honour the old by rising before them, and love the foreigner as yourself, remembering that you were once strangers in Egypt.

Stand up before the gray head. Respect for the old is put into a single action: not a feeling about the elderly but a movement, made with the body, in a room, when someone comes in. And the same clause is attached again, “you shall fear your God”, because nobody can legislate for whether a man rises from his seat.

A culture afraid of grey hair. Our culture’s ideal human being is young, and the old are too often moved out of sight, valued, if at all, for what they once produced. Simone de Beauvoir, in her study Old Age (1970), argued that modern society treats its elderly as though they stop being full persons once they stop being useful. Leviticus says the opposite: their worth lies not in their output but in their Maker. Proverbs calls grey hair “a crown of glory” (Proverbs 16:31), and when John saw the risen Christ, “The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow” (Revelation 1:14), the likeness of the Ancient of Days in Daniel’s vision. The Bible’s last picture of glory is not a young body, so we need not dread ageing: “even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you” (Isaiah 46:4).

Love him as yourself. In verses 33–34 the command of verse 18 returns with the neighbour redefined, now a foreigner. The reason given is memory. A people who knew what it was to be aliens must not treat anyone as an outsider. The Lord himself was carried into Egypt as a refugee child (Matthew 2:14–15), and he will say to those who welcomed the stranger, “I was a stranger and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35).

Does this settle immigration policy? It binds how God’s people treat the foreigner among them: with love, justice and hospitality (Hebrews 13:2). It does not lay down a nation’s laws of entry; that is for governments to decide justly, and faithful Christians may disagree about it. But the church must never treat foreigners with contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall do no wrong in judgment, in measures of length or weight or quantity. You shall have just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. And you shall observe all my statutes and all my rules, and do them: I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Use honest measures in every trade, because the LORD who rescued Israel from Egypt sees every scale.

Just balances, just weights. The chapter ends in honest trade. A merchant with two sets of weights, a heavy one for buying and a light one for selling, could rob a whole town a fraction at a time and never be caught. “A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight” (Proverbs 11:1). Today the scales are the timesheet, the expense claim, the product description and the small print: the places where a little dishonesty pays and nobody would ever know, except the LORD who brought his people out of Egypt (v. 36).

Holiness spelled out. Holiness, which in this book has meant blood and veils and an unapproachable fire, is spelled out for ordinary Israelites as: feed the poor without humiliating them, pay workers before dark, tell the truth in court, protect the disabled, say the hard thing to a brother’s face, stand up for the old, love the foreigner, and keep honest scales.

The Holy One among us. So nobody should be surprised at what God was like when he became man. The Holy One spent his time with the poor, the disabled, the foreigners and the despised, not because he had set this chapter aside, but because he was the only one who ever kept it. He kept it for us, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19); so the reader this list convicts has a way back in confession, and the Spirit he gives grows this very love in us (Galatians 5:22).

keyVerse.quote: You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge against the sons of your own people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD.
keyVerse.note: Jesus named this the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39), and Paul says the whole law is fulfilled in it (Galatians 5:14). It gathers up the chapter: every command about wages, courts, the poor and the stranger is love of neighbour spelled out, grounded in “I am the LORD”.

19.reflection:
Verse 2 says, “You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy,” and then talks about parents, wages, the deaf and honest scales. What does that teach you about what holiness really is?

The gleaning law gave the poor dignity as well as food (vv. 9–10). How might your church or household leave margins for others in an ordinary week?

Verse 17 says that love tells the truth to a neighbour’s face rather than nursing a grudge. Is there a conversation you have been avoiding, and how would Christ’s love shape it?

Israel was to love the stranger “as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt” (v. 34). How does remembering what God has rescued you from change the way you treat the old, the foreigner and the outsider?

20.title: Penalties for Violations: The Seriousness of Sin
20.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Say to the people of Israel, Any one of the people of Israel or of the strangers who sojourn in Israel who gives any of his children to Molech shall surely be put to death. The people of the land shall stone him with stones.<sup>3</sup>I myself will set my face against that man and will cut him off from among his people, because he has given one of his children to Molech, to make my sanctuary unclean and to profane my holy name.<sup>4</sup>And if the people of the land do at all close their eyes to that man when he gives one of his children to Molech, and do not put him to death,<sup>5</sup>then I will set my face against that man and against his clan and will cut them off from among their people, him and all who follow him in whoring after Molech.<sup>6</sup>"If a person turns to mediums and necromancers, whoring after them, I will set my face against that person and will cut him off from among his people.<sup>7</sup>Consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy, for I am the LORD your God.<sup>8</sup>Keep my statutes and do them; I am the LORD who sanctifies you.<sup>9</sup>For anyone who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death; he has cursed his father or his mother; his blood is upon him.<sup>10</sup>"If a man commits adultery with the wife of his neighbor, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death.<sup>11</sup>If a man lies with his father's wife, he has uncovered his father's nakedness; both of them shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them.<sup>12</sup>If a man lies with his daughter-in-law, both of them shall surely be put to death; they have committed perversion; their blood is upon them.<sup>13</sup>If a man lies with a male as with a woman, both of them have committed an abomination; they shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them.<sup>14</sup>If a man takes a woman and her mother also, it is depravity; he and they shall be burned with fire, that there may be no depravity among you.<sup>15</sup>If a man lies with an animal, he shall surely be put to death, and you shall kill the animal.<sup>16</sup>If a woman approaches any animal and lies with it, you shall kill the woman and the animal; they shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them.<sup>17</sup>"If a man takes his sister, a daughter of his father or a daughter of his mother, and sees her nakedness, and she sees his nakedness, it is a disgrace, and they shall be cut off in the sight of the children of their people. He has uncovered his sister's nakedness, and he shall bear his iniquity.<sup>18</sup>If a man lies with a woman during her menstrual period and uncovers her nakedness, he has made naked her fountain, and she has uncovered the fountain of her blood. Both of them shall be cut off from among their people.<sup>19</sup>You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother's sister or of your father's sister, for that is to make naked one's relative; they shall bear their iniquity.<sup>20</sup>If a man lies with his uncle's wife, he has uncovered his uncle's nakedness; they shall bear their sin; they shall die childless.<sup>21</sup>If a man takes his brother's wife, it is impurity. He has uncovered his brother's nakedness; they shall be childless.<sup>22</sup>"You shall therefore keep all my statutes and all my rules and do them, that the land where I am bringing you to live may not vomit you out.<sup>23</sup>And you shall not walk in the customs of the nation that I am driving out before you, for they did all these things, and therefore I detested them.<sup>24</sup>But I have said to you, 'You shall inherit their land, and I will give it to you to possess, a land flowing with milk and honey.' I am the LORD your God, who has separated you from the peoples.<sup>25</sup>You shall therefore separate the clean beast from the unclean, and the unclean bird from the clean. You shall not make yourselves detestable by beast or by bird or by anything with which the ground crawls, which I have set apart for you to hold unclean.<sup>26</sup>You shall be holy to me, for I the LORD am holy and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine.<sup>27</sup>"A man or a woman who is a medium or a necromancer shall surely be put to death. They shall be stoned with stones; their blood shall be upon them."
20.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 18 and 19 set out how a holy people are to live. Chapter 20 returns to many of the sins of chapter 18, child sacrifice to Molech, consulting the dead and sexual offences, and now attaches penalties, often death. It is among the hardest chapters in the Bible.

The message. Sin against the holy God who lives among his people is deadly serious, and a community that shuts its eyes to it shares the guilt. Yet the chapter is finally about holiness and belonging. Twice it calls Israel to be holy (vv. 7, 26), it names the LORD as the one “who sanctifies you” (v. 8), and it ends with his purpose: “that you should be mine” (v. 26).

Why it was said. Israel was a nation ruled directly by God through his law, with his dwelling in the middle of the camp, and set apart as the people from whom the promised Saviour would come. These were its criminal laws (see the introduction on the moral, ceremonial and civil law).

How the chapter makes its case. Whoever gives a child to Molech must die, and God will set his face against any clan that looks away (vv. 1–5). Turning to mediums is unfaithfulness, and the remedy is holiness, which the LORD supplies (vv. 6–8). Cursing a parent and the gravest sexual sins are capital crimes (vv. 9–16); other sexual sins bring lesser penalties, being cut off or dying childless (vv. 17–21). Then the reason for it all: God has separated Israel from the peoples to be his (vv. 22–27).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes. Every sentence of death in this chapter says that these things deserve death, and the gospel does not dispute it: “the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23). It announces that the sentence fell on someone else: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). So the holiness the chapter demands, God gives: Christ gave himself “to purify for himself a people for his own possession” (Titus 2:14).

For us. We do not wield Israel’s civil sword, but we can recover the true weight of sin, and with it a deeper wonder at the grace that bore its penalty. Churches and families must never look away from harm done to the vulnerable. And those who have done these things are not beyond reach: the way back is confession and the mercy God has promised (1 John 1:9).
20.theology:
The seriousness of sin. The death penalties reveal how gravely God regards sin among his people.

Israel, not the church. These civil penalties belonged to Israel as a nation under God's direct rule; the church lives under grace and church discipline, not the sword.

Separated to be his own. God's purpose in setting Israel apart is fulfilled as Christ purifies "a people for his own possession" (Titus 2:14).
20.examples:
Then: Israel learned that sin against a holy God is deadly serious.

Now: we do not wield Israel's civil sword, but we can recover sin's true weight, and with it a deeper wonder at the grace that made us God's own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-27 — Penalties, and a People Set Apart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The holy God who lives among his people treats sin among them with deadly seriousness, yet his purpose is to make them his own. Giving a child to Molech brings death, and God himself will act against anyone who looks away (vv. 1–5). Turning to mediums is unfaithfulness, answered by the call to be holy and the promise that the LORD sanctifies (vv. 6–8). Cursing parents and the gravest sexual sins are capital offences (vv. 9–16), while others bring lesser penalties (vv. 17–21). The chapter closes with the reason: the land will vomit out a defiled people, and God has separated Israel from the peoples “that you should be mine” (vv. 22–27).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who demands holiness is the God who gives it. Even in a chapter of penalties, he says, "I am the LORD who sanctifies you."
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a community that looked away was treated as complicit. Now: a church or family that ignores the abuse of a child is not neutral either; it must act to protect the vulnerable.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Say to the people of Israel, Any one of the people of Israel or of the strangers who sojourn in Israel who gives any of his children to Molech shall surely be put to death. The people of the land shall stone him with stones. I myself will set my face against that man and will cut him off from among his people, because he has given one of his children to Molech, to make my sanctuary unclean and to profane my holy name. And if the people of the land do at all close their eyes to that man when he gives one of his children to Molech, and do not put him to death, then I will set my face against that man and against his clan and will cut them off from among their people, him and all who follow him in whoring after Molech.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Giving a child to Molech was to be punished by death, and God himself would act against the offender and against any community that shut its eyes to it.

Gives any of his children to Molech. Chapter 18 forbade it (18:21); chapter 20 attaches the penalty. The reason given includes its effect on God’s dwelling: it makes his sanctuary unclean and profanes his name.

Close their eyes. Then a clause with teeth: if the people close their eyes, God will act himself, against the man “and against his clan”. A community that looks away is not neutral; it is named alongside the offender. Jesus, who welcomed little children, spoke as sternly of those who harm them (Matthew 18:6).

verseByVerse.quote: "If a person turns to mediums and necromancers, whoring after them, I will set my face against that person and will cut him off from among his people. Consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy, for I am the LORD your God. Keep my statutes and do them; I am the LORD who sanctifies you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turning to mediums is unfaithfulness to God, and the answer is holiness, which the LORD himself gives: “I am the LORD who sanctifies you.”

Whoring after them. Seeking the dead for guidance is adultery against the LORD, as Saul found at Endor (1 Samuel 28).

I am the LORD who sanctifies you. In the middle of a chapter of penalties comes the call of chapter 19, “be holy”, followed at once by the promise. The one who demands holiness is the one who supplies it, as he now does by the Spirit he gives to all who are in Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:7–8). That clause is the only reason a chapter like this is bearable.

verseByVerse.quote: For anyone who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death; he has cursed his father or his mother; his blood is upon him. "If a man commits adultery with the wife of his neighbor, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death.
