If a man lies with his father's wife, he has uncovered his father's nakedness; both of them shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them. If a man lies with his daughter-in-law, both of them shall surely be put to death; they have committed perversion; their blood is upon them. If a man lies with a male as with a woman, both of them have committed an abomination; they shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them. If a man takes a woman and her mother also, it is depravity; he and they shall be burned with fire, that there may be no depravity among you. If a man lies with an animal, he shall surely be put to death, and you shall kill the animal. If a woman approaches any animal and lies with it, you shall kill the woman and the animal; they shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Israel, cursing a parent and the gravest sexual sins carried the death penalty, showing how seriously God regards them; these civil penalties belonged to Israel as a nation and are not carried into the church.

Facing the difficulty. A modern reader cannot read this page without difficulty, and it should be faced honestly rather than explained away.

A nation’s criminal code. Israel was not a church but a nation, with a criminal code, and this was that code. As in every legal system, the severity of a sentence states how gravely the society regards the act.

Witnesses and ransom. Two further facts help. A death sentence required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:6), so private sins were rarely capital cases. And Numbers 35:31 forbids a ransom for a murderer’s life, which suggests to many scholars that for other offences a ransom could replace death, so that these penalties marked the most the crime deserved. That reading is debated.

Not carried into the church. These penalties were given to one nation, in one land, under one covenant, and the New Testament does not carry them across. The church has no sword: for the gravest sin in Corinth Paul put a man out of the fellowship, not to death (1 Corinthians 5:13), and even that aimed at his restoration (perhaps 2 Corinthians 2:5–8).

Neither do I condemn you. When a woman caught in adultery was brought to Jesus with verse 10 in hand, he said, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more” (John 8:11; the earliest manuscripts do not include this account). He did not call adultery harmless; he could release her because he would bear the sentence himself.

Why the acts are still sin. Why do Christians still call the acts of verse 13 sin, while dropping the penalty and the food laws (11:10)? Because the New Testament sorts them. The food laws marked Israel off from the nations and are lifted explicitly (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). The sexual laws rest on creation (Genesis 2:24), bound the Canaanites too (18:24–25), and are repeated by the apostles (Romans 1:26–27; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11). The death penalty belonged to Israel’s civil law and ended with that nation’s state. Christians are not picking and choosing; they are following the apostles, and the gospel offers washing to every sinner: “such were some of you” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

Where Christians differ: should nations today adopt these penalties? Theonomists would apply Israel’s civil laws, penalties included, to modern states. This commentary’s view: Israel’s civil law was fulfilled and ended with Israel as a nation; the moral law it expressed remains the rule of life.

Uncertain wording. Burned with fire (v. 14) may mean burning alive, or burning the bodies after execution, as at Achan’s death, where Israel “stoned him with stones” and “burned them with fire” (Joshua 7:25). The text does not say which.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man takes his sister, a daughter of his father or a daughter of his mother, and sees her nakedness, and she sees his nakedness, it is a disgrace, and they shall be cut off in the sight of the children of their people. He has uncovered his sister's nakedness, and he shall bear his iniquity. If a man lies with a woman during her menstrual period and uncovers her nakedness, he has made naked her fountain, and she has uncovered the fountain of her blood. Both of them shall be cut off from among their people. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother's sister or of your father's sister, for that is to make naked one's relative; they shall bear their iniquity. If a man lies with his uncle's wife, he has uncovered his uncle's nakedness; they shall bear their sin; they shall die childless. If a man takes his brother's wife, it is impurity. He has uncovered his brother's nakedness; they shall be childless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other sexual sins carried lesser penalties, being cut off or dying childless, for each offence was weighed, but none was treated as trivial.

Weighed, not alike. Not everything is punished alike: each offence was weighed, and some are left to God’s own hand. Yet the New Testament nowhere lowers the estimate of these sins; it raises it, tracing adultery back to the lustful look and murder back to anger (Matthew 5:21–28).

Who bears the sentence. What changes is not the gravity of sin but who bears its sentence. The gospel reports that it was carried out on someone else, who also kept the law we broke (Romans 5:19). So the way back for anyone who has done these things is confession and the mercy God promised (1 John 1:9).

Uncertain wording. They shall die childless (vv. 20–21) may mean that God would withhold children, or that their children would not count as their heirs. Either way it is left in God’s hands.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall therefore keep all my statutes and all my rules and do them, that the land where I am bringing you to live may not vomit you out. And you shall not walk in the customs of the nation that I am driving out before you, for they did all these things, and therefore I detested them. But I have said to you, 'You shall inherit their land, and I will give it to you to possess, a land flowing with milk and honey.' I am the LORD your God, who has separated you from the peoples. You shall therefore separate the clean beast from the unclean, and the unclean bird from the clean. You shall not make yourselves detestable by beast or by bird or by anything with which the ground crawls, which I have set apart for you to hold unclean. You shall be holy to me, for I the LORD am holy and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine. "A man or a woman who is a medium or a necromancer shall surely be put to death. They shall be stoned with stones; their blood shall be upon them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God separated Israel from the nations to be his own, and the daily separation of clean from unclean food was to remind them of it. The chapter’s last word is not death but belonging.

Who has separated you from the peoples. The word “separated” appears twice, and it carries the whole logic of the book: holy means set apart. But Israel’s distinctiveness was never an end in itself, and the final clause says what it was for: that you should be mine. Separating clean animals from unclean at every meal mirrored God’s separating Israel from the peoples (v. 25). That is why, when the wall between Jew and Gentile came down, the food laws went with it, and Peter learned that he “should not call any person common or unclean” (Acts 10:28).

A people for his own possession. The New Testament describes the church in the same terms: “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession” (1 Peter 2:9), words first spoken to Israel. The church is still set apart, and for the same reason: not to be admired for its separation, but to belong to him.

A medium or a necromancer. Verse 27 returns to verse 6, now naming the medium’s own penalty: the chapter closes on the danger of seeking any voice but the LORD’s.

keyVerse.quote: You shall be holy to me, for I the LORD am holy and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine.
keyVerse.note: After a chapter of penalties, this verse gives the reason for them all: God set Israel apart not to make it proud but to make it his own. The same purpose runs through the cross, where Christ gave himself “to purify for himself a people for his own possession” (Titus 2:14).

20.reflection:
Many readers find this chapter one of the hardest in the Bible. What does it show you about how seriously God takes sin, and why might our own discomfort expose how lightly we take it?

Verses 4–5 warn a community that “close their eyes” to the harm of a child. What would it mean for your church and family never to look away from harm done to the vulnerable?

Israel’s civil penalties are not carried into the church, yet the New Testament still calls these acts sin. How would you explain the difference to a friend who thinks Christians pick and choose?

The chapter ends, “that you should be mine” (v. 26). How does knowing that Christ bore the sentence of death for us change the way you think about holiness and belonging?

21.title: Holiness for the Priests: A Higher Standard
21.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them, No one shall make himself unclean for the dead among his people,<sup>2</sup>except for his closest relatives, his mother, his father, his son, his daughter, his brother,<sup>3</sup>or his virgin sister (who is near to him because she has had no husband; for her he may make himself unclean).<sup>4</sup>He shall not make himself unclean as a husband among his people and so profane himself.<sup>5</sup>They shall not make bald patches on their heads, nor shave off the edges of their beards, nor make any cuts on their body.<sup>6</sup>They shall be holy to their God and not profane the name of their God. For they offer the LORD's food offerings, the bread of their God; therefore they shall be holy.<sup>7</sup>They shall not marry a prostitute or a woman who has been defiled, neither shall they marry a woman divorced from her husband, for the priest is holy to his God.<sup>8</sup>You shall sanctify him, for he offers the bread of your God. He shall be holy to you, for I, the LORD, who sanctify you, am holy.<sup>9</sup>And the daughter of any priest, if she profanes herself by whoring, profanes her father; she shall be burned with fire.<sup>10</sup>"The priest who is chief among his brothers, on whose head the anointing oil is poured and who has been consecrated to wear the garments, shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes.<sup>11</sup>He shall not go in to any dead bodies nor make himself unclean, even for his father or for his mother.<sup>12</sup>He shall not go out of the sanctuary, lest he profane the sanctuary of his God, for the consecration of the anointing oil of his God is on him: I am the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And he shall take a wife in her virginity.<sup>14</sup>A widow, or a divorced woman, or a woman who has been defiled, or a prostitute, these he shall not marry. But he shall take as his wife a virgin of his own people,<sup>15</sup>that he may not profane his offspring among his people, for I am the LORD who sanctifies him."<sup>16</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>17</sup>"Speak to Aaron, saying, None of your offspring throughout their generations who has a blemish may approach to offer the bread of his God.<sup>18</sup>For no one who has a blemish shall draw near, a man blind or lame, or one who has a mutilated face or a limb too long,<sup>19</sup>or a man who has an injured foot or an injured hand,<sup>20</sup>or a hunchback or a dwarf or a man with a defect in his sight or an itching disease or scabs or crushed testicles.<sup>21</sup>No man of the offspring of Aaron the priest who has a blemish shall come near to offer the LORD's food offerings; since he has a blemish, he shall not come near to offer the bread of his God.<sup>22</sup>He may eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy and of the holy things,<sup>23</sup>but he shall not go through the veil or approach the altar, because he has a blemish, that he may not profane my sanctuaries, for I am the LORD who sanctifies them."<sup>24</sup>So Moses spoke to Aaron and to his sons and to all the people of Israel.
21.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 17–20 carried holiness into the camp for every Israelite. Now chapters 21–22 turn to those who stood nearest to God, the priests, and to the holy things they handled. This chapter is about the men themselves.

The message. The nearer you stand to God, the more plainly your life must say that he is holy. The priests were to keep away from death, marry with care and come to the altar whole, because they were living pictures of the holy God and of the perfect offering. Yet it is the LORD who makes them holy (vv. 8, 15, 23), and the priest barred from the altar is still fed at his table.

Why it was said. Israel had already seen two priests die for careless worship (10:1–3), and the peoples around them mourned with gashes and shaved heads (see the introduction). Israel needed priests whose very lives showed that the LORD is the living God.

How the chapter makes its case. Every priest may be defiled by a death only in his closest family, must not mourn in pagan ways, and must marry a woman of good name, because he offers “the bread of his God” (vv. 1–9). The high priest is held more strictly still: no open mourning, no contact with any dead body, even a parent’s, and a virgin of his own people for a bride (vv. 10–15). A descendant of Aaron with a physical defect may not offer at the altar, yet he still eats the most holy food (vv. 16–24).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. Aaron’s sons could be outwardly whole for a while, but none was whole within; the priest this chapter describes is found only in Jesus, “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26). And the pattern takes a surprising turn: the high priest who could not go near a corpse is fulfilled in one who touched the dead and raised them. Because he is the unblemished priest, the blind, the lame and the scarred are welcomed in him and made “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9).

For us. Those who lead God’s people are still held to a higher standard (James 3:1), and every believer is now a priest whose life should say that God is holy. But our access does not rest on our own wholeness. If you feel disqualified by what is broken in you, in body or in history, look to the priest who is whole for you, and come.
21.theology:
A higher standard for leaders. Those who draw nearest to God bear greater accountability; teachers in the church will be judged with greater strictness (James 3:1).

The unblemished priest. The demand for a flawless priest and sacrifice points to Christ, the spotless Lamb (1 Pet 1:19).

Grace for the blemished. In Christ the broken are welcomed and made priests, clothed in his perfection.
21.examples:
Then: Israel's priests kept a stricter holiness, a living parable of the perfection God requires.

Now: no believer is kept back from God by disability, illness or scars. We rest in Christ, who clothes blemished sinners in his own perfection, and a church should make its welcome as wide as his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-24 — The Holiness of the Priests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who serve nearest to God must show his holiness most plainly, and God himself makes them holy. Ordinary priests may be defiled by a death only for their closest family, must not mourn with pagan cuts and shaving, and must marry a woman of good name, because they offer the bread of their God (vv. 1–9). The high priest may not mourn openly or go near any dead body, even a parent’s, and must marry a virgin of his own people (vv. 10–15). A descendant of Aaron with a physical defect may not offer at the altar, yet he still eats the holy food, for the rule guards a picture, not his worth (vv. 16–24).
verseByVerse.theology: The priests' life was a living picture of the holiness of the God they served, who is the God of life and wholeness. The cost of that picture fell on real people, and the law softened it where it could.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a priest might have to stay away from a funeral he longed to attend. Now: ministers still carry costs others do not see, and their people can pray for them and bear with them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them, No one shall make himself unclean for the dead among his people, except for his closest relatives, his mother, his father, his son, his daughter, his brother, or his virgin sister (who is near to him because she has had no husband; for her he may make himself unclean). He shall not make himself unclean as a husband among his people and so profane himself. They shall not make bald patches on their heads, nor shave off the edges of their beards, nor make any cuts on their body. They shall be holy to their God and not profane the name of their God. For they offer the LORD's food offerings, the bread of their God; therefore they shall be holy. They shall not marry a prostitute or a woman who has been defiled, neither shall they marry a woman divorced from her husband, for the priest is holy to his God. You shall sanctify him, for he offers the bread of your God. He shall be holy to you, for I, the LORD, who sanctify you, am holy. And the daughter of any priest, if she profanes herself by whoring, profanes her father; she shall be burned with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because priests stood nearest to the living God, they were to keep away from death and keep their homes above reproach.

Except for his closest relatives. Grief is not forbidden him; his wife is probably included among “his closest relatives”. But where an ordinary Israelite could attend any funeral, the priest could attend almost none. Death, the wage of sin, is the great uncleanness, and the servant of the living God could not be continually in contact with it.

Nor make any cuts on their body. The pagan mourning rites are forbidden, as in 19:27–28, because they say something untrue about death. His marriage is guarded too, for the priest is holy to his God (v. 7): the man who offered the bread of their God (v. 6), the food of God’s table, was to have a household above reproach.

A priest’s daughter. Verse 9 is the hardest line here: a priest’s daughter who turns to prostitution is to be burned. It probably includes the cult prostitution of Canaan’s shrines, which profaned her father’s office. Whether the burning was the means of death or, as with Achan, of the body after execution (Joshua 7:15, 25) is debated. This was Israel’s civil law, which ended with that nation; the church answers such sin with the welcome of Christ, who sent a sinful woman away forgiven (Luke 7:47–50).

What it does not mean. These rules fenced an office that was a picture; they do not make divorced women, or women with a past, second-class before God.

Uncertain wording. As a husband (v. 4) can also mean “as a chief”: either he may not be defiled for relatives by marriage, or his rank forbids it. A woman who has been defiled (v. 7) may be one violated or one who lived immorally.

verseByVerse.quote: "The priest who is chief among his brothers, on whose head the anointing oil is poured and who has been consecrated to wear the garments, shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes. He shall not go in to any dead bodies nor make himself unclean, even for his father or for his mother. He shall not go out of the sanctuary, lest he profane the sanctuary of his God, for the consecration of the anointing oil of his God is on him: I am the LORD. And he shall take a wife in her virginity. A widow, or a divorced woman, or a woman who has been defiled, or a prostitute, these he shall not marry. But he shall take as his wife a virgin of his own people, that he may not profane his offspring among his people, for I am the LORD who sanctifies him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest, anointed to stand before God for all Israel, was to show no sign of mourning, go near no dead body, even his parents’, and marry a virgin of his own people.

Even for his father or for his mother. The high priest could not even let his hair hang loose or tear his clothes (compare 10:6). The man who bore the LORD’s name on his forehead could not stand at his own mother’s graveside, because the consecration of the anointing oil of his God is on him. His bride had to be a virgin of his own people, because the office passed to his sons (v. 15).

Jesus touched the dead. That sets up something the Gospels record without comment. In Nain Jesus “came up and touched the bier” of a widow’s only son (Luke 7:14); in a ruler’s house he “took her by the hand” (Matthew 9:25); at Bethany he called a man four days dead out of the tomb (John 11:39–44). The one holier than Aaron walked straight up to the dead and touched them, because uncleanness did not pass from them to him. Life passed from him to them, and the dead sat up. And he wept there (John 11:35): Aaron could not mourn in public, but our high priest is able “to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron, saying, None of your offspring throughout their generations who has a blemish may approach to offer the bread of his God. For no one who has a blemish shall draw near, a man blind or lame, or one who has a mutilated face or a limb too long, or a man who has an injured foot or an injured hand, or a hunchback or a dwarf or a man with a defect in his sight or an itching disease or scabs or crushed testicles. No man of the offspring of Aaron the priest who has a blemish shall come near to offer the LORD's food offerings; since he has a blemish, he shall not come near to offer the bread of his God. He may eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy and of the holy things, but he shall not go through the veil or approach the altar, because he has a blemish, that he may not profane my sanctuaries, for I am the LORD who sanctifies them." So Moses spoke to Aaron and to his sons and to all the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A descendant of Aaron with a physical defect could not offer at the altar, yet he remained a priest and ate the holy food: the rule guarded a picture of wholeness, not his worth.

What the rule is doing. Everything presented at the altar had to be unblemished, and the same word is used of the animals in the next chapter (22:20–25). The priest at the altar was himself a living picture of a whole offering; he who could not serve as that picture lost nothing of his worth.

Barred from serving, not from eating. Verse 22 is easy to miss: he may eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy and of the holy things. He remains a priest, supported by the offerings and belonging wholly to the household of God. What he loses is one task, not his place.

Brought in to the banquet. Then the gospel does something startling with these very people. In Jesus’ parable the master sends for “the poor and crippled and blind and lame” (Luke 14:21): much of the list of Leviticus 21, carried through the door and seated at the table. The altar admitted only the unblemished; the kingdom has one unblemished man, Christ, and admits all the rest on his account.

What it does not mean. Disability is not a sign of sin (John 9:2–3). People with disabilities bear God’s image and are indispensable members of the church (1 Corinthians 12:22), and church leaders are qualified by character, not body (1 Timothy 3:1–7).

Uncertain wording. Several words in vv. 18–20 are rare: a mutilated face may mean a split nose, a dwarf translates a word meaning “thin”, and the skin conditions cannot be identified. The general sense, a visible bodily defect, is clear.

keyVerse.quote: You shall sanctify him, for he offers the bread of your God. He shall be holy to you, for I, the LORD, who sanctify you, am holy.
keyVerse.note: Every rule in the chapter rests on this verse: the priest must be holy because he serves at the table of the holy God, and that holiness is the LORD’s gift before it is the priest’s duty. It looks ahead to the priest who said, “for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth” (John 17:19).

21.reflection:
The priests were held to a higher standard because they stood nearest to God (vv. 1–9). What does this teach about the responsibilities of those who lead in the church today (James 3:1), and how can we pray for and support them?

The high priest could not go near even a parent’s body, yet Jesus touched the dead and raised them (Luke 7:14). What does that contrast show you about Christ’s holiness, and about how he meets us in our grief?

A priest with a blemish could not offer at the altar but still ate the bread of his God (vv. 22–23). How does that distinction help us read this hard passage, and how can our church welcome and value people with disabilities?

Three times God says that he is the LORD who sanctifies (vv. 8, 15, 23). Where are you tempted to think your standing with God depends on your own wholeness, and how does Christ, the unblemished priest, answer that?

22.title: Holy Offerings: Nothing Blemished for God
22.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to Aaron and his sons so that they abstain from the holy things of the people of Israel, which they dedicate to me, so that they do not profane my holy name: I am the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Say to them, 'If any one of all your offspring throughout your generations approaches the holy things that the people of Israel dedicate to the LORD, while he has an uncleanness, that person shall be cut off from my presence: I am the LORD.<sup>4</sup>None of the offspring of Aaron who has a leprous disease or a discharge may eat of the holy things until he is clean. Whoever touches anything that is unclean through contact with the dead or a man who has had an emission of semen,<sup>5</sup>and whoever touches a swarming thing by which he may be made unclean or a person from whom he may take uncleanness, whatever his uncleanness may be—<sup>6</sup>the person who touches such a thing shall be unclean until the evening and shall not eat of the holy things unless he has bathed his body in water.<sup>7</sup>When the sun goes down he shall be clean, and afterward he may eat of the holy things, because they are his food.<sup>8</sup>He shall not eat what dies of itself or is torn by beasts, and so make himself unclean by it: I am the LORD.'<sup>9</sup>They shall therefore keep my charge, lest they bear sin for it and die thereby when they profane it: I am the LORD who sanctifies them.<sup>10</sup>"A lay person shall not eat of a holy thing; no foreign guest of the priest or hired worker shall eat of a holy thing,<sup>11</sup>but if a priest buys a slave as his property for money, the slave may eat of it, and anyone born in his house may eat of his food.<sup>12</sup>If a priest's daughter marries a layman, she shall not eat of the contribution of the holy things.<sup>13</sup>But if a priest's daughter is widowed or divorced and has no child and returns to her father's house, as in her youth, she may eat of her father's food; yet no lay person shall eat of it.<sup>14</sup>And if anyone eats of a holy thing unintentionally, he shall add the fifth of its value to it and give the holy thing to the priest.<sup>15</sup>They shall not profane the holy things of the people of Israel, which they contribute to the LORD,<sup>16</sup>and so cause them to bear iniquity and guilt, by eating their holy things: for I am the LORD who sanctifies them."<sup>17</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>18</sup>"Speak to Aaron and his sons and all the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of the house of Israel or of the sojourners in Israel presents a burnt offering as his offering, for any of their vows or freewill offerings that they offer to the LORD,<sup>19</sup>if it is to be accepted for you it shall be a male without blemish, of the bulls or the sheep or the goats.<sup>20</sup>You shall not offer anything that has a blemish, for it will not be acceptable for you.<sup>21</sup>And when anyone offers a sacrifice of peace offerings to the LORD to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering from the herd or from the flock, to be accepted it must be perfect; there shall be no blemish in it.<sup>22</sup>Animals blind or disabled or mutilated or having a discharge or an itch or scabs you shall not offer to the LORD or give them to the LORD as a food offering on the altar.<sup>23</sup>You may present a bull or a lamb that has a part too long or too short for a freewill offering, but for a vow offering it cannot be accepted.<sup>24</sup>Any animal that has its testicles bruised or crushed or torn or cut you shall not offer to the LORD; you shall not do it within your land,<sup>25</sup>neither shall you offer as the bread of your God any such animals gotten from a foreigner. Since there is a blemish in them, because of their mutilation, they will not be accepted for you."<sup>26</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>27</sup>"When an ox or sheep or goat is born, it shall remain seven days with its mother, and from the eighth day on it shall be acceptable as a food offering to the LORD.<sup>28</sup>But you shall not kill an ox or a sheep and her young in one day.<sup>29</sup>And when you sacrifice a sacrifice of thanksgiving to the LORD, you shall sacrifice it so that you may be accepted.<sup>30</sup>It shall be eaten on the same day; you shall leave none of it until morning: I am the LORD.<sup>31</sup>"So you shall keep my commandments and do them: I am the LORD.<sup>32</sup>And you shall not profane my holy name, that I may be sanctified among the people of Israel. I am the LORD who sanctifies you,<sup>33</sup>who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God: I am the LORD."
22.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 21 set the standard for the priests themselves. Chapter 22 turns to the holy things they handled: first who may eat the holy food and when, then what the people may bring to the altar. It closes the section on the priests (chapters 21–22).

The message. Holy things must be handled as holy, and God must be given what is whole and best. A priest who is unclean waits before he eats; only his household shares the holy food; and no blind, lame or maimed animal may be offered, because it would say that God deserves only what we can spare. Behind every rule stands the God who brought Israel out of Egypt to be their God (vv. 32–33).

Why it was said. The priests lived on the offerings, so it was easy to treat holy food as ordinary dinner; and every farmer had a lame animal worth nothing at market. Centuries later Malachi found both temptations winning (Malachi 1:6–14).

How the chapter makes its case. Priests must not eat the holy things while unclean (vv. 1–9). Only the priest’s household may eat them, including a bought slave and a daughter come home, but not a guest or hired worker; anyone who eats by mistake repays with a fifth added (vv. 10–16). Offerings for vows, freewill gifts and peace offerings must be without blemish (vv. 17–25). Newborn animals stay seven days with their mother, mother and young are not killed on one day, the thanksgiving meat is eaten the same day, and the chapter ends with its reason: “I am the LORD who sanctifies you” (vv. 26–33).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern. Every inspection of a lamb rehearsed one perfect sacrifice: Christ “offered himself without blemish to God” (Hebrews 9:14), and we were ransomed “with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19). Where Israel searched its flocks for a flawless lamb, God gave his own Son: the perfect sacrifice he required, he himself provided.

For us. Do we give God the first and best, or the leftovers: the prime of our strength, or the dregs of our exhaustion? Because Christ’s offering is accepted, ours can be too: “present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God” (Romans 12:1). And the God who accepted a poor man’s handful of flour does not despise the weary who have little left to give (Mark 12:43–44).
22.theology:
Without blemish. The demand for a flawless offering sets a standard no earthly lamb could meet, and points to Christ, who alone met it.

God deserves our best. To offer the maimed or leftover is to despise God's name; he is worthy of our first and finest.

The LORD who sanctifies. Holiness is God's gift and work, grounded in redemption and applied by the Spirit (22:32).
22.examples:
Then: an Israelite searched his flock for a flawless animal.

Now: we bring God our best, not our leftovers, yet we rest our acceptance not on our flawed offerings but on the one spotless Lamb.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Holy food must be eaten by the right people in the right state, so that the priests do not profane God’s holy name. A priest who is unclean, through skin disease, a discharge, contact with the dead or anything else, must keep away from the holy things until he has bathed and the sun has set; to eat while unclean is to be cut off from God’s presence (vv. 1–9). The holy food belongs to the priest’s household: not to a guest or hired worker, but to a slave he has bought, those born in his house, and a widowed or divorced daughter come home. Anyone who eats it by mistake repays it with a fifth added (vv. 10–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Holy things belong to God and to those he brings into his household. Access to them rests on belonging, not on rank, wages or a professional exemption.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: priests had no exemption from the rules they enforced. Now: pastors and church leaders need the same grace, and the same accountability, as everyone they serve.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and his sons so that they abstain from the holy things of the people of Israel, which they dedicate to me, so that they do not profane my holy name: I am the LORD. Say to them, 'If any one of all your offspring throughout your generations approaches the holy things that the people of Israel dedicate to the LORD, while he has an uncleanness, that person shall be cut off from my presence: I am the LORD. None of the offspring of Aaron who has a leprous disease or a discharge may eat of the holy things until he is clean. Whoever touches anything that is unclean through contact with the dead or a man who has had an emission of semen, and whoever touches a swarming thing by which he may be made unclean or a person from whom he may take uncleanness, whatever his uncleanness may be— the person who touches such a thing shall be unclean until the evening and shall not eat of the holy things unless he has bathed his body in water. When the sun goes down he shall be clean, and afterward he may eat of the holy things, because they are his food. He shall not eat what dies of itself or is torn by beasts, and so make himself unclean by it: I am the LORD.' They shall therefore keep my charge, lest they bear sin for it and die thereby when they profane it: I am the LORD who sanctifies them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Priests had to be clean before they ate the holy offerings: the men who ran the system were not exempt from it.

That person shall be cut off from my presence. There is no professional exemption: a priest with a skin disease waits outside like anybody else. Yet the uncleanness is not endless: he bathes, the sun goes down, and he eats again (v. 7).

Because they are his food. The holy offerings were the priests’ daily bread, and that was the danger: what you handle every day you stop noticing. Those who handle holy things most often, pastors among them, are most at risk of treating them as ordinary (compare 1 Corinthians 11:27). The paragraph closes on grace: I am the LORD who sanctifies them (v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: "A lay person shall not eat of a holy thing; no foreign guest of the priest or hired worker shall eat of a holy thing, but if a priest buys a slave as his property for money, the slave may eat of it, and anyone born in his house may eat of his food. If a priest's daughter marries a layman, she shall not eat of the contribution of the holy things. But if a priest's daughter is widowed or divorced and has no child and returns to her father's house, as in her youth, she may eat of her father's food; yet no lay person shall eat of it. And if anyone eats of a holy thing unintentionally, he shall add the fifth of its value to it and give the holy thing to the priest. They shall not profane the holy things of the people of Israel, which they contribute to the LORD, and so cause them to bear iniquity and guilt, by eating their holy things: for I am the LORD who sanctifies them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The holy food belonged to the priest’s household, and the line was drawn by belonging, not by employment.

If a priest buys a slave. A hired man who works on the premises every day may not eat; a purchased slave who lives there may. Israel’s servant laws trouble modern readers, and rightly ask for care; here at least the bought slave is counted as family at the holy table. It is a small picture of the gospel: we sit at God’s table not as employees but as those who “were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:20).

If a priest’s daughter is widowed or divorced. A daughter whose marriage has ended, with no child to support her, is restored to the provision she grew up with. She does not fall between two households.

Add the fifth of its value. Repaying the value plus a fifth is the rule already given for holy things in 5:16. Even an honest mistake with holy things carries a cost.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God must be given what is whole, not what is spare. Every burnt offering and peace offering, whether from an Israelite or a sojourner, must be without blemish; a blind, injured or diseased animal will not be accepted, nor a castrated one, even if bought from a foreigner, and only a freewill gift may have a limb too long or short (vv. 17–25). Small mercies follow: a newborn stays seven days with its mother, mother and young are not killed on one day, and the thanksgiving offering is eaten on the day it is made. All of it rests on the LORD who sanctifies Israel and brought them out of Egypt (vv. 26–33).
verseByVerse.theology: God is worthy of the best, and he is also kind: the same laws that demand perfect offerings stop to protect a newborn animal and its mother.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God would not be worshipped with what was going spare. Now: the time, money and energy we give him can be our first and best, even when there is not much of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and his sons and all the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of the house of Israel or of the sojourners in Israel presents a burnt offering as his offering, for any of their vows or freewill offerings that they offer to the LORD, if it is to be accepted for you it shall be a male without blemish, of the bulls or the sheep or the goats. You shall not offer anything that has a blemish, for it will not be acceptable for you. And when anyone offers a sacrifice of peace offerings to the LORD to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering from the herd or from the flock, to be accepted it must be perfect; there shall be no blemish in it. Animals blind or disabled or mutilated or having a discharge or an itch or scabs you shall not offer to the LORD or give them to the LORD as a food offering on the altar. You may present a bull or a lamb that has a part too long or too short for a freewill offering, but for a vow offering it cannot be accepted. Any animal that has its testicles bruised or crushed or torn or cut you shall not offer to the LORD; you shall not do it within your land, neither shall you offer as the bread of your God any such animals gotten from a foreigner. Since there is a blemish in them, because of their mutilation, they will not be accepted for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Offerings had to be whole, because to give God what is damaged says he is worth only what we can spare.

Anything that has a blemish. The temptation in any farming community is obvious: an animal has broken its leg and is worth nothing at market, so give that one to God. The law shuts the door on worship funded by whatever was going spare, even rejects bought cheaply from a foreigner (v. 25). Only a freewill gift, not a vow already owed, may have a limb too long or short (v. 23).

Malachi’s sarcasm. Centuries later Malachi found Israel’s priests doing precisely this, and his sarcasm is withering: “When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not evil? And when you offer those that are lame or sick, is that not evil? Present that to your governor; will he accept you or show you favor?” (Malachi 1:8).

Uncertain wording. Too long or too short (v. 23) translates two rare words, probably describing a deformed or stunted limb. You shall not do it within your land (v. 24) may forbid offering such animals, or, as Jewish tradition took it, castrating animals at all.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "When an ox or sheep or goat is born, it shall remain seven days with its mother, and from the eighth day on it shall be acceptable as a food offering to the LORD. But you shall not kill an ox or a sheep and her young in one day. And when you sacrifice a sacrifice of thanksgiving to the LORD, you shall sacrifice it so that you may be accepted. It shall be eaten on the same day; you shall leave none of it until morning: I am the LORD. "So you shall keep my commandments and do them: I am the LORD. And you shall not profane my holy name, that I may be sanctified among the people of Israel. I am the LORD who sanctifies you, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God: I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the sacrifices showed mercy to God’s creatures, and every rule rested on the God who had rescued Israel to make them his own.

An ox or a sheep and her young. A newborn stays seven days with its mother (compare Exodus 22:30), and a mother and her young may not be killed on one day. Nothing in the sacrificial system required these mercies; they show God’s care for his creatures (Deuteronomy 22:6; 25:4). And the reason for all of it is grace already given: the LORD who sanctifies Israel is the one who brought them out of Egypt (vv. 32–33).

The Lamb of God. The demand for an unblemished offering ran for centuries, and no animal could truly take away sin. Then John the Baptist looked at Jesus walking towards him and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). Peter uses this chapter’s vocabulary of him: “a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19). Every inspection Israel made of every animal it brought was a rehearsal for one examination, conducted by a Roman governor who said, “I find no guilt in him” (John 18:38), and then handed him over anyway.

keyVerse.quote: You shall not offer anything that has a blemish, for it will not be acceptable for you.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this rule: God is to be given what is whole, never what is spare. No animal could finally meet it, and it points to the one offering that did, Christ, “a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19), through whom our own imperfect gifts are made acceptable.

22.reflection:
The holy food was the priests’ daily bread (v. 7). How can familiarity with holy things, such as Bible reading, worship or the Lord’s Supper, make us careless, and what helps us to keep them holy?

The bought slave could eat at the holy table, but the hired worker could not (vv. 10–11). What does it mean for you that you belong to God’s household because you were “bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:20), not because you have earned a place?

Malachi rebuked priests who offered God the blind and the lame (Malachi 1:8). Where are you most tempted to give God your leftovers, of time, money or energy, rather than your first and best?

Israel inspected every lamb for blemishes, and Pilate said of Jesus, “I find no guilt in him” (John 18:38). How does Christ’s perfect offering free us both to give our best and to rest when our best is poor?

23.title: The Feasts of the LORD: A Rehearsal of Redemption
23.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, These are the appointed feasts of the LORD that you shall proclaim as holy convocations; they are my appointed feasts.<sup>3</sup>"Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, a holy convocation. You shall do no work. It is a Sabbath to the LORD in all your dwelling places.<sup>4</sup>"These are the appointed feasts of the LORD, the holy convocations, which you shall proclaim at the time appointed for them.<sup>5</sup>In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at twilight, is the LORD's Passover.<sup>6</sup>And on the fifteenth day of the same month is the Feast of Unleavened Bread to the LORD; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread.<sup>7</sup>On the first day you shall have a holy convocation; you shall not do any ordinary work.<sup>8</sup>But you shall present a food offering to the LORD for seven days. On the seventh day is a holy convocation; you shall not do any ordinary work."<sup>9</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land that I give you and reap its harvest, you shall bring the sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest to the priest,<sup>11</sup>and he shall wave the sheaf before the LORD, so that you may be accepted. On the day after the Sabbath the priest shall wave it.<sup>12</sup>And on the day when you wave the sheaf, you shall offer a male lamb a year old without blemish as a burnt offering to the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And the grain offering with it shall be two tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil, a food offering to the LORD with a pleasing aroma, and the drink offering with it shall be of wine, a fourth of a hin.<sup>14</sup>And you shall eat neither bread nor grain parched or fresh until this same day, until you have brought the offering of your God: it is a statute forever throughout your generations in all your dwellings.<sup>15</sup>"You shall count seven full weeks from the day after the Sabbath, from the day that you brought the sheaf of the wave offering.<sup>16</sup>You shall count fifty days to the day after the seventh Sabbath. Then you shall present a grain offering of new grain to the LORD.<sup>17</sup>You shall bring from your dwelling places two loaves of bread to be waved, made of two tenths of an ephah. They shall be of fine flour, and they shall be baked with leaven, as firstfruits to the LORD.<sup>18</sup>And you shall present with the bread seven lambs a year old without blemish, and one bull from the herd and two rams. They shall be a burnt offering to the LORD, with their grain offering and their drink offerings, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>19</sup>And you shall offer one male goat for a sin offering, and two male lambs a year old as a sacrifice of peace offerings.<sup>20</sup>And the priest shall wave them with the bread of the firstfruits as a wave offering before the LORD, with the two lambs. They shall be holy to the LORD for the priest.<sup>21</sup>And you shall make a proclamation on the same day. You shall hold a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work. It is a statute forever in all your dwelling places throughout your generations.<sup>22</sup>"And when you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field right up to its edge, nor shall you gather the gleanings after your harvest. You shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner: I am the LORD your God."<sup>23</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>24</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, you shall observe a day of solemn rest, a memorial proclaimed with blast of trumpets, a holy convocation.<sup>25</sup>You shall not do any ordinary work, and you shall present a food offering to the LORD."<sup>26</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>27</sup>"Now on the tenth day of this seventh month is the Day of Atonement. It shall be for you a time of holy convocation, and you shall afflict yourselves and present a food offering to the LORD.<sup>28</sup>And you shall not do any work on that very day, for it is a Day of Atonement, to make atonement for you before the LORD your God.<sup>29</sup>For whoever is not afflicted on that very day shall be cut off from his people.<sup>30</sup>And whoever does any work on that very day, that person I will destroy from among his people.<sup>31</sup>You shall not do any work. It is a statute forever throughout your generations in all your dwelling places.<sup>32</sup>It shall be to you a Sabbath of solemn rest, and you shall afflict yourselves. On the ninth day of the month beginning at evening, from evening to evening shall you keep your Sabbath."<sup>33</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>34</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, On the fifteenth day of this seventh month and for seven days is the Feast of Booths to the LORD.<sup>35</sup>On the first day shall be a holy convocation; you shall not do any ordinary work.<sup>36</sup>For seven days you shall present food offerings to the LORD. On the eighth day you shall hold a holy convocation and present a food offering to the LORD. It is a solemn assembly; you shall not do any ordinary work.<sup>37</sup>"These are the appointed feasts of the LORD, which you shall proclaim as times of holy convocation, for presenting to the LORD food offerings, burnt offerings and grain offerings, sacrifices and drink offerings, each on its proper day,<sup>38</sup>besides the LORD's Sabbaths and besides your gifts and besides all your vow offerings and besides all your freewill offerings, which you give to the LORD.<sup>39</sup>"On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you have gathered in the produce of the land, you shall celebrate the feast of the LORD seven days. On the first day shall be a solemn rest, and on the eighth day shall be a solemn rest.<sup>40</sup>And you shall take on the first day the fruit of splendid trees, branches of palm trees and boughs of leafy trees and willows of the brook, and you shall rejoice before the LORD your God seven days.<sup>41</sup>You shall celebrate it as a feast to the LORD for seven days in the year. It is a statute forever throughout your generations; you shall celebrate it in the seventh month.<sup>42</sup>You shall dwell in booths for seven days. All native Israelites shall dwell in booths,<sup>43</sup>that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God."<sup>44</sup>Thus Moses declared to the people of Israel the appointed feasts of the LORD.
23.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 21–22 dealt with the priests and the holy things they handled. Now holiness reaches the calendar: chapter 23 sets out “the appointed feasts of the LORD”, the fixed times when all Israel met with God, from the weekly Sabbath through the spring and autumn feasts.

The message. Israel’s time belongs to God, and he fills their year with appointments with himself. Week by week and season by season the calendar was to remind them that he had redeemed them, that every harvest was his gift, and that sin must be dealt with before they could rejoice in his presence. Their year was to preach his grace from one end to the other.

Why it was said. Israel was about to move from a wilderness camp to farms whose rhythm would be set by seedtime and harvest, among peoples who kept their harvest festivals to gods of rain and fertility (see the introduction). God claims the seasons for himself and ties each one to what he has done.

How the chapter makes its case. The weekly Sabbath comes first (vv. 1–3). Then the spring feasts: Passover and Unleavened Bread (vv. 4–8), the first sheaf of the harvest waved before the LORD (vv. 9–14), and fifty days later the Feast of Weeks, with leavened loaves and a reminder to leave gleanings for the poor (vv. 15–22). Then the autumn feasts of the seventh month: trumpets on its first day (vv. 23–25), the Day of Atonement on the tenth, a day of fasting and rest (vv. 26–32), and from the fifteenth the Feast of Booths, a week of joy in shelters of branches (vv. 33–44).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and fulfilment, and the New Testament says so plainly: these are “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:17). He died at Passover as “our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7), rose on the day of firstfruits as “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20), and poured out the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:1–4). The Day of Atonement was fulfilled at the cross (Hebrews 9:11–12), while Trumpets and Booths look ahead to the last trumpet and to God dwelling with his people for ever (Revelation 21:3).

For us. Christians are not bound to Israel’s calendar, but we still need our time shaped by what God has done: the Lord’s Day, the Lord’s Supper, gathered worship. Let your week and your year tell the gospel, rest in the work Christ has finished, and make room in your celebrations for the poor (v. 22).
23.theology:
Time belongs to God. The feasts are appointments God made, not festivals Israel invented, and they teach that the whole year is lived before him.

Shadow and substance. Each feast was a shadow pointing beyond itself to Christ, the substance (Col 2:17), and the order in which they were fulfilled was arranged by God, not by the people it happened to.

Hope still ahead. The calendar ends with God's people camping in joy, a picture of the day when he will dwell with them for ever.
23.examples:
Then: Israel kept the feasts, unknowingly rehearsing the gospel.

Now: Christians mark their weeks by the Lord’s Day, remember his death at his table, and wait for the final harvest, when God will make his home with his people for ever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-44 — The Appointed Feasts of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sets Israel’s year around fixed meetings with himself, and each one tells part of the story of redemption. The weekly Sabbath comes first (vv. 1–3). The spring feasts follow: Passover and Unleavened Bread remember the exodus (vv. 4–8), the first sheaf of the harvest is given to God before anyone eats (vv. 9–14), and fifty days later the Feast of Weeks offers the finished loaves, with a reminder to leave the edges of the field for the poor (vv. 15–22). The autumn feasts of the seventh month open with trumpets (vv. 23–25), pass through the Day of Atonement, a day of fasting and rest (vv. 26–32), and end with a week of joy in booths (vv. 33–44).
verseByVerse.theology: The calendar is built around rest, remembrance and joy. God did not only command Israel's work; he commanded their holidays.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the feasts rehearsed Israel's redemption every year. Now: a Christian's diary can also be shaped by worship, with fixed times for gathering, remembering and rejoicing, received as gifts rather than burdens.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, These are the appointed feasts of the LORD that you shall proclaim as holy convocations; they are my appointed feasts. "Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, a holy convocation. You shall do no work. It is a Sabbath to the LORD in all your dwelling places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God claims Israel’s time for himself, and his first appointment is the weekly Sabbath.

My appointed feasts. The Hebrew word, moʿadim, means appointed times, fixed meetings, and God calls them his own twice in one verse. They are not festivals Israel invented to mark its own history, but appointments God made, entered in a calendar he wrote. A holy convocation is a sacred assembly for worship.

A Sabbath of solemn rest. The first appointment is not annual at all: the weekly Sabbath, kept in all your dwelling places, with no journey, no animal and no priest. The most frequent appointment God kept with his people cost nothing at all.

Must Christians keep these feasts? They were shadows fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17): “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7), and the Lord’s Supper has taken the Passover’s place. Keeping them is a matter of freedom, not obligation (Romans 14:5–6), and never a condition of standing with God (Galatians 4:10–11).

Where Christians differ. Does the Sabbath bind Christians today? It was the sign of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 31:13). Many godly Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment; Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds.

This commentary’s view. The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), because Colossians places Sabbaths among the shadows, so no day binds the conscience (Romans 14:5). Rest and gathering for worship on the Lord’s Day remain good gifts, gladly received. Faithful Christians differ here, and should bear with one another.
verseByVerse.note: Israel's months were lunar; the first month (later called Nisan) fell in March–April.

verseByVerse.quote: "These are the appointed feasts of the LORD, the holy convocations, which you shall proclaim at the time appointed for them. In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at twilight, is the LORD's Passover. And on the fifteenth day of the same month is the Feast of Unleavened Bread to the LORD; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day you shall have a holy convocation; you shall not do any ordinary work. But you shall present a food offering to the LORD for seven days. On the seventh day is a holy convocation; you shall not do any ordinary work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Passover and the week of Unleavened Bread remembered the night God redeemed Israel from Egypt, and both are fulfilled in Christ, our Passover lamb.

The LORD’s Passover. Passover, on the fourteenth day of the first month at twilight, marked the night Israel came out of Egypt, kept every year since as a family meal with a lamb (Exodus 12).

The Feast of Unleavened Bread. Then came seven days with no leaven (yeast) in the house: a week of searching for crumbs, so that a nation would learn that a little evil, like a little yeast, works through the whole batch. On its first and last days no ordinary work was done, probably meaning daily labour, since food could still be prepared (Exodus 12:16).

Christ our Passover. Paul states the fulfilment in one sentence: “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The Gospels place the crucifixion at precisely this point in the calendar, and John notes that the soldiers did not break his legs, “that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘Not one of his bones will be broken’” (John 19:36), the rule for the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46). Paul takes up the feast that follows in the same breath: “Let us therefore celebrate the festival… with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians 5:8). We do not put away sin to be redeemed; we put it away because the lamb has already been sacrificed.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land that I give you and reap its harvest, you shall bring the sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest to the priest, and he shall wave the sheaf before the LORD, so that you may be accepted. On the day after the Sabbath the priest shall wave it. And on the day when you wave the sheaf, you shall offer a male lamb a year old without blemish as a burnt offering to the LORD. And the grain offering with it shall be two tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil, a food offering to the LORD with a pleasing aroma, and the drink offering with it shall be of wine, a fourth of a hin. And you shall eat neither bread nor grain parched or fresh until this same day, until you have brought the offering of your God: it is a statute forever throughout your generations in all your dwellings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first sheaf of the harvest was given to God before anyone ate, a pledge that the whole harvest was his; Christ rose as the firstfruits of all who will be raised.

The sheaf of the firstfruits. The law was given in a desert, for fields Israel did not yet own (v. 10). No one was to eat from the new harvest until God had been given the first of it (v. 14). The priest waved the sheaf before the LORD, so that you may be accepted, with a lamb without blemish. Israel waved that sheaf every spring for centuries without knowing what it was rehearsing.

Christ the firstfruits. Paul’s word for the resurrection is this feast’s word: “But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). One sheaf, lifted up early, on the first day of the week, and the point of firstfruits is that they guarantee a harvest still standing in the field. It is not a sample but a promise about the rest: all who are his will rise.

For us. Giving God the first of our income and time, not what is left (Proverbs 3:9), is an act of trust that he will provide the rest.

Uncertain wording. Which “Sabbath” is meant in verse 11? The Sadducees took it as the weekly Sabbath, so the firstfruits always fell on a Sunday; the Pharisees, as the first day of Unleavened Bread. Either way, Christ rose on the first day of the week.
verseByVerse.note: The barley harvest came first, in early spring; the wheat harvest followed about seven weeks later, at the Feast of Weeks.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall count seven full weeks from the day after the Sabbath, from the day that you brought the sheaf of the wave offering. You shall count fifty days to the day after the seventh Sabbath. Then you shall present a grain offering of new grain to the LORD. You shall bring from your dwelling places two loaves of bread to be waved, made of two tenths of an ephah. They shall be of fine flour, and they shall be baked with leaven, as firstfruits to the LORD. And you shall present with the bread seven lambs a year old without blemish, and one bull from the herd and two rams. They shall be a burnt offering to the LORD, with their grain offering and their drink offerings, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And you shall offer one male goat for a sin offering, and two male lambs a year old as a sacrifice of peace offerings. And the priest shall wave them with the bread of the firstfruits as a wave offering before the LORD, with the two lambs. They shall be holy to the LORD for the priest. And you shall make a proclamation on the same day. You shall hold a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work. It is a statute forever in all your dwelling places throughout your generations. "And when you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field right up to its edge, nor shall you gather the gleanings after your harvest. You shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner: I am the LORD your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fifty days after the firstfruits Israel offered loaves from the new wheat and remembered the poor; on this very feast God poured out his Spirit.

You shall count fifty days. Seven full weeks and a day: this is the Feast of Weeks, which Greek-speaking Jews called Pentecost, from the word for fiftieth.

Baked with leaven. The two loaves waved at this feast are explicitly baked with leaven, though leaven has been banned from the offerings since chapter 2. The likeliest reason is that this feast celebrates not the raw sheaf but the finished loaf, bread as people actually eat it; and the loaves went to the priests, not onto the altar (v. 20).

Pentecost fulfilled. Fifty days after the resurrection, on the day this chapter appoints, the disciples were “all together in one place” when a sound like a mighty rushing wind filled the house (Acts 2:1–2). Luke did not choose that date; Leviticus did, centuries earlier. And the leavened loaves fit the day: the harvest gathered in was three thousand ordinary people, forgiven but far from faultless.

Gleaning at the festival. Verse 22 is a gleaning law, dropped without transition into the festival calendar (compare 19:9–10). Israel could not hold a harvest festival without being reminded to leave part of the harvest for people who owned no field. By this law Ruth the Moabite gleaned, and came into the line of David and of Christ (Ruth 2:23; 4:17). Worship and care for the poor are commanded together.
verseByVerse.note: In later Jewish tradition the Feast of Weeks also came to celebrate the giving of the law at Sinai.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, you shall observe a day of solemn rest, a memorial proclaimed with blast of trumpets, a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work, and you shall present a food offering to the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A day of rest and trumpet blasts opened the seventh month, the solemn month in which Israel’s sins would be dealt with.

A memorial proclaimed with blast of trumpets. The autumn feasts begin, and the calendar changes character. No event is remembered and no ritual described beyond the blast, the rest and the offering; the day announces that the Day of Atonement is nine days away. Later Jewish tradition made it New Year’s Day, Rosh Hashanah (see Feast of Trumpets).

A warning before the reckoning. The trumpet sounds before the reckoning, giving a nation time to prepare. Scripture keeps that pattern: the warning comes first, and early enough to act on. The last trumpet will sound for the whole world (1 Thessalonians 4:16), and until then “now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew says only a memorial of blast; no instrument is named. Memorial may mean that Israel remembers, or that the blast calls on God to remember his people, as the silver trumpets were “a reminder of you before your God” (Numbers 10:10).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Now on the tenth day of this seventh month is the Day of Atonement. It shall be for you a time of holy convocation, and you shall afflict yourselves and present a food offering to the LORD. And you shall not do any work on that very day, for it is a Day of Atonement, to make atonement for you before the LORD your God. For whoever is not afflicted on that very day shall be cut off from his people. And whoever does any work on that very day, that person I will destroy from among his people. You shall not do any work. It is a statute forever throughout your generations in all your dwelling places. It shall be to you a Sabbath of solemn rest, and you shall afflict yourselves. On the ninth day of the month beginning at evening, from evening to evening shall you keep your Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the Day of Atonement Israel was to humble itself and rest from all work while the high priest made atonement: empty-handed repentance, and complete rest in another’s work.

The Day of Atonement. The ceremony was given in chapter 16 (see Day of Atonement); this passage adds what the people do while the high priest works, from evening to evening (v. 32), as Israel’s days were counted (see How days were counted).

You shall afflict yourselves. Two commands pull against each other: afflict yourselves, and do not do any work. Fast, and rest. To afflict oneself meant above all fasting (Psalm 35:13), so that by New Testament times this was simply “the Fast” (Acts 27:9): the one fast the law commands, and also a Sabbath of solemn rest.

Fast and rest. Both halves are the gospel. Israel comes empty-handed and mourning, then sits still, because the work being done that day is the priest’s, not theirs. So we come to Christ, who entered the holy places “by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12): sorry for our sin, and resting wholly on what he has done.

Shall be cut off from his people. The warning is the sharpest attached to any feast in the chapter. There is no neutral way to spend the Day of Atonement, and no neutral response to the cross.

Where Christians differ. Are the autumn feasts fulfilled at the cross or at Christ’s return? Some dispensational readers expect the feasts to be literally restored in a millennial kingdom.

This commentary’s view. The Day of Atonement was fulfilled once for all at the cross (Hebrews 9:11–12, 24–26); Trumpets and Booths look ahead to the last trumpet (1 Thessalonians 4:16) and God dwelling with his people (Revelation 21:3). Holding the amillennial view, this commentary takes the feasts as shadows whose substance is Christ, while gladly owning as brothers those who read the prophecies otherwise.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, On the fifteenth day of this seventh month and for seven days is the Feast of Booths to the LORD. On the first day shall be a holy convocation; you shall not do any ordinary work. For seven days you shall present food offerings to the LORD. On the eighth day you shall hold a holy convocation and present a food offering to the LORD. It is a solemn assembly; you shall not do any ordinary work. "These are the appointed feasts of the LORD, which you shall proclaim as times of holy convocation, for presenting to the LORD food offerings, burnt offerings and grain offerings, sacrifices and drink offerings, each on its proper day, besides the LORD's Sabbaths and besides your gifts and besides all your vow offerings and besides all your freewill offerings, which you give to the LORD. "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you have gathered in the produce of the land, you shall celebrate the feast of the LORD seven days. On the first day shall be a solemn rest, and on the eighth day shall be a solemn rest. And you shall take on the first day the fruit of splendid trees, branches of palm trees and boughs of leafy trees and willows of the brook, and you shall rejoice before the LORD your God seven days. You shall celebrate it as a feast to the LORD for seven days in the year. It is a statute forever throughout your generations; you shall celebrate it in the seventh month. You shall dwell in booths for seven days. All native Israelites shall dwell in booths, that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God." Thus Moses declared to the people of Israel the appointed feasts of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Feast of Booths was a week of joy at harvest’s end, spent in shelters of branches to remember the wilderness; it points to God dwelling with his people for ever.

The Feast of Booths. The last feast is the longest and the happiest: you shall rejoice before the LORD your God seven days (v. 40). A settled people with vineyards and stone walls moved out of their houses and lived under leaves for a week, so that no one could forget that the land was a gift and their forefathers had crossed a desert with nothing.

Against forgetting. Prosperity forgets, and the booths were built to stop it. The command was given before Israel had a single house to move out of: God made a law against a forgetfulness still forty years away.

Living water at the feast. It was at this feast, “on the last day of the feast, the great day”, that Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). By later Jewish custom a priest poured out water from the pool of Siloam at the altar during the feast, with prayers for rain and the words of Isaiah 12:3. Jesus offered himself as the water.

God’s tent with man. The autumn feasts open with a trumpet, pass through the day sin was dealt with, and end with God’s people rejoicing in shelters. Scripture takes up that last image at the very end: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people” (Revelation 21:3), where dwell is the word for pitching a tent, the word John uses when the Word became flesh and “dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The week of camping was a rehearsal for God moving in for ever.

Uncertain wording. The fruit of splendid trees (v. 40) is not identified; later Jewish custom used the citron. It is also unclear whether the branches were for building the booths, as in Nehemiah 8:15, or for carrying in celebration.
verseByVerse.note: The Feast of Booths is also called Tabernacles (ESV note); its Hebrew name is Sukkot.

keyVerse.quote: These are the appointed feasts of the LORD that you shall proclaim as holy convocations; they are my appointed feasts.
keyVerse.note: The feasts are God’s appointments before they are Israel’s celebrations: he sets the times and calls his people to meet him. Each one tells part of the story of redemption, and together they are “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:17).

23.reflection:
God calls the feasts “my appointed feasts” (v. 2), fixed meetings with his people. What regular rhythms of worship shape your week and your year, and how could they tell the gospel more clearly?

Christ died at Passover, rose on the day of firstfruits and poured out the Spirit at Pentecost (1 Corinthians 5:7; 15:20; Acts 2:1). What does it do for your faith to see God’s plan worked out so precisely, centuries in advance?

On the Day of Atonement Israel was to fast and to rest, because the work that day was the priest’s (vv. 27–32). How do repentance and resting in Christ’s finished work belong together in the Christian life?

A gleaning law sits in the middle of the harvest festivals (v. 22). How can our celebrations, at church and at home, make room for those who have little?

24.title: The Lampstand, the Bread, and the Holiness of the Name
24.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel to bring you pure oil from beaten olives for the lamp, that a light may be kept burning regularly.<sup>3</sup>Outside the veil of the testimony, in the tent of meeting, Aaron shall arrange it from evening to morning before the LORD regularly. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations.<sup>4</sup>He shall arrange the lamps on the lampstand of pure gold before the LORD regularly.<sup>5</sup>"You shall take fine flour and bake twelve loaves from it; two tenths of an ephah shall be in each loaf.<sup>6</sup>And you shall set them in two piles, six in a pile, on the table of pure gold before the LORD.<sup>7</sup>And you shall put pure frankincense on each pile, that it may go with the bread as a memorial portion as a food offering to the LORD.<sup>8</sup>Every Sabbath day Aaron shall arrange it before the LORD regularly; it is from the people of Israel as a covenant forever.<sup>9</sup>And it shall be for Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat it in a holy place, since it is for him a most holy portion out of the LORD's food offerings, a perpetual due."<sup>10</sup>Now an Israelite woman's son, whose father was an Egyptian, went out among the people of Israel. And the Israelite woman's son and a man of Israel fought in the camp,<sup>11</sup>and the Israelite woman's son blasphemed the Name, and cursed. Then they brought him to Moses. His mother's name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan.<sup>12</sup>And they put him in custody, till the will of the LORD should be clear to them.<sup>13</sup>Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>14</sup>"Bring out of the camp the one who cursed, and let all who heard him lay their hands on his head, and let all the congregation stone him.<sup>15</sup>And speak to the people of Israel, saying, Whoever curses his God shall bear his sin.<sup>16</sup>Whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall stone him. The sojourner as well as the native, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death.<sup>17</sup>"Whoever takes a human life shall surely be put to death.<sup>18</sup>Whoever takes an animal's life shall make it good, life for life.<sup>19</sup>If anyone injures his neighbor, as he has done it shall be done to him,<sup>20</sup>fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth; whatever injury he has given a person shall be given to him.<sup>21</sup>Whoever kills an animal shall make it good, and whoever kills a person shall be put to death.<sup>22</sup>You shall have the same rule for the sojourner and for the native, for I am the LORD your God."<sup>23</sup>So Moses spoke to the people of Israel, and they brought out of the camp the one who had cursed and stoned him with stones. Thus the people of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses.
24.overview:
Where we are. After the yearly calendar of chapter 23, chapter 24 turns to what happened every night and every week inside the Holy Place: the lamp and the bread (vv. 1–9). Then, without warning, comes one of the book’s two stories (compare chapters 8–10): a man who cursed the name of God (vv. 10–23).

The message. God’s people live continually before his face, lit and fed by his provision, and his name among them is holy. The lamp burning through the night and the twelve loaves on the golden table say that Israel is always before the LORD; the blasphemer’s death says that the name of the God who dwells with them may not be cursed, by native or foreigner. The God who gives light and bread will not have his name despised.

Why it was said. Israel was a mixed camp, with many who were not born Israelites (Exodus 12:38), and the case raised a real question: did God’s law bind a man with an Egyptian father? God’s answer is that one law holds for all (v. 22).

How the chapter makes its case. The people supply pure olive oil for the lamp that burns from evening to morning (vv. 1–4), and fine flour for twelve loaves set out every Sabbath before the LORD (vv. 5–9). Then the son of an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father curses the Name in a fight, and is held until the LORD speaks (vv. 10–12). God commands that he be stoned outside the camp and makes it law for all who curse him (vv. 13–16), restates the laws of life and injury with one rule for sojourner and native (vv. 17–22), and Israel does as the LORD commanded (v. 23).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. He is “the light of the world” (John 8:12) and “the bread of life” (John 6:35), and in him his people are kept before God’s face for ever. And the blasphemy case points to the cross. Jesus was condemned as a blasphemer (Mark 14:64) and “suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12). The man in Leviticus was guilty; Christ had told the truth about who he was, and bore the curse that we, who have dishonoured God’s name, deserved.
