For us. Take God’s name on your lips with reverence, in anger as well as in worship, for we will give account for every careless word (Matthew 12:36). And rest in the one who keeps you before God continually: his light does not go out, and his table is never empty.
24.theology:
Christ the light. The continual lampstand points to Jesus, 'the light of the world' (John 8:12), and to his people who shine with borrowed light (Matt 5:14).

Christ the bread. The bread of the Presence points to Jesus, 'the bread of life' (John 6:35), who keeps us continually present and nourished before the Father.

The holiness of the Name. The judgment on the blasphemer enforces reverence for God's name, the name Jesus taught us to hallow (Matt 6:9).
24.examples:
Then: the priests tended the light and the bread, and Israel learned that the Name must never be cursed.

Now: we live by Christ our light and bread, kept continually before the Father, and we learn to speak God's name with reverence in a culture that uses it as a curse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — The Lamp and the Bread of the Presence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lamp and the bread keep Israel continually before the LORD. The people provide the purest olive oil, and Aaron tends the lamps on the golden lampstand from evening to morning, every night, as a statute for ever (vv. 1–4). Twelve loaves of fine flour, one for each tribe, are set in two piles on the golden table with frankincense, renewed every Sabbath as a covenant for ever, and then eaten by the priests in a holy place (vv. 5–9). The word that runs through it all is “regularly”: God’s presence among his people is not occasional, and neither is their place before him.
verseByVerse.theology: God's people were kept continually before him. The light never went out, and every tribe was represented at his table, week in and week out.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a priest trimmed the wicks every night in a room no one else saw. Now: much faithful service is hidden and repetitive, and God sees all of it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command the people of Israel to bring you pure oil from beaten olives for the lamp, that a light may be kept burning regularly. Outside the veil of the testimony, in the tent of meeting, Aaron shall arrange it from evening to morning before the LORD regularly. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations. He shall arrange the lamps on the lampstand of pure gold before the LORD regularly. "You shall take fine flour and bake twelve loaves from it; two tenths of an ephah shall be in each loaf. And you shall set them in two piles, six in a pile, on the table of pure gold before the LORD. And you shall put pure frankincense on each pile, that it may go with the bread as a memorial portion as a food offering to the LORD. Every Sabbath day Aaron shall arrange it before the LORD regularly; it is from the people of Israel as a covenant forever. And it shall be for Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat it in a holy place, since it is for him a most holy portion out of the LORD's food offerings, a perpetual due."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lamp burning every night and the twelve loaves set out every week kept Israel continually before the LORD, lit and fed by his provision.

Regularly. Both arrangements in the Holy Place are defined by this word, used four times. The oil was the finest grade, pure oil from beaten olives (see Olive Tree and Olive Oil), and the people themselves supplied it. Somebody trimmed those wicks night after night, for centuries, in a room the public never entered.

Twelve loaves. Twelve loaves for twelve tribes: the whole nation, set out in bread, permanently in God’s presence. Each was large, made from two tenths of an ephah of flour, and the frankincense on them was the memorial portion, offered to the LORD. Nobody was missing from that table, including the tribes that would later be lost to history.

Light and bread. Jesus claimed both: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12) and “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). In the city to come no lamp is needed, for “its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23), and every name of his people is kept before God.

David and the bread. The old loaves went to the priests, and centuries later David, a hungry fugitive with no right to it, ate that bread at Nob (1 Samuel 21:1–6). When Jesus was challenged about his disciples picking grain on the Sabbath, that was the incident he cited (Mark 2:25–26). He used the holiest bread in Israel to show that God’s law was never meant to stand in the way of human need; it was made with that need in view.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-23 — The Blasphemer, and Just Measure
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The name of the LORD is holy, and one law protects it for native and foreigner alike. A man with an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father curses the Name in a fight, and Israel holds him until the LORD makes his will clear (vv. 10–12). God commands that the witnesses lay their hands on his head and the whole congregation stone him outside the camp, and he makes it law for all who curse him (vv. 13–16). He then restates the laws of murder, the killing of animals and injury, with the same rule for sojourner and native (vv. 17–22), and the people do exactly what he commanded (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: God's name is holy, and his justice is even-handed: the same law for foreigner and native, and penalties limited to the harm done.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the penalty could not exceed the damage. Now: when we are wronged, we may still seek justice, but Christ calls us to let go of revenge.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an Israelite woman's son, whose father was an Egyptian, went out among the people of Israel. And the Israelite woman's son and a man of Israel fought in the camp, and the Israelite woman's son blasphemed the Name, and cursed. Then they brought him to Moses. His mother's name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan. And they put him in custody, till the will of the LORD should be clear to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a camp quarrel a man of mixed parentage cursed the name of the LORD, and Israel waited for God to say what should be done. This is one of the few stories in the book.

Whose father was an Egyptian. The man was probably one of the “mixed multitude” that left Egypt with Israel (Exodus 12:38): an Israelite by his mother, an Egyptian by his father. The narrator names his mother, Shelomith of the tribe of Dan, perhaps so that the family is remembered, and perhaps to make plain that through her he belonged to the camp and stood under its law.

Blasphemed the Name, and cursed. A fight turned into a curse, and the curse was aimed at God. “The Name” is a reverent way of speaking of the LORD’s own name. Words spoken in anger are still words, and Jesus says we will give account for every careless one (Matthew 12:36).

Till the will of the LORD should be clear. There was no precedent, so they waited and asked rather than acting on instinct. Even an obvious outrage was not left to the anger of the moment.

Uncertain wording. Blasphemed translates a verb that usually means to pierce or to name specifically. It may mean he pronounced the divine name in his curse, or simply that he reviled it. Later Jewish custom of not pronouncing the name at all was probably shaped in part by this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Bring out of the camp the one who cursed, and let all who heard him lay their hands on his head, and let all the congregation stone him. And speak to the people of Israel, saying, Whoever curses his God shall bear his sin. Whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall stone him. The sojourner as well as the native, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commanded that the blasphemer be stoned outside the camp by the whole congregation, and made it law: whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD, native or foreigner, must die.

Bring out of the camp. The camp was where the LORD lived among his people, so death and defilement were taken outside it, as with the Sabbath-breaker in Numbers 15:35–36. Before the sentence, all who heard the curse laid their hands on the man’s head (v. 14): the witnesses publicly owned their testimony, and probably laid back on the speaker the guilt of the words they had been made to hear. Then “all the congregation” stoned him: the whole people under God’s word, not the man he fought with, and not in the heat of the quarrel.

Whoever curses his God shall bear his sin. Verse 15 states the principle: the one who curses God is answerable for it. Verse 16 names the penalty when the name of the LORD himself is blasphemed, and applies it to sojourner and native alike.

Outside the camp. Christ was accused of blaspheming the Name (Mark 14:64), led outside the city, and killed for it: “Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). The difference is that he had told the truth about who he was, and he bore that death for those who had truly dishonoured God’s name.

Was stoning for blasphemy fair? In Israel, cursing the name of the God who was the nation’s King was treason against the covenant itself. The penalty belonged to that civil law and ended with it; the church answers blasphemy with the word and discipline (1 Corinthians 5:12–13), and most Christians today agree that the state should not compel true worship.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever takes a human life shall surely be put to death. Whoever takes an animal's life shall make it good, life for life. If anyone injures his neighbor, as he has done it shall be done to him, fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth; whatever injury he has given a person shall be given to him. Whoever kills an animal shall make it good, and whoever kills a person shall be put to death. You shall have the same rule for the sojourner and for the native, for I am the LORD your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God restated the basic laws of life and injury for everyone alike: a human life for a life, an animal’s life made good, and a penalty matched to the injury and no more.

Whoever takes a human life. Why do laws about murder and injury appear in the middle of a blasphemy case? Probably because the case raised the question of whether God’s law bound a man of mixed descent, and God answers by restating the basic laws of life and injury, all of them binding on everyone: the same rule for the sojourner and for the native (v. 22). Their order teaches too: an animal killed is paid for (vv. 18, 21), a human life is not, because a human being is made in the image of God (Genesis 9:6).

Eye for eye. The formula is almost always quoted as though it licensed revenge, and it did the opposite. In a world where an injury to a chief’s son could cost a village, it set a ceiling: one eye, not two; one tooth, not a family. It restrained retaliation, administered by a court and not by the injured party. Many think lesser injuries could be settled by payment, since only a murderer’s life could not be ransomed (Numbers 35:31).

Jesus and the eye for an eye. That is what makes Jesus’ handling of it so precise: “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil” (Matthew 5:38–39). He is not correcting the law. He takes a rule that limits what a court may exact and tells his followers to go further, to surrender what they are owed in their own quarrels; and then he did it himself before a court: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses spoke to the people of Israel, and they brought out of the camp the one who had cursed and stoned him with stones. Thus the people of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people did exactly what the LORD commanded, no more and no less.

Thus the people of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses. The story ends with obedience. The people had waited for God’s word (v. 12), and now they do what it says. Centuries later Stephen was dragged out of Jerusalem and stoned on a charge of blasphemy (Acts 6:11; 7:58), by men who had not waited to hear the will of the LORD; and the one he died confessing had himself been taken outside the city to die (see the note on vv. 13–16).

keyVerse.quote: Whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s story turns on this law: the God who keeps his people continually before him, with light and bread, will not have his name despised, by native or foreigner. It exposes how serious our own careless words about God are, and it points to the one condemned as a blasphemer outside the city, who bore that death for those who had truly dishonoured God’s name.

24.reflection:
The lamp burned every night and the bread was renewed every Sabbath, “regularly” (vv. 2–8). What does that tell you about God’s constant care, and about the place his people always have before him in Christ, the light of the world and the bread of life?

Israel held the blasphemer “till the will of the LORD should be clear” (v. 12). When you face a hard situation, how can you wait for God’s word instead of acting on instinct or anger?

The man’s curse began in a fight (vv. 10–11). How do you speak of God, and to God, when you are angry, and what does Jesus’ warning about careless words (Matthew 12:36) mean for you?

“Eye for eye” limited what a court could exact, but Jesus calls his followers to give up what they are owed (Matthew 5:38–39). Where is God asking you to let go of a right to repay, trusting him who judges justly?

25.title: The Jubilee: The Year of the LORD's Favor
25.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land that I give you, the land shall keep a Sabbath to the LORD.<sup>3</sup>For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather in its fruits,<sup>4</sup>but in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a Sabbath to the LORD. You shall not sow your field or prune your vineyard.<sup>5</sup>You shall not reap what grows of itself in your harvest, or gather the grapes of your undressed vine. It shall be a year of solemn rest for the land.<sup>6</sup>The Sabbath of the land shall provide food for you, for yourself and for your male and female slaves and for your hired worker and the sojourner who lives with you,<sup>7</sup>and for your cattle and for the wild animals that are in your land: all its yield shall be for food.<sup>8</sup>"You shall count seven weeks of years, seven times seven years, so that the time of the seven weeks of years shall give you forty-nine years.<sup>9</sup>Then you shall sound the loud trumpet on the tenth day of the seventh month. On the Day of Atonement you shall sound the trumpet throughout all your land.<sup>10</sup>And you shall consecrate the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you, when each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan.<sup>11</sup>That fiftieth year shall be a jubilee for you; in it you shall neither sow nor reap what grows of itself nor gather the grapes from the undressed vines.<sup>12</sup>For it is a jubilee. It shall be holy to you. You may eat the produce of the field.<sup>13</sup>"In this year of jubilee each of you shall return to his property.<sup>14</sup>And if you make a sale to your neighbor or buy from your neighbor, you shall not wrong one another.<sup>15</sup>You shall pay your neighbor according to the number of years after the jubilee, and he shall sell to you according to the number of years for crops.<sup>16</sup>If the years are many, you shall increase the price, and if the years are few, you shall reduce the price, for it is the number of the crops that he is selling to you.<sup>17</sup>You shall not wrong one another, but you shall fear your God, for I am the LORD your God.<sup>18</sup>"Therefore you shall do my statutes and keep my rules and perform them, and then you will dwell in the land securely.<sup>19</sup>The land will yield its fruit, and you will eat your fill and dwell in it securely.<sup>20</sup>And if you say, 'What shall we eat in the seventh year, if we may not sow or gather in our crop?'<sup>21</sup>I will command my blessing on you in the sixth year, so that it will produce a crop sufficient for three years.<sup>22</sup>When you sow in the eighth year, you will be eating some of the old crop; you shall eat the old until the ninth year, when its crop arrives.<sup>23</sup>"The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me.<sup>24</sup>And in all the country you possess, you shall allow a redemption of the land.<sup>25</sup>"If your brother becomes poor and sells part of his property, then his nearest redeemer shall come and redeem what his brother has sold.<sup>26</sup>If a man has no one to redeem it and then himself becomes prosperous and finds sufficient means to redeem it,<sup>27</sup>let him calculate the years since he sold it and pay back the balance to the man to whom he sold it, and then return to his property.<sup>28</sup>But if he does not have sufficient means to recover it, then what he sold shall remain in the hand of the buyer until the year of jubilee. In the jubilee it shall be released, and he shall return to his property.<sup>29</sup>"If a man sells a dwelling house in a walled city, he may redeem it within a year of its sale. For a full year he shall have the right of redemption.<sup>30</sup>If it is not redeemed within a full year, then the house in the walled city shall belong in perpetuity to the buyer, throughout his generations; it shall not be released in the jubilee.<sup>31</sup>But the houses of the villages that have no wall around them shall be classified with the fields of the land. They may be redeemed, and they shall be released in the jubilee.<sup>32</sup>As for the cities of the Levites, the Levites may redeem at any time the houses in the cities they possess.<sup>33</sup>And if one of the Levites exercises his right of redemption, then the house that was sold in a city they possess shall be released in the jubilee. For the houses in the cities of the Levites are their possession among the people of Israel.<sup>34</sup>But the fields of pastureland belonging to their cities may not be sold, for that is their possession forever.<sup>35</sup>"If your brother becomes poor and cannot maintain himself with you, you shall support him as though he were a stranger and a sojourner, and he shall live with you.<sup>36</sup>Take no interest from him or profit, but fear your God, that your brother may live beside you.<sup>37</sup>You shall not lend him your money at interest, nor give him your food for profit.<sup>38</sup>I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to give you the land of Canaan, and to be your God.<sup>39</sup>"If your brother becomes poor beside you and sells himself to you, you shall not make him serve as a slave:<sup>40</sup>he shall be with you as a hired worker and as a sojourner. He shall serve with you until the year of the jubilee.<sup>41</sup>Then he shall go out from you, he and his children with him, and go back to his own clan and return to the possession of his fathers.<sup>42</sup>For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt; they shall not be sold as slaves.<sup>43</sup>You shall not rule over him ruthlessly but shall fear your God.<sup>44</sup>As for your male and female slaves whom you may have: you may buy male and female slaves from among the nations that are around you.<sup>45</sup>You may also buy from among the strangers who sojourn with you and their clans that are with you, who have been born in your land, and they may be your property.<sup>46</sup>You may bequeath them to your sons after you to inherit as a possession forever. You may make slaves of them, but over your brothers the people of Israel you shall not rule, one over another ruthlessly.<sup>47</sup>"If a stranger or sojourner with you becomes rich, and your brother beside him becomes poor and sells himself to the stranger or sojourner with you or to a member of the stranger's clan,<sup>48</sup>then after he is sold he may be redeemed. One of his brothers may redeem him,<sup>49</sup>or his uncle or his cousin may redeem him, or a close relative from his clan may redeem him. Or if he grows rich he may redeem himself.<sup>50</sup>He shall calculate with his buyer from the year when he sold himself to him until the year of jubilee, and the price of his sale shall vary with the number of years. The time he was with his owner shall be rated as the time of a hired worker.<sup>51</sup>If there are still many years left, he shall pay proportionately for his redemption some of his sale price.<sup>52</sup>If there remain but a few years until the year of jubilee, he shall calculate and pay for his redemption in proportion to his years of service.<sup>53</sup>He shall treat him as a worker hired year by year. He shall not rule ruthlessly over him in your sight.<sup>54</sup>And if he is not redeemed by these means, then he and his children with him shall be released in the year of jubilee.<sup>55</sup>For it is to me that the people of Israel are servants. They are my servants whom I brought out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
25.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 23 set out Israel’s holy calendar of feasts. Now the calendar stretches from days to years: a Sabbath for the land every seventh year and, every fiftieth year, the Jubilee. It is the last block of laws before the blessings and curses of chapter 26.

The message. The land belongs to God, and so do his people: “the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me” (v. 23). Because God owns the land and has bought Israel out of slavery, no family could lose its inheritance for ever and no Israelite could be owned for ever. The God who sets people free builds rest, release and redemption into the economy itself.

Why it was said. Israel was about to become a farming people in Canaan (see the introduction). Bad harvests, debt and forced sales would slowly gather the land into fewer hands and push families into servitude. This chapter answered that slide before it began, and met the farmer’s fear of letting his fields rest with a promise of food.

How the chapter makes its case. The land rests every seventh year, and what grows untended feeds everyone (vv. 1–7). Every fiftieth year, announced by trumpet on the Day of Atonement, liberty is proclaimed and families return to their land (vv. 8–12); so every sale is really a lease priced by the harvests left, and God promises enough to eat (vv. 13–22). Because the land is his, it can always be bought back (vv. 23–34). The poor brother is helped without interest (vv. 35–38), and an Israelite who sells himself is treated as a hired worker and set free, because Israel belongs to the God who brought them out of Egypt (vv. 39–55).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by promise. The kinsman-redeemer who had to be related, willing and able finds his fulfilment in the Son who became our brother to buy us back, “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Isaiah took up the Jubilee’s words for the coming Servant (Isaiah 61:1–2), and at Nazareth Jesus read them and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21). The Jubilee began on the Day of Atonement; our liberty begins at the cross.

For us. We are tenants, not owners: what we have is God’s, to be held loosely and used generously. And the Jubilee’s liberty is a homecoming: Christ frees us not from God but back to him, and into his family.
25.theology:
The gospel as Jubilee. Liberty for captives, cancelled debts and restored inheritance are fulfilled in Christ, who announced that the year of the Lord's favour had come in him (Luke 4:21).

Everything belongs to God. We hold what we have as his tenants, and so we are not free to keep others in permanent poverty or bondage.

The kinsman-redeemer. The relative who buys back lost land and frees the enslaved points to Christ, who became our flesh and blood in order to redeem us (Heb 2:14-17).
25.examples:
Then: every fiftieth year slaves went free and families returned to their lost lands.

Now: those whom Christ has set free are made open-handed by his Spirit: slow to hold on to what others owe them, and quick to help a struggling family keep its footing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-22 — The Sabbath Year and the Year of Jubilee
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The land’s rest teaches Israel that God, not ceaseless work, is the source of their food, and that the land they farm is his. Every seventh year the fields lie fallow, and whatever grows of itself feeds owner, slave, worker, sojourner, cattle and wild animals alike (vv. 1–7). Every fiftieth year, from a trumpet blown on the Day of Atonement, the Jubilee proclaims liberty and sends each family home to its land and clan (vv. 8–12). So every sale of land is priced by the harvests left until the next Jubilee, and no one may wrong his neighbour (vv. 13–17). To the farmer’s question, “What shall we eat?”, God answers with a sixth-year harvest large enough for three years (vv. 18–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Rest and release are built into God's order. He provides for those who stop when he says stop, and he will not let his people's poverty become permanent.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God answered the farmer's question, "What shall we eat?", with provision in advance. Now: resting one day in seven, or turning down work that would swallow every hour, is an act of trust that God will still provide.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land that I give you, the land shall keep a Sabbath to the LORD. For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather in its fruits, but in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a Sabbath to the LORD. You shall not sow your field or prune your vineyard. You shall not reap what grows of itself in your harvest, or gather the grapes of your undressed vine. It shall be a year of solemn rest for the land. The Sabbath of the land shall provide food for you, for yourself and for your male and female slaves and for your hired worker and the sojourner who lives with you, and for your cattle and for the wild animals that are in your land: all its yield shall be for food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every seventh year the land itself was to rest, and Israel was to trust God to feed them through it.

The land shall keep a Sabbath to the LORD. The commandment about the seventh day is extended to the seventh year, the Sabbath year, with the same logic. Israel is asked to believe that provision does not depend on unbroken work, and to prove it by stopping: not for a day, which anyone can manage, but for a farming year, which means trusting God with the food supply.

Food for all. Whatever grows untended belongs to everyone: the list runs past the household and the workers to the sojourner, the cattle and even the wild animals. In the year the owner stops owning, the field feeds whoever comes to it.

Does the Jubilee bind today? It was part of Israel’s civil law in the land, and it ended with Israel’s life as a nation under God’s direct rule. Jesus announced the true Jubilee, “the year of the Lord’s favor” (Luke 4:18–21): release for the captives of sin. Its principles remain: the earth is the Lord’s, the poor are not to be left in permanent bondage, and generosity is a duty.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall count seven weeks of years, seven times seven years, so that the time of the seven weeks of years shall give you forty-nine years. Then you shall sound the loud trumpet on the tenth day of the seventh month. On the Day of Atonement you shall sound the trumpet throughout all your land. And you shall consecrate the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you, when each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan. That fiftieth year shall be a jubilee for you; in it you shall neither sow nor reap what grows of itself nor gather the grapes from the undressed vines. For it is a jubilee. It shall be holy to you. You may eat the produce of the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every fiftieth year, beginning on the Day of Atonement, liberty was proclaimed and every family went home to its land and its clan.

On the Day of Atonement. The Jubilee begins on the one day in the year when the nation’s sin is dealt with. Liberty is proclaimed in the hours after the scapegoat is led away: forgiveness in the sanctuary and release in the marketplace begin on the same day.

The reset. Over fifty years land piles up in fewer hands. Bad harvests and bad decisions bring debt, debt forces sales, and families slip from owning land to renting it and then to servitude. Every fiftieth year a horn sounded and the whole process reset: land went back to the family that had lost it, and people who had sold themselves walked home.

Liberty as homecoming. Verse 10 is cast into the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia, and we mostly hear its key word as the freedom to choose for ourselves. But the sentence goes on: “each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan.” The Jubilee’s liberty is not escape from belonging but restoration to it. Modern freedom often delivers a kind of homelessness: endless options, shallow roots, and no one obliged to take us back when we fail. Jesus told a story about the difference. The younger son took the first kind of liberty and ended in a far country among the pigs. On the road home he met the second kind: his father running to him, the best robe, a ring, and his place in the family given back before he had finished his speech (Luke 15:20–24). That is the Jubilee the gospel proclaims: we are freed not from God but back to him, and nothing we have lost or sold is beyond the reach of the Father’s welcome.

Was the Jubilee ever kept? The Old Testament never records one, and it shows Israel neglecting the land’s Sabbath years (2 Chronicles 36:21) and breaking a solemn release of slaves (Jeremiah 34:8–17). The law stood, largely unkept, as a promise waiting for someone who would keep it, which is part of why Jesus’ words at Nazareth landed as they did.
verseByVerse.note: The word “jubilee” comes from the Hebrew yobel, the ram's horn blown to announce it.

verseByVerse.quote: "In this year of jubilee each of you shall return to his property. And if you make a sale to your neighbor or buy from your neighbor, you shall not wrong one another. You shall pay your neighbor according to the number of years after the jubilee, and he shall sell to you according to the number of years for crops. If the years are many, you shall increase the price, and if the years are few, you shall reduce the price, for it is the number of the crops that he is selling to you. You shall not wrong one another, but you shall fear your God, for I am the LORD your God. "Therefore you shall do my statutes and keep my rules and perform them, and then you will dwell in the land securely. The land will yield its fruit, and you will eat your fill and dwell in it securely. And if you say, 'What shall we eat in the seventh year, if we may not sow or gather in our crop?' I will command my blessing on you in the sixth year, so that it will produce a crop sufficient for three years. When you sow in the eighth year, you will be eating some of the old crop; you shall eat the old until the ninth year, when its crop arrives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because every field returned at the Jubilee, a sale of land was really a lease of its harvests, and God promised enough food for the years of rest.

The number of the crops. The law is blunt about what is being sold: “it is the number of the crops that he is selling to you” (v. 16). Every land deal was a lease with a known expiry date: a buyer near the Jubilee paid little, a buyer just after it paid much. The reason is verse 23, which governs the whole chapter. Israel did not own Canaan; it rented it, from a landlord with strong views about how tenants treat each other, and “you shall not wrong one another, but you shall fear your God” (v. 17).

What shall we eat? Then comes the objection any farmer would raise. God does not rebuke the asking. He answers with a promise of a sixth-year harvest “sufficient for three years” (v. 21), given in advance of the obedience he asks for. Jesus met the same anxiety the same way: “your heavenly Father knows that you need them all” (Matthew 6:32).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23-55 — Redemption of Land and of People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the land is God’s and Israel are his servants, no family can lose its land for ever and no Israelite can be owned for ever. Land sold in poverty may be bought back by the nearest kinsman or by the seller, and it returns at the Jubilee in any case (vv. 23–28); houses in walled towns are the exception, while the Levites’ houses and pastures are protected (vv. 29–34). A poor brother is to be supported without interest, so that he can go on living beside you (vv. 35–38). An Israelite who sells himself is to be treated as a hired worker, not a slave, and released at the Jubilee, because the LORD brought his people out of Egypt (vv. 39–55).
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption is a family duty. When a relative falls into poverty, the nearest kinsman steps in, and behind every human redeemer stands the God who brought his people out of Egypt and calls them his own servants.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the aim of the law was that a struggling brother could go on living beside you. Now: helping someone in debt keep his home and dignity is still the shape of Christian love.

verseByVerse.quote: "The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me. And in all the country you possess, you shall allow a redemption of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land could never be sold outright, because it belonged to God, and Israel lived on it as his guests.

For you are strangers and sojourners with me. This is the reason behind all the land laws. Israel lived on the land as resident guests of its owner, “with me”, in God’s own household, as Abraham called himself “a sojourner and foreigner” in the land he had been promised (Genesis 23:4). David prayed in the same words (1 Chronicles 29:15), and Peter calls Christians “sojourners and exiles” (1 Peter 2:11). Those who know they are guests hold what they have loosely and use it as the owner wishes.

You shall allow a redemption of the land. Every sale of land carried a right to buy it back. No transaction, however desperate the seller, could cut a family off from its inheritance for good.

verseByVerse.quote: "If your brother becomes poor and sells part of his property, then his nearest redeemer shall come and redeem what his brother has sold. If a man has no one to redeem it and then himself becomes prosperous and finds sufficient means to redeem it, let him calculate the years since he sold it and pay back the balance to the man to whom he sold it, and then return to his property. But if he does not have sufficient means to recover it, then what he sold shall remain in the hand of the buyer until the year of jubilee. In the jubilee it shall be released, and he shall return to his property.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When poverty forced a sale, the nearest relative was to buy the land back; failing him, the seller could, and failing both, the Jubilee would.

His nearest redeemer. Here a word enters that will matter enormously: go’el, the kinsman-redeemer. Redeeming is a family duty, not an optional kindness: the nearest able kinsman pays to buy back what was lost. He must be related, willing and able. Ruth’s story is this law in action, with Boaz as her go’el (Ruth 4:1–10). The same word is used of God as Israel’s Redeemer, and in Christ he met all three conditions (see the note on vv. 47–55).

Let him calculate the years. If the seller later prospers, he buys the land back by paying for the harvests remaining before the Jubilee, the reckoning of verses 15–16. Neither side is wronged. And if no redeemer appears, the man is not abandoned: the property returns at the Jubilee anyway.
verseByVerse.note: The same word, go'el, is used of God himself as Israel's Redeemer (Isaiah 41:14).

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man sells a dwelling house in a walled city, he may redeem it within a year of its sale. For a full year he shall have the right of redemption. If it is not redeemed within a full year, then the house in the walled city shall belong in perpetuity to the buyer, throughout his generations; it shall not be released in the jubilee. But the houses of the villages that have no wall around them shall be classified with the fields of the land. They may be redeemed, and they shall be released in the jubilee. As for the cities of the Levites, the Levites may redeem at any time the houses in the cities they possess. And if one of the Levites exercises his right of redemption, then the house that was sold in a city they possess shall be released in the jubilee. For the houses in the cities of the Levites are their possession among the people of Israel. But the fields of pastureland belonging to their cities may not be sold, for that is their possession forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Town houses could be sold for good after a year, but village houses and the Levites’ homes and pastures stayed under the protection of the Jubilee.

A dwelling house in a walled city. The Jubilee protects a family’s land, its livelihood. A house in a walled town was not farmland, so after a year’s grace it could be sold outright. Village houses belonged to the farming life around them, so they are “classified with the fields of the land” (v. 31) and return at the Jubilee.

The cities of the Levites. The Levites received no tribal territory, only towns and the pasture around them (Numbers 35:1–8). Their houses could always be redeemed, and their pastures never sold, so the tribe that served at God’s altar would never become landless.

Uncertain wording. Verse 33 is one of the hardest sentences in the chapter. The Hebrew reads literally something like and whoever redeems from the Levites, and translators differ over whether it speaks of a Levite buying back his own house or of a house bought from a Levite. The point is clear either way: a Levite’s house goes back to him in the Jubilee.

verseByVerse.quote: "If your brother becomes poor and cannot maintain himself with you, you shall support him as though he were a stranger and a sojourner, and he shall live with you. Take no interest from him or profit, but fear your God, that your brother may live beside you. You shall not lend him your money at interest, nor give him your food for profit. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to give you the land of Canaan, and to be your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A brother who falls into poverty is to be helped to stay on his feet, with no profit made from his need.

Fear your God. A loan at interest to a desperate man was entirely legal in every surrounding nation, and no court could police a refusal to charge it. So the law appeals to conscience, and gives the reason in verse 38: the God who brought them out of Egypt and gave them the land. They had been given everything; they could not profit from a brother’s ruin.

That your brother may live beside you. The stated aim is not repayment. It is that the man stays your neighbour, in the same street, on speaking terms. Jesus pressed it further: “lend, expecting nothing in return” (Luke 6:35).

Is charging interest sin? The law forbade profiting from a poor brother’s need (v. 36). It allowed interest from a foreigner in trade (Deuteronomy 23:20), and Jesus speaks of money with bankers earning interest (Matthew 25:27). Commercial lending and borrowing are not sin; exploiting the desperate is.

verseByVerse.quote: "If your brother becomes poor beside you and sells himself to you, you shall not make him serve as a slave: he shall be with you as a hired worker and as a sojourner. He shall serve with you until the year of the jubilee. Then he shall go out from you, he and his children with him, and go back to his own clan and return to the possession of his fathers. For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt; they shall not be sold as slaves. You shall not rule over him ruthlessly but shall fear your God. As for your male and female slaves whom you may have: you may buy male and female slaves from among the nations that are around you. You may also buy from among the strangers who sojourn with you and their clans that are with you, who have been born in your land, and they may be your property. You may bequeath them to your sons after you to inherit as a possession forever. You may make slaves of them, but over your brothers the people of Israel you shall not rule, one over another ruthlessly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An Israelite driven by poverty to sell himself was to be treated as a hired worker and freed at the Jubilee, because Israel already belonged to God.

They are my servants. The reason is stated twice (vv. 42, 55): they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. A people already bought out of slavery are not available to be owned, because they already belong to someone. So he may not be ruled “ruthlessly” (v. 43), the word used of Egypt’s rule over Israel (Exodus 1:13), and at the Jubilee he goes home with his children.

Foreign slaves. Verses 44–46 then permit the purchase of foreign slaves as permanent property, and it would be dishonest to soften it. The law regulated an institution that existed everywhere in the ancient world (see Slavery in the Ancient World); it did not abolish it here. It did forbid, on pain of death, the kidnapping on which the Atlantic slave trade was built (Exodus 21:16), and it gave refuge to a slave who escaped a master (Deuteronomy 23:15–16). What Scripture does is plant within slavery a truth that eventually destroyed it: that every human being bears the image of God. When Paul wrote to Philemon about a runaway, he asked him to receive the man back “no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16), and slavery cannot last where that sentence is taken seriously.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a stranger or sojourner with you becomes rich, and your brother beside him becomes poor and sells himself to the stranger or sojourner with you or to a member of the stranger's clan, then after he is sold he may be redeemed. One of his brothers may redeem him, or his uncle or his cousin may redeem him, or a close relative from his clan may redeem him. Or if he grows rich he may redeem himself. He shall calculate with his buyer from the year when he sold himself to him until the year of jubilee, and the price of his sale shall vary with the number of years. The time he was with his owner shall be rated as the time of a hired worker. If there are still many years left, he shall pay proportionately for his redemption some of his sale price. If there remain but a few years until the year of jubilee, he shall calculate and pay for his redemption in proportion to his years of service. He shall treat him as a worker hired year by year. He shall not rule ruthlessly over him in your sight. And if he is not redeemed by these means, then he and his children with him shall be released in the year of jubilee. For it is to me that the people of Israel are servants. They are my servants whom I brought out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even an Israelite sold to a wealthy foreigner kept his right to be redeemed, and went free at the Jubilee, because Israel belonged to the LORD.

He may be redeemed. A brother, uncle, cousin or any close relative may buy him back, or he may redeem himself at a hired worker’s rate for the years left; and the whole community must see that he is not ruled ruthlessly (vv. 48–53). The chapter ends on the sentence beneath all of it: “it is to me that the people of Israel are servants” (v. 55).

A Sabbath in Nazareth. Now hold this chapter next to a Sabbath morning in Nazareth. Jesus stood up in the synagogue, was handed the scroll of Isaiah, and read: “to proclaim liberty to the captives … to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.” Then he rolled it up, sat down and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:18–21). Isaiah’s phrase is Jubilee language, and what Jesus announced in that room was that the true Jubilee had begun.

Our kinsman-redeemer. Everything in this chapter turns out to be a picture of him and his work: a people who cannot free themselves; a kinsman who must be related to them, willing to act and able to pay; a debt discharged with someone else’s money; captives walking home to a property they had forfeited, on a day that began with atonement. “You were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). He became man so that he could be our kinsman, and the price he paid was not silver. So we are free from every other master, because “you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:20).

keyVerse.quote: The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the reason behind every law in the chapter: the land is God’s, and Israel lives on it as his guests. It is why no sale could be final and no Israelite could be owned for ever, and it teaches every believer to hold what he has as the steward of a God who has made him a pilgrim and a member of his household.

25.reflection:
The land had to rest every seventh year, and God promised enough to eat (vv. 4, 20–21). Where do you find it hardest to stop working and trust God to provide?

“The land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me” (v. 23). How would your attitude to your home, money and possessions change if you saw yourself as God’s guest rather than their owner?

The Jubilee’s liberty was a homecoming: each one returned to his property and his clan (v. 10). How does the gospel free us not from God but back to him and to his family, and how can a church show that freedom?

Boaz was Ruth’s kinsman-redeemer: related, willing and able. What does it mean to you that Christ became your kinsman to buy you back, and how might it shape the way you treat people in debt or poverty around you (vv. 35–38)?

26.title: Blessings and Curses: The Covenant's Heart

26.overview:
Where we are. The laws given at Sinai are complete, and chapter 25 ended with the LORD claiming Israel as his servants, brought out of Egypt. Now, as covenants in the ancient world often did, the book sets out blessings for faithfulness and curses for unfaithfulness. Chapter 27 is an appendix; this chapter is the climax of Leviticus.

The message. God offers his people himself: “I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people” (v. 12). To walk with him is life, harvest and peace; to walk against him is to find him walking against them, in discipline that grows heavier until it ends in exile. Yet the last word is mercy. Even in exile, a humbled people who confess their sin will find that God has not broken his covenant, “for I am the LORD their God” (v. 44).

Why it was said. Israel was about to enter a land full of idols and shrines (see the introduction). These words were set before them in advance, so that when harvests failed and enemies came they would know why, and know the way back. In exile, centuries later, the promise of verses 40–45 was all they had left.

How the chapter makes its case. Two commands head the chapter: no idols, and keep the Sabbaths (vv. 1–2). Faithfulness brings rain, harvest, peace, victory and fruitfulness, crowned by God dwelling and walking among his people (vv. 3–13). Unfaithfulness brings five rounds of discipline, each “sevenfold”: disease and defeat (vv. 14–17), drought (vv. 18–20), wild beasts (vv. 21–22), sword, plague and famine (vv. 23–26), and at last siege, ruin and exile, while the land enjoys the Sabbaths it was denied (vv. 27–39). But confession will find God remembering his covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham (vv. 40–46).

Where it leads. To Christ, by covenant and by the need it exposes. Israel did walk contrary to God, and the curses fell. No one could keep this covenant from the human side until Christ obeyed in our place and “redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us”, “so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles” (Galatians 3:13–14). The promise of verse 12 is fulfilled in him: God dwells among his people now (2 Corinthians 6:16), and will for ever in the new creation (Revelation 21:3).

For us. God’s warnings are mercies, doors held open. A believer’s hardships are a Father’s discipline, never the curse, because Christ has borne it. And the covenant is held from God’s side, so no one who confesses his sin is beyond the reach of the God who remembers his promises.
26.theology:
The covenant's two roads. Blessing follows faithfulness and curse follows unfaithfulness, and the greatest blessing is God's own presence.

Mercy outlasts judgment. Even in exile, confession reopens the door, for the covenant rests on God's faithfulness, not ours: "I will for their sake remember the covenant" (26:45).

Christ bore the curse. Jesus "redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Gal 3:13), bearing the full covenant judgment, even the exile of being forsaken by God, so that the blessing might come to us.
26.examples:
Then: Israel was warned of discipline and exile, and promised that confession would meet a remembering God.

Now: a believer who has wandered need not wonder whether the door is still open. Confession meets the same remembering God, and in Christ the blessing is ours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-46 — Blessing, Discipline, and Covenant Faithfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter sets two ways before Israel, and at the far end of the worse way it leaves a door open. After the two commands on which everything hangs, no idols and keep the Sabbaths (vv. 1–2), the blessings of faithfulness rise from rain and harvest to peace, victory and fruitfulness, and reach their summit in God walking among his people (vv. 3–13). The curses run more than twice as long, in five rounds that grow heavier each time Israel refuses to listen: disease, drought, wild beasts, siege, famine and exile (vv. 14–39). Then comes the way back: confession, a humbled heart, and a God who remembers his covenant and will not abhor his people so as to destroy them (vv. 40–46).
verseByVerse.theology: God's judgments on his people are meant to bring them back, not to destroy them, and his covenant holds because of who he is.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was warned plainly and in advance. Now: God's warnings in Scripture are also mercies, given early enough for us to turn.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not make idols for yourselves or erect an image or pillar, and you shall not set up a figured stone in your land to bow down to it, for I am the LORD your God. You shall keep my Sabbaths and reverence my sanctuary: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the blessings and curses stand two commands, whom Israel worships and when: no idols, and God’s Sabbaths kept.

You shall not make idols for yourselves. The pillar was a standing stone of the kind set up at Canaanite shrines and the figured stone a carved one, and the land Israel was about to enter was full of both. Both commands were given before (19:3–4, 30); everything that follows hangs on them, and they are a fair summary of the whole covenant: the right God, honoured at the right times, in the place he appointed. The Sabbaths return at the end, when the land enjoys the rest Israel denied it (vv. 34–35), and John’s last word to the church is still the first command: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21).

verseByVerse.quote: "If you walk in my statutes and observe my commandments and do them, then I will give you your rains in their season, and the land shall yield its increase, and the trees of the field shall yield their fruit. Your threshing shall last to the time of the grape harvest, and the grape harvest shall last to the time for sowing. And you shall eat your bread to the full and dwell in your land securely.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel walked in God’s ways, he would send the rains, and harvest would run into harvest.

If you walk in my statutes. “Walk” is the key word of the chapter. Israel is to walk in God’s statutes (v. 3), and God promises to walk among them (v. 12); if they walk contrary to him (vv. 21, 23, 27), he will walk contrary to them (vv. 24, 28). Everything turns on which way the two are walking.

Rains in their season. Egypt was watered by the Nile; Canaan depended on the early rains of autumn and the late rains of spring (Deuteronomy 11:10–14). The land itself taught Israel to look up: every harvest came from God’s sky.

Does this promise health and wealth to obedient believers? These were the covenant terms for Israel as a nation in the land (Deuteronomy 28). Christ bore the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13), and believers have “every spiritual blessing” in him (Ephesians 1:3), while being told to expect trouble in the world (John 16:33). God promises to meet his people’s needs, not to make them rich.

verseByVerse.quote: I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid. And I will remove harmful beasts from the land, and the sword shall not go through your land. You shall chase your enemies, and they shall fall before you by the sword. Five of you shall chase a hundred, and a hundred of you shall chase ten thousand, and your enemies shall fall before you by the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faithfulness would bring peace in the land and victory out of all proportion, because God would fight for his people.

I will give peace in the land. The peace promised is the full Hebrew shalom: lying down at night with no one to make you afraid, no wild beasts and no invading sword. The prophets used the same words for the coming kingdom: “they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid” (Micah 4:4).

Five of you shall chase a hundred. Victory would not depend on numbers, because God would fight for them, as with Gideon’s three hundred (Judges 7) and as Jonathan said: “nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few” (1 Samuel 14:6). The curses turn this round: they will flee when no one is chasing them (vv. 17, 36).

verseByVerse.quote: I will turn to you and make you fruitful and multiply you and will confirm my covenant with you. You shall eat old store long kept, and you shall clear out the old to make way for the new.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God would turn to his people in favour, make them fruitful, keep his covenant and fill their barns.

I will turn to you and make you fruitful. “Fruitful” and “multiply” echo the blessing at creation (Genesis 1:28) and the promise to Abraham (Genesis 17:6–7). To “confirm my covenant” is to keep his word and see it through.

Clear out the old to make way for the new. Last year’s grain would still be in store when the new harvest came in. Compare the famine of verse 26, where bread is weighed out and no one is satisfied.

verseByVerse.quote: I will make my dwelling among you, and my soul shall not abhor you. And I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, that you should not be their slaves. And I have broken the bars of your yoke and made you walk erect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The highest blessing is not harvest or safety but God himself, living and walking among the people he set free.

I will make my dwelling among you. The word for “dwelling” (mishkan) is the word for the tabernacle, the tent just set up at Sinai. “My soul shall not abhor you” is God’s pledge that he will not tire of them; the words come back reversed in verse 30, and even then he will not abhor them so as to destroy them (v. 44).

Made you walk erect. The blessings rest on what God had already done: he had broken their yoke. Slaves stoop; he straightened their backs.

I will walk among you. The word walk is the one used of God in Eden, walking in the garden in the cool of the day (Genesis 3:8). Everything the tabernacle was built to make possible is compressed into that sentence: not prosperity, not safety, but God at ease in the middle of his people. Paul applies the promise to the church in Corinth, Gentiles and Jews together: “we are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6:16). In Christ it has begun to come true, and in the new creation it will be complete (Revelation 21:3).

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you will not listen to me and will not do all these commandments, if you spurn my statutes, and if your soul abhors my rules, so that you will not do all my commandments, but break my covenant, then I will do this to you: I will visit you with panic, with wasting disease and fever that consume the eyes and make the heart ache. And you shall sow your seed in vain, for your enemies shall eat it. I will set my face against you, and you shall be struck down before your enemies. Those who hate you shall rule over you, and you shall flee when none pursues you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel rejected God’s commands and broke his covenant, he would set his face against them: disease, defeat, and fear without cause.

If you will not listen to me. The curses run more than twice as long as the blessings, in five escalating rounds. The refrain is not I will destroy you but if you will not listen: each round is a door held open, another attempt to make them listen when gentler measures had failed.

If your soul abhors my rules. The sin in view is not a single lapse but a settled turning against God (vv. 14–15): the curses answer a heart that has already rejected him.

I will set my face against you. The first round brings terror, wasting disease and fever, and harvests sown for enemies to eat. It is the reverse of the priestly blessing, “the LORD make his face to shine upon you” (Numbers 6:25), and its fruit is fear without cause: “you shall flee when none pursues you”, the opposite of verse 8. “The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion” (Proverbs 28:1).
verseByVerse.note: Deuteronomy 28 gives a longer list of covenant blessings and curses in the same pattern.

verseByVerse.quote: And if in spite of this you will not listen to me, then I will discipline you again sevenfold for your sins, and I will break the pride of your power, and I will make your heavens like iron and your earth like bronze. And your strength shall be spent in vain, for your land shall not yield its increase, and the trees of the land shall not yield their fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel still would not listen, God would break their pride in their own strength with drought, so that all their work came to nothing.

Sevenfold for your sins. Seven is the number of completeness, so “sevenfold” means in full measure, not an exact multiple. Each refusal brings a heavier blow (vv. 18, 21, 24, 28).

I will break the pride of your power. The second round strikes Israel’s confidence in its own strength. Drought is described as metal: a sky like iron that gives no rain, ground like bronze that yields nothing, so that “your strength shall be spent in vain”. Elijah’s drought in the days of Ahab (1 Kings 17:1) was this warning come true.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then if you walk contrary to me and will not listen to me, I will continue striking you, sevenfold for your sins. And I will let loose the wild beasts against you, which shall bereave you of your children and destroy your livestock and make you few in number, so that your roads shall be deserted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Continued defiance would bring wild beasts, bereaved homes and empty roads.

I will let loose the wild beasts against you. The third round reverses the promise of verse 6. As people grow few, wild animals take over (compare Exodus 23:29), as lions did among the settlers in Samaria (2 Kings 17:25). “Your roads shall be deserted”: in the dark days of the judges “the highways were abandoned” (Judges 5:6).

Uncertain wording. The word translated contrary occurs only in this chapter. It probably means walking in opposition to God; some take it as treating his dealings as mere chance, as though the troubles were bad luck rather than his call to return.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if by this discipline you are not turned to me but walk contrary to me, then I also will walk contrary to you, and I myself will strike you sevenfold for your sins. And I will bring a sword upon you, that shall execute vengeance for the covenant. And if you gather within your cities, I will send pestilence among you, and you shall be delivered into the hand of the enemy. When I break your supply of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in a single oven and shall dole out your bread again by weight, and you shall eat and not be satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When discipline failed to turn them, God would walk contrary to them: sword, plague in the crowded cities, and famine.

Then I also will walk contrary to you. The fourth round answers them in kind: as they treat God, so he treats them. “With the crooked you make yourself seem tortuous” (Psalm 18:26).

A sword … that shall execute vengeance for the covenant. War is the covenant’s own penalty: God takes his covenant so seriously that its breach is avenged. When the people crowd into their walled cities for safety, plague breaks out among them and they fall to the enemy, the pattern of every siege that came.

Ten women shall bake your bread in a single oven. Each household normally had its own oven. Now there is so little flour that ten families share one, and bread is weighed out like a ration. Ezekiel uses the same words of the siege of Jerusalem: “I will break the supply of bread in Jerusalem. They shall eat bread by weight and with anxiety” (Ezekiel 4:16). “You shall eat and not be satisfied” is still the verdict on a life lived away from God (Haggai 1:6).

verseByVerse.quote: "But if in spite of this you will not listen to me, but walk contrary to me, then I will walk contrary to you in fury, and I myself will discipline you sevenfold for your sins. You shall eat the flesh of your sons, and you shall eat the flesh of your daughters. And I will destroy your high places and cut down your incense altars and cast your dead bodies upon the dead bodies of your idols, and my soul will abhor you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth and worst round brings siege famine, ruined shrines and God’s abhorrence; yet even this is meant to heal.

You shall eat the flesh of your sons. Scripture does not look away. This is siege famine at its most terrible, and it happened in Samaria when the Syrians besieged it (2 Kings 6:28–29) and in Jerusalem when Babylon did (Lamentations 4:10).

I will destroy your high places. The idols forbidden in verse 1 come back at the end: the high places, the incense altars, and the people’s corpses thrown on the “dead bodies” of their idols, as lifeless as they are. “My soul will abhor you” reverses the promise of verse 11.

Meant to heal. Two things should be said about a passage this dark. The first is that it is meant to heal, not to take revenge. Verse 41 names the goal: that their uncircumcised heart, a heart closed to God, might be humbled. The purpose is not the ruin but the repentance it is meant to produce.

Is my hardship a curse? A Christian in hardship may wonder whether this is God’s curse on him. It is not. Christ bore the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13), and the troubles of a believer are the discipline of a Father who loves his children, never the punishment of an enemy (Hebrews 12:5–11).

Uncertain wording. The word translated incense altars is rare; older translations guessed images. Small stone incense altars, found at many ancient sites, are the likeliest meaning.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will lay your cities waste and will make your sanctuaries desolate, and I will not smell your pleasing aromas. And I myself will devastate the land, so that your enemies who settle in it shall be appalled at it. And I will scatter you among the nations, and I will unsheathe the sword after you, and your land shall be a desolation, and your cities shall be a waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the end God would refuse even their sacrifices, lay the land waste and scatter his people among the nations.

I will not smell your pleasing aromas. Worship carried on while the heart walks contrary to God is not accepted, as the prophets would repeat (Isaiah 1:11–15; Amos 5:21–22). The “sanctuaries” laid waste came true when the temple was burned in 587/586 BC.

I will scatter you among the nations. Exile is the last stage: the land so ruined that even the conquerors who settle in it are appalled, and the people scattered with the sword drawn after them, so that there is no safety even in flight (compare Jeremiah 9:16).

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths as long as it lies desolate, while you are in your enemies' land; then the land shall rest, and enjoy its Sabbaths. As long as it lies desolate it shall have rest, the rest that it did not have on your Sabbaths when you were dwelling in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Israel was in exile, the land would at last receive the Sabbath years they had denied it.

Then the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths. This looks back to the Sabbath year of 25:1–7. The land is the LORD’s (25:23), and it will have its rest, either through Israel’s obedience or through Israel’s absence.

All of it happened. The second thing to say about this dark passage (see the note on vv. 27–30) is that all of it happened. This chapter was read in Israel for centuries as something that might happen, and then Assyria came, and then Babylon, and the land lay empty. When the writer of Chronicles explained the exile, he reached back to these verses and to the seventy years foretold by Jeremiah: “until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths. All the days that it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years” (2 Chronicles 36:21).

verseByVerse.quote: And as for those of you who are left, I will send faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies. The sound of a driven leaf shall put them to flight, and they shall flee as one flees from the sword, and they shall fall when none pursues. They shall stumble over one another, as if to escape a sword, though none pursues. And you shall have no power to stand before your enemies. And you shall perish among the nations, and the land of your enemies shall eat you up. And those of you who are left shall rot away in your enemies' lands because of their iniquity, and also because of the iniquities of their fathers they shall rot away like them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The survivors in exile would live in fear and waste away, carrying on in their fathers’ sins.

The sound of a driven leaf shall put them to flight. A rustling leaf sends them running, and they stumble over one another escaping a sword that is not there. The promise of verse 8 has been turned inside out, and the threat of verse 17 fulfilled.

The land of your enemies shall eat you up. The scattered would be swallowed up among the nations, as the northern tribes were after Assyria took Samaria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6).

Because of the iniquities of their fathers. They waste away in their own iniquity and their fathers’ too: not punished for sins in which they had no part (Ezekiel 18:20), but carrying them on. That is why the way back in verse 40 begins with confessing “their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers”.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if they confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers in their treachery that they committed against me, and also in walking contrary to me, so that I walked contrary to them and brought them into the land of their enemies—if then their uncircumcised heart is humbled and they make amends for their iniquity, then I will remember my covenant with Jacob, and I will remember my covenant with Isaac and my covenant with Abraham, and I will remember the land. But the land shall be abandoned by them and enjoy its Sabbaths while it lies desolate without them, and they shall make amends for their iniquity, because they spurned my rules and their soul abhorred my statutes. Yet for all that, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them, for I am the LORD their God. But I will for their sake remember the covenant with their forefathers, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt in the sight of the nations, that I might be their God: I am the LORD." These are the statutes and rules and laws that the LORD made between himself and the people of Israel through Moses on Mount Sinai.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the exiles confessed their sin and humbled their hearts, God would remember his covenant: he would not destroy them or break it, because he is the LORD their God.

If they confess. The way back is left open at the far end of the worst that could happen, and it begins with honest confession of their own sin and their fathers’ and a humbled heart. Daniel prayed this way in exile (Daniel 9:4–19), and so did the people after the return (Nehemiah 9:2).

I will remember my covenant. It is not a new covenant offered on better behaviour; it is the old one, remembered, with the patriarchs named in reverse order, as though God were walking back up the family line to where the promise started.

He does not break the covenant. Verse 44 is the sentence to take away from the chapter. Even in exile, after judgments they were warned of in advance, he does not break the covenant, and the reason given is nothing about them. It is for I am the LORD their God. The covenant holds because of who is keeping it. That is exactly Paul’s logic as he looks at his own unbelieving nation: “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). A covenant that depended on Israel would have ended somewhere in the book of Judges. This one is held up from God’s side, which is why a believer can be sure of his promises at all.

What a covenant is. We live in a world of contracts, which either side can leave when they stop paying. A covenant is a bond in which one person binds himself to another by solemn promise, and God’s covenant comes down to verse 12. Timothy Keller often pointed out that a consumer relationship lasts only as long as it meets my needs, while a covenant relationship holds even when it costs me. Israel treated God like a supplier, to be dropped whenever other gods seemed to offer more. He did not treat them that way. In the end he kept the covenant from both sides: Christ obeyed where Israel failed and bore its curse, and on the night he was betrayed he lifted the cup and said, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). So keep your own promises when they have become costly, at home, at work and in your church, because you are held by One who kept his. See also Covenant in the Theological Dictionary.

Where Christians differ: does verse 42 promise a future return to the land? Dispensational readers hold that it promises a future national and territorial restoration for Israel, with Romans 11:29 as support. Many Reformed readers answer that the return from Babylon fulfilled verses 40–45 in its first sense, and that the New Testament sees the covenant with Abraham fulfilled in Christ and his people (Galatians 3:29); many also expect a great turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:26), without a separate promise of land. This commentary’s view: the promise was first kept in the return from exile and is fulfilled in Christ, whose people will inherit the whole new earth; with humility it also reads Romans 11 as looking for a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ, within the one people of God. All agree that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1–2) and that for Jew and Gentile alike the way home is Christ.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated make amends (vv. 41, 43) is the one translated enjoy of the land’s Sabbaths (vv. 34, 43): to accept, or pay off, what is due. It may mean that the exiles pay off their debt as the land is paid its Sabbaths, or that they accept their punishment as just. Either way they no longer argue with God’s judgment.

keyVerse.quote: And I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people.
keyVerse.note: This is the summit of the blessings and the heart of the covenant: not harvest or safety but God himself among his people. It is what the curses threaten to take away and what Christ secures; Paul applies it to the church (2 Corinthians 6:16), and Revelation sees it fulfilled for ever (Revelation 21:3).

26.reflection:
The highest blessing in the chapter is God walking among his people (v. 12). Do you value God’s presence above his gifts, and how would you know?

Each round of discipline came because Israel would not listen (vv. 14, 18, 21, 27). How have hard times turned you back to God, and how does Hebrews 12:5–11 help us see a believer’s troubles as a Father’s discipline rather than the curse Christ has already borne?

The way back began with confessing “their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers” (v. 40). What does honest confession look like for us, and why is it the door to mercy rather than to condemnation?

God kept his covenant though Israel broke it, “for I am the LORD their God” (v. 44). How does that give you assurance, and how should it shape the promises you keep to others?

27.title: Vows and Dedications: All Things Are His
27.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, If anyone makes a special vow to the LORD involving the valuation of persons,<sup>3</sup>then the valuation of a male from twenty years old up to sixty years old shall be fifty shekels of silver, according to the shekel of the sanctuary.<sup>4</sup>If the person is a female, the valuation shall be thirty shekels.<sup>5</sup>If the person is from five years old up to twenty years old, the valuation shall be for a male twenty shekels, and for a female ten shekels.<sup>6</sup>If the person is from a month old up to five years old, the valuation shall be for a male five shekels of silver, and for a female the valuation shall be three shekels of silver.<sup>7</sup>And if the person is sixty years old or over, then the valuation for a male shall be fifteen shekels, and for a female ten shekels.<sup>8</sup>And if someone is too poor to pay the valuation, then he shall be made to stand before the priest, and the priest shall value him; the priest shall value him according to what the vower can afford.<sup>9</sup>"If the vow is an animal that may be offered as an offering to the LORD, all of it that he gives to the LORD is holy.<sup>10</sup>He shall not exchange it or make a substitute for it, good for bad, or bad for good; as the priest values it, so it shall be.<sup>13</sup>But if he wishes to redeem it, he shall add a fifth to the valuation.<sup>14</sup>"When a man dedicates his house as a holy gift to the LORD, the priest shall value it as either good or bad;
