A homer of barley seed shall be valued at fifty shekels of silver.<sup>17</sup>If he dedicates his field from the year of jubilee, the valuation shall stand,<sup>18</sup>but if he dedicates his field after the jubilee, then the priest shall calculate the price according to the years that remain until the year of jubilee, and a deduction shall be made from the valuation.<sup>19</sup>And if he who dedicates the field wishes to redeem it, then he shall add a fifth to its valuation price, and it shall remain his.<sup>20</sup>But if he does not wish to redeem the field, or if he has sold the field to another man, it shall not be redeemed anymore.<sup>21</sup>But the field, when it is released in the jubilee, shall be a holy gift to the LORD, like a field that has been devoted. The priest shall be in possession of it.<sup>22</sup>If he dedicates to the LORD a field that he has bought, which is not a part of his possession,<sup>23</sup>then the priest shall calculate the amount of the valuation for it up to the year of jubilee, and the man shall give the valuation on that day as a holy gift to the LORD.<sup>24</sup>In the year of jubilee the field shall return to him from whom it was bought, to whom the land belongs as a possession.<sup>25</sup>Every valuation shall be according to the shekel of the sanctuary: twenty gerahs shall make a shekel.<sup>26</sup>"But a firstborn of animals, which as a firstborn belongs to the LORD, no man may dedicate; whether ox or sheep, it is the LORD's.<sup>27</sup>And if it is an unclean animal, then he shall buy it back at the valuation, and add a fifth to it; or, if it is not redeemed, it shall be sold at the valuation.<sup>28</sup>"But no devoted thing that a man devotes to the LORD, of anything that he has, whether man or beast, or of his inherited field, shall be sold or redeemed; every devoted thing is most holy to the LORD.<sup>29</sup>No one devoted, who is to be devoted for destruction from mankind, shall be ransomed; he shall surely be put to death.<sup>30</sup>"Every tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is the LORD's; it is holy to the LORD.<sup>31</sup>If a man wishes to redeem some of his tithe, he shall add a fifth to it.<sup>32</sup>And every tithe of herds and flocks, every tenth animal of all that pass under the herdsman's staff, shall be holy to the LORD.<sup>33</sup>One shall not differentiate between good or bad, neither shall he make a substitute for it; and if he does substitute for it, then both it and the substitute shall be holy; it shall not be redeemed."<sup>34</sup>These are the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses for the people of Israel on Mount Sinai.
27.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 26 brought the covenant to its climax with blessings and curses, and closed by saying the laws given at Sinai were complete (26:46). Leviticus ends with an appendix on vows, things devoted to God and the tithe, and a last line that takes us back to Sinai (27:34).

The message. Everything belongs to God, and what we promise him we must give. After all the commanded offerings, the book turns to offerings no one commands, the vows of a grateful or desperate heart. Such promises are serious; God is kind to the poor who make them; and some things cannot be vowed at all, because they are already his: the firstborn, the devoted thing and the tithe.

Why it was said. Israelites made vows in thanks or in trouble, as Hannah did (1 Samuel 1:11). Vows could be rash, haggled over or quietly undone. This chapter fixed fair prices in advance, protected the poor, and made sure a vow was never a bargain struck with God but a gift given back to him.

How the chapter makes its case. A person vowed to the LORD is redeemed at a fixed price set by age and sex, lowered for the poor (vv. 1–8). A vowed animal may not be swapped; an unclean animal, a house or a field may be bought back with a fifth added, and fields follow the Jubilee calendar of chapter 25 (vv. 9–25). The firstborn cannot be vowed, because it is already the LORD’s; what is devoted can never be redeemed; and the tithe of land and flock is holy to the LORD (vv. 26–33). The book closes with the commandments given “on Mount Sinai” (v. 34).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern. A person given to God had to be bought back, and we could never pay our own price: we were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). And Christ is himself the one wholly devoted to God, who came saying, “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7), and held nothing back. The whole book, from the tent no one could enter to the herdsman’s staff, is answered in him.

For us. We do not buy God’s favour with promises; we give back what was already his, in gratitude to the One who gave himself. So make promises to God soberly and keep them, give regularly and generously, and offer yourself: “present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (Romans 12:1).
27.theology:
All things belong to God. The tithe and the devoted thing confess that everything is the LORD's: "The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof" (Ps 24:1).

Voluntary consecration. Worship that begins with God's gift to us ends with our glad gift to him.

Christ our ransom. We could never pay our own redemption price; we were redeemed by "the precious blood of Christ" (1 Pet 1:19).
27.examples:
Then: a grateful Israelite might vow himself or his field, confessing that all he had was God's.

Now: we present our whole selves to God, not to buy his favour but because Christ first gave himself wholly for us. And a promise made to God in a crisis is worth keeping, or bringing honestly to him if it cannot be kept.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-34 — Vows, the Devoted Thing, and the Tithe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What is vowed to God is holy, and what already belongs to God cannot be vowed at all. A person vowed to the LORD is redeemed at a published price, set by age and sex and lowered to what the poor can pay (vv. 1–8). A vowed clean animal may not be exchanged, and if it is, both are holy; an unclean animal, a house or a field may be bought back for its value plus a fifth, with fields priced by the harvests left before the Jubilee (vv. 9–25). The firstborn already belongs to the LORD; a devoted thing can never be sold or redeemed; and the tenth of crop and flock is holy to the LORD, taken as it comes without picking (vv. 26–34).
verseByVerse.theology: A vow to God is serious, and so is his kindness: the law fixes a price and then bends it for those who cannot pay.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a published price list protected the worshipper from being exploited at the sanctuary door. Now: churches should be just as careful that no one is pressured into giving, or shamed for giving little.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, If anyone makes a special vow to the LORD involving the valuation of persons, then the valuation of a male from twenty years old up to sixty years old shall be fifty shekels of silver, according to the shekel of the sanctuary. If the person is a female, the valuation shall be thirty shekels. If the person is from five years old up to twenty years old, the valuation shall be for a male twenty shekels, and for a female ten shekels. If the person is from a month old up to five years old, the valuation shall be for a male five shekels of silver, and for a female the valuation shall be three shekels of silver. And if the person is sixty years old or over, then the valuation for a male shall be fifteen shekels, and for a female ten shekels. And if someone is too poor to pay the valuation, then he shall be made to stand before the priest, and the priest shall value him; the priest shall value him according to what the vower can afford.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A person vowed to the LORD was normally redeemed by paying a fixed price to the sanctuary, and the poor paid only what they could afford.

A special vow to the LORD. After chapter 26 this looks like an anticlimax. It is not. It is about what happens when somebody, moved by gratitude or desperation, promises God something, and then has to work out what that costs.

Fifty shekels of silver. The sums are substantial: fifty shekels for a man in his prime. They are not statements of human worth but a schedule of redemption prices, published in advance so that nobody haggled over a person at the sanctuary door and no priest could set his own rate. Most people vowed were not Levites and could not serve at the sanctuary, so the vow was usually kept by paying the price. Hannah, who gave Samuel himself, is the rare exception (1 Samuel 1:11, 28).

According to what the vower can afford. As with the sin offering (chapter 5) and the cleansed leper (chapter 14), a fixed price bends to what the man actually has. Nobody in Israel was priced out of the sanctuary. It happens so often in this book that it stops looking like an exception and starts looking like the character of the God who gave the law.

Why are women valued less (vv. 3–7)? The valuations reflect the labour a person could give in a farming economy; children and the elderly are valued less too. They are not a measure of worth before God, in whose image man and woman are made alike (Genesis 1:27; Galatians 3:28).
verseByVerse.note: A shekel was about 11 grams (2/5 ounce) of silver (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "If the vow is an animal that may be offered as an offering to the LORD, all of it that he gives to the LORD is holy. He shall not exchange it or make a substitute for it, good for bad, or bad for good; and if he does in fact substitute one animal for another, then both it and the substitute shall be holy. And if it is any unclean animal that may not be offered as an offering to the LORD, then he shall stand the animal before the priest, and the priest shall value it as either good or bad; as the priest values it, so it shall be. But if he wishes to redeem it, he shall add a fifth to the valuation. "When a man dedicates his house as a holy gift to the LORD, the priest shall value it as either good or bad; as the priest values it, so it shall stand. And if the donor wishes to redeem his house, he shall add a fifth to the valuation price, and it shall be his. "If a man dedicates to the LORD part of the land that is his possession, then the valuation shall be in proportion to its seed. A homer of barley seed shall be valued at fifty shekels of silver. If he dedicates his field from the year of jubilee, the valuation shall stand, but if he dedicates his field after the jubilee, then the priest shall calculate the price according to the years that remain until the year of jubilee, and a deduction shall be made from the valuation. And if he who dedicates the field wishes to redeem it, then he shall add a fifth to its valuation price, and it shall remain his. But if he does not wish to redeem the field, or if he has sold the field to another man, it shall not be redeemed anymore. But the field, when it is released in the jubilee, shall be a holy gift to the LORD, like a field that has been devoted. The priest shall be in possession of it. If he dedicates to the LORD a field that he has bought, which is not a part of his possession, then the priest shall calculate the amount of the valuation for it up to the year of jubilee, and the man shall give the valuation on that day as a holy gift to the LORD. In the year of jubilee the field shall return to him from whom it was bought, to whom the land belongs as a possession. Every valuation shall be according to the shekel of the sanctuary: twenty gerahs shall make a shekel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Animals, houses and fields vowed to God became his; buying one back cost its value plus a fifth, because a vow is a gift, not a loan.

He shall not exchange it. A vowed animal cannot be swapped, “good for bad, or bad for good”; anyone who tries loses both (v. 10). Fields follow the Jubilee calendar of chapter 25, so even a gift to God cannot cut a family off from its land (vv. 22–24).

The added fifth. It does the same work every time: buying back what you gave away costs more than giving it did. No one had to vow; Peter told Ananias, “While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own?” (Acts 5:4). But a promise once made must be kept. The Preacher draws the lesson: “It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay” (Ecclesiastes 5:5). So promise God soberly and keep your word, as one held by a God who keeps all of his.

Uncertain wording. In proportion to its seed (v. 16) most likely means by the seed needed to sow the field, not by its harvest. Who sells the field in verse 20, the owner or the priest, is also unclear; either way, the owner who will not redeem his gift loses it.

verseByVerse.quote: "But a firstborn of animals, which as a firstborn belongs to the LORD, no man may dedicate; whether ox or sheep, it is the LORD's. And if it is an unclean animal, then he shall buy it back at the valuation, and add a fifth to it; or, if it is not redeemed, it shall be sold at the valuation. "But no devoted thing that a man devotes to the LORD, of anything that he has, whether man or beast, or of his inherited field, shall be sold or redeemed; every devoted thing is most holy to the LORD. No one devoted, who is to be devoted for destruction from mankind, shall be ransomed; he shall surely be put to death. "Every tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is the LORD's; it is holy to the LORD. If a man wishes to redeem some of his tithe, he shall add a fifth to it. And every tithe of herds and flocks, every tenth animal of all that pass under the herdsman's staff, shall be holy to the LORD. One shall not differentiate between good or bad, neither shall he make a substitute for it; and if he does substitute for it, then both it and the substitute shall be holy; it shall not be redeemed." These are the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses for the people of Israel on Mount Sinai.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What already belongs to God, the firstborn, the devoted thing and the tithe, cannot be vowed, sold or swapped; and with these words Leviticus closes at Sinai.

It is the LORD’s. The firstborn of the animals already is the LORD’s: nobody can dedicate what was never his to give. Anything devoted (Hebrew herem, handed over wholly to God, often for destruction) is beyond redemption entirely, as Achan found when he kept devoted things from Jericho (Joshua 7).

Whatever comes tenth. The tenth of crop and flock is “holy to the LORD” (v. 30). With the tithe of the flock there was to be no inspecting the animals to make sure the tenth was the runt: whichever passed tenth under the staff went.

Holiness moving outward. The book stops in administrative detail, a strange place to end until you measure the distance travelled. It opened with God calling out of a tent nobody could enter; it ends with a herdsman counting animals. Holiness runs outward from the Most Holy Place, through the priests and the camp, into the kitchen, the marketplace and the working day, and there is no point along that line where God is not interested. The last word of the book is Sinai, and everything in these twenty-seven chapters was arranged so that the God on top of the mountain could live at the bottom of it, among his people, without consuming them.

Replaced by a person. That arrangement was always temporary. When it was replaced, it was replaced not by a better system but by a person, who did not come down the mountain to a tent but “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and in whom the whole book is answered: the offering, the priest, the blood, the mercy seat, the scapegoat, the Jubilee trumpet and the lamb without blemish, all of it, in one man, once.

Does the tithe bind Christians today? Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and belonged to that order. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and for churches to support those who teach them (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14). Many believers find a tenth a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.

Can “devoted to destruction” justify a vow to kill a person, as Jephthah did? No. This concerns what God himself had placed under judgment, such as the Canaanites or an idolatrous town (Deuteronomy 13:15), and it is no licence for violence today. The law forbids child sacrifice absolutely (18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31).

Uncertain wording. Verse 29 is compressed, and its scope is debated. Most take it to mean a person already under God’s sentence of destruction, such as an idolater condemned by the law (Exodus 22:20), who could not be bought off. It does not allow anyone to devote another person to death by a vow.

keyVerse.quote: Every tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is the LORD’s; it is holy to the LORD.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s logic in one sentence: some things are not ours to give, because they already belong to God. The tithe was Israel’s standing confession that the whole harvest came from him, and the New Testament takes the confession further: we ourselves are not our own, for we were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

27.reflection:
Vows were voluntary, but once made they had to be kept, and buying back a gift cost a fifth more (vv. 13, 15, 19). What promises have you made to God or to others that have become costly, and what would it mean to keep them?

The priest set the price “according to what the vower can afford” (v. 8). What does this repeated care for the poor in Leviticus tell you about God, and how should it shape the way a church treats those with little to give?

The firstborn and the tithe could not be vowed because they already belonged to the LORD (vv. 26, 30). If everything you have is already God’s, how does that change the way you think about giving?

Leviticus ends at Sinai, with God making a way to live among his people (v. 34). Looking back over the whole book, where have you seen Christ most clearly: as the offering, the priest, or the one wholly devoted to God?
